M10. Simplify (put x = sin θ, tan θ or cos θ as suitable; the condition keeps
     the angle in the principal range).
     a) tan⁻¹(x/√(1 − x²)), |x| < 1
     b) sin⁻¹(x/√(1 + x²)), all x
     c) cos(tan⁻¹x), all x
     d) sin(cot⁻¹x), x > 0
     e) tan(cos⁻¹x), 0 < x ≤ 1
     f) sin⁻¹(2x√(1 − x²)), |x| ≤ √2/2
     g) tan⁻¹(2x/(1 − x²)), |x| < 1
     h) cos⁻¹((1 − x²)/(1 + x²)), x ≥ 0
     i) sin⁻¹(2x/(1 + x²)), |x| ≤ 1
     j) tan⁻¹((1 + x)/(1 − x)), x < 1
     k) cos⁻¹(2x² − 1), 0 ≤ x ≤ 1
     l) sin⁻¹(3x − 4x³), |x| ≤ 1/2
     m) tan⁻¹(√((1 − cos x)/(1 + cos x))), 0 < x < π
     n) tan⁻¹(cos x/(1 + sin x)), −π/2 < x < π/2
     o) tan⁻¹((cos x − sin x)/(cos x + sin x)), −π/4 < x < 3π/4
     p) cot⁻¹(√(1 + x²) − x), all x
     Answers:
       a) sin⁻¹x
       b) tan⁻¹x
       c) 1/√(1 + x²)
       d) 1/√(1 + x²)
       e) √(1 − x²)/x
       f) 2 sin⁻¹x
       g) 2 tan⁻¹x
       h) 2 tan⁻¹x
       i) 2 tan⁻¹x
       j) π/4 + tan⁻¹x
       k) 2 cos⁻¹x
       l) 3 sin⁻¹x
       m) x/2
       n) π/4 − x/2
       o) π/4 − x
       p) π/4 + (1/2) tan⁻¹x

M11. True (T) or false (F)? (For a false statement find a value of x where it
     fails.)
     a) sin⁻¹x = 1/sin x
     b) sin⁻¹(−x) = −sin⁻¹x for all x in [−1, 1]
     c) cos⁻¹(−x) = −cos⁻¹x for all x in [−1, 1]
     d) cos⁻¹(−x) = π − cos⁻¹x for all x in [−1, 1]
     e) tan⁻¹(−x) = −tan⁻¹x for all real x
     f) sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 for all x in [−1, 1]
     g) tan⁻¹x + cot⁻¹x = π
     h) sin(sin⁻¹x) = x for all x in [−1, 1]
     i) sin⁻¹(sin x) = x for all real x
     j) cos(cos⁻¹x) = x for all x in [−1, 1]
     k) tan⁻¹(tan x) = x for all x in (−π/2, π/2)
     l) tan(tan⁻¹x) = x for all real x
     m) sin⁻¹x + sin⁻¹x = sin⁻¹(2x) for all x in [−1/2, 1/2]
     n) 2 tan⁻¹x = tan⁻¹(2x/(1 − x²)) for all x in (−1, 1)
     o) cos⁻¹x = sin⁻¹(√(1 − x²)) for all x in [−1, 1]
     p) cos⁻¹x = sin⁻¹(√(1 − x²)) for all x in [0, 1]
     q) tan⁻¹x ≤ π/2 for all real x
     r) cos⁻¹x ≥ 0 for all x in [−1, 1]
     Answers: a) F   b) T   c) F   d) T   e) T   f) T   g) F   h) T   i) F
              j) T   k) T   l) T   m) F   n) T   o) F   p) T   q) T   r) T

M12. State the range of each function of x (on its full domain).
     a) 2 sin⁻¹x       b) sin⁻¹x + π/2
     c) cos⁻¹x − π/2   d) tan⁻¹x + π/2
     e) sin⁻¹(x²)      f) cos⁻¹(x²)
     g) tan⁻¹(x²)      h) sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x
     i) 3 tan⁻¹(2x)    j) π − 2 cos⁻¹x
     k) sin⁻¹(|x|)     l) tan⁻¹(1/x), x ≠ 0
     m) cos⁻¹(sin x)   n) sin⁻¹(cos x)
     Answers: a) [−π, π]   b) [0, π]   c) [−π/2, π/2]   d) (0, π)   e) [0, π/2]
              f) [0, π/2]   g) [0, π/2)   h) π/2 only   i) (−3π/2, 3π/2)
              j) [−π, π]   k) [0, π/2]   l) (−π/2, 0) or (0, π/2)   m) [0, π]
              n) [−π/2, π/2]

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw the three principal ranges as arcs on the unit circle
  (sin⁻¹ and tan⁻¹ on the right half, cos⁻¹ on the upper half) and check every
  answer lands on its arc; for sin(cos⁻¹x) always draw the triangle; for
  sin⁻¹(sin θ) sketch the zigzag graph. Harder: prove Machin's formula
  π/4 = 4 tan⁻¹(1/5) − tan⁻¹(1/239); show that
  tan⁻¹(1/(1 + 1·2)) + tan⁻¹(1/(1 + 2·3)) + ... + tan⁻¹(1/(1 + n(n + 1)))
  = tan⁻¹(n + 1) − π/4 (telescoping: each term is tan⁻¹(k + 1) − tan⁻¹k), and
  find the sum to infinity (π/4); solve sin⁻¹x + sin⁻¹(2x) = π/3 (x = √21/14);
  sketch y = sin⁻¹(sin x) and y = cos⁻¹(cos x) for −2π ≤ x ≤ 2π.


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.12 — SINE RULE, COSINE RULE; SOLUTION OF TRIANGLES
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - NOTATION: in triangle ABC the side a = BC is opposite angle A, b = CA
    opposite B, c = AB opposite C; A + B + C = 180°. The largest side is
    opposite the largest angle.
  - SINE RULE: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C = 2R, where R is the radius of the
    circumcircle. Use it when you know a side and its OPPOSITE angle (AAS, ASA
    after finding the third angle, SSA).
  - COSINE RULE: a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A (and the two cyclic versions); for an
    angle: cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc). Use it for SAS (two sides and the
    included angle) and SSS. If A = 90° it is Pythagoras; cos A < 0 (A obtuse)
    exactly when a² > b² + c².
  - AREA: Δ = ½ab sin C = ½bc sin A = ½ca sin B; Heron:
    Δ = √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)) with s = (a + b + c)/2; also R = abc/(4Δ) and
    inradius r = Δ/s.
  - PROJECTION FORMULAS: a = b cos C + c cos B, b = c cos A + a cos C,
    c = a cos B + b cos A.
  - AMBIGUOUS CASE (SSA: given a, b and angle A): let h = b sin A. If A is
    acute: a < h no triangle; a = h one (right-angled at B); h < a < b TWO
    triangles (B and 180° − B); a ≥ b one. If A is right or obtuse: a ≤ b none,
    a > b one. With the sine rule, sin B > 1 means no triangle; always test
    whether 180° − B also works.
  - SOLVING A TRIANGLE means finding all three sides and all three angles. Keep
    full calculator accuracy in the middle of a calculation and round only the
    final answers (sides and angles to 2 d.p.); give exact values (surds) when
    the data allow it.
  - APPLICATIONS: bearings (measured clockwise from north, three figures: 060°),
    heights and distances with two observation points, surveying plots of land.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. In triangle ABC, A = 40°, B = 65° and a = 12 cm. Solve the triangle.
    Answer: C = 75°, b ≈ 16.92 cm, c ≈ 18.03 cm.
    Teacher explains: A side and its opposite angle are known (a and A), so the
    sine rule works. First the third angle: C = 180° − 40° − 65° = 75°.
       b = a sin B/sin A = 12 × sin 65°/sin 40° = 12 × 0.90631/0.64279 = 16.92
       c = a sin C/sin A = 12 × sin 75°/sin 40° = 12 × 0.96593/0.64279 = 18.03
    Check the order: the angles 40° < 65° < 75° and the sides 12 < 16.92 < 18.03
    match (largest side opposite largest angle). Also 2R = a/sin A = 18.67, so
    R ≈ 9.33 cm. Common mistake: using the calculator in radian mode (sin 40 in
    radians is 0.745, giving nonsense). Now you try: A = 50°, C = 70°, c = 20;
    find a and b. (B = 60°; a ≈ 16.30, b ≈ 18.43)

D2. Two sides of a triangle are b = 7 cm and c = 5 cm and the angle between them
    is A = 60°. Find a, the other angles and the area.
    Answer: a = √39 ≈ 6.24 cm, B ≈ 76.10°, C ≈ 43.90°, area = 35√3/4 ≈ 15.16
    cm².
    Teacher explains: SAS: use the cosine rule for the third side.
       a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A = 49 + 25 − 2(7)(5)(1/2) = 74 − 35 = 39
       a = √39 ≈ 6.245
    Now find the SMALLER unknown angle with the sine rule (it cannot be obtuse),
    or use the cosine rule for either angle (the cosine rule is never
    ambiguous):
       cos C = (a² + b² − c²)/(2ab) = (39 + 49 − 25)/(2 × 7 × √39) = 0.72058
       C = 43.90°,   B = 180° − 60° − 43.90° = 76.10°
    Area = ½bc sin A = ½ × 7 × 5 × √3/2 = 35√3/4 ≈ 15.16 cm². Common mistake:
    finding the LARGEST angle with the sine rule, sin B = 0.9707, then taking
    B = 76.10° without asking whether 103.90° is possible (it is not here,
    because 60° + 103.90° + 43.90° ≠ 180°, but the cosine rule avoids the
    worry). Now you try: b = 5, c = 8, A = 60°: find a. (a = 7 exactly)

D3. Find the angles of the triangle with sides 7, 8 and 9 cm, and its area.
    Answer: Angles 48.19°, 58.41°, 73.40°; area 12√5 ≈ 26.83 cm².
    Teacher explains: SSS: cosine rule in the form cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc).
    Let a = 7, b = 8, c = 9.
       cos A = (64 + 81 − 49)/(2 × 8 × 9) = 96/144 = 2/3     A = 48.19°
       cos B = (49 + 81 − 64)/(2 × 7 × 9) = 66/126 = 11/21   B = 58.41°
       C = 180° − 48.19° − 58.41° = 73.40°
    (check with the rule: cos C = (49 + 64 − 81)/112 = 2/7, C = 73.40°.) Area by
    Heron: s = 12, Δ = √(12 × 5 × 4 × 3) = √720 = 12√5 ≈ 26.83. Or Δ = ½bc
    sin A = ½ × 8 × 9 × √5/3 = 12√5, since sin A = √(1 − 4/9) = √5/3. Common
    mistake: in cos A = (b² + c² − a²)/(2bc) putting the wrong side on the
    minus: the side OPPOSITE the angle is the one subtracted. Now you try:
    angles of the triangle with sides 3, 5, 7. (the largest angle is 120°
    exactly; the others 21.79° and 38.21°)

D4. In triangle ABC, A = 30°, a = 6 cm and b = 10 cm. Show that there are two
    possible triangles and solve both.
    Answer: Triangle 1: B ≈ 56.44°, C ≈ 93.56°, c ≈ 11.98 cm. Triangle 2:
    B ≈ 123.56°, C ≈ 26.44°, c ≈ 5.34 cm.
    Teacher explains: The height from C to the line AB is
    h = b sin A = 10 × 0.5 = 5. Since 5 < 6 < 10 (h < a < b), the side a can
    reach the line AB in TWO places:
                    C
                  / /|\
             10 /  / | \  6
              /  6/  |5 \
            /30° /   |   \
          A-----B2---+----B1       AB2 = 5.34, AB1 = 11.98
    Sine rule: sin B = b sin A/a = 10 × 0.5/6 = 5/6. B = sin⁻¹(5/6) = 56.44° OR
    B = 180° − 56.44° = 123.56°; both leave room for C (A + B < 180°).
       B1 = 56.44°:  C = 93.56°,  c = a sin C/sin A = 6 × 0.99807/0.5 = 11.98
       B2 = 123.56°: C = 26.44°,  c = 6 × 0.44530/0.5 = 5.34
    Check: the two values of c add to 2b cos A = 20 × 0.8660 = 17.32 (they are
    the roots of c² − 2bc cos A + b² − a² = 0, which is the cosine rule written
    as a quadratic in c). Common mistake: giving only the calculator value
    56.44°. Now you try: A = 30°, b = 10: how many triangles when a = 4, 5, 8,
    12? (0; 1, right-angled; 2; 1)

D5. Explain all the cases of SSA (angle A, sides a and b given) when A is acute,
    using h = b sin A. Then decide the number of triangles for A = 40°, b = 12
    and a = 7, 12 sin 40°, 9, 15.
    Answer: a < h: none; a = h: one; h < a < b: two; a ≥ b: one. For the data
    (h = 7.71): a = 7: none; a = h: one; a = 9: two; a = 15: one.
    Teacher explains: Swing the side a like a door hinged at C: it must reach
    the ray from A.
       a < h           a = h            h < a < b          a ≥ b
       too short       touches once     cuts the ray       cuts once (the other
                       (right angle)    twice              point is behind A)
    With A = 40°, b = 12: h = 12 × sin 40° = 7.713. a = 7 < h: no triangle (sine
    rule would give sin B = 12 sin 40°/7 = 1.1019 > 1, impossible). a = h:
    B = 90° exactly, one triangle. a = 9: 7.71 < 9 < 12, two triangles,
    sin B = 0.8571, B = 58.99° or 121.01°. a = 15 ≥ 12: one triangle, B = 30.95°
    (the value 149.05° is impossible because then A + B > 180°). If A is obtuse
    or right: one triangle when a > b, none otherwise. Now you try: A = 120°,
    b = 5: how many triangles for a = 4 and a = 7? (none; one)

D6. Find the area of triangle PQR with PQ = 9 cm, PR = 14 cm and ∠P = 40°. If
    instead the area is 42 cm² with the same two sides, find ∠P.
    Answer: Area ≈ 40.50 cm². ∠P ≈ 41.81° or 138.19°.
    Teacher explains: With two sides and the INCLUDED angle: area
    = ½ × PQ × PR × sin P = ½ × 9 × 14 × sin 40° = 63 × 0.64279 = 40.50 cm².
    Why: the height from Q to PR is 9 sin P, and area = ½ × base × height. For
    the reverse problem: 42 = 63 sin P, sin P = 2/3, P = 41.81° or
    180° − 41.81° = 138.19°. BOTH give the same area, because
    sin P = sin(180° − P): two different triangles (one acute at P, one obtuse).
    Common mistake: using a side and an angle that are not included, such as
    ½ × PQ × QR × sin P. Now you try: area of a triangle with sides 5 and 8 and
    included angle 150°. (½ × 5 × 8 × ½ = 10)

D7. Prove the sine rule in the form a/sin A = 2R, and prove the projection
    formula a = b cos C + c cos B. Deduce the cosine rule.
    Answer: Proofs below.
    Teacher explains: Sine rule: draw the circumcircle (centre O, radius R) and
    the diameter BD. The angle BDC equals A (angles in the same segment; if A is
    obtuse, BDC = 180° − A, and sin is the same). Angle BCD = 90° (angle in a
    semicircle). In the right triangle BCD: BC = BD sin(BDC), i.e. a = 2R sin A.
    The same for b and c gives a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C = 2R. Projection:
    drop the perpendicular from A to BC at D. If B and C are acute, BD = c cos B
    and DC = b cos C, so a = BD + DC = b cos C + c cos B (the formula stays true
    when an angle is obtuse, because then the cosine is negative). Cosine rule:
    write the three projection formulas, multiply them by a, −b, −c and add:
       a² − b² − c² = ab cos C + ac cos B − bc cos A − ba cos C − ca cos B
                     − cb cos A = −2bc cos A
    so a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A. Check with a = 7, b = 8, c = 9 (D3):
    cos C = 2/7 and cos B = 11/21, so b cos C + c cos B = 16/7 + 33/7 = 49/7 = 7
    = a. Now you try: verify c = a cos B + b cos A for the 7, 8, 9 triangle.
    (7 × 11/21 + 8 × 2/3 = 11/3 + 16/3 = 9)

D8. A ship leaves port P and sails 40 km on a bearing of 060° to Q, then 25 km
    on a bearing of 130° to R. Find the distance PR and the bearing of R from P.
    Answer: PR ≈ 53.94 km on a bearing of about 085.82°.
    Teacher explains: Draw north lines at P and Q. At Q the direction back to P
    is the bearing 240° (060° + 180°), and QR is on 130°, so the angle
    PQR = 240° − 130° = 110°.
        N           N
        |           |   Q
        |        .  +-----.  130°
        |     .   110°      .
        |  .  40              . 25
        P  060°                  R
    Cosine rule: PR² = 40² + 25² − 2 × 40 × 25 × cos 110°. Since
    2000 × cos 110° = −684.04, PR² = 1600 + 625 + 684.04 = 2909.04 and
    PR = 53.94 km. Then the angle QPR from the sine rule:
    sin QPR = 25 sin 110°/53.94 = 0.43556, QPR = 25.82°, and the bearing of R is
    060° + 25.82° = 085.82°. Common mistake: using the angle 130° − 60° = 70° as
    the angle inside the triangle; draw the north lines! Now you try: find the
    bearing of P from R. (085.82° + 180° = 265.82°)

D9. From a point A on level ground the angle of elevation of the top T of a
    tower is 30°. After walking 20 m towards the tower, to B, it is 45°. Find
    the height of the tower exactly and to 2 d.p.
    Answer: Height = 10(√3 + 1) ≈ 27.32 m.
    Teacher explains: In triangle ABT: angle A = 30°, angle
    ABT = 180° − 45° = 135°, so angle ATB = 180° − 30° − 135° = 15°. Sine rule
    for BT:
       BT/sin 30° = AB/sin 15°   →   BT = 20 × (1/2)/sin 15° = 10/sin 15°
    Height h = BT sin 45° = 10 sin 45°/sin 15°. With sin 15° = (√6 − √2)/4
    (topic 8.9):
       h = 10 × (√2/2) × 4/(√6 − √2) = 20√2/(√6 − √2) = 20/(√3 − 1)
         = 20(√3 + 1)/2 = 10(√3 + 1) ≈ 27.32 m
    Check with right triangles: h = x tan 45° = (x + 20) tan 30° gives
    x = (x + 20)/√3, x(√3 − 1) = 20, x = 10(√3 + 1), the same. The sine-rule
    method also works when the ground is sloping or the tower leans, where right
    triangles fail. Now you try: with angles 30° and 60° and AB = 30 m, find the
    height. (15√3 ≈ 25.98 m)

D10. Prove that in any triangle (b² − c²)/a² = sin(B − C)/sin A. Check it for
     the triangle A = 50°, B = 70°, C = 60°.
     Answer: Proof below; both sides ≈ 0.2267 for that triangle.
     Teacher explains: By the sine rule a = 2R sin A etc., so
        (b² − c²)/a² = (sin²B − sin²C)/sin²A
     From topic 8.9, sin²B − sin²C = sin(B + C) sin(B − C), and
     sin(B + C) = sin(180° − A) = sin A. So the right side is
     sin A sin(B − C)/sin²A = sin(B − C)/sin A. Check:
     sin 10°/sin 50° = 0.17365/0.76604 = 0.22668; with 2R = 1, b² − c²
     = sin²70° − sin²60° = 0.88302 − 0.75 = 0.13302 and a² = sin²50° = 0.58682,
     ratio 0.22668. The method "replace sides by 2R sin" turns side identities
     into angle identities. Now you try: prove a cos A + b cos B = c cos(A − B).
     (the left side is R(sin 2A + sin 2B) = 2R sin(A + B) cos(A − B)
     = c cos(A − B))

D11. For the triangle with sides a = 13, b = 14, c = 15 find the area, the
     circumradius R, the inradius r and the length of the median from A.
     Answer: Area 84; R = 65/8 = 8.125; r = 4; median m_a = √(673)/2 ≈ 12.97.
     Teacher explains: s = (13 + 14 + 15)/2 = 21; Heron:
     Δ = √(21 × 8 × 7 × 6) = √7056 = 84.
        R = abc/(4Δ) = 13 × 14 × 15/336 = 2730/336 = 65/8
        r = Δ/s = 84/21 = 4
     For the median AM (M the midpoint of BC, BM = 6.5) use the cosine rule in
     triangles ABM and ABC with the common angle B: cos B = (a² + c² − b²)/(2ac)
     = (169 + 225 − 196)/390 = 198/390 = 33/65, then AM²
     = c² + (a/2)² − 2c(a/2) cos B = 225 + 42.25 − 195 × 33/65 = 267.25 − 99
     = 168.25, AM = √168.25 = √673/2 ≈ 12.97. General formula (Apollonius): m_a²
     = (2b² + 2c² − a²)/4 = (392 + 450 − 169)/4 = 673/4. The 13-14-15 triangle
     is famous because its area and its altitude to side 14 (12) are whole
     numbers. Now you try: find R and r for the triangle with sides 3, 4, 5.
     (R = 5/2, r = 1)

D12. A farmer's field ABCD has sides AB = 40 m, BC = 55 m, CD = 35 m, DA = 50 m,
     and the diagonal AC = 60 m (measured with a chain). Find the area of the
     field in m² and in hectares, and the angles ABC and ADC.
     Answer: Area ≈ 1944.18 m² ≈ 0.19 hectare; ∠ABC ≈ 76.53°, ∠ADC ≈ 87.95°.
     Teacher explains: A surveyor splits the field along the diagonal into two
     triangles whose three sides are known, then uses Heron's formula for each.
        ΔABC: s = (40 + 55 + 60)/2 = 77.5
              area = √(77.5 × 37.5 × 22.5 × 17.5) = 1069.74 m²
        ΔACD: s = (35 + 50 + 60)/2 = 72.5
              area = √(72.5 × 37.5 × 22.5 × 12.5) = 874.44 m²
     Total 1944.18 m²; 1 hectare = 10,000 m², so about 0.19 ha. Angles by the
     cosine rule: cos ABC = (40² + 55² − 60²)/(2 × 40 × 55) = 1025/4400
     = 41/176, ∠ABC = 76.53°; cos ADC = (35² + 50² − 60²)/(2 × 35 × 50)
     = 125/3500 = 1/28, ∠ADC = 87.95°. The four sides alone do NOT fix the shape
     of a quadrilateral (it can flex), which is why the diagonal is measured.
     Common mistake: using Heron's formula on all four sides at once
     (Brahmagupta's formula works only for cyclic quadrilaterals). Now you try:
     a triangular plot has sides 30 m, 40 m and 50 m. Find its area. (600 m²; it
     is right-angled)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Use the sine rule (sides to 2 d.p.).
    a) A = 40°, B = 65°, a = 12: find b and c
    b) A = 35°, B = 80°, a = 10: find b and c

    n) A = 88°, B = 41°, a = 5.4: find b and c
    o) A = 33°, B = 99°, a = 25: find b and c
    p) A = 60°, B = 75°, a = 10: find b and c
    Answers:

      g) b = 10.15, c = 15.56

      i) b = 7.00, c = 8.03
      j) b = 7.50, c = 12.30
      k) b = 4.90, c = 5.46
      l) b = 5.20, c = 5.20
      m) b = 35.72, c = 38.01
      n) b = 3.54, c = 4.20
      o) b = 45.34, c = 34.11
      p) b = 11.15, c = 8.16

M2. Use the sine rule to find the angles (a ≥ b, so B is acute and there is one
    triangle).
    a) a = 10, b = 7, A = 50°: find B and C
    b) a = 12, b = 9, A = 64°: find B and C
    c) a = 8, b = 5, A = 110°: find B and C
    d) a = 15, b = 11, A = 30°: find B and C
    e) a = 6.5, b = 4, A = 72°: find B and C
    f) a = 20, b = 13, A = 95°: find B and C

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always draw and label the triangle, putting each side opposite its
  angle; decide first which rule fits (a side with its opposite angle known:
  sine rule; otherwise cosine rule); keep the calculator in DEGREE mode; store
  intermediate values in memory instead of retyping rounded numbers; in SSA
  problems always test 180° − B. Harder: prove Heron's formula from the cosine
  rule and ½bc sin A; show that r = 4R sin(A/2) sin(B/2) sin(C/2) and check it
  for the 13-14-15 triangle; for which values of a does A = 35°, b = 20 give
  exactly one triangle? (a = 20 sin 35° ≈ 11.47 or a ≥ 20); a triangle has sides
  x, x + 1, x + 2 and its largest angle is twice its smallest: find x (x = 4,
  sides 4, 5, 6).


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.13 — COMPLEX NUMBERS: ALGEBRA, ARGAND PLANE, MODULUS-ARGUMENT FORM
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - i is a number with i² = −1. A COMPLEX NUMBER is z = a + bi with a, b real:
    a = Re z (real part), b = Im z (imaginary part, a REAL number). Two complex
    numbers are equal only if their real parts are equal AND their imaginary
    parts are equal.
  - POWERS OF i repeat with period 4: i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1; so iⁿ
    depends on the remainder of n ÷ 4. Also 1/i = −i.
  - ARITHMETIC: add and multiply like algebra, replacing i² by −1. Divide by
    multiplying top and bottom by the CONJUGATE of the denominator:
    (a + bi)(a − bi) = a² + b².
  - CONJUGATE z̄ = a − bi: z + z̄ = 2 Re z, z − z̄ = 2i Im z, z z̄ = |z|²; the
    conjugate of a sum/product/quotient is the sum/product/quotient of the
    conjugates. z is real ⇔ z = z̄.
  - ARGAND PLANE: z = a + bi is the point (a, b). MODULUS |z| = √(a² + b²)
    (distance from 0); |z₁ − z₂| is the distance between the points.
    |z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂|, |z₁/z₂| = |z₁|/|z₂|, |z₁ + z₂| ≤ |z₁| + |z₂| (triangle
    inequality).
  - ARGUMENT: the angle θ from the positive real axis to the point. The
    PRINCIPAL argument satisfies −π < θ ≤ π. Find the reference angle tan⁻¹|b/a|
    and place it in the right quadrant (QII: π − α, QIII: −π + α, QIV: −α).
    arg 0 is not defined.
  - MODULUS-ARGUMENT (POLAR) FORM: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) = re^(iθ) (Euler).
    Multiplying MULTIPLIES moduli and ADDS arguments; dividing divides moduli
    and subtracts arguments (adjust by 2π to stay in (−π, π]). Multiplying by i
    rotates a point by 90° anticlockwise.
  - LOCI: |z − z₀| = r is a circle, centre z₀, radius r; |z − z₁| = |z − z₂| is
    the perpendicular bisector of z₁z₂; arg(z − z₀) = θ is a half-line from z₀
    (z₀ excluded). Replace z by x + iy to get the Cartesian equation.
  - SQUARE ROOTS of a + bi: put (x + iy)² = a + bi, so x² − y² = a, 2xy = b, and
    use x² + y² = √(a² + b²). There are always exactly two roots, negatives of
    each other.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Simplify i⁵, i¹⁰, i²⁰²⁶, i⁻³ and 1 + i + i² + ... + i¹⁰⁰.
    Answer: i⁵ = i, i¹⁰ = −1, i²⁰²⁶ = −1, i⁻³ = i, and the sum is 1.
    Teacher explains: The powers cycle every 4:
       n mod 4      0     1     2     3
       iⁿ           1     i    −1    −i
    i⁵: 5 = 4 + 1, so i⁵ = i. i¹⁰: 10 = 8 + 2, so −1. i²⁰²⁶: 2026 = 4 × 506 + 2,
    so −1. i⁻³ = 1/i³ = 1/(−i) = i (or: −3 = −4 + 1, remainder 1). The sum has
    101 terms; each block of four consecutive powers adds to 1 + i − 1 − i = 0,
    and 101 = 4 × 25 + 1, so after 25 zero blocks only the last term i¹⁰⁰ = 1
    remains. (Or use the geometric series:
    (1 − i¹⁰¹)/(1 − i) = (1 − i)/(1 − i) = 1.) Common mistake:
    √(−4) × √(−9) = √36 = 6. Wrong! √(−4) = 2i and √(−9) = 3i, and
    2i × 3i = 6i² = −6: the rule √a √b = √(ab) holds only for a, b ≥ 0. Now you
    try: i⁹⁹ and i⁻¹. (−i; −i)

D2. Write (3 + 4i)(2 − i) and (3 + 4i)/(1 − 2i) in the form a + bi.
    Answer: 10 + 5i and −1 + 2i.
    Teacher explains: Multiply like brackets (FOIL), then use i² = −1:
       (3 + 4i)(2 − i) = 6 − 3i + 8i − 4i² = 6 + 5i + 4 = 10 + 5i
    For division, multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the bottom,
    1 + 2i, which makes the bottom REAL:
       (3 + 4i)(1 + 2i)   3 + 6i + 4i + 8i²   −5 + 10i
       ---------------- = ----------------- = -------- = −1 + 2i
       (1 − 2i)(1 + 2i)        1 − 4i²            5
    Check by multiplying back: (−1 + 2i)(1 − 2i) = −1 + 2i + 2i − 4i² = 3 + 4i.
    The denominator is always a² + b² = 1 + 4 = 5. Common mistake: dividing real
    parts and imaginary parts separately: 3/1 + (4/−2)i = 3 − 2i is wrong. Now
    you try: (2 + i)² and 1/(1 + i). (3 + 4i; 1/2 − i/2)

D3. Find the complex number z with z + 2z̄ = 6 − i. Show that z z̄ is always
    real and non-negative.
    Answer: z = 2 + i. z z̄ = a² + b² = |z|².
    Teacher explains: Put z = x + iy, so z̄ = x − iy:
       x + iy + 2(x − iy) = 6 − i   →   3x − iy = 6 − i
    Equate REAL parts: 3x = 6, x = 2. Equate IMAGINARY parts: −y = −1, y = 1. So
    z = 2 + i. Check: 2 + i + 2(2 − i) = 6 − i. In general
    (a + bi)(a − bi) = a² − (bi)² = a² + b², which is real and ≥ 0, and equals 0
    only when z = 0. This is why multiplying by the conjugate clears i from a
    denominator. Common mistake: treating z and z̄ as the same unknown
    ("3z = 6 − i"). Now you try: solve 2z − z̄ = 3 + 6i. (x = 3, 3y = 6:
    z = 3 + 2i)

D4. Find the modulus and principal argument of z₁ = 1 + i√3, z₂ = −1 + i,
    z₃ = −√3 − i and z₄ = 2 − 2i. Mark them on an Argand diagram.
    Answer: |z₁| = 2, arg π/3; |z₂| = √2, arg 3π/4; |z₃| = 2, arg −5π/6;
    |z₄| = 2√2, arg −π/4.
    Teacher explains: Plot each point first, THEN find the angle:
                       Im
         z₂ (−1, 1) *   |   * z₁ (1, √3)
                        |
         ---------------+--------------- Re
       z₃ (−√3, −1) *   |
                        |   * z₄ (2, −2)
    Reference angle α = tan⁻¹|b/a|: for z₁, tan⁻¹√3 = π/3, QI, so arg = π/3. z₂:
    α = π/4, QII, arg = π − π/4 = 3π/4. z₃: α = tan⁻¹(1/√3) = π/6, QIII,
    arg = −π + π/6 = −5π/6 (principal: between −π and π, so NOT 7π/6). z₄:
    α = π/4, QIV, arg = −π/4. Moduli: |z₁| = √(1 + 3) = 2, |z₂| = √2, |z₃| = 2,
    |z₄| = √8 = 2√2. Common mistake: calculator tan⁻¹(b/a) for z₃ gives
    tan⁻¹(−1/−√3) = π/6, which is the wrong quadrant. Now you try: modulus and
    argument of −4 and −3i. (4, π; 3, −π/2)

D5. Write z = −2 + 2i in modulus-argument form and in exponential form. Write
    w = 4(cos(2π/3) + i sin(2π/3)) in the form a + bi.
    Answer: z = 2√2(cos(3π/4) + i sin(3π/4)) = 2√2 e^(3iπ/4); w = −2 + 2√3 i.
    Teacher explains: |z| = √(4 + 4) = 2√2; z is in QII with reference angle
    π/4, so arg z = 3π/4. Polar form r(cos θ + i sin θ), exponential form
    re^(iθ) (Euler's formula e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ). For w: cos(2π/3) = −1/2
    and sin(2π/3) = √3/2, so w = 4(−1/2) + 4(√3/2)i = −2 + 2√3 i. Check:
    |w|² = 4 + 12 = 16. Polar form is often written r cis θ. Special case:
    e^(iπ) = −1, so e^(iπ) + 1 = 0 (Euler's identity, linking five famous
    numbers). Common mistake: writing 2√2(cos(−π/4) + i sin(−π/4)), the angle
    from tan⁻¹(2/(−2)) = −π/4, which is the point 2 − 2i. Now you try: write −5i
    and 3e^(−iπ/6) in the other form. (5(cos(−π/2) + i sin(−π/2)); 3√3/2 − 3i/2)

D6. If z₁ = 2(cos(π/3) + i sin(π/3)) and z₂ = 3(cos(π/4) + i sin(π/4)), find
    z₁z₂ and z₁/z₂ in polar form. What does multiplication by i do to a point?
    Answer: z₁z₂ = 6(cos(7π/12) + i sin(7π/12));
    z₁/z₂ = (2/3)(cos(π/12) + i sin(π/12)). Multiplying by i rotates by 90°
    anticlockwise.
    Teacher explains: Expand (cos A + i sin A)(cos B + i sin B)
    = (cos A cos B − sin A sin B) + i(sin A cos B + cos A sin B)
    = cos(A + B) + i sin(A + B), by the compound-angle formulas (8.9). So moduli
    MULTIPLY and arguments ADD:
       z₁z₂:  r = 2 × 3 = 6,    θ = π/3 + π/4 = 7π/12
       z₁/z₂: r = 2/3,          θ = π/3 − π/4 = π/12
    Since i = 1(cos(π/2) + i sin(π/2)), multiplying by i keeps the modulus and
    adds π/2 to the argument: a quarter turn anticlockwise. Example:
    i(3 + i) = −1 + 3i; the point (3, 1) moves to (−1, 3). As a check in
    Cartesian form: z₁ = 1 + √3 i, z₂ = (3√2/2)(1 + i), z₁z₂
    = (3√2/2)(1 − √3 + i(1 + √3)) ≈ −1.553 + 5.796i, and 6 cos(105°) = −1.553,
    6 sin(105°) = 5.796. Now you try: find (1 + i)(√3 + i) in polar form.
    (2√2(cos(5π/12) + i sin(5π/12)))

D7. Describe the locus of z when (i) |z − (1 + 2i)| = 3, (ii) |z − 1| = |z + i|.
    Give Cartesian equations.
    Answer: (i) The circle centre (1, 2), radius 3: (x − 1)² + (y − 2)² = 9.
    (ii) The perpendicular bisector of the points 1 and −i: the line y = −x.
    Teacher explains: |z − w| is the DISTANCE between the points z and w. (i)
    All points at distance 3 from 1 + 2i: a circle. Algebra:
    z − (1 + 2i) = (x − 1) + (y − 2)i, so its modulus squared is
    (x − 1)² + (y − 2)² = 9. (ii) Points equally far from 1 and from −i: the
    perpendicular bisector of the segment from (1, 0) to (0, −1). Algebra:
    (x − 1)² + y² = x² + (y + 1)², so −2x + 1 = 2y + 1, y = −x. Check:
    z = 2 − 2i gives |1 − 2i| = √5 and |2 − i| = √5. Common mistake: reading
    |z + i| as distance from +i (it is distance from −i, since
    z + i = z − (−i)). Now you try: the locus |z + 2| = 2|z − 1|.
    ((x + 2)² + y² = 4((x − 1)² + y²): x² + y² − 4x = 0, circle centre (2, 0),
    radius 2)

D8. Find the square roots of 5 + 12i and of −8 − 6i.
    Answer: ±(3 + 2i) and ±(1 − 3i).
    Teacher explains: Let (x + iy)² = 5 + 12i. Then x² − y² + 2ixy = 5 + 12i:
       x² − y² = 5,   2xy = 12,   and   x² + y² = |5 + 12i| = 13
    Adding: 2x² = 18, x = ±3; subtracting: 2y² = 8, y = ±2. Since xy = 6 > 0, x
    and y have the SAME sign: 3 + 2i or −3 − 2i. Check:
    (3 + 2i)² = 9 + 12i − 4 = 5 + 12i. For −8 − 6i: x² − y² = −8, 2xy = −6,
    x² + y² = 10, so x² = 1, y² = 9, and xy = −3 < 0 means opposite signs:
    1 − 3i or −1 + 3i. The third equation (from the moduli) avoids a quartic.
    Common mistake: forgetting to use the sign of xy and listing four "roots".
    Now you try: square roots of −3 + 4i and of 2i. (±(1 + 2i); ±(1 + i))

D9. Find real numbers x and y such that (x + iy)(2 − 3i) = 4 + i.
    Answer: x = 5/13, y = 14/13.
    Teacher explains: Method 1: divide. x + iy = (4 + i)/(2 − 3i)
    = (4 + i)(2 + 3i)/13 = (8 + 12i + 2i + 3i²)/13 = (5 + 14i)/13. Method 2:
    expand and equate parts: (2x + 3y) + (2y − 3x)i = 4 + i, so
       2x + 3y = 4
       −3x + 2y = 1     →   x = 5/13,  y = 14/13
    (multiply the first by 3, the second by 2 and add: 13y = 14). Both give the
    same answer. Equating real and imaginary parts turns ONE complex equation
    into TWO real equations; this is the key idea for solving equations in
    complex numbers. Now you try: find real x, y with
    (x − 2y) + (2x + y)i = 1 + 7i. (x = 3, y = 1)

D10. Prove that |z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂| and that |z₁ + z₂| ≤ |z₁| + |z₂|. When is
     there equality in the second? Check with z₁ = 3 + 4i, z₂ = 5 − 12i.
     Answer: Proofs below; |z₁z₂| = 65 = 5 × 13 and
     |z₁ + z₂| = √128 ≈ 11.31 ≤ 18. Equality holds when one number is a
     non-negative real multiple of the other.
     Teacher explains: Use |z|² = z z̄: |z₁z₂|² = z₁z₂ × conj(z₁z₂) = z₁z̄₁
     z₂z̄₂ = |z₁|²|z₂|²; take square roots. For the triangle inequality:
        |z₁ + z₂|² = (z₁ + z₂)(z̄₁ + z̄₂) = |z₁|² + |z₂|² + 2 Re(z₁z̄₂)
                   ≤ |z₁|² + |z₂|² + 2|z₁||z₂| = (|z₁| + |z₂|)²
     because Re w ≤ |w| and |z₁z̄₂| = |z₁||z₂|. Geometrically: one side of a
     triangle is shorter than the sum of the other two. Check:
     z₁z₂ = 15 − 36i + 20i − 48i² = 63 − 16i, |63 − 16i| = √(3969 + 256) = √4225
     = 65 = 5 × 13. z₁ + z₂ = 8 − 8i, |8 − 8i| = 8√2 ≈ 11.31 < 5 + 13 = 18. Now
     you try: show |z₁ − z₂| ≥ ||z₁| − |z₂|| for the same numbers.
     (|−2 + 16i| = √260 ≈ 16.12 ≥ 8)

D11. If |z − 3 − 4i| = 2, find the greatest and least values of |z|. Describe
     the region |z − 3i| < |z + 3i| and the half-line arg(z − 1) = π/4.
     Answer: Greatest |z| = 7, least 3. |z − 3i| < |z + 3i| is the upper
     half-plane y > 0. arg(z − 1) = π/4 is the half-line y = x − 1 with x > 1.
     Teacher explains: z lies on the circle with centre 3 + 4i and radius 2. The
     centre is at distance |3 + 4i| = 5 from the origin. The line from 0 through
     the centre meets the circle at distances 5 − 2 = 3 and 5 + 2 = 7: these are
     the least and greatest values of |z| (triangle inequality:
     5 − 2 ≤ |z| ≤ 5 + 2). The nearest point is (3/5)(3 + 4i) = 1.8 + 2.4i, the
     farthest (7/5)(3 + 4i) = 4.2 + 5.6i. For the region: points nearer to 3i
     than to −3i; the perpendicular bisector of these two points is the real
     axis, so the region is Im z > 0 (strict, so the axis is excluded). For
     arg(z − 1) = π/4: the vector from 1 to z makes 45° with the real axis, so
     z = 1 + t + ti with t > 0, i.e. y = x − 1, x > 1 (the point 1 itself has no
     argument). Now you try: least and greatest |z + 1| when |z − 2i| = 1.
     (√5 − 1; √5 + 1)

D12. In AC circuits engineers use complex impedances (and write j for i). Two
     branches with impedances Z₁ = 3 + 4j ohms and Z₂ = 6 − 8j ohms are joined
     in parallel. Find the total impedance Z = Z₁Z₂/(Z₁ + Z₂) and its modulus.
     Answer: Z = (450 + 200j)/97 ≈ 4.64 + 2.06j ohms; |Z| = 50/√97 ≈ 5.08 ohms.
     Teacher explains: Numerator: (3 + 4j)(6 − 8j) = 18 − 24j + 24j − 32j²
     = 18 + 32 = 50. Denominator: Z₁ + Z₂ = 9 − 4j. So
        Z = 50/(9 − 4j) = 50(9 + 4j)/(81 + 16) = (450 + 200j)/97
          ≈ 4.639 + 2.062j
        |Z| = 50/|9 − 4j| = 50/√97 ≈ 5.077
     The real part is the resistance (4.64 Ω) and the imaginary part the
     reactance (2.06 Ω). The modulus rule |w₁/w₂| = |w₁|/|w₂| gives |Z| without
     the division. Notice |Z₁| = 5 and |Z₂| = 10, yet |Z| ≈ 5.08 is NOT
     (5 × 10)/(5 + 10) = 3.33: moduli do not add. Now you try: find Z₁ + Z₂ and
     Z₁Z₂ for Z₁ = 2 + j, Z₂ = 1 − 3j. (3 − 2j; 5 − 5j)

M11. Describe the locus of z = x + iy and give its Cartesian equation.

     o) z z̄ = 4
     p) Re(z²) = 0
     q) z + z̄ = |z|²
     r) Im(1/z) = 1/2
     Answers:
       a) circle x² + y² = 9 (centre 0, radius 3)
       b) circle (x − 2)² + y² = 1
       c) circle (x + 1)² + (y − 1)² = 4
       d) circle x² + (y − 3)² = 16
       e) line x = 2
       f) line y = 0 (the real axis)
       g) line y = 2x − 3
       h) line y = −x
       i) half-line y = x, x > 0
       j) half-line x = 1, y > 0
       k) half-line y = −x − 1, x > 0
       l) line x = 2
       m) line y = 4
       n) circle (x + 5/3)² + y² = 16/9
       o) circle x² + y² = 4
       p) the two lines y = x and y = −x
       q) circle (x − 1)² + y² = 1
       r) circle x² + (y + 1)² = 1, without 0

M12. True (T) for all complex numbers (where defined) or false (F)? For a false
     one give a counterexample.
     a) |z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂|
     b) |z₁ + z₂| = |z₁| + |z₂|
     c) conj(z₁z₂) = z̄₁z̄₂
     d) conj(z₁ + z₂) = z̄₁ + z̄₂
     e) z z̄ = |z|²
     f) z + z̄ = 2 Re z
     g) z − z̄ = 2 Im z
     h) |z̄| = |z|
     i) |1/z| = 1/|z| (z ≠ 0)
     j) |z|² = z²
     k) Re(z₁z₂) = Re z₁ Re z₂
     l) |Re z| ≤ |z|
     m) |z₁ − z₂| ≥ ||z₁| − |z₂||
     n) arg(z₁z₂) = arg z₁ + arg z₂ (principal arguments)
     o) arg(z̄) = −arg z (principal, z not a negative real number)
     p) arg(z̄) = −arg z (principal, every z ≠ 0)
     q) z = z̄ exactly when z is real
     r) |z₁ + z₂|² + |z₁ − z₂|² = 2|z₁|² + 2|z₂|²
     s) (z̄)ⁿ = conj(zⁿ)
     t) |zⁿ| = |z|ⁿ
     Answers: a) T   b) F   c) T   d) T   e) T   f) T   g) F   h) T   i) T
              j) F   k) F   l) T   m) T   n) F   o) T   p) F   q) T   r) T
              s) T   t) T

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw EVERY complex number as a point on squared paper before
  finding its argument; make a table of the four quadrant rules for the
  principal argument; practise i-powers with the cycle i, −1, −i, 1; when
  dividing, write the conjugate step in full; for loci, first say it in words
  ("distance from 2 equals 1"). Harder: prove that if |z| = 1 then
  (z − 1)/(z + 1) is purely imaginary (z ≠ −1); find the complex numbers with
  z² = z̄ (0, 1, and −1/2 ± (√3/2)i); show that the points z₁, z₂, z₃ form an
  equilateral triangle when z₁² + z₂² + z₃² = z₁z₂ + z₂z₃ + z₃z₁ and test it
  with 1, ω, ω² (8.14); find the least value of |z − 1| + |z − 3i| (√10, on the
  segment).


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.14 — DE MOIVRE'S THEOREM; ROOTS OF UNITY
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - DE MOIVRE'S THEOREM: (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ for every
    integer n (proved by induction for n ≥ 1, and for negative n using
    1/(cos θ + i sin θ) = cos θ − i sin θ). In exponential form:
    (e^(iθ))ⁿ = e^(inθ).
  - POWERS: to find (a + bi)ⁿ write a + bi = r(cos θ + i sin θ); then
    (a + bi)ⁿ = rⁿ(cos nθ + i sin nθ). Much faster than the binomial expansion:
    (1 + i)¹⁰ = (√2)¹⁰(cos(10π/4) + i sin(10π/4)) = 32i.
  - nth ROOTS OF UNITY: the solutions of zⁿ = 1 are
    z = cos(2kπ/n) + i sin(2kπ/n) = e^(2kπi/n), k = 0, 1, ..., n − 1. They are
    the vertices of a regular n-gon on the unit circle, one vertex at 1. If
    α = e^(2πi/n), the roots are 1, α, α², ..., αⁿ⁻¹.
  - SUM AND PRODUCT: for n ≥ 2 the n roots add to 0
    (1 + α + ... + αⁿ⁻¹ = (αⁿ − 1)/(α − 1) = 0); their product is (−1)ⁿ⁺¹. The
    sum of their m-th powers is n if n divides m, otherwise 0.
  - CUBE ROOTS OF UNITY: 1, ω, ω² with ω = (−1 + i√3)/2 = e^(2πi/3),
    ω² = (−1 − i√3)/2 = ω̄ = 1/ω. KEY FACTS: ω³ = 1 and 1 + ω + ω² = 0. Reduce
    powers using ω³ = 1 (ω¹⁰⁰ = ω) and replace 1 + ω by −ω², 1 + ω² by −ω,
    ω + ω² by −1.
  - nth ROOTS OF ANY z = r(cos θ + i sin θ): w_k
    = r^(1/n)(cos((θ + 2kπ)/n) + i sin((θ + 2kπ)/n)), k = 0, ..., n − 1: n
    equally spaced points on the circle of radius r^(1/n).
  - TRIGONOMETRY FROM DE MOIVRE: expand (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ by the binomial
    theorem and compare real and imaginary parts to get cos nθ, sin nθ in powers
    of cos θ, sin θ. Conversely, with z = e^(iθ): z + 1/z = 2 cos θ,
    z − 1/z = 2i sin θ, zⁿ + z⁻ⁿ = 2 cos nθ, which turns powers such as cos⁴θ
    into sums of multiple angles.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. State De Moivre's theorem and prove it for positive integers n by induction.
    Show that it also holds for n = −1.
    Answer: (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ; proof below.
    Teacher explains: Let P(n) be the statement. P(1) is obvious. Assume P(k):
    (cos θ + i sin θ)ᵏ = cos kθ + i sin kθ. Then
       (cos θ + i sin θ)ᵏ⁺¹ = (cos kθ + i sin kθ)(cos θ + i sin θ)
         = (cos kθ cos θ − sin kθ sin θ) + i(sin kθ cos θ + cos kθ sin θ)
         = cos(k + 1)θ + i sin(k + 1)θ          (compound angles, 8.9)
    so P(k + 1) is true, and by induction (8.6) P(n) holds for all n ≥ 1. For
    n = −1: 1/(cos θ + i sin θ) = (cos θ − i sin θ)/(cos²θ + sin²θ)
    = cos θ − i sin θ = cos(−θ) + i sin(−θ). Applying this to the positive case
    gives every negative n; n = 0 gives 1 = 1. In words: to raise a number of
    modulus 1 to the power n, multiply its angle by n. Check θ = π/2, n = 2:
    i² = cos π + i sin π = −1. Now you try: simplify (cos(π/9) + i sin(π/9))⁶.
    (cos(2π/3) + i sin(2π/3) = −1/2 + √3 i/2)

D2. Find (1 + i)¹⁰ and (1 + i)⁻⁴.
    Answer: (1 + i)¹⁰ = 32i; (1 + i)⁻⁴ = −1/4.
    Teacher explains: Change to polar form: |1 + i| = √2, arg = π/4, so
    1 + i = √2(cos(π/4) + i sin(π/4)).
     (1 + i)¹⁰ = (√2)¹⁰(cos(10π/4) + i sin(10π/4)) = 32(cos(5π/2) + i sin(5π/2))
              = 32(0 + i) = 32i
     (1 + i)⁻⁴ = (√2)⁻⁴(cos(−π) + i sin(−π)) = (1/4)(−1) = −1/4
    Quick check for the first: (1 + i)² = 2i, so (1 + i)¹⁰ = (2i)⁵ = 32i⁵ = 32i.
    The binomial theorem would need eleven terms. Common mistake: raising the
    modulus to the power but forgetting to multiply the ANGLE (writing
    32(cos(π/4) + i sin(π/4))). Now you try: (1 − i)⁸ and (1 + i)⁵. (16;
    −4 − 4i)

D3. Find (√3 + i)⁶ and (1 − √3 i)⁵ in the form a + bi.
    Answer: (√3 + i)⁶ = −64; (1 − √3 i)⁵ = 16 + 16√3 i.
    Teacher explains: √3 + i = 2(cos(π/6) + i sin(π/6)), so (√3 + i)⁶
    = 2⁶(cos π + i sin π) = 64(−1) = −64. 1 − √3 i = 2(cos(−π/3) + i sin(−π/3))
    (QIV), so
       (1 − √3 i)⁵ = 32(cos(−5π/3) + i sin(−5π/3))
                  = 32(cos(π/3) + i sin(π/3)) = 32(1/2 + (√3/2)i)
                  = 16 + 16√3 i
    (−5π/3 and π/3 differ by 2π.) Reality check with moduli:
    |16 + 16√3 i| = 16 × 2 = 32 = 2⁵. Common mistake: taking arg(1 − √3 i) = π/3
    (wrong quadrant). Now you try: (−1 + i)⁴ and (√3 − i)³. (−4; −8i)

D4. Find the three cube roots of unity and prove that 1 + ω + ω² = 0 and
    ω² = ω̄.
    Answer: 1, ω = (−1 + i√3)/2 and ω² = (−1 − i√3)/2.
    Teacher explains: z³ = 1 means z³ − 1 = (z − 1)(z² + z + 1) = 0. So z = 1 or
    z² + z + 1 = 0, whose roots are z = (−1 ± √(1 − 4))/2 = (−1 ± i√3)/2. By De
    Moivre these are cos(2π/3) ± i sin(2π/3) = e^(±2πi/3). Call ω = e^(2πi/3);
    then ω² = e^(4πi/3) = e^(−2πi/3), the other root, which is the conjugate ω̄.
    And 1 + ω + ω² = 0 because ω satisfies z² + z + 1 = 0 (or: the sum of the
    roots of z³ − 1 = 0 is 0). On the Argand diagram the three roots are the
    vertices of an equilateral triangle inscribed in the unit circle.
                 ω *      |
                          |
            --------------+-----------* 1
                          |
                ω² *      |
    Also ω³ = 1, so 1/ω = ω² and ω⁴ = ω. Now you try: find ω² × ω̄ and ω⁵ + ω⁷.
    (ω⁴ = ω; ω² + ω = −1)

D5. Simplify (1 + ω − ω²)(1 − ω + ω²), (1 + ω)⁷ and ω¹⁰⁰ + ω²⁰⁰ + 1.
    Answer: 4; −ω²; 0.
    Teacher explains: Use 1 + ω = −ω², 1 + ω² = −ω and ω³ = 1:
       1 + ω − ω² = −ω² − ω² = −2ω²      1 − ω + ω² = −ω − ω = −2ω
       product = (−2ω²)(−2ω) = 4ω³ = 4
       (1 + ω)⁷ = (−ω²)⁷ = −ω¹⁴ = −ω² (as 14 = 12 + 2)
       ω¹⁰⁰ = ω (100 = 99 + 1),  ω²⁰⁰ = ω² (200 = 198 + 2): sum ω + ω² + 1 = 0
    Always reduce the exponent modulo 3 first. Numerically: ω = −0.5 + 0.866i,
    (1 + ω)⁷ = (0.5 + 0.866i)⁷ = e^(7πi/3) = e^(πi/3) = 0.5 + 0.866i and
    −ω² = 0.5 + 0.866i, which agrees. Common mistake: replacing 1 + ω by −ω (it
    is −ω²). Now you try: (1 − ω)(1 − ω²) and (1 − ω + ω²)³. (3; −8)

D6. Find the sixth roots of unity, mark them, and check that their sum is 0 and
    their product is −1.
    Answer: 1, 1/2 + √3 i/2, −1/2 + √3 i/2, −1, −1/2 − √3 i/2, 1/2 − √3 i/2.
    Teacher explains: z = cos(2kπ/6) + i sin(2kπ/6) = cos(kπ/3) + i sin(kπ/3),
    k = 0, ..., 5:
       k      0     1          2           3     4           5
       angle  0     π/3        2π/3        π     4π/3        5π/3
       z      1   1/2+√3i/2  −1/2+√3i/2   −1   −1/2−√3i/2   1/2−√3i/2
    They form a regular hexagon with side 1. Sum: the real parts
    1 + 1/2 − 1/2 − 1 − 1/2 + 1/2 = 0 and the imaginary parts cancel in pairs.
    Product: the roots pair into conjugates (product |z|² = 1) except 1 and −1,
    so the product is 1 × (−1) = −1 = (−1)⁶⁺¹. Notice the sixth roots include
    the cube roots (k even) and the square roots ±1 (k = 0, 3). Now you try:
    list the 4th roots of unity and their product. (1, i, −1, −i; −1)

D7. Prove that for n ≥ 2 the n-th roots of unity add to 0 and multiply to
    (−1)ⁿ⁺¹. Find 1 + α + α² + α³ + α⁴ where α = e^(2πi/5), and the sum of the
    squares of the 4th roots of unity.
    Answer: Proof below; the first sum is 0; the sum of squares is 0.
    Teacher explains: The roots are the n roots of zⁿ − 1 = 0, a polynomial with
    no zⁿ⁻¹ term and constant term −1. By the relations between roots and
    coefficients (sum of roots = −(coefficient of zⁿ⁻¹),
    product = (−1)ⁿ × constant): sum = 0, product = (−1)ⁿ(−1) = (−1)ⁿ⁺¹.
    Alternatively with α = e^(2πi/n): 1 + α + ... + αⁿ⁻¹ = (αⁿ − 1)/(α − 1) = 0
    since αⁿ = 1 and α ≠ 1. For n = 5 the sum is 0. Squares of 1, i, −1, −i:
    1 − 1 + 1 − 1 = 0. In general the sum of the m-th powers is n when n divides
    m (every term is 1) and 0 otherwise (it is a geometric series with ratio
    αᵐ ≠ 1). Example: fourth powers of the 4th roots: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4. Now you
    try: product of the 5th roots of unity and sum of their cubes. (1; 0)

D8. Find the cube roots of 8i and show them on an Argand diagram.
    Answer: √3 + i, −√3 + i, −2i.
    Teacher explains: 8i = 8(cos(π/2) + i sin(π/2)). A cube root has modulus
    ∛8 = 2 and argument (π/2 + 2kπ)/3, k = 0, 1, 2:
       k = 0:  2(cos(π/6) + i sin(π/6))   = √3 + i
       k = 1:  2(cos(5π/6) + i sin(5π/6)) = −√3 + i
       k = 2:  2(cos(3π/2) + i sin(3π/2)) = −2i
    They lie on the circle of radius 2, 120° apart (an equilateral triangle).
    Check: (−2i)³ = −8i³ = 8i. Also each root is the first one times 1, ω, ω²:
    (√3 + i)ω = −√3 + i. Common mistake: dividing only π/2 by 3 and forgetting
    the + 2kπ, which gives just one root. Now you try: the cube roots of −27.
    (3/2 + 3√3 i/2, −3, 3/2 − 3√3 i/2)

D9. Solve z⁴ = −16 and write the roots in the form a + bi. Hence factorise
    z⁴ + 16 into two real quadratic factors.
    Answer: z = ±√2 ± √2 i (all four sign choices);
    z⁴ + 16 = (z² − 2√2 z + 4)(z² + 2√2 z + 4).
    Teacher explains: −16 = 16(cos π + i sin π); roots have modulus 16^(1/4) = 2
    and arguments (π + 2kπ)/4 = π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4, 7π/4:
       2 cis(π/4) = √2 + √2 i      2 cis(3π/4) = −√2 + √2 i
       2 cis(5π/4) = −√2 − √2 i    2 cis(7π/4) = √2 − √2 i
    (cis θ is short for cos θ + i sin θ.) Pair each root with its conjugate:
    (z − (√2 + √2 i))(z − (√2 − √2 i)) = z² − 2√2 z + 4, and similarly
    z² + 2√2 z + 4. Multiply out to check: (z² + 4)² − 8z² = z⁴ + 8z² + 16 − 8z²
    = z⁴ + 16. Real polynomials always factor into real linear and quadratic
    factors this way. Now you try: solve z⁴ = −4. (±1 ± i)

D10. Use De Moivre's theorem to express cos 3θ and sin 3θ in powers of cos θ and
     sin θ, and deduce a formula for tan 3θ.
     Answer: cos 3θ = 4cos³θ − 3 cos θ; sin 3θ = 3 sin θ − 4 sin³θ;
     tan 3θ = (3t − t³)/(1 − 3t²) with t = tan θ.
     Teacher explains: Write c = cos θ, s = sin θ. By De Moivre and the binomial
     theorem:
        cos 3θ + i sin 3θ = (c + is)³ = c³ + 3c²(is) + 3c(is)² + (is)³
                          = (c³ − 3cs²) + i(3c²s − s³)
     Equate real parts: cos 3θ = c³ − 3c(1 − c²) = 4c³ − 3c. Imaginary parts:
     sin 3θ = 3(1 − s²)s − s³ = 3s − 4s³. Divide the two expressions by c³:
     tan 3θ = (3c²s − s³)/(c³ − 3cs²) = (3t − t³)/(1 − 3t²). Check at θ = 20°:
     4(0.93969)³ − 3(0.93969) = 0.5 = cos 60°. This is quicker than repeated
     compound-angle formulas, especially for 5θ. Now you try: express cos 4θ in
     powers of cos θ. (8cos⁴θ − 8cos²θ + 1)

D11. Let z = cos θ + i sin θ. Show that zⁿ + 1/zⁿ = 2 cos nθ and use it to write
     cos⁴θ in terms of cos 4θ and cos 2θ. Hence find the exact value of
     cos⁴(π/8) + cos⁴(3π/8).
     Answer: cos⁴θ = (cos 4θ + 4 cos 2θ + 3)/8; the value is 3/4.
     Teacher explains: By De Moivre zⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ and
     z⁻ⁿ = cos nθ − i sin nθ; adding, zⁿ + z⁻ⁿ = 2 cos nθ. So 2 cos θ = z + 1/z
     and
        16cos⁴θ = (z + 1/z)⁴ = z⁴ + 4z² + 6 + 4/z² + 1/z⁴
                = (z⁴ + 1/z⁴) + 4(z² + 1/z²) + 6 = 2 cos 4θ + 8 cos 2θ + 6
     so cos⁴θ = (cos 4θ + 4 cos 2θ + 3)/8. At θ = π/8: cos(π/2) = 0,
     cos(π/4) = √2/2, giving (2√2 + 3)/8; at θ = 3π/8: cos(3π/2) = 0,
     cos(3π/4) = −√2/2, giving (3 − 2√2)/8. Sum: 6/8 = 3/4. Numerically
     0.72855 + 0.02145 = 0.75. Such "linearised" forms are exactly what is
     needed to integrate cos⁴θ (8.44). Now you try: write sin³θ in terms of
     sin 3θ and sin θ. ((3 sin θ − sin 3θ)/4)

D12. Using the fifth roots of unity, prove that cos(2π/5) = (√5 − 1)/4.
     Answer: Proof below.
     Teacher explains: Let z = e^(2πi/5) ≠ 1. From
     z⁵ − 1 = (z − 1)(z⁴ + z³ + z² + z + 1) = 0 we get z⁴ + z³ + z² + z + 1 = 0.
     Divide by z²:
        (z² + 1/z²) + (z + 1/z) + 1 = 0
     Put w = z + 1/z = 2 cos(2π/5); then z² + 1/z² = w² − 2, so w² + w − 1 = 0
     and w = (−1 ± √5)/2. Since 2π/5 = 72° is acute, w > 0, so w = (√5 − 1)/2
     and cos 72° = (√5 − 1)/4 ≈ 0.30902 (calculator: cos 72° = 0.30902). The
     other root (−1 − √5)/2 = 2 cos(4π/5) gives cos 144° = −(1 + √5)/4. This
     links roots of unity with the regular pentagon, which Gauss extended to
     construct the regular 17-gon with ruler and compasses. Now you try: use the
     same method with z = e^(2πi/7) to show
     cos(2π/7) + cos(4π/7) + cos(6π/7) = −1/2. (the sum of the six non-real
     roots is −1)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Use De Moivre's theorem; answer in the form a + bi.

    b) (cos(π/4) + i sin(π/4))⁸

M2. Change to polar form, then use De Moivre. Answer as a + bi.
    a) (1 + i)²         b) (1 + i)⁴            c) (1 + i)⁶      d) (1 + i)⁸

    Answers: a) 2i   b) −4   c) −8i   d) 16   e) −64   f) 8 + 8i   g) 8i

M3. Evaluate (use De Moivre with a negative power). Answer as a + bi.

M4. List all the n-th roots of unity (exact a + bi form where the angles are
    standard; otherwise exponential form and decimals).
    a) zⁿ = 1 for n = 2
    b) zⁿ = 1 for n = 3
    c) zⁿ = 1 for n = 4

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: before using De Moivre ALWAYS write the number in polar form with
  a sketch; keep a card with ω facts (ω³ = 1, 1 + ω + ω² = 0, ω² = ω̄) and
  reduce every power of ω mod 3 first; draw the n-th roots as a regular polygon
  to see sums and products. Harder: prove that the product of sin(kπ/n) for
  k = 1 to n − 1 equals n/2ⁿ⁻¹ (use zⁿ − 1 = (z − 1)(z − α)...(z − αⁿ⁻¹) at
  z = 1); show that if 1, α, α², ..., αⁿ⁻¹ are the n-th roots of unity then
  (1 − α)(1 − α²)...(1 − αⁿ⁻¹) = n; solve (z + 1)⁵ = z⁵
  (z = −1/2 − (i/2) cot(kπ/5), k = 1, 2, 3, 4); find
  cos(π/7) − cos(2π/7) + cos(3π/7) (1/2).


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.15 — QUADRATIC EQUATIONS WITH COMPLEX ROOTS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - For ax² + bx + c = 0 with a, b, c real and a ≠ 0, the DISCRIMINANT is
    Δ = b² − 4ac. Δ > 0: two distinct real roots; Δ = 0: one repeated real root;
    Δ < 0: two NON-REAL roots, a conjugate pair.
  - When Δ < 0 write √Δ = i√(−Δ) = i√(4ac − b²). The quadratic formula still
    works: x = (−b ± i√(4ac − b²))/(2a). Completing the square gives the same
    result: a(x + b/(2a))² = −(4ac − b²)/(4a).
  - CONJUGATE ROOT THEOREM: if a polynomial has REAL coefficients and p + qi
    (q ≠ 0) is a root, then p − qi is also a root. So
    (x − p)² + q² = x² − 2px + (p² + q²) is a real quadratic factor. With
    complex coefficients this can fail.
  - ROOTS AND COEFFICIENTS (true for complex roots too): α + β = −b/a, αβ = c/a.
    The quadratic with roots α, β is x² − (α + β)x + αβ = 0. For the pair p ±
    qi: x² − 2px + (p² + q²) = 0 (sum 2p, product = |root|²).
  - SYMMETRIC EXPRESSIONS are found from the sum and product without solving:
    α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ, α³ + β³ = (α + β)³ − 3αβ(α + β),
    1/α + 1/β = (α + β)/(αβ), (α − β)² = (α + β)² − 4αβ. An equation whose roots
    are α², 1/α, α + k, ... is built from its new sum and product.
  - HIGHER DEGREE: given one non-real root of a real cubic or quartic, multiply
    out the conjugate pair to get a real quadratic factor, divide, and solve
    what is left. Equations such as x⁴ + 5x² + 4 = 0 or x³ = 8 reduce to
    quadratics.
  - COMPLEX COEFFICIENTS: the formula z = (−b ± √Δ)/(2a) still holds, but √Δ is
    a complex square root (8.13); the roots need not be conjugates. Always check
    a root by substituting it back.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Solve x² + 4x + 13 = 0 and check one root by substitution.
    Answer: x = −2 + 3i or x = −2 − 3i (written x = −2 ± 3i).
    Teacher explains: Here a = 1, b = 4, c = 13, so
    Δ = b² − 4ac = 16 − 52 = −36 < 0: no real roots, but two complex ones. Since
    √(−36) = √36 × i = 6i,
       x = (−4 ± √(−36))/2 = (−4 ± 6i)/2 = −2 ± 3i
    Check x = −2 + 3i: x² = 4 − 12i + 9i² = −5 − 12i and 4x = −8 + 12i, so
    x² + 4x + 13 = −5 − 12i − 8 + 12i + 13 = 0. On the Argand plane the two
    roots are mirror images in the real axis, and both lie on the vertical line
    Re x = −2 = −b/(2a), the axis of symmetry of the parabola y = x² + 4x + 13,
    which never meets the x-axis. Common mistake: writing √(−36) = −6. Now you
    try: x² − 6x + 10 = 0. (3 ± i)

D2. Solve 2x² − 3x + 5 = 0 by completing the square, and compare with the
    formula.
    Answer: x = (3 ± i√31)/4.
    Teacher explains: Divide by 2 and move the constant:
       x² − (3/2)x = −5/2
       x² − (3/2)x + 9/16 = −5/2 + 9/16 = −31/16
       (x − 3/4)² = −31/16
       x − 3/4 = ±i√31/4,  so  x = (3 ± i√31)/4
    Formula: Δ = 9 − 40 = −31, x = (3 ± √(−31))/4 = (3 ± i√31)/4, the same.
    Decimals: x ≈ 0.75 ± 1.392i. A square equal to a NEGATIVE number is
    impossible for real x; allowing x to be complex removes the obstacle. Common
    mistake: halving the coefficient of x before dividing by 2 (adding 9/4
    instead of 9/16). Now you try: 3x² + 2x + 1 = 0. ((−1 ± i√2)/3)

D3. Explain why the non-real roots of a quadratic with REAL coefficients always
    come as a conjugate pair. Can x² + (1 + i)x + i = 0 have roots that are not
    conjugates?
    Answer: Taking conjugates of aα² + bα + c = 0 shows ᾱ is also a root. Yes:
    the second equation has roots −1 and −i, not a conjugate pair.
    Teacher explains: Suppose α is a root: aα² + bα + c = 0. Take the conjugate
    of both sides. The conjugate of a sum is the sum of the conjugates, the
    conjugate of a product is the product of the conjugates, and real numbers
    equal their own conjugates (ā = a, b̄ = b, c̄ = c):
       a(ᾱ)² + b(ᾱ) + c = 0 (the conjugate of 0 is 0)
    So ᾱ is also a root. If α is non-real then ᾱ ≠ α, so the two roots are α and
    ᾱ. The same proof works for real polynomials of ANY degree. In the second
    equation the coefficient 1 + i is not real, so the step b̄ = b fails:
    (x + 1)(x + i) = x² + (1 + i)x + i has roots −1 and −i. Now you try: one
    root of x² − 8x + c = 0 (c real) is 4 + 3i; find the other root and c.
    (4 − 3i; c = 25)

D4. A ball is thrown straight up at 20 m/s; its height after t seconds is
    h = 20t − 5t² metres. Does it ever reach 25 m? What does the discriminant
    tell us?
    Answer: No. 5t² − 20t + 25 = 0 has Δ = −100 < 0; the roots t = 2 ± i are not
    real, so the height 25 m is never reached. The greatest height is 20 m.
    Teacher explains: Set h = 25: 20t − 5t² = 25, i.e. 5t² − 20t + 25 = 0, or
    t² − 4t + 5 = 0. Then Δ = 16 − 20 = −4 < 0 and t = (4 ± 2i)/2 = 2 ± i. A
    time cannot be a non-real number, so there is no moment when h = 25.
    Completing the square explains why: h = 20 − 5(t − 2)², which is at most 20
    (at t = 2 s). In applied problems, non-real roots are a message: "this never
    happens". For h = 15: t² − 4t + 3 = 0 gives t = 1 or 3 (going up and coming
    down), and for h = 20: Δ = 0, t = 2 (just touching the top). Now you try:
    can h = 20t − 5t² equal 21? (No: t² − 4t + 4.2 = 0 has Δ = −0.8 < 0)

D5. For which real k does x² + kx + 9 = 0 have non-real roots? Solve it when
    k = 4.
    Answer: −6 < k < 6. For k = 4: x = −2 ± i√5.
    Teacher explains: Non-real roots need Δ < 0:
       k² − 4 × 1 × 9 < 0   ⇔   k² < 36   ⇔   −6 < k < 6
    At k = ±6 the roots are equal (x = ∓3) and for |k| > 6 they are real and
    distinct. For k = 4: Δ = 16 − 36 = −20 and √(−20) = i√20 = 2i√5, so
       x = (−4 ± 2i√5)/2 = −2 ± i√5
    Check with the product: (−2)² + (√5)² = 4 + 5 = 9 = c. Common mistake:
    solving k² < 36 as k < 6 only (forgetting negative k such as k = −10, which
    gives real roots). Now you try: for which k does x² + 4x + k = 0 have
    non-real roots? (k > 4)

D6. Find a quadratic with real coefficients that has 3 + 2i as a root. Do the
    same for 2 − i√3.
    Answer: x² − 6x + 13 = 0 and x² − 4x + 7 = 0.
    Teacher explains: With real coefficients the other root must be the
    conjugate 3 − 2i.
       sum     = (3 + 2i) + (3 − 2i) = 6
       product = (3 + 2i)(3 − 2i) = 9 − 4i² = 9 + 4 = 13
    so x² − (sum)x + product = x² − 6x + 13 = 0. Shortcut for p ± qi: sum 2p,
    product p² + q². For 2 ± i√3: sum 4, product 4 + 3 = 7, giving
    x² − 4x + 7 = 0. Check: Δ = 16 − 28 = −12, x = (4 ± 2i√3)/2 = 2 ± i√3. Any
    non-zero multiple, such as 2x² − 12x + 26 = 0, has the same roots. Common
    mistake: product (3 + 2i)(3 − 2i) = 9 − 4 = 5 (forgetting i² = −1). Now you
    try: roots −1 ± 4i. (x² + 2x + 17 = 0)

D7. α and β are the roots of x² − 2x + 5 = 0. Without solving, find α² + β²,
    1/α + 1/β and α³ + β³. Then check by solving.
    Answer: α² + β² = −6; 1/α + 1/β = 2/5; α³ + β³ = −22.
    Teacher explains: α + β = −b/a = 2 and αβ = c/a = 5 (these rules come from
    a(x − α)(x − β) = ax² − a(α + β)x + aαβ, so they hold for complex roots).
       α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ = 4 − 10 = −6
       1/α + 1/β = (α + β)/(αβ) = 2/5
       α³ + β³ = (α + β)³ − 3αβ(α + β) = 8 − 30 = −22
    Check: the roots are 1 ± 2i. (1 + 2i)² = −3 + 4i and (1 − 2i)² = −3 − 4i,
    sum −6. (1 + 2i)³ = (−3 + 4i)(1 + 2i) = −11 − 2i, and with the conjugate the
    sum is −22. A sum of two SQUARES that is negative is only possible because
    the roots are not real. Now you try: for the same equation find (α − β)².
    ((α + β)² − 4αβ = −16)

D8. α and β are the roots of x² − 2x + 5 = 0. Find the quadratic equations whose
    roots are (i) α², β² and (ii) 1/α, 1/β.
    Answer: (i) x² + 6x + 25 = 0; (ii) 5x² − 2x + 1 = 0.
    Teacher explains: Work out the new sum S and product P, then write
    x² − Sx + P = 0.
       (i)  S = α² + β² = −6,      P = α²β² = (αβ)² = 25
       (ii) S = 1/α + 1/β = 2/5,   P = 1/(αβ) = 1/5
    (i) gives x² + 6x + 25 = 0. (ii) gives x² − (2/5)x + 1/5 = 0; multiply by 5:
    5x² − 2x + 1 = 0. Checks: α² = (1 + 2i)² = −3 + 4i, and x² + 6x + 25 = 0 has
    roots −3 ± 4i. Also 1/(1 + 2i) = (1 − 2i)/5, and the roots of
    5x² − 2x + 1 = 0 are
       x = (2 ± √(4 − 20))/10 = (2 ± 4i)/10 = (1 ± 2i)/5
    Shortcut for reciprocals: reverse the coefficients, so ax² + bx + c = 0
    becomes cx² + bx + a = 0. Now you try: the equation with roots α + 1, β + 1.
    (x² − 4x + 8 = 0)

D9. Given that 2 + 3i is a root of x³ − 5x² + 17x − 13 = 0, find the other two
    roots.
    Answer: 2 − 3i and 1.
    Teacher explains: The coefficients are real, so 2 − 3i is also a root, and
    (x − 2 − 3i)(x − 2 + 3i) = (x − 2)² + 9 = x² − 4x + 13 is a factor. Divide:
                      x  − 1
                  ------------------------
       x² − 4x + 13 ) x³ − 5x² + 17x − 13
                      x³ − 4x² + 13x
                      ------------------
                           −x² +  4x − 13
                           −x² +  4x − 13
                           --------------
                                        0
    So x³ − 5x² + 17x − 13 = (x² − 4x + 13)(x − 1) and the third root is 1.
    Quick check with the sum of roots of a cubic (−b/a = 5):
    (2 + 3i) + (2 − 3i) + 1 = 5; product of roots (−d/a = 13): 13 × 1 = 13. Now
    you try: x³ − x² + 2 = 0 has root 1 + i; find the others. (1 − i, −1)

D10. Show that 3i is a root of x⁴ − 4x³ + 14x² − 36x + 45 = 0 and solve the
     equation completely.
     Answer: x = ±3i and x = 2 ± i.
     Teacher explains: Substitute x = 3i: x² = −9, x³ = −27i, x⁴ = 81, so
        81 − 4(−27i) + 14(−9) − 36(3i) + 45 = 81 + 108i − 126 − 108i + 45 = 0
     The coefficients are real, so −3i is a root too, and
     (x − 3i)(x + 3i) = x² + 9 is a factor. Compare coefficients in
     x⁴ − 4x³ + 14x² − 36x + 45 = (x² + 9)(x² + px + q): x³: p = −4; constant:
     9q = 45, q = 5 (check x²: q + 9 = 14; x: 9p = −36). So the other factor is
     x² − 4x + 5, with Δ = 16 − 20 = −4 and x = (4 ± 2i)/2 = 2 ± i. A real
     quartic always splits into real linear and quadratic factors. Now you try:
     solve x⁴ + 5x² + 4 = 0. (±i, ±2i)

D11. Solve z² − (3 + i)z + (2 + 2i) = 0. Why are the roots not conjugates?
     Answer: z = 2 or z = 1 + i. The coefficients are not all real.
     Teacher explains: Use the formula with a = 1, b = −(3 + i), c = 2 + 2i:
        Δ = (3 + i)² − 4(2 + 2i) = 9 + 6i − 1 − 8 − 8i = −2i
     Find √(−2i) as in 8.13: (x + iy)² = −2i gives x² − y² = 0 and 2xy = −2, so
     x = 1, y = −1 (or the negatives): √(−2i) = ±(1 − i). Then
        z = ((3 + i) ± (1 − i))/2 = 4/2 or (2 + 2i)/2 = 2 or 1 + i
     Checks: sum 2 + (1 + i) = 3 + i = −b, product 2(1 + i) = 2 + 2i = c. The
     conjugate-pair rule needs REAL coefficients; here b and c are not real, so
     nothing forces 1 − i to be a root (indeed it is not). Common mistake:
     writing the roots as (3 + i ± √(−2i))/2 and stopping; always simplify √Δ.
     Now you try: z² − 2iz − 5 = 0. (z = 2 + i or −2 + i)

D12. In 1545 Cardano asked for two numbers whose sum is 10 and whose product is
     40, and called the answer "as subtle as it is useless". Find them and check
     the conditions.
     Answer: 5 + i√15 and 5 − i√15.
     Teacher explains: The numbers are the roots of x² − (sum)x + product = 0:
        x² − 10x + 40 = 0,   Δ = 100 − 160 = −60,   √(−60) = 2i√15
        x = (10 ± 2i√15)/2 = 5 ± i√15
     Check the sum: (5 + i√15) + (5 − i√15) = 10. Product:
     5² − (i√15)² = 25 + 15 = 40. No two REAL numbers work: real numbers with
     sum 10 have product at most 5 × 5 = 25 (since xy = 25 − (x − 5)²).
     Cardano's "useless" numbers later turned out to be essential in physics and
     engineering. Now you try: two numbers with sum 6 and product 13. (3 ± 2i)
