      j) Δ = 2, Δ₁ = 2, Δ₂ = 2, Δ₃ = 2; x = 1, y = 1, z = 1
      k) Δ = 5, Δ₁ = 5, Δ₂ = 10, Δ₃ = 15; x = 1, y = 2, z = 3
      l) Δ = 4, Δ₁ = 4, Δ₂ = 8, Δ₃ = 12; x = 1, y = 2, z = 3

M9. Find |A| and decide: unique solution (give it), no solution, or infinitely
    many solutions.
    a) x + 2y = 3, 2x + 4y = 6
    b) x + 2y = 3, 2x + 4y = 7
    c) x + 2y = 3, 2x + 3y = 5
    d) 3x − y = 4, −6x + 2y = 1
    e) 3x − y = 4, −6x + 2y = −8
    f) 2x + 5y = 7, 4x + 10y = 14
    g) x − y = 1, 3x − 3y = 3
    h) 5x + 2y = 4, 3x + y = 2
    i) x + y + z = 1, x + 2y + 3z = 2, 3x + 4y + 5z = 4
    j) x + y + z = 1, x + 2y + 3z = 2, 3x + 4y + 5z = 5
    k) x + y + z = 1, 2x + 2y + 2z = 2, 3x + 3y + 3z = 3
    l) x + y + z = 1, 2x + 2y + 2z = 2, 3x + 3y + 3z = 4
    m) x − y + z = 4, 2x + y − 3z = 0, x + y + z = 2
    n) 2x − y + 3z = 5, x + y + z = 2, 3x + 4z = 7
    o) 2x − y + 3z = 5, x + y + z = 2, 3x + 4z = 8
    p) x + 2y + 3z = 0, 4x + 5y + 6z = 0, 7x + 8y + 9z = 0
    Answers:
      a) |A| = 0; infinitely many
      b) |A| = 0; none (inconsistent)
      c) |A| = −1; unique: x = 1, y = 1
      d) |A| = 0; none (inconsistent)
      e) |A| = 0; infinitely many
      f) |A| = 0; infinitely many
      g) |A| = 0; infinitely many
      h) |A| = −1; unique: x = 0, y = 2
      i) |A| = 0; infinitely many
      j) |A| = 0; none (inconsistent)
      k) |A| = 0; infinitely many
      l) |A| = 0; none (inconsistent)
      m) |A| = 10; unique: x = 2, y = −1, z = 1
      n) |A| = 0; infinitely many
      o) |A| = 0; none (inconsistent)
      p) |A| = 0; infinitely many

M10. Find the values of the parameters.
     a) x + 2y = 3, 2x + ky = 6: k for a unique solution
     b) x + 2y = 3, 2x + ky = 6: k for infinitely many
     c) x + 2y = 3, 2x + 4y = m: m for no solution
     d) kx + y = 1, x + ky = 1: k for no solution
     e) kx + y = 1, x + ky = 1: k for infinitely many
     f) kx + y = 1, x + ky = 1: solution when k ≠ ±1
     g) x + y + z = 1, x + 2y + 3z = 2, 3x + 4y + kz = 4: k for a unique
        solution
     h) x + ky + 3z = 0, 3x + ky − 2z = 0, 2x + 3y − 4z = 0: k for non-trivial
        solutions
     i) x + y + z = 0, x − y + z = 0, x + y + kz = 0: k for non-trivial
        solutions
     j) 2x + y = 5, 4x + 2y = k: k for a solution to exist
     k) x + y + z = 6, x + 2y + 3z = 10, x + 2y + λz = μ: λ, μ for no solution
     l) the same system: λ, μ for infinitely many
     m) the same system: λ, μ for a unique solution
     Answers: a) k ≠ 4   b) k = 4   c) m ≠ 6   d) k = −1   e) k = 1
              f) x = y = 1/(k + 1)   g) k ≠ 5   h) k = 33/2   i) k = 1
              j) k = 10   k) λ = 3, μ ≠ 10   l) λ = 3, μ = 10   m) λ ≠ 3 (any μ)

M11. Inverses from matrix identities.
     a) A = [1 2; 3 4]: show A² − 5A − 2I = O, then A⁻¹
     b) A = [2 1; 1 3]: show A² − 5A + 5I = O, then A⁻¹
     c) A = [3 1; −1 2]: show A² − 5A + 7I = O, then A⁻¹
     d) A = [2 3; 1 2]: show A² − 4A + I = O, then A⁻¹
     e) A = [4 −1; 2 1]: show A² − 5A + 6I = O, then A⁻¹
     f) A³ = I: A⁻¹
     g) A² = A (and A invertible): A
     h) A² − 3A + 2I = O: A⁻¹
     i) A² = 2I: A⁻¹
     j) A = [1 1 1; 1 1 1; 1 1 1]: show A² = 3A; does A⁻¹ exist?
     k) A = [0 1; −1 0]: A⁻¹ = −A? (T or F)
     Answers: a) A⁻¹ = (A − 5I)/2 = [−2 1; 3/2 −1/2]
              b) A⁻¹ = (5I − A)/5 = [3/5 −1/5; −1/5 2/5]
              c) A⁻¹ = (5I − A)/7 = [2/7 −1/7; 1/7 3/7]
              d) A⁻¹ = 4I − A = [2 −3; −1 2]
              e) A⁻¹ = (5I − A)/6 = [1/6 1/6; −1/3 2/3]   f) A²   g) I
              h) (3I − A)/2   i) A/2   j) no (|A| = 0)   k) T

M12. Row-reduction inverses; True (T) or False (F).
     a) by row operations: [2 1; 5 3]⁻¹
     b) by row operations: [1 2; 3 7]⁻¹
     c) by row operations: [1 1 1; 1 2 3; 1 3 6]⁻¹
     d) by row operations: [1 2 0; 0 1 2; 0 0 1]⁻¹
     e) by row operations: [1 0 1; 0 1 0; 1 0 −1]⁻¹
     f) T or F: every square matrix has an inverse
     g) T or F: (AB)⁻¹ = A⁻¹B⁻¹
     h) T or F: (A⁻¹)ᵀ = (Aᵀ)⁻¹
     i) T or F: if |A| = 0, AX = B has no solution
     j) T or F: AX = O with |A| ≠ 0 has only X = O
     k) T or F: Cramer's rule works when Δ = 0
     l) T or F: an invertible matrix has exactly one inverse
     m) T or F: if AB = AC and |A| ≠ 0 then B = C
     n) T or F: the inverse of a symmetric matrix is symmetric
     o) T or F: |adj A| = |A| for every 3 × 3 matrix
     Answers: a) [3 −1; −5 2]   b) [7 −2; −3 1]   c) [3 −3 1; −3 5 −2; 1 −2 1]
              d) [1 −2 4; 0 1 −2; 0 0 1]   e) (1/2)[1 0 1; 0 2 0; 1 0 −1]   f) F
              g) F (B⁻¹A⁻¹)   h) T   i) F (none or infinitely many)   j) T
              k) F   l) T   m) T   n) T   o) F (|A|²)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: follow a fixed routine for a 3 × 3 inverse: determinant, nine
  cofactors in a grid, TRANSPOSE, divide; check A × A⁻¹ = I every time; keep
  1/|A| outside until the end; write missing variables with coefficient 0; check
  solutions in every original equation; draw the two lines for 2 × 2 systems to
  see "unique, parallel, same line". Harder: prove that adj(AB) = (adj B)(adj A)
  and adj(adj A) = |A|ⁿ⁻²A; solve a 4 × 4 system by Gaussian elimination and
  count the operations compared with Cramer's rule; use a matrix to encode and
  decode a message (Hill cipher) with an integer matrix whose determinant is ±1;
  fit a parabola y = ax² + bx + c through three data points by solving a 3 × 3
  system.


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.24 — STRAIGHT LINES: FORMS OF EQUATIONS, ANGLE BETWEEN LINES, DISTANCE
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - SLOPE of the line through (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂): m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) =
    tan θ, where θ (0° ≤ θ < 180°) is the INCLINATION to the positive x-axis.
    Horizontal lines have m = 0; vertical lines have no slope (x = constant).
  - FORMS: point-slope y − y₁ = m(x − x₁); slope-intercept y = mx + c; two-point
    (y − y₁)/(y₂ − y₁) = (x − x₁)/(x₂ − x₁); intercept x/a + y/b = 1; NORMAL
    form x cos α + y sin α = p (p = length of the perpendicular from O, α = its
    angle with the x-axis, p > 0); GENERAL form Ax + By + C = 0 with slope −A/B,
    x-intercept −C/A, y-intercept −C/B.
  - To change Ax + By + C = 0 to normal form, move C to the right so that it is
    positive and divide by √(A² + B²).
  - PARALLEL lines: equal slopes (Ax + By + k = 0 is parallel to Ax + By +
    C = 0). PERPENDICULAR: m₁m₂ = −1 (Bx − Ay + k = 0 is perpendicular to Ax +
    By + C = 0). ANGLE θ between lines: tan θ = |(m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)| for the
    acute angle.
  - DISTANCE from (x₁, y₁) to Ax + By + C = 0: d = |Ax₁ + By₁ + C|/√(A² + B²).
    Between parallel lines Ax + By + C₁ = 0 and Ax + By + C₂ = 0 (same A, B):
    d = |C₁ − C₂|/√(A² + B²).
  - FOOT of the perpendicular (h, k) from (x₁, y₁) to Ax + By + C = 0: (h −
    x₁)/A = (k − y₁)/B = −(Ax₁ + By₁ + C)/(A² + B²); the IMAGE (mirror point)
    uses −2(Ax₁ + By₁ + C)/(A² + B²). Points are on the same side of the line
    when Ax + By + C has the same sign at both.
  - FAMILY of lines through the intersection of L₁ = 0 and L₂ = 0: L₁ + λL₂ = 0.
    Three lines are CONCURRENT (meet at one point) when the intersection of two
    of them lies on the third; for lines no two of which are parallel this is
    |a₁ b₁ c₁; a₂ b₂ c₂; a₃ b₃ c₃| = 0.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Find the slope and the inclination of the line through (−2, 3) and (4, −6).
    Find the slope of a line inclined at 60° and at 135°. Use slopes to show
    that (1, 1), (3, 5) and (4, 7) are collinear.
    Answer: m = −3/2, θ ≈ 123.69°; slopes √3 and −1; the slopes AB and BC are
    both 2, so the points are collinear.
    Teacher explains:
    m = (−6 − 3)/(4 − (−2)) = −9/6 = −3/2
    tan θ = −3/2:  θ = 180° − tan⁻¹(3/2) ≈ 180° − 56.31° = 123.69°
    tan 60° = √3,   tan 135° = −1
    AB: (5 − 1)/(3 − 1) = 2,   BC: (7 − 5)/(4 − 3) = 2
    A negative slope means the line goes DOWN from left to right, so the
    inclination is obtuse. The calculator gives tan⁻¹(−1.5) = −56.31°, which is
    not in 0° ≤ θ < 180°; add 180°. AB and BC have the same slope AND share the
    point B, so they are the same line. Common mistake: mixing the order, (y₂ −
    y₁)/(x₁ − x₂), which flips the sign. Now you try: the slope of the line
    through (2, 5) and (2, −1). (undefined: the line x = 2 is vertical)

D2. Find the equation of the line (a) through (2, −3) with slope 4 (b) with
    inclination 135° and y-intercept 5. (c) A taxi charges ₹50 plus ₹12 per km.
    Write the fare y (₹) for x km as a line; what do the slope and intercept
    mean? What does a 17 km ride cost?
    Answer: (a) y = 4x − 11 (4x − y − 11 = 0) (b) y = −x + 5 (x + y − 5 = 0) (c)
    y = 12x + 50; ₹254.
    Teacher explains:
    (a) y − (−3) = 4(x − 2):  y + 3 = 4x − 8,  y = 4x − 11
    (b) m = tan 135° = −1, c = 5:  y = −x + 5
    (c) y = 12x + 50;  x = 17:  y = 204 + 50 = 254
    The point-slope form comes straight from the slope: every point (x, y) of
    the line satisfies (y − y₁)/(x − x₁) = m. In the taxi model the slope 12 is
    the RATE (₹ per km) and the intercept 50 is the fixed charge (the fare for
    0 km). Check (a): x = 2 gives y = 8 − 11 = −3. Common mistake:
    y − 3 = 4(x − 2) (sign of y₁ lost). Now you try: the line through (−1, 4)
    with slope −2/3. (2x + 3y − 10 = 0)

D3. Find the line (a) through (1, −1) and (3, 5) (b) with x-intercept 3 and
    y-intercept −4 (c) through (2, 3) with equal intercepts (d) whose segment
    between the axes is bisected at (−2, 3).
    Answer: (a) 3x − y − 4 = 0 (b) 4x − 3y − 12 = 0 (c) x + y − 5 = 0 (d)
    3x − 2y + 12 = 0.
    Teacher explains:
    (a) m = (5 + 1)/(3 − 1) = 3:  y + 1 = 3(x − 1),  y = 3x − 4
    (b) x/3 + y/(−4) = 1;  × 12:  4x − 3y = 12
    (c) x/a + y/a = 1, i.e. x + y = a;  (2, 3):  a = 5
    (d) midpoint of (a, 0) and (0, b) is (a/2, b/2) = (−2, 3):
        a = −4, b = 6:  x/(−4) + y/6 = 1,  3x − 2y = −12
    The intercept form x/a + y/b = 1 is ideal when the line meets the axes at
    (a, 0) and (0, b): check (b) by putting y = 0 (x = 3) and x = 0 (y = −4). In
    (c) "equal intercepts" means a = b (and a ≠ 0); the line y = (3/2)x through
    the origin has both intercepts 0 and is sometimes accepted as a second
    answer. Common mistake: in (d) taking the intercepts as −2 and 3 instead of
    doubling them. Now you try: the line through (4, 1) and (−2, 4).
    (x + 2y − 6 = 0)

D4. Find the line whose perpendicular from the origin has length 5 and makes 30°
    with the positive x-axis. Reduce √3x + y − 8 = 0 and x − y + 4 = 0 to normal
    form, and find p and α.
    Answer: √3x + y = 10; √3x + y − 8 = 0: p = 4, α = 30°; x − y + 4 = 0:
    p = 2√2, α = 135°.
    Teacher explains:
    x cos 30° + y sin 30° = 5:  (√3/2)x + (1/2)y = 5,  √3x + y = 10
    √3x + y = 8;  √(3 + 1) = 2:  (√3/2)x + (1/2)y = 4
       cos α = √3/2, sin α = 1/2:  α = 30°,  p = 4
    x − y + 4 = 0  →  −x + y = 4  (right side positive)
       √(1 + 1) = √2:  (−1/√2)x + (1/√2)y = 4/√2 = 2√2
       cos α = −1/√2, sin α = 1/√2:  α = 135°,  p = 2√2
    p is a DISTANCE, so it must be positive: move the constant to the right and
    make it positive BEFORE dividing. Then cos α and sin α must both fit the
    same angle (check the signs: here cos α < 0 and sin α > 0, so α is in the
    second quadrant). p is also the distance from the origin to the line. Common
    mistake: dividing by A² + B² instead of √(A² + B²). Now you try: normal form
    of 3x + 4y + 10 = 0. (−(3/5)x − (4/5)y = 2: p = 2, cos α = −3/5, sin α =
    −4/5, α ≈ 233.13°)

D5. For the line 3x − 4y + 12 = 0 find the slope, the intercepts and the
    slope-intercept and intercept forms. Which of the points (0, 3), (4, 6) and
    (1, 1) lie on it, and which side of it is the origin on?
    Answer: m = 3/4; x-intercept −4, y-intercept 3; y = (3/4)x + 3; x/(−4) +
    y/3 = 1. (0, 3) and (4, 6) are on it; (1, 1) and O are on the same side.
    Teacher explains:
    solve for y:  4y = 3x + 12,  y = (3/4)x + 3:  m = 3/4, c = 3
    y = 0:  3x = −12,  x = −4;   x = 0:  y = 3
    intercept form:  3x − 4y = −12  ÷ (−12):  x/(−4) + y/3 = 1
    (0, 3):  0 − 12 + 12 = 0    on the line
    (4, 6):  12 − 24 + 12 = 0   on the line
    (1, 1):  3 − 4 + 12 = 11 > 0;   O:  0 − 0 + 12 = 12 > 0
    From Ax + By + C = 0: slope −A/B = −3/(−4) = 3/4, x-intercept −C/A = −4,
    y-intercept −C/B = 3. The expression 3x − 4y + 12 is ZERO on the line and
    has one sign on each side, so (1, 1) and the origin (both positive) lie on
    the same side. Common mistake: slope = A/B (the sign is lost). Now you try:
    slope and intercepts of 2x + 5y − 10 = 0. (−2/5; 5 and 2)

D6. Find the acute angle between the lines y = (1/2)x + 1 and y = 3x − 2, and
    between y = 3x + 1 and x + 2y = 4. Find the slopes of the lines that make
    45° with a line of slope 1/2.
    Answer: 45°; tan θ = 7, θ ≈ 81.87°; m = 3 or m = −1/3.
    Teacher explains:
    tan θ = |(3 − 1/2)/(1 + 3 × 1/2)| = |(5/2)/(5/2)| = 1:  θ = 45°
    x + 2y = 4 has m = −1/2:
    tan θ = |(3 − (−1/2))/(1 + 3(−1/2))| = |(7/2)/(−1/2)| = 7
    θ = tan⁻¹ 7 ≈ 81.87°
    |(m − 1/2)/(1 + m/2)| = 1:
       (2m − 1)/(2 + m) = 1   → m = 3
       (2m − 1)/(2 + m) = −1  → 3m = −1,  m = −1/3
    The formula comes from θ = θ₁ − θ₂ and tan(θ₁ − θ₂) = (tan θ₁ − tan θ₂)/(1 +
    tan θ₁ tan θ₂). The absolute value picks the ACUTE angle (the obtuse one is
    180° − θ). When 1 + m₁m₂ = 0 the lines are perpendicular (θ = 90°); when one
    line is vertical use the inclinations directly. Both answers in the last
    part are genuine: two lines through any point make 45° with a given line.
    Common mistake: dropping the absolute value and getting a negative "angle".
    Now you try: the angle between y = x and y = √3x. (15°)

D7. Find the lines through (1, 2) parallel and perpendicular to 3x + 4y = 7.
    Find the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining (1, 3) and (5, 7).
    For which k are (k − 1)x + 2y = 5 and 3x − y = 2 perpendicular?
    Answer: Parallel 3x + 4y − 11 = 0; perpendicular 4x − 3y + 2 = 0; bisector
    x + y − 8 = 0; k = 5/3.
    Teacher explains:
    parallel:       3x + 4y = k;  (1, 2):  k = 3 + 8 = 11
    perpendicular:  4x − 3y = k;  (1, 2):  k = 4 − 6 = −2
    bisector: midpoint (3, 5); slope of segment (7 − 3)/(5 − 1) = 1
              perpendicular slope −1:  y − 5 = −(x − 3),  x + y = 8
    slopes −(k − 1)/2 and 3:  −3(k − 1)/2 = −1,  k − 1 = 2/3,  k = 5/3
    Short cut: a line PARALLEL to Ax + By + C = 0 keeps A and B and only changes
    the constant; a PERPENDICULAR one swaps A and B and changes one sign. The
    perpendicular bisector is the set of points equally far from the two ends:
    check (3, 5): both distances are √8. Common mistake: m₁m₂ = 1 instead of −1.
    Now you try: the line through (−2, 1) perpendicular to y = 2x + 3.
    (x + 2y = 0)

D8. Derive the distance from P(x₁, y₁) to Ax + By + C = 0 in outline, and find
    (a) the distance from (3, −5) to 3x − 4y − 26 = 0 (b) the distance between
    the parallel lines 3x − 4y + 7 = 0 and 6x − 8y − 6 = 0 (c) the points on the
    x-axis at distance 4 from 4x + 3y = 12.
    Answer: (a) 3/5 (b) 2 (c) (−2, 0) and (8, 0).
    Teacher explains: Outline: the line meets the axes at Q(−C/A, 0) and
    R(0, −C/B). The area of triangle PQR is (1/2) × QR × d, and also
    (1/2)|determinant| of the three points (topic 8.22). Equating the two and
    simplifying gives d = |Ax₁ + By₁ + C|/√(A² + B²): substitute the point into
    the left-hand side and divide by the length √(A² + B²).
    (a) |3(3) − 4(−5) − 26|/√(9 + 16) = |9 + 20 − 26|/5 = 3/5
    (b) make A, B equal:  6x − 8y − 6 = 0  →  3x − 4y − 3 = 0
        d = |7 − (−3)|/√(9 + 16) = 10/5 = 2
    (c) (h, 0):  |4h − 12|/5 = 4,  4h − 12 = ±20,  h = 8 or −2
    In (b) the coefficients of x and y must be the SAME before using |C₁ − C₂|;
    otherwise the answer is wrong by a factor. Check (c): (8, 0) gives
    |32 − 12|/5 = 4. Common mistake: forgetting the absolute value, or dividing
    by A² + B². Now you try: the distance of the origin from 5x + 12y = 26. (2)

D9. Find the foot of the perpendicular from (3, 8) to the line x + 3y = 7, and
    the image (reflection) of (3, 8) in the line.
    Answer: Foot (1, 2); image (−1, −4).
    Teacher explains:
    write the line as x + 3y − 7 = 0;  value at (3, 8):
       3 + 24 − 7 = 20,   A² + B² = 1 + 9 = 10
    foot:   (h − 3)/1 = (k − 8)/3 = −20/10 = −2
            h = 1,  k = 2:   foot (1, 2)
    image:  (h − 3)/1 = (k − 8)/3 = −2(20)/10 = −4
            h = −1,  k = −4:  image (−1, −4)
    Why it works: the perpendicular from P goes in the direction (A, B) (the
    NORMAL direction of the line), so the foot is P + t(A, B); putting it into
    the line gives t = −(Ax₁ + By₁ + C)/(A² + B²). The image is twice as far: t
    doubled. Checks: (1, 2) lies on the line (1 + 6 = 7); the foot is the
    midpoint of P and its image: ((3 − 1)/2, (8 − 4)/2) = (1, 2). Common
    mistake: using the direction (B, −A), which runs ALONG the line. Now you
    try: the image of (1, 2) in the line y = x. ((2, 1))

D10. Find the intersection of 2x + y = 5 and x − 3y = −8. Find the line through
     this point and (a) the origin (b) parallel to the x-axis (c) perpendicular
     to 3x + 4y = 1, using the family (2x + y − 5) + λ(x − 3y + 8) = 0.
     Answer: Intersection (1, 3); (a) 3x − y = 0 (b) y = 3 (c) 4x − 3y + 5 = 0.
     Teacher explains:
     solve: x = 3y − 8;  2(3y − 8) + y = 5,  7y = 21,  y = 3,  x = 1
     family:  (2 + λ)x + (1 − 3λ)y + (8λ − 5) = 0
     (a) through O:     8λ − 5 = 0,  λ = 5/8
         (21/8)x − (7/8)y = 0,  i.e. 3x − y = 0
     (b) no x-term:     2 + λ = 0,  λ = −2:  7y − 21 = 0,  y = 3
     (c) slope 4/3:     −(2 + λ)/(1 − 3λ) = 4/3
         −6 − 3λ = 4 − 12λ,  9λ = 10,  λ = 10/9
         (28/9)x − (21/9)y + 35/9 = 0,  i.e. 4x − 3y + 5 = 0
     Every line L₁ + λL₂ = 0 passes through the common point, because there both
     L₁ and L₂ are 0; λ is then chosen to meet the extra condition. The family
     trick avoids finding the intersection at all (useful when it has ugly
     fractions), but here we can check: (1, 3) satisfies 4 − 9 + 5 = 0. Note
     that L₂ = 0 itself is not in the family for any λ, so check it separately.
     Common mistake: substituting the point into only one of L₁, L₂. Now you
     try: the line through the intersection of x + y = 4 and x − y = 2 with
     slope 2. (2x − y − 5 = 0)

D11. Show that the lines x + y = 3, 2x − y = 0 and 3x + 2y = 7 are concurrent.
     Find k so that x + 2y = 5, 3x − y = 1 and kx + y = 3 are concurrent.
     Answer: They meet at (1, 2) (determinant 0); k = 1.
     Teacher explains:
     |1 1 −3; 2 −1 0; 3 2 −7| = 1(7 − 0) − 1(−14 − 0) − 3(4 + 3)
                             = 7 + 14 − 21 = 0   → concurrent
     first two: x + y = 3, 2x = y  →  3x = 3, x = 1, y = 2
     third: 3(1) + 2(2) = 7  ✓
     x + 2y = 5, 3x − y = 1  →  x = 1, y = 2;   k(1) + 2 = 3,  k = 1
     Two methods: find where two lines meet and test the third, or use the
     determinant of the coefficients (write each line as ax + by + c = 0). The
     determinant test needs the lines not to be parallel: three parallel lines
     also give determinant 0 but never meet. Common mistake: writing the
     constants with the wrong sign in the determinant. Now you try: are x −
     y = 0, x + y = 2 and 3x − 2y = 1 concurrent? (yes, at (1, 1))

D12. A ray of light from P(1, 2) strikes the x-axis at A and, after reflection,
     passes through Q(5, 3). Find A. Are P and Q on the same side of the line
     2x + y = 6?
     Answer: A = (13/5, 0); P and Q are on opposite sides of 2x + y = 6.
     Teacher explains: The law of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of
     reflection) means that the reflected ray, extended backwards, passes
     through the IMAGE of P in the mirror. The image of (1, 2) in the x-axis is
     P′(1, −2). So A is where the line P′Q meets the x-axis:
     slope of P′Q = (3 − (−2))/(5 − 1) = 5/4
     y + 2 = (5/4)(x − 1);  y = 0:  2 = (5/4)(x − 1),  x = 1 + 8/5
     A = (13/5, 0)
     side test:  2x + y − 6 at P: 2 + 2 − 6 = −2 < 0
                              at Q: 10 + 3 − 6 = 7 > 0   opposite
     This also gives the SHORTEST path from P to the mirror to Q: PA + AQ =
     P′A + AQ, and a straight line P′Q is the shortest route. Check: slopes of
     PA and AQ are 2/(1 − 13/5) = −5/4 and 3/(5 − 13/5) = 5/4, equal and
     opposite, so the angles with the mirror are equal. Common mistake: joining
     P to Q directly. Now you try: the image of (4, −3) in the y-axis.
     ((−4, −3))

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw a quick sketch for every question (a line with a positive
  slope rises to the right; intercepts are where it crosses the axes); always
  convert to Ax + By + C = 0 before using distance, foot or image formulas;
  check an equation by substituting the given points; for "parallel" keep A and
  B, for "perpendicular" swap them and change one sign. Harder: find the
  equations of the lines through (1, 2) making 60° with x + √3y = 0; show that
  the bisectors of the angles between two lines are (a₁x + b₁y + c₁)/√(a₁² +
  b₁²) = ±(a₂x + b₂y + c₂)/√(a₂² + b₂²) and find the incentre of a triangle with
  them; prove that the medians, altitudes and perpendicular bisectors of a
  triangle are each concurrent (centroid, orthocentre, circumcentre) and that
  these three points are collinear (the Euler line).


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.25 — CONIC SECTIONS: CIRCLE, PARABOLA, ELLIPSE, HYPERBOLA
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A CONIC is the curve cut from a double cone by a plane. Focus-directrix
    definition: a conic is the locus of P with PS = e × PM, where S is the
    FOCUS, PM the distance from P to the DIRECTRIX and e the ECCENTRICITY.
    e = 1: parabola; 0 < e < 1: ellipse; e > 1: hyperbola; a circle is the limit
    e = 0.
  - CIRCLE with centre (h, k) and radius r: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². GENERAL
    FORM x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (−g, −f) and radius
    √(g² + f² − c): a real circle if g² + f² − c > 0, a point circle if it is 0,
    no real locus if it is negative. Divide first if x² and y² have a common
    coefficient other than 1. Circle on the DIAMETER from (x₁, y₁) to (x₂, y₂):
    (x − x₁)(x − x₂) + (y − y₁)(y − y₂) = 0. Circle through three points: put
    each point into the general form and solve for g, f, c.
  - PARABOLA (vertex at the origin, a > 0). y² = 4ax: focus (a, 0), directrix
    x = −a, axis y = 0, opens right. y² = −4ax: focus (−a, 0), directrix x = a,
    opens left. x² = 4ay: focus (0, a), directrix y = −a, opens up. x² = −4ay:
    focus (0, −a), directrix y = a, opens down. In every case the LATUS RECTUM
    (the focal chord perpendicular to the axis) has length 4a; for y² = 4ax its
    ends are (a, ±2a).
  - SHIFTED PARABOLA: (y − k)² = 4a(x − h) has vertex (h, k), focus (h + a, k),
    directrix x = h − a, axis y = k (a may be negative: then it opens left).
    (x − h)² = 4a(y − k): vertex (h, k), focus (h, k + a), directrix y = k − a,
    axis x = h. Complete the square to reach these forms.
  - ELLIPSE x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 with a > b > 0: c² = a² − b², e = c/a < 1, foci
    (±c, 0) = (±ae, 0), vertices (±a, 0), ends of the minor axis (0, ±b),
    directrices x = ±a/e, latus rectum 2b²/a. Major axis 2a, minor axis 2b. For
    every point P on it, PS + PS' = 2a. If the bigger number is under y² the
    major axis is vertical: foci (0, ±c), directrices y = ±a/e.
  - HYPERBOLA x²/a² − y²/b² = 1: c² = a² + b², e = c/a > 1, foci (±c, 0),
    vertices (±a, 0), directrices x = ±a/e, latus rectum 2b²/a, ASYMPTOTES
    y = ±(b/a)x, and |PS − PS'| = 2a. y²/a² − x²/b² = 1 opens up and down: foci
    (0, ±c), asymptotes y = ±(a/b)x. RECTANGULAR hyperbola: a = b, e = √2
    (x² − y² = a², or xy = c² after a 45° turn).
  - SHIFTED ellipse or hyperbola: complete the square to reach (x − h)²/A ±
    (y − k)²/B = 1; the centre is (h, k) and everything else moves with it (foci
    (h ± c, k) for a horizontal major or transverse axis).
  - IDENTIFYING Ax² + Bxy + Cy² + Dx + Ey + F = 0: with no xy term, A = C gives
    a circle, AC = 0 a parabola, AC > 0 an ellipse, AC < 0 a hyperbola; in
    general B² − 4AC < 0 ellipse (or circle), = 0 parabola, > 0 hyperbola.
    Degenerate cases (a point, a pair of lines, no real points) show up when
    completing the square.
  - TANGENT at (x₁, y₁) on the curve: replace x² by xx₁, y² by yy₁, x by
    (x + x₁)/2, y by (y + y₁)/2, xy by (xy₁ + x₁y)/2. So x² + y² = r² gives
    xx₁ + yy₁ = r², y² = 4ax gives yy₁ = 2a(x + x₁), and x²/a² ± y²/b² = 1 gives
    xx₁/a² ± yy₁/b² = 1. The line y = mx + c touches x² + y² = r² when
    c² = r²(1 + m²), y² = 4ax when c = a/m, x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 when
    c² = a²m² + b².

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A garden sprinkler at the point (2, −3) (units: metres) waters every point
    within 5 m of it. Write the equation of the boundary circle in centre-radius
    form and in general form. Is the tap at (5, 1) on the boundary, inside or
    outside? The bench at (6, 1)? The flower bed at (3, −1)?
    Answer: (x − 2)² + (y + 3)² = 25, i.e. x² + y² − 4x + 6y − 12 = 0. The tap
    is ON the circle, the bench is outside and the flower bed is inside.
    Teacher explains: A circle is the set of points at distance r from the
    centre (h, k). By the distance formula √((x − h)² + (y − k)²) = r, and
    squaring gives (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². Here h = 2, k = −3, r = 5:
       (x − 2)² + (y − (−3))² = 5²
       (x − 2)² + (y + 3)² = 25
       x² − 4x + 4 + y² + 6y + 9 = 25
       x² + y² − 4x + 6y − 12 = 0
    To test a point, work out (x − 2)² + (y + 3)² and compare it with 25:
       tap (5, 1):         3² + 4² = 25      = 25, on the circle
       bench (6, 1):       4² + 4² = 32      > 25, outside
       flower bed (3, −1): 1² + 2² = 5       < 25, inside
    In general form the same test is the sign of S = x² + y² − 4x + 6y − 12 at
    the point: S = 0 on, S > 0 outside, S < 0 inside. Common mistake: writing
    (y − 3)² for the centre (2, −3); the sign inside the bracket is the opposite
    of the coordinate. Another: forgetting to square the radius. Now you try:
    the circle with centre (−1, 4) and radius 3, in general form.
    (x² + y² + 2x − 8y + 8 = 0)

D2. Find the centre and radius of x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 12 = 0, first by
    completing the square and then by the formula. What do
    x² + y² + 2x + 4y + 5 = 0 and x² + y² + 2x + 4y + 6 = 0 represent?
    Answer: Centre (3, −2), radius 5. The second is the single point (−1, −2) (a
    point circle); the third has no real points.
    Teacher explains: Group the x terms and the y terms and complete each
    square:
       (x² − 6x + 9) + (y² + 4y + 4) = 12 + 9 + 4
       (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 25
    so the centre is (3, −2) and r = 5. FORMULA: compare with
    x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0: 2g = −6, 2f = 4, c = −12, so g = −3, f = 2. The
    centre is (−g, −f) = (3, −2) and r = √(g² + f² − c) = √(9 + 4 + 12) = √25
    = 5. For x² + y² + 2x + 4y + 5 = 0: g = 1, f = 2, c = 5 and g² + f² − c = 0,
    so the 'circle' has radius 0: only the point (−1, −2) satisfies it, since
    (x + 1)² + (y + 2)² = 0 forces both squares to be 0. With c = 6,
    g² + f² − c = −1 < 0: a sum of squares cannot be negative, so there are no
    real points at all. If the equation is 2x² + 2y² − 8x + 12y − 6 = 0, DIVIDE
    by 2 first: the formula needs the coefficient of x² and y² to be 1. Now you
    try: centre and radius of x² + y² + 8x − 2y + 8 = 0. ((−4, 1), 3)

D3. Find the circle through A(5, 3), B(−1, 3) and C(−3, −1). Also find the
    circle that has the points (1, 2) and (5, 6) as the ends of a diameter.
    Answer: x² + y² − 4x + 2y − 20 = 0 (centre (2, −1), radius 5);
    x² + y² − 6x − 8y + 17 = 0 (centre (3, 4), radius 2√2).
    Teacher explains: Let the circle be x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 and
    substitute each point:
       A(5, 3):    25 + 9 + 10g + 6f + c = 0     10g + 6f + c = −34
       B(−1, 3):   1 + 9 − 2g + 6f + c = 0       −2g + 6f + c = −10
       C(−3, −1):  9 + 1 − 6g − 2f + c = 0       −6g − 2f + c = −10
    Subtract to remove c: (A) − (B) gives 12g = −24, so g = −2; (B) − (C) gives
    4g + 8f = 0, so f = 1. Then c = −10 + 2g − 6f = −10 − 4 − 6 = −20. The
    circle is x² + y² − 4x + 2y − 20 = 0, centre (2, −1), r = √(4 + 1 + 20) = 5.
    CHECK every point: for C, 9 + 1 + 12 − 2 − 20 = 0. Geometric idea: the
    centre is where the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC meet (AB is
    horizontal, so its bisector is x = 2 at once). DIAMETER FORM: P(x, y) is on
    the circle exactly when the angle in the semicircle is 90°, i.e. the slopes
    from P to the two ends multiply to −1: (x − 1)(x − 5) + (y − 2)(y − 6) = 0,
    giving x² + y² − 6x − 8y + 17 = 0; centre = midpoint (3, 4),
    r = √(9 + 16 − 17) = √8. Now you try: the circle through (0, 0), (8, 0) and
    (0, 6). (x² + y² − 8x − 6y = 0; centre (4, 3), r = 5)

D4. A satellite dish is a paraboloid: its cross-section is the parabola y² = 4ax
    with the vertex at the bottom of the dish. The dish is 1.2 m across and
    0.15 m deep. Where must the receiver go? Then write down the focus,
    directrix, axis and latus rectum of y² = 12x.
    Answer: At the focus, 0.6 m from the vertex along the axis. For y² = 12x:
    focus (3, 0), directrix x = −3, axis y = 0, latus rectum 12 with ends
    (3, ±6).
    Teacher explains: Put the vertex of the dish at O with the axis along the
    x-axis. The rim is 0.6 m from the axis (half of 1.2 m) and 0.15 m along it,
    so (0.15, 0.6) is on y² = 4ax: 0.36 = 4a × 0.15 = 0.6a, a = 0.6. The focus
    is (a, 0) = (0.6, 0). Every ray parallel to the axis reflects through the
    focus — this is why dishes, car headlights and solar cookers are parabolic.
    For y² = 12x: 4a = 12, a = 3.
       focus (a, 0) = (3, 0)        directrix x = −a, i.e. x = −3
       axis y = 0 (the x-axis)      vertex (0, 0)
       latus rectum 4a = 12, ends (a, ±2a) = (3, ±6)
    Check with the definition PS = PM for the point (3, 6): PS = 6 (straight up
    from the focus) and PM = 3 − (−3) = 6. Common mistake: taking a = 12 (the
    number in the equation is 4a). Now you try: focus, directrix and latus
    rectum of y² = 20x. ((5, 0), x = −5, 20)

D5. Find the focus, directrix, axis and length of the latus rectum of (a)
    y² = −8x, (b) x² = 16y, (c) x² = −6y. Sketch which way each opens.
    Answer: (a) (−2, 0), x = 2, y = 0, 8; opens left. (b) (0, 4), y = −4, x = 0,
    16; opens up. (c) (0, −3/2), y = 3/2, x = 0, 6; opens down.
    Teacher explains: Match each equation to one of the four standard forms
    (a > 0):
       equation    focus      directrix   axis    opens
       y² = 4ax    (a, 0)     x = −a      y = 0   right
       y² = −4ax   (−a, 0)    x = a       y = 0   left
       x² = 4ay    (0, a)     y = −a      x = 0   up
       x² = −4ay   (0, −a)    y = a       x = 0   down
    The SQUARED variable tells you the axis is the OTHER one: y² goes with the
    x-axis. The sign on the other side tells you the direction. (a) 4a = 8,
    a = 2: focus (−2, 0), directrix x = 2. (b) 4a = 16, a = 4: focus (0, 4),
    directrix y = −4. (c) 4a = 6, a = 3/2: focus (0, −3/2), directrix y = 3/2.
    The focus is always INSIDE the curve and the directrix outside, the same
    distance a from the vertex. The latus rectum is 4a in each case: 8, 16, 6.
    Now you try: x² = −12y. ((0, −3), y = 3, LR 12)

D6. Find the vertex, focus, directrix and axis of y² − 4y − 8x + 28 = 0. Then
    find the parabola with focus (2, 3) and directrix y = −1.
    Answer: Vertex (3, 2), focus (5, 2), directrix x = 1, axis y = 2.
    (x − 2)² = 8(y − 1), i.e. x² − 4x − 8y + 12 = 0.
    Teacher explains: Complete the square in the variable that is squared:
       y² − 4y = 8x − 28
       y² − 4y + 4 = 8x − 24
       (y − 2)² = 8(x − 3)
    Compare with (y − k)² = 4a(x − h): vertex (3, 2) and 4a = 8, a = 2.
    Everything shifts with the vertex: focus (3 + 2, 2) = (5, 2), directrix
    x = 3 − 2 = 1, axis y = 2. For the second part use the DEFINITION: P(x, y)
    is as far from the focus as from the directrix:
    √((x − 2)² + (y − 3)²) = |y + 1|. Square:
    (x − 2)² + y² − 6y + 9 = y² + 2y + 1, so (x − 2)² = 8y − 8 = 8(y − 1).
    Check: the vertex is halfway between focus and directrix, (2, 1), and a = 2
    (focus 2 above the vertex). Common mistake: writing (y − 2)² = 8x − 3
    (forgetting to take out the factor 8). Now you try: vertex and focus of
    x² + 6x − 4y + 1 = 0. (V(−3, −2), F(−3, −1))

D7. For the ellipse x²/25 + y²/9 = 1 find a, b, c, e, the foci, vertices,
    directrices and latus rectum. Prove that PS + PS' = 2a for every point P on
    it, and check at P(0, 3).
    Answer: a = 5, b = 3, c = 4, e = 4/5; foci (±4, 0); vertices (±5, 0);
    directrices x = ±25/4; latus rectum 18/5.
    Teacher explains: a² = 25 and b² = 9 (the bigger number is under x², so the
    major axis is along the x-axis).
       c² = a² − b² = 25 − 9 = 16,  c = 4        e = c/a = 4/5
       foci (±c, 0) = (±4, 0)                  vertices (±5, 0), (0, ±3)
       directrices x = ±a/e = ±25/4            latus rectum 2b²/a = 18/5
    PROOF: for P(x, y) on the ellipse, y² = b²(1 − x²/a²) and b² = a² − c², so
    PS² = (x − c)² + y² = x² − 2cx + c² + b² − b²x²/a² = a² − 2cx + c²x²/a²
    = (a − ex)². Since |x| ≤ a and e < 1, a − ex > 0, so PS = a − ex; in the
    same way PS' = a + ex. Adding: PS + PS' = 2a, whatever P is. At P(0, 3):
    PS = √(16 + 9) = 5 and PS' = 5, sum 10 = 2a. This is the 'pins and string'
    construction: fix a string of length 2a at the two foci and trace. Now you
    try: e and the foci of x²/100 + y²/36 = 1. (e = 4/5, (±8, 0))

D8. An elliptical 'whispering gallery' is 20 m long and 12 m wide. A whisper at
    one focus is heard clearly at the other. How far from the centre are the
    foci? Then find the ellipse with foci (0, ±3) and major axis 10.
    Answer: 8 m from the centre on the long axis. x²/16 + y²/25 = 1.
    Teacher explains: Put the centre at O with the long axis on the x-axis:
    2a = 20, 2b = 12, so a = 10, b = 6 and c = √(a² − b²) = √(100 − 36) = 8. The
    foci are (±8, 0): 8 m either side of the centre (sound from one focus
    reflects off the wall to the other focus, and all paths have the same length
    2a, so the sound arrives together). Second part: the foci are on the y-axis,
    so the major axis is VERTICAL and the form is x²/b² + y²/a² = 1 with a > b.
    2a = 10 gives a = 5, c = 3, b² = a² − c² = 25 − 9 = 16:
       x²/16 + y²/25 = 1        (vertices (0, ±5), e = 3/5)
    Common mistake: writing x²/25 + y²/16 = 1, which has its foci on the x-axis.
    Now you try: the ellipse with vertices (±6, 0) and e = 2/3.
    (x²/36 + y²/20 = 1)

D9. For the hyperbola 9x² − 16y² = 144 find a, b, c, e, the foci, vertices,
    directrices, latus rectum and asymptotes. Check |PS − PS'| = 2a at the end
    of a latus rectum.
    Answer: x²/16 − y²/9 = 1: a = 4, b = 3, c = 5, e = 5/4; foci (±5, 0);
    vertices (±4, 0); directrices x = ±16/5; latus rectum 9/2; asymptotes
    y = ±(3/4)x.
    Teacher explains: Divide by 144 to get 1 on the right: x²/16 − y²/9 = 1, so
    a² = 16, b² = 9. For a HYPERBOLA the squares ADD: c² = a² + b² = 25, c = 5
    and e = c/a = 5/4 > 1.
       foci (±5, 0)       vertices (±4, 0)     directrices x = ±a/e = ±16/5
       latus rectum 2b²/a = 18/4 = 9/2        asymptotes y = ±(b/a)x = ±(3/4)x
    The asymptotes come from x²/16 − y²/9 = 0: for large x the curve hugs these
    lines. At x = 5, y² = 9(25/16 − 1) = 81/16, so P(5, 9/4) is an end of the
    latus rectum. PS = 9/4 (straight up from S(5, 0)) and
    PS' = √(10² + (9/4)²) = √(1681/16) = 41/4. PS' − PS = 32/4 = 8 = 2a. Common
    mistake: c² = a² − b² (that is the ellipse). Now you try: e and the
    asymptotes of x²/4 − y²/5 = 1. (e = 3/2, y = ±(√5/2)x)

D10. Reduce 4x² + 9y² − 16x + 18y − 11 = 0 to standard form and find its centre,
     vertices, foci and eccentricity. Then do the same for
     9x² − 4y² − 36x − 8y − 4 = 0.
     Answer: (x − 2)²/9 + (y + 1)²/4 = 1: centre (2, −1), vertices (5, −1) and
     (−1, −1), foci (2 ± √5, −1), e = √5/3. Second: (x − 2)²/4 − (y + 1)²/9 = 1:
     centre (2, −1), vertices (4, −1) and (0, −1), foci (2 ± √13, −1),
     e = √13/2.
     Teacher explains: Take out the coefficient of x² and of y² BEFORE
     completing the square:
        4(x² − 4x) + 9(y² + 2y) = 11
        4(x² − 4x + 4) + 9(y² + 2y + 1) = 11 + 16 + 9 = 36
        4(x − 2)² + 9(y + 1)² = 36
        (x − 2)²/9 + (y + 1)²/4 = 1
     So the centre is (2, −1), a = 3 (along x), b = 2, c = √(9 − 4) = √5 and
     e = √5/3. Vertices (2 ± 3, −1) = (5, −1), (−1, −1); foci (2 ± √5, −1). Note
     we added 4 × 4 = 16 and 9 × 1 = 9 to the right side, not just 4 and 1: that
     is the most common mistake. Second curve:
     9(x − 2)² − 4(y + 1)² = 4 + 36 − 4 = 36, so (x − 2)²/4 − (y + 1)²/9 = 1,
     a = 2, b = 3, c = √13, e = √13/2. Now you try: x² + 4y² − 2x − 3 = 0.
     ((x − 1)²/4 + y² = 1, centre (1, 0), e = √3/2)

D11. Name the conic: (a) x² + y² − 4x = 5, (b) y² − 4x + 2y = 0, (c)
     4x² + 9y² − 8x = 32, (d) x² − 4y² + 2x = 3, (e) x² − y² = 0. Then find the
     locus of a point whose distance from (3, 0) is half its distance from the
     line x = 12.
     Answer: (a) circle (b) parabola (c) ellipse (d) hyperbola (e) a pair of
     lines y = ±x. The locus is the ellipse x²/36 + y²/27 = 1.
     Teacher explains: With no xy term, look at the coefficients A of x² and C
     of y²:
        A = C (same sign)   circle        A or C = 0    parabola
        AC > 0              ellipse       AC < 0        hyperbola
     (a) A = C = 1: circle ((x − 2)² + y² = 9). (b) no x² term: parabola. (c)
     AC = 36 > 0: ellipse. (d) AC = −4 < 0: hyperbola. (e) looks like a
     hyperbola but factorises: (x − y)(x + y) = 0, two lines — a DEGENERATE
     conic, the plane passing through the vertex of the cone. Always complete
     the square before trusting the name. For the locus use PS = e × PM with
     e = 1/2: √((x − 3)² + y²) = (1/2)|x − 12|; square and multiply by 4:
     4x² − 24x + 36 + 4y² = x² − 24x + 144, so 3x² + 4y² = 108,
     x²/36 + y²/27 = 1. Check: a = 6, e = 1/2, so c = ae = 3 (the focus) and
     a/e = 12 (the directrix). Now you try: name 2x² + 2y² − 3x = 0 and
     3x² − y² = 3. (circle; hyperbola)

D12. Find the tangent to x² + y² = 25 at (3, 4), to y² = 8x at (2, 4) and to
     x²/25 + y²/9 = 1 at (4, 9/5). Find the tangents to x²/16 + y²/9 = 1 with
     slope 1.
     Answer: 3x + 4y = 25; y = x + 2; 4x + 5y = 25; y = x ± 5.
     Teacher explains: Rule for the tangent at a point (x₁, y₁) ON the curve: x²
     → xx₁, y² → yy₁, x → (x + x₁)/2, y → (y + y₁)/2.
        x² + y² = 25 at (3, 4):         3x + 4y = 25
        y² = 8x at (2, 4):              4y = 4(x + 2), so y = x + 2
        x²/25 + y²/9 = 1 at (4, 9/5):   4x/25 + y/5 = 1, so 4x + 5y = 25
     For the circle the tangent is perpendicular to the radius: the radius to
     (3, 4) has slope 4/3 and the tangent slope −3/4. Slope form: the line
     y = mx + c meets x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 in points given by a quadratic in x; it
     TOUCHES when the discriminant is zero, which simplifies to c² = a²m² + b².
     With m = 1: c² = 16 + 9 = 25, c = ±5, giving y = x + 5 and y = x − 5 (an
     ellipse has two parallel tangents of every slope). Check y = x + 2 with
     y² = 8x: (x + 2)² = 8x gives x² − 4x + 4 = 0, (x − 2)² = 0, a double root,
     so it touches at x = 2. Now you try: the tangent to x²/16 − y²/9 = 1 at
     (5, 9/4). (5x − 4y = 16)

M3. Find the circle through the three points; give its centre C and radius r.
    a) (5, 3), (−1, 3), (−3, −1)   b) (0, 0), (8, 0), (0, 6)
    c) (1, 0), (0, 1), (−1, 0)     d) (3, 4), (4, −3), (−5, 0)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw every conic on squared paper and mark the focus, directrix
  and vertices before writing formulas; keep a one-page table of the four
  parabolas and of ellipse versus hyperbola (c² = a² − b² against c² = a² + b²);
  always divide to get 1 on the right side; complete the square slowly, writing
  the numbers added to BOTH sides; check every answer by substituting a vertex
  or a latus-rectum end. Harder: prove the reflection property of the parabola
  (the tangent at P makes equal angles with PS and with the line through P
  parallel to the axis); show that the product of the distances from the foci of
  an ellipse to any tangent is b²; find the locus of the midpoints of focal
  chords of y² = 4ax (y² = 2a(x − a)); show that the tangents at the ends of a
  focal chord of a parabola meet at right angles on the directrix; find the
  equation of the director circle x² + y² = a² + b² of an ellipse.


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.26 — INTRODUCTION TO 3D COORDINATE GEOMETRY
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - Three mutually perpendicular axes OX, OY, OZ through the origin O form a
    RIGHT-HANDED system: curl the fingers of the right hand from OX to OY and
    the thumb points along OZ. They fix three COORDINATE PLANES: the xy-plane
    (z = 0), the yz-plane (x = 0) and the zx-plane (y = 0).
  - A point P(x, y, z): x is its signed distance from the yz-plane, y from the
    zx-plane, z from the xy-plane. Points on the x-axis are (x, 0, 0), on the
    y-axis (0, y, 0), on the z-axis (0, 0, z); points on the xy-plane are
    (x, y, 0), and so on.
  - The three planes cut space into 8 OCTANTS, named by the signs of (x, y, z):
    I (+, +, +), II (−, +, +), III (−, −, +), IV (+, −, +), V (+, +, −), VI
    (−, +, −), VII (−, −, −), VIII (+, −, −). A point with a zero coordinate
    lies on a coordinate plane and is in no octant.
  - FEET and DISTANCES from P(x, y, z): the foot on the xy-plane is (x, y, 0)
    and the distance is |z|; the foot on the x-axis is (x, 0, 0) and the
    distance is √(y² + z²); the distance from O is √(x² + y² + z²).
  - DISTANCE FORMULA: PQ = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)² + (z₂ − z₁)²) (Pythagoras
    twice). Use it to test right-angled, isosceles and equilateral triangles,
    parallelograms, and to find loci (points equidistant from A and B form a
    plane).
  - SECTION FORMULA: the point dividing PQ internally in the ratio m : n is
    ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n), (mz₂ + nz₁)/(m + n)); externally,
    replace n by −n: ((mx₂ − nx₁)/(m − n), ...). MIDPOINT: m = n = 1. To find
    the ratio in which a plane (e.g. the yz-plane) cuts PQ, take the ratio k : 1
    and set that coordinate equal to 0 (k > 0 internal, k < 0 external).
  - CENTROID of the triangle ABC: ((x₁ + x₂ + x₃)/3, (y₁ + y₂ + y₃)/3,
    (z₁ + z₂ + z₃)/3); of a tetrahedron: the average of the four vertices.
    Fourth vertex of the parallelogram ABCD: D = A + C − B (coordinate by
    coordinate).
  - COLLINEAR points: A, B, C lie on one line when one distance is the sum of
    the other two (AB + BC = AC), or when the differences B − A and C − A are
    proportional.
  - DIRECTION COSINES of a line making angles α, β, γ with OX, OY, OZ:
    l = cos α, m = cos β, n = cos γ, and l² + m² + n² = 1. For OP with
    P(x, y, z) and r = OP: l = x/r, m = y/r, n = z/r. DIRECTION RATIOS are any
    numbers a, b, c proportional to l, m, n; the line through (x₁, y₁, z₁) and
    (x₂, y₂, z₂) has direction ratios x₂ − x₁, y₂ − y₁, z₂ − z₁ and
    l = ±a/√(a² + b² + c²) etc.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A drone takes off from the corner O of a school ground. Take x metres east,
    y metres north and z metres up. It hovers at P(12, −4, 3). In which octant
    is it? Where is the point on the ground directly below it, how high is it,
    and how far is it from O? How far is it from the east-west boundary line
    (the x-axis)?
    Answer: Octant IV (+, −, +). The point below it is (12, −4, 0); it is 3 m
    high, 13 m from O, and 5 m from the x-axis.
    Teacher explains: Read the coordinates as three moves from O: 12 m east, 4 m
    SOUTH (y is negative), 3 m up. The signs (+, −, +) give octant IV. The
    ground is the xy-plane (z = 0), so the point straight below is (12, −4, 0)
    and the height is |z| = 3 m.
       OP² = 12² + (−4)² + 3² = 144 + 16 + 9 = 169,  OP = 13 m
    Why: O to the foot F(12, −4, 0) is a flat distance √(144 + 16) = √160; then
    F to P is 3 m straight up, at right angles, so OP² = 160 + 9 = 169. The
    distance from the x-axis: the foot on the x-axis is (12, 0, 0), and from
    there P is 4 m across and 3 m up: √(4² + 3²) = 5 m. In general the distance
    of (x, y, z) from the x-axis is √(y² + z²) — leave out the coordinate of
    THAT axis. Common mistake: answering |x| = 12 (that is the distance from the
    yz-plane). Now you try: P(−6, 2, −3): octant, distance from O, distance from
    the z-axis. (VI; 7; 2√10)

D2. The three coordinate planes cut space into eight octants. List the sign
    pattern of every octant, and place (−3, 1, −2), (2, −5, −1), (−4, −4, 9) and
    (0, 3, −4).
    Answer: VI, VIII, III; (0, 3, −4) lies on the yz-plane (in no octant).
    Teacher explains: The numbering goes round the top four first (z > 0),
    anticlockwise from the +x, +y quarter, then the same four underneath
    (z < 0):
       octant    I   II   III   IV     V   VI   VII   VIII
       x         +   −    −     +      +   −    −     +
       y         +   +    −     −      +   +    −     −
       z         +   +    +     +      −   −    −     −
    (−3, 1, −2) is (−, +, −): VI. (2, −5, −1) is (+, −, −): VIII. (−4, −4, 9) is
    (−, −, +): III. (0, 3, −4) has x = 0, so it is ON the yz-plane, the wall
    between octants; a point with two zero coordinates is on an axis, e.g.
    (0, 0, −6) is on the z-axis. Only the SIGNS matter, not the sizes:
    (−0.001, 500, −2) is in VI as well. Common mistake: numbering V to VIII in a
    different order — memorise that V to VIII are I to IV with z made negative.
    Now you try: (5, −1, 7), (−2, −2, −2), (4, 0, 0). (IV; VII; on the x-axis)

D3. Derive the distance formula in three dimensions and find the distance
    between A(1, −2, 3) and B(4, 2, 15).
    Answer: AB = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)² + (z₂ − z₁)²); here AB = 13.
    Teacher explains: Draw the box (cuboid) with A and B at opposite corners and
    edges parallel to the axes. Its edges are |x₂ − x₁|, |y₂ − y₁| and
    |z₂ − z₁|. Let C be the corner level with A and directly below B. In the
    bottom face, Pythagoras gives AC² = (x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)². CB is vertical,
    so the angle ACB is 90° and AB² = AC² + CB²
    = (x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)² + (z₂ − z₁)².
       AB² = (4 − 1)² + (2 − (−2))² + (15 − 3)²
           = 9 + 16 + 144 = 169,   AB = 13
    Setting A = O gives OP = √(x² + y² + z²). Squares make the order of
    subtraction irrelevant, but watch double negatives: 2 − (−2) = 4. Common
    mistake: forgetting one of the three squares. Now you try: the distance
    between (2, −1, 3) and (−2, 1, 3). (2√5)

D4. Show that A(0, 7, 10), B(−1, 6, 6) and C(−4, 9, 6) are the vertices of a
    right-angled isosceles triangle. Where is the right angle?
    Answer: AB = BC = 3√2 and AB² + BC² = CA² = 36; the right angle is at B.
    Teacher explains: Work with SQUARED lengths to avoid roots:
       AB² = (−1 − 0)² + (6 − 7)² + (6 − 10)² = 1 + 1 + 16 = 18
       BC² = (−4 + 1)² + (9 − 6)² + (6 − 6)² = 9 + 9 + 0 = 18
       CA² = (0 + 4)² + (7 − 9)² + (10 − 6)² = 16 + 4 + 16 = 36
    AB = BC, so the triangle is isosceles; 18 + 18 = 36 means AB² + BC² = CA²,
    so by the converse of Pythagoras the angle opposite CA, the angle at B, is
    90°. Test checklist for three points: all three sides equal (equilateral),
    two equal (isosceles), the biggest square equal to the sum of the other two
    (right-angled), the biggest length equal to the sum of the other two
    (collinear — not a triangle at all). Now you try: show that (1, 0, 0),
    (0, 1, 0) and (0, 0, 1) form an equilateral triangle. (each side √2)

D5. Find the locus of points equidistant from A(1, 2, 3) and B(3, 2, −1). Then
    find the point on the y-axis equidistant from (3, 1, 2) and (5, 5, 2).
    Answer: The plane x = 2z (x − 2z = 0). The point (0, 5, 0).
    Teacher explains: Let P(x, y, z) with PA² = PB²:
       (x − 1)² + (y − 2)² + (z − 3)² = (x − 3)² + (y − 2)² + (z + 1)²
       −2x + 1 − 6z + 9 = −6x + 9 + 2z + 1
       4x − 8z = 0,   so x = 2z
    The x², y², z² terms cancel, so the locus is a PLANE (the perpendicular
    bisector plane of AB: in 3D the 'perpendicular bisector' is a plane, not a
    line). Check the midpoint (2, 2, 1): x = 2 = 2 × 1. For the second part a
    point on the y-axis is (0, y, 0):
       9 + (y − 1)² + 4 = 25 + (y − 5)² + 4
       y² − 2y + 14 = y² − 10y + 54,  8y = 40,  y = 5
    Check: the distances are √(9 + 16 + 4) = √29 and √(25 + 0 + 4) = √29. Common
    mistake: writing a general point on the y-axis as (y, 0, 0). Now you try:
    the point on the x-axis equidistant from (1, 2, 3) and (3, 4, 1).
    ((3, 0, 0))

D6. Find the point R that divides the join of P(2, −3, 4) and Q(8, 0, 10) in the
    ratio 1 : 2 internally. Explain the section formula.
    Answer: R(4, −2, 6).
    Teacher explains: R divides PQ in the ratio m : n when PR : RQ = m : n. Drop
    perpendiculars from P, R, Q to the xy-plane: the feet lie on a line and the
    similar-triangle argument of 2D works for each coordinate separately, so
       R = ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n), (mz₂ + nz₁)/(m + n))
    With m = 1 (next to Q) and n = 2 (next to P):
       x = (1 × 8 + 2 × 2)/3 = 12/3 = 4
       y = (1 × 0 + 2 × (−3))/3 = −6/3 = −2
       z = (1 × 10 + 2 × 4)/3 = 18/3 = 6
    Check: R is one third of the way from P to Q: P + (1/3)(Q − P) = (2 + 2,
    −3 + 1, 4 + 2) = (4, −2, 6). Memory trick: CROSS multiply — m goes with the
    FAR point Q. Common mistake: (mx₁ + nx₂)/(m + n), which gives the point 1/3
    of the way from Q instead. Now you try: the point dividing (1, 2, 3) and
    (4, 5, 6) in the ratio 2 : 1. ((3, 4, 5))

D7. Find the point dividing P(1, −2, 3) and Q(3, 4, −5) externally in the ratio
    2 : 3. In what ratio does the yz-plane divide the join of A(−2, 4, 7) and
    B(3, −5, 8), and at which point?
    Answer: (−3, −14, 19). The yz-plane divides AB internally in the ratio 2 : 3
    at (0, 2/5, 37/5).
    Teacher explains: EXTERNAL division: the point is outside the segment, and
    the formula is the internal one with n replaced by −n:
       x = (2 × 3 − 3 × 1)/(2 − 3) = 3/(−1) = −3
       y = (2 × 4 − 3 × (−2))/(2 − 3) = 14/(−1) = −14
       z = (2 × (−5) − 3 × 3)/(2 − 3) = −19/(−1) = 19
    For the ratio, let the point divide AB in k : 1. Its x-coordinate is
    (3k − 2)/(k + 1), and on the yz-plane x = 0, so 3k − 2 = 0 and k = 2/3. The
    ratio is 2/3 : 1 = 2 : 3, positive, so INTERNAL. The point:
       y = (2 × (−5) + 3 × 4)/5 = 2/5,   z = (2 × 8 + 3 × 7)/5 = 37/5
    A negative k would mean external division (the plane misses the segment).
    Tip: A and B have x-coordinates of opposite signs, so the yz-plane must
    cross between them. Now you try: the ratio in which the xy-plane divides the
    join of (1, 2, −3) and (4, −1, 6). (1 : 2 internally, at (2, 1, 0))

D8. A(1, 2, 3), B(−2, 0, 5) and C(4, −5, 1) are three vertices of a
    parallelogram ABCD. Find the centroid of the triangle ABC and the fourth
    vertex D. If the centroid of a triangle is (1, 1, 1) and two vertices are
    (3, −5, 7) and (−1, 7, −6), find the third vertex.
    Answer: Centroid (1, −1, 3); D(7, −3, −1); third vertex (1, 1, 2).
    Teacher explains: The centroid is the average of the three vertices:
       G = ((1 − 2 + 4)/3, (2 + 0 − 5)/3, (3 + 5 + 1)/3) = (1, −1, 3)
    In a parallelogram the diagonals bisect each other, so the midpoints of AC
    and BD are the same: A + C = B + D, so D = A + C − B:
       D = (1 + 4 + 2, 2 − 5 − 0, 3 + 1 − 5) = (7, −3, −1)
    Check: the midpoint of AC is (2.5, −1.5, 2) and of BD is ((−2 + 7)/2,
    (0 − 3)/2, (5 − 1)/2) = (2.5, −1.5, 2). For the third vertex:
    A + B + C = 3G, so C = 3G − A − B = (3 − 3 + 1, 3 + 5 − 7,
    3 − 7 + 6) = (1, 1, 2). Common mistake: D = A + B − C (that is the
    parallelogram ABDC in a different order). Now you try: the centroid of the
    tetrahedron with vertices (0, 0, 0), (4, 0, 0), (0, 8, 0) and (0, 0, 12).
    ((1, 2, 3))

D9. Show that A(2, 3, 4), B(−1, −2, 1) and C(5, 8, 7) are collinear. Which point
    is between the other two?
    Answer: BA = AC = √43 and BC = 2√43 = BA + AC, so they are collinear, with A
    in the middle (A is the midpoint of BC).
    Teacher explains: Method 1 (distances):
       AB² = 9 + 25 + 9 = 43        AB = √43
       AC² = 9 + 25 + 9 = 43        AC = √43
       BC² = 36 + 100 + 36 = 172    BC = √172 = 2√43
    BC = AB + AC exactly, so the 'triangle' is flat: the three points are on one
    line, A between B and C. Method 2 (proportional differences):
    B − A = (−3, −5, −3) and C − A = (3, 5, 3) = −(B − A); the same direction
    (reversed), so the points are collinear, and the factor −1 says A is halfway
    between. Method 2 avoids square roots and is quicker. Common mistake with
    method 1: rounded decimals (6.56 + 6.56 and 13.11) only suggest equality;
    keep the surds exact. Now you try: are (1, 2, 3), (3, 5, 7) and (5, 8, 10)
    collinear? (no: the differences (2, 3, 4) and (4, 6, 7) are not
    proportional)

D10. Find the direction cosines of OP, where P is (2, −3, 6), and the angles OP
     makes with the axes. Prove that l² + m² + n² = 1 for every line.
     Answer: l = 2/7, m = −3/7, n = 6/7; α ≈ 73.4°, β ≈ 115.4°, γ ≈ 31.0°.
     Teacher explains: Let r = OP = √(4 + 9 + 36) = 7. Drop a perpendicular from
     P to the x-axis; it meets it at (2, 0, 0), and in the right triangle
     formed, cos α = x/r. Likewise cos β = y/r and cos γ = z/r:
        l = 2/7,   m = −3/7,   n = 6/7
        α = arccos(2/7) ≈ 73.4°,  β = arccos(−3/7) ≈ 115.4°,
        γ = arccos(6/7) ≈ 31.0°
     A negative cosine means an obtuse angle (P is on the −y side). PROOF:
     l² + m² + n² = (x² + y² + z²)/r² = r²/r² = 1. So the three angles cannot be
     chosen freely: once two are known, cos²γ = 1 − cos²α − cos²β. Check here:
     4/49 + 9/49 + 36/49 = 49/49 = 1. Common mistake: using the angles with the
     coordinate PLANES instead of the axes. Now you try: the direction cosines
     of OP for P(1, 2, 2). ((1/3, 2/3, 2/3))

D11. Find the direction ratios and direction cosines of the line through
     A(1, 2, −1) and B(3, −4, 2). Can a line make angles 45°, 60°, 60° with the
     axes? 45°, 45°, 45°? Find the direction cosines of a line equally inclined
     to the three axes.
     Answer: Direction ratios 2, −6, 3; direction cosines ±(2/7, −6/7, 3/7).
     Yes; no; ±(1/√3, 1/√3, 1/√3).
     Teacher explains: Direction ratios of AB are the differences
     B − A = (2, −6, 3) (any multiple, e.g. −4, 12, −6, is also a set of
     direction ratios). To get direction cosines divide by
     √(a² + b² + c²) = √(4 + 36 + 9) = 7. A line has TWO directions, so the
     signs can all be reversed: ±(2/7, −6/7, 3/7). For the angles test
     l² + m² + n² = 1:
        45°, 60°, 60°:  1/2 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 1     possible
        45°, 45°, 45°:  1/2 + 1/2 + 1/2 = 3/2   impossible
     Equally inclined: l = m = n, so 3l² = 1 and l = ±1/√3 = ±√3/3 (each angle
     about 54.7°, the direction of the diagonal of a cube). Direction ratios are
     NOT unique, direction cosines are unique up to sign. Common mistake:
     calling 2, −6, 3 the direction cosines (their squares add to 49, not 1).
     Now you try: a line makes 90° with the x-axis and 60° with the y-axis; find
     its angle with the z-axis. (30° or 150°)

D12. A classroom is a cuboid 5 m long, 4 m wide and 3 m high. Put one corner of
     the floor at O with the edges along the axes. Find the length of the
     longest rod that fits in the room, the centre of the room, and how far the
     far top corner is from the vertical edge through O and from the floor.
     Answer: The longest rod is the space diagonal 5√2 ≈ 7.07 m; the centre is
     (2.5, 2, 1.5); the far top corner (5, 4, 3) is √41 ≈ 6.40 m from the
     vertical edge (the z-axis) and 3 m from the floor.
     Teacher explains: The far top corner is P(5, 4, 3). The longest straight
     rod joins O and P:
        OP = √(5² + 4² + 3²) = √50 = 5√2 ≈ 7.07 m
     (longer than the floor diagonal √41 ≈ 6.40 m). The centre of the room is
     the midpoint of OP: (2.5, 2, 1.5). The vertical edge through O is the
     z-axis, so the distance from it ignores z:
     √(x² + y²) = √(25 + 16) = √41 ≈ 6.40 m; the distance from the floor (the
     xy-plane) is |z| = 3 m. Summary for a point (x, y, z):
        from the x-axis √(y² + z²)     from the yz-plane |x|
        from the y-axis √(z² + x²)     from the zx-plane |y|
        from the z-axis √(x² + y²)     from the xy-plane |z|
     Common mistake: mixing up 'distance from the x-axis' with 'distance from
     the yz-plane'. Now you try: for P(3, 4, 12), find OP and the distance from
     each axis. (13; 4√10, 3√17, 5)

M5. Classify: equilateral, isosceles, right-angled, right-angled isosceles,
    scalene (not right-angled), or collinear (no triangle).
    a) (0, 7, 10), (−1, 6, 6), (−4, 9, 6)
    b) (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (0, 0, 1)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: build a model: the corner of a room (two walls and the floor) is
  the three coordinate planes; stand pencils along the edges as axes and point
  to (2, 3, 1) with a finger; draw the cuboid with the two points as opposite
  corners before using the distance formula; say 'leave out that axis's
  coordinate' for the distance from an axis; keep a sign table of the octants on
  the desk. Harder: prove that the centroid of a tetrahedron divides each line
  joining a vertex to the centroid of the opposite face in the ratio 3 : 1; show
  that the points (0, 0, 0), (a, 0, 0), (0, a, 0), (0, 0, a) and (a, a, a) are
  not all at the same distance from any point (or find the sphere through the
  first four); find the equation of the sphere with centre (1, −2, 3) and radius
  4; show that the angle θ between lines with direction cosines (l₁, m₁, n₁) and
  (l₂, m₂, n₂) satisfies cos θ = l₁l₂ + m₁m₂ + n₁n₂.


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.27 — POLAR COORDINATES AND PARAMETRIC EQUATIONS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - POLAR COORDINATES (r, θ): r is the distance from the POLE O and θ the angle
    from the INITIAL LINE (the positive x-axis), anticlockwise positive, in
    RADIANS. Convention in this topic: the PRINCIPAL form has r > 0 and
    −π < θ ≤ π; the pole is r = 0 with any θ.
  - CONVERSION: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ; r = √(x² + y²), and θ is the angle
    with cos θ = x/r and sin θ = y/r. tan θ = y/x alone is NOT enough: draw the
    point and choose the quadrant ((−1, −1) has θ = −3π/4, not π/4).
    Non-standard angles are written with arctan: (3, 4) is (5, arctan(4/3)).
  - One point has infinitely many polar names: (r, θ) = (r, θ + 2nπ) = (−r,
    θ + π). A NEGATIVE r means: face the direction θ and walk backwards.
  - CONVERTING EQUATIONS: polar to Cartesian — replace r cos θ by x, r sin θ by
    y and r² by x² + y² (multiply by r first if needed: r = 2a cos θ gives
    r² = 2ar cos θ, i.e. x² + y² = 2ax, a circle of centre (a, 0) and radius a).
    Cartesian to polar — substitute x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ and simplify.
  - STANDARD POLAR CURVES: r = a (circle, centre O); θ = α (line through O);
    r cos θ = a (line x = a); r = 2a cos θ, r = 2a sin θ (circles through O);
    r = a(1 ± cos θ), a(1 ± sin θ) (CARDIOIDS); r = a cos nθ or a sin nθ (ROSES:
    n petals if n is odd, 2n petals if n is even); r = a + b cos θ (LIMAÇON,
    inner loop when b > a); r = aθ (Archimedean SPIRAL); r² = a² cos 2θ
    (LEMNISCATE); r = l/(1 + e cos θ) (a conic with focus O and eccentricity e).
  - DISTANCE between (r₁, θ₁) and (r₂, θ₂): √(r₁² + r₂² − 2r₁r₂ cos(θ₁ − θ₂))
    (cosine rule); area of the triangle they make with the pole:
    (1/2)r₁r₂|sin(θ₁ − θ₂)|.
  - PARAMETRIC EQUATIONS x = f(t), y = g(t): as the parameter t runs, the point
    traces the curve in a definite direction (t is often time). Standard forms:
    line x = x₁ + at, y = y₁ + bt (direction (a, b)); circle x = h + r cos t,
    y = k + r sin t; ellipse x = a cos t, y = b sin t; parabola x = at²,
    y = 2at; hyperbola x = a sec t, y = b tan t; rectangular hyperbola x = ct,
    y = c/t.
  - ELIMINATING THE PARAMETER: make t the subject of one equation and
    substitute, or use an identity (cos²t + sin²t = 1, sec²t − tan²t = 1,
    cos 2t = 1 − 2sin²t). Always state RESTRICTIONS: x = t², y = t² gives only
    the half-line y = x, x ≥ 0. (Derivatives of parametric curves come in topic
    8.36.)

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A radar at O reports a ship at distance 10 km in the direction θ = π/3 from
    due east (the initial line), and a fishing boat at (4, 3π/4). Find their
    Cartesian coordinates (x east, y north, in km).
    Answer: Ship (5, 5√3) ≈ (5, 8.66); boat (−2√2, 2√2) ≈ (−2.83, 2.83).
    Teacher explains: Drop a perpendicular from the point to the initial line:
    the right triangle has hypotenuse r and angle θ at O, so
       x = r cos θ,     y = r sin θ
       ship: x = 10 cos(π/3) = 10 × 1/2 = 5,  y = 10 sin(π/3) = 5√3
       boat: x = 4 cos(3π/4) = −2√2,          y = 4 sin(3π/4) = 2√2
    The formulas work in every quadrant because cos and sin carry the signs:
    3π/4 is in the second quadrant, so x < 0 and y > 0. Check with Pythagoras:
    5² + (5√3)² = 25 + 75 = 100 = 10². Radar screens, the positions of fielders
    round a cricket pitch and the rotation of a ceiling fan are naturally polar.
    Common mistake: using degrees mode on the calculator with a radian angle.
    Now you try: (6, −π/6) and (2, π). ((3√3, −3); (−2, 0))

D2. Convert to polar form (r > 0, −π < θ ≤ π): (−2, 2), (−√3, −1), (3, −3√3),
    (0, −5) and (3, 4).
    Answer: (2√2, 3π/4), (2, −5π/6), (6, −π/3), (5, −π/2), (5, arctan(4/3)) with
    arctan(4/3) ≈ 0.927.
    Teacher explains: Step 1: r = √(x² + y²). Step 2: find the reference angle
    from tan φ = |y/x|. Step 3: place it in the correct quadrant:
       point       r     reference   quadrant   θ
       (−2, 2)     2√2   π/4         II         π − π/4 = 3π/4
       (−√3, −1)   2     π/6         III        −π + π/6 = −5π/6
       (3, −3√3)   6     π/3         IV         −π/3
       (0, −5)     5     on an axis  −y-axis    −π/2
       (3, 4)      5     arctan(4/3) I          arctan(4/3) ≈ 0.927
    Common mistake: a calculator gives arctan(−1/−√3) = arctan(1/√3) = π/6 for
    (−√3, −1), which is the first-quadrant point (√3, 1). Always sketch. Check
    (−√3, −1): 2 cos(−5π/6) = −√3 and 2 sin(−5π/6) = −1. Now you try: (−1, √3)
    and (4, −4). ((2, 2π/3); (4√2, −π/4))

D3. Show that (3, π/6), (3, 13π/6), (3, −11π/6), (−3, 7π/6) and (−3, −5π/6) are
    all the same point. Why is the pole special?
    Answer: All give (x, y) = (3√3/2, 3/2).
    Teacher explains: Adding 2π to θ turns a full circle and lands in the same
    place, so (3, π/6) = (3, 13π/6) = (3, −11π/6). A NEGATIVE r means: face
    along θ and walk backwards r units, which is the same as walking forwards in
    the direction θ + π (or θ − π). So (−3, 7π/6) is the point at distance 3 in
    the direction 7π/6 − π = π/6, the same point again, and so is (−3, −5π/6).
    Check one with the formulas: x = −3 cos(7π/6) = −3 × (−√3/2) = 3√3/2 and
    y = −3 sin(7π/6) = −3 × (−1/2) = 3/2. The pole O is r = 0 and ANY θ, so
    (0, 1) and (0, 2) in polar form are both the origin. This is why we fix the
    PRINCIPAL form r > 0, −π < θ ≤ π for answers. Now you try: write (2, −3π/4)
    with θ in [0, 2π) and also with a negative r. ((2, 5π/4); (−2, π/4))

D4. Convert to Cartesian form and describe: r = 4, θ = π/4, r = 6 cos θ,
    r sin θ = 3 and r = 4 sin θ.
    Answer: x² + y² = 16 (circle, centre O, radius 4); y = x (line through O);
    x² + y² = 6x, i.e. (x − 3)² + y² = 9 (circle, centre (3, 0), radius 3);
    y = 3 (horizontal line); x² + y² = 4y, i.e. x² + (y − 2)² = 4 (circle,
    centre (0, 2), radius 2).
    Teacher explains: The dictionary is x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, r² = x² + y².
    r = 4: square, r² = 16, so x² + y² = 16. θ = π/4: tan θ = y/x = 1 so y = x
    (negative r gives the other half of the line). r = 6 cos θ: multiply by r to
    make recognisable pieces:
       r² = 6r cos θ   →   x² + y² = 6x   →   (x − 3)² + y² = 9
    a circle through the pole with centre (3, 0). r sin θ = 3 is just y = 3.
    r = 4 sin θ: r² = 4r sin θ, x² + y² = 4y, x² + (y − 2)² = 4. In general
    r = 2a cos θ and r = 2a sin θ are circles of radius |a| through O, centred
    on the x-axis and y-axis. Common mistake: turning r = 6 cos θ into
    √(x² + y²) = 6x/√(x² + y²) and giving up; multiply by r first. Now you try:
    r = −8 cos θ and r cos θ = −2. (x² + y² + 8x = 0, circle centre (−4, 0),
    radius 4; x = −2)

D5. Convert to polar form: x² + y² = 9, x = 5, x² + y² − 4x = 0, y = x²,
    x² − y² = 1, xy = 4 and x + y = 2.
    Answer: r = 3; r = 5 sec θ; r = 4 cos θ; r = tan θ sec θ; r² cos 2θ = 1;
    r² sin 2θ = 8; r(cos θ + sin θ) = 2.
    Teacher explains: Substitute x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ and simplify with
    identities:
       x² + y² = 9:      r² = 9, r = 3
       x = 5:            r cos θ = 5, r = 5 sec θ
       x² + y² = 4x:     r² = 4r cos θ, r = 4 cos θ (r = 0 is included)
       y = x²:           r sin θ = r² cos²θ, r = sin θ/cos²θ = tan θ sec θ
       x² − y² = 1:      r²(cos²θ − sin²θ) = 1, r² cos 2θ = 1
       xy = 4:           r² sin θ cos θ = 4, r² sin 2θ = 8
       x + y = 2:        r(cos θ + sin θ) = 2
    When we divide by r we lose the pole, so check whether r = 0 is on the curve
    (for x² + y² = 4x it is, and r = 4 cos θ gives r = 0 at θ = π/2, so nothing
    is lost). Polar form is best for curves with circular symmetry about O;
    Cartesian form is best for lines not through O. Now you try: polar form of
    x² + y² + 6y = 0 and of y = −2. (r = −6 sin θ; r = −2 cosec θ)

D6. Sketch the cardioid r = 2(1 + cos θ) from a table of values, and describe
    its shape and symmetry.
    Answer: r = 4, 3, 2, 1, 0 at θ = 0, π/3, π/2, 2π/3, π; a heart-shaped curve,
    symmetric about the initial line, with a cusp at the pole.
    Teacher explains: Make a table (cos is known exactly at these angles):
       θ            0     π/3    π/2    2π/3    π
       cos θ        1     1/2    0      −1/2    −1
       r            4     3      2      1       0
    Plot each point at distance r in direction θ: (4, 0), (3, π/3), (2, π/2),
    (1, 2π/3) and the pole at θ = π. SYMMETRY TEST: replacing θ by −θ does not
    change cos θ, so the lower half is the mirror image of the upper half in the
    initial line. The curve passes through the pole with a sharp point (a cusp)
    when θ = π. Its widest point is (4, 0), and it crosses the y-axis at
    (0, ±2). Cardioid means 'heart-shaped'; the cross-section of a coffee cup
    caustic and the pickup pattern of some microphones are cardioids. Now you
    try: the values of r = 3(1 − sin θ) at θ = 0, π/2, π and −π/2. (3, 0, 3, 6)

D7. How many petals do the roses r = 3 cos 2θ and r = 3 sin 3θ have, and how
    long is each petal? What do r = 1 + 2 cos θ, r = θ (θ ≥ 0) and r² = 4 cos 2θ
    look like?
    Answer: r = 3 cos 2θ: 4 petals; r = 3 sin 3θ: 3 petals; each petal has
    length 3. r = 1 + 2 cos θ is a limaçon with an inner loop; r = θ an
    Archimedean spiral; r² = 4 cos 2θ a lemniscate (figure of eight) with loops
    of length 2.
    Teacher explains: For r = a cos nθ or a sin nθ each petal reaches the
    maximum r = |a|. RULE: n odd gives n petals, n even gives 2n petals. Why:
    when n is odd, the negative values of r retrace the same petals (the curve
    repeats after θ = π); when n is even they draw new petals. For r = 3 cos 2θ
    the petals point along θ = 0, π/2, π, 3π/2 (where cos 2θ = ±1). For
    r = 3 sin 3θ they point along θ = π/6, 5π/6 and 3π/2. LIMAÇON
    r = a + b cos θ: b > a gives an inner loop (r becomes negative for some θ;
    here when cos θ < −1/2), b = a is the cardioid, b < a a dimpled or oval
    shape. SPIRAL r = θ: r grows steadily, so each turn is 2π further out.
    LEMNISCATE r² = 4 cos 2θ exists only where cos 2θ ≥ 0, that is
    −π/4 ≤ θ ≤ π/4 and 3π/4 ≤ θ ≤ 5π/4, giving two loops of length 2 through O.
    Now you try: petals of r = 2 sin 4θ and of r = cos 5θ. (8; 5)

D8. Find the distance between A(3, π/6) and B(4, 2π/3), and the area of the
    triangle OAB. Then find the distance between (2, π/3) and (4, 0).
    Answer: AB = 5, area 6; the second distance is 2√3.
    Teacher explains: In triangle OAB, OA = r₁, OB = r₂ and the angle
    AOB = |θ₁ − θ₂|, so the COSINE RULE gives
       AB² = r₁² + r₂² − 2r₁r₂ cos(θ₁ − θ₂)
       area = (1/2) r₁ r₂ |sin(θ₁ − θ₂)|
    Here θ₂ − θ₁ = 2π/3 − π/6 = π/2, so cos = 0 and sin = 1:
       AB² = 9 + 16 − 0 = 25, AB = 5;   area = (1/2)(3)(4)(1) = 6
    Second: AB² = 4 + 16 − 2(2)(4) cos(π/3) = 20 − 8 = 12, AB = 2√3. Check by
    converting: (2, π/3) = (1, √3) and (4, 0) = (4, 0), distance
    √(9 + 3) = √12 = 2√3. The formula saves converting and is exact. Common
    mistake: subtracting r values or forgetting the factor 2 in the cosine rule.
    Now you try: the distance between (1, π/3) and (2, −π/3). (√7)

D9. An ant walks in a straight line so that at time t seconds it is at
    x = 1 + 3t, y = 2 − 4t (in cm). Where is it at t = 0 and t = 2? How fast
    does it move? Find the Cartesian equation of its path and where it crosses
    the x-axis.
    Answer: (1, 2) and (7, −6); 5 cm/s; 4x + 3y = 10; it crosses the x-axis at
    (5/2, 0) when t = 1/2.
    Teacher explains: Substitute t: at t = 0, (1, 2); at t = 2, (1 + 6,
    2 − 8) = (7, −6). Each second x grows by 3 and y falls by 4, so the
    direction vector is (3, −4) and the speed is √(3² + 4²) = 5 cm/s. Eliminate
    t:
       t = (x − 1)/3   →   y = 2 − 4(x − 1)/3   →   3y = 6 − 4x + 4
       4x + 3y = 10
    On the x-axis y = 0: 2 − 4t = 0, t = 1/2, x = 1 + 3/2 = 5/2. In general
    x = x₁ + at, y = y₁ + bt is the line through (x₁, y₁) with direction (a, b);
    the parametric form also tells us WHEN the ant is where, which the Cartesian
    equation does not. Now you try: the line through (2, −1) and (5, 3) in
    parametric form, and its Cartesian equation. (x = 2 + 3t, y = −1 + 4t;
    4x − 3y = 11)

D10. Eliminate the parameter: (a) x = 2 + 5 cos t, y = −1 + 5 sin t; (b)
     x = 4 cos t, y = 3 sin t. Which way does each point move as t increases,
     and what part is traced for 0 ≤ t ≤ π?
     Answer: (a) (x − 2)² + (y + 1)² = 25, a circle; (b) x²/16 + y²/9 = 1, an
     ellipse. Both are traced anticlockwise; for 0 ≤ t ≤ π we get the upper half
     of each.
     Teacher explains: Isolate cos t and sin t and use cos²t + sin²t = 1:
        (a) cos t = (x − 2)/5, sin t = (y + 1)/5
            (x − 2)²/25 + (y + 1)²/25 = 1, (x − 2)² + (y + 1)² = 25
        (b) cos t = x/4, sin t = y/3,  x²/16 + y²/9 = 1
     At t = 0 the points are (7, −1) and (4, 0); at t = π/2 they are (2, 4) and
     (0, 3): moving anticlockwise. For 0 ≤ t ≤ π, sin t ≥ 0, so y ≥ −1 in (a)
     and y ≥ 0 in (b): the upper halves. For the ellipse, t is NOT the polar
     angle of the point (it is the 'eccentric angle'): at t = π/4 the point is
     (2√2, 3√2/2), whose polar angle is arctan(3/4), not π/4. Common mistake:
     squaring and adding without dividing first, getting x² + y² = ... for (b).
     Now you try: eliminate t from x = 1 + 2 cos t, y = 3 + 2 sin t.
     ((x − 1)² + (y − 3)² = 4)

D11. A batter hits a cricket ball from ground level. With g = 10 m/s² its
     position after t seconds is x = 15t, y = 20t − 5t² (metres). Find the
     Cartesian equation of the path, when and where it lands, and its greatest
     height. Also show that x = at², y = 2at is the parabola y² = 4ax.
     Answer: y = (4/3)x − x²/45; it lands after 4 s, 60 m away; greatest height
     20 m (at t = 2 s, x = 30 m).
     Teacher explains: From x = 15t, t = x/15. Substitute:
        y = 20(x/15) − 5(x/15)² = (4/3)x − x²/45
     a parabola opening downwards, as a thrown ball should. It lands when y = 0:
     5t(4 − t) = 0, so t = 0 (the hit) or t = 4 s, and then x = 15 × 4 = 60 m.
     By symmetry the top is halfway in time, t = 2: y = 40 − 20 = 20 m at
     x = 30 m. Check with the Cartesian form: (4/3)(30) − 900/45 = 40 − 20 = 20.
     For the standard parabola: from y = 2at, t = y/(2a), so
     x = a × y²/(4a²) = y²/(4a), that is y² = 4ax. Every point (at², 2at) is on
     y² = 4ax, which is why this is the standard parametric form (used in topic
     8.25). Common mistake: squaring (x/15) as x²/15. Now you try: eliminate t
     from x = 3t², y = 6t. (y² = 12x)

D12. Eliminate the parameter, stating any restriction: (a) x = t², y = t²; (b)
     x = cos 2t, y = sin t; (c) x = sec t, y = tan t; (d) x = t + 1/t,
     y = t − 1/t.
     Answer: (a) y = x with x ≥ 0 (a half-line); (b) x = 1 − 2y², −1 ≤ y ≤ 1;
     (c) x² − y² = 1; (d) x² − y² = 4.
     Teacher explains: (a) y = x, but x = t² can never be negative, so only the
     half-line from O is traced (twice: t and −t give the same point). (b)
     Use cos 2t = 1 − 2sin²t: x = 1 − 2y². Since y = sin t, −1 ≤ y ≤ 1, so only
     the arc of this parabola from (−1, −1) to (−1, 1) is traced. (c)
     sec²t − tan²t = 1 gives x² − y² = 1, a rectangular hyperbola. (d) Square
     and subtract:
        x² = t² + 2 + 1/t²,   y² = t² − 2 + 1/t²,   x² − y² = 4
     Also |x| = |t + 1/t| ≥ 2, which the hyperbola x² − y² = 4 satisfies
     automatically. A famous parametric curve with no simple Cartesian equation
     is the CYCLOID x = a(t − sin t), y = a(1 − cos t): the path of a mark on a
     rolling bicycle wheel of radius a. Now you try: eliminate t from x = cos t,
     y = cos 2t. (y = 2x² − 1, −1 ≤ x ≤ 1)

M10. Eliminate the parameter t.
     a) x = 3 cos t, y = 3 sin t
     b) x = 2 + 5 cos t, y = −1 + 5 sin t
     c) x = 4 cos t, y = 3 sin t
     d) x = 5 sin t, y = 5 cos t
     e) x = 1 + 2 cos t, y = 3 + 2 sin t
     f) x = 2 cos t, y = 7 sin t
     g) x = −3 + 4 cos t, y = 2 + 3 sin t
     h) x = cos t, y = 2 sin t
     i) x = 6 cos t, y = −6 sin t
     j) x = 3 + cos t, y = sin t
     k) x = 5 cos t, y = 4 sin t
     l) x = √2 cos t, y = √3 sin t
     Answers:
       a) x² + y² = 9

       c) x²/16 + y²/9 = 1

       e) (x − 1)² + (y − 3)² = 4
       f) x²/4 + y²/49 = 1
       g) (x + 3)²/16 + (y − 2)²/9 = 1

M11. Eliminate the parameter t and state any restriction on x or y.
     a) x = 3t², y = 6t
     b) x = t², y = 2t
     c) x = 2t, y = t²
     d) x = 4 sec t, y = 3 tan t
     e) x = 2t, y = 2/t

     j) x = t², y = t³
     k) x = 1 + t, y = 1 − t²
     l) x = sec t, y = tan t
     m) x = 15t, y = 20t − 5t²
     n) x = t/(1 + t), y = 1/(1 + t)

       k) y = 2x − x²
       l) x² − y² = 1
       m) 45y = 60x − x²

       o) 2x + y = 7, x ≥ 2

M12. Write parametric equations (one possible answer), or find the parameter of
     the point.

     b) parametric form of (x − 2)² + (y + 1)² = 9

     k) t for (0, −3) on x = 3 cos t, y = 3 sin t (−π < t ≤ π)
     l) t for (7, −6) on x = 1 + 3t, y = 2 − 4t
