TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: use polar graph paper (circles and rays) and plot points by
  turning then walking; ALWAYS sketch the point before choosing θ; keep the
  conversion dictionary x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ, r² = x² + y² on the board; for
  parametric curves make a table of t, x, y and plot the points in order with
  arrows; check every elimination by substituting one value of t. Harder: find
  the area enclosed by the cardioid r = a(1 + cos θ) using (1/2)∫r² dθ (3πa²/2);
  show that the polar equation of a conic with focus at O and directrix x = −d
  is r = ed/(1 − e cos θ); find the Cartesian equation of the curve traced by
  the midpoint of a ladder sliding down a wall (a quarter circle); investigate
  the curves x = sin at, y = sin bt (Lissajous figures) with a graphing tool.


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.28 — VECTORS: ADDITION, SCALAR MULTIPLE, COMPONENTS, POSITION VECTORS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A VECTOR has magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, force); a
    SCALAR has magnitude only. AB is the vector from A to B, |AB| its length.
    Special vectors: the ZERO vector 0; a UNIT vector (length 1); EQUAL vectors
    (same length and direction, anywhere in space); the NEGATIVE −a; COLLINEAR
    (parallel) vectors, which lie along parallel lines.
  - COMPONENTS: with unit vectors i, j, k along the x-, y- and z-axes,
    a = a₁i + a₂j + a₃k, also written (a₁, a₂, a₃). |a| = √(a₁² + a₂² + a₃²) and
    the UNIT VECTOR in the direction of a is â = a/|a|.
  - ADDITION: TRIANGLE law AB + BC = AC; PARALLELOGRAM law (the sum of two
    vectors from one point is the diagonal); POLYGON law AB + BC + CD = AD. In
    components, add (or subtract) coordinate by coordinate. Addition is
    commutative and associative; a + 0 = a and a + (−a) = 0; |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|
    (triangle inequality).
  - SCALAR MULTIPLE: λa has length |λ||a|, the same direction as a if λ > 0 and
    the opposite direction if λ < 0. a and b (b ≠ 0) are PARALLEL exactly when
    a = λb, i.e. when their components are proportional: a₁/b₁ = a₂/b₂ = a₃/b₃.
  - POSITION VECTORS: the position vector of P(x, y, z) is OP = xi + yj + zk.
    For any two points AB = b − a ('end minus start') and |AB| is the distance
    AB.
  - SECTION FORMULA: R dividing AB internally in the ratio m : n has
    r = (mb + na)/(m + n); externally r = (mb − na)/(m − n). Midpoint (a + b)/2;
    centroid of a triangle (a + b + c)/3.
  - COLLINEAR POINTS: A, B, C are collinear exactly when AB = λAC for some
    scalar λ (the vectors are parallel AND share the point A).
  - DIRECTION COSINES of a are the components of â: (a₁/|a|, a₂/|a|, a₃/|a|)
    = (cos α, cos β, cos γ), the angles with the axes; a₁, a₂, a₃ are its
    direction ratios. The vector of length k in the direction of a is kâ.
  - LINEAR COMBINATIONS: any vector in the plane is xa + yb for two non-parallel
    vectors a, b; any vector in space is xa + yb + zc for three non-coplanar a,
    b, c. Find x, y, z by equating components.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A delivery drone starts at the point (1, 1, 0) (metres) and flies with the
    constant velocity v = 6i + 2j + 3k m/s. What is its speed? Where is it after
    5 s? How far has it travelled?
    Answer: Speed 7 m/s; it reaches (31, 11, 15); it has travelled 35 m.
    Teacher explains: The components say how fast the drone moves in each axis
    direction: 6 m/s east, 2 m/s north and 3 m/s up. The SPEED is the magnitude
    of the velocity:
       |v| = √(6² + 2² + 3²) = √(36 + 4 + 9) = √49 = 7 m/s
    In 5 s the displacement is 5v = 30i + 10j + 15k, so the new position vector
    is
       (i + j) + (30i + 10j + 15k) = 31i + 11j + 15k,  the point (31, 11, 15)
    The distance travelled is |5v| = 5 × 7 = 35 m (for a straight flight at
    constant velocity, distance = speed × time). Velocity is a vector; speed is
    its magnitude, a scalar. Common mistake: adding the components,
    6 + 2 + 3 = 11 m/s, as the speed. Now you try: the speed for
    v = 2i − 3j + 6k km/h, and the position after 2 h from the origin. (7 km/h;
    (4, −6, 12))

D2. Find |a| and the unit vector â for a = 2i − 3j + 6k. Check that â has length
    1.
    Answer: |a| = 7; â = (2/7)i − (3/7)j + (6/7)k.
    Teacher explains: Magnitude by Pythagoras in three dimensions:
       |a| = √(2² + (−3)² + 6²) = √(4 + 9 + 36) = √49 = 7
    Divide every component by the length:
       â = a/|a| = (2/7)i − (3/7)j + (6/7)k
       check: 4/49 + 9/49 + 36/49 = 49/49 = 1
    â points the same way as a but has length 1; its components are also the
    DIRECTION COSINES of a (the cosines of the angles with the axes). Only the
    zero vector has no unit vector. Common mistake: dividing by 2 − 3 + 6 = 5.
    Now you try: the unit vector along i + j + k. ((1/√3)(i + j + k), i.e.
    (√3/3)(i + j + k))

D3. a = i + 2j − 3k and b = 2i − j + 5k. Find a + b, a − b and |a + b|, and
    check the triangle inequality. Explain the triangle, parallelogram and
    polygon laws.
    Answer: a + b = 3i + j + 2k, a − b = −i + 3j − 8k, |a + b| = √14 ≈ 3.74,
    which is less than |a| + |b| = √14 + √30 ≈ 9.22.
    Teacher explains: Add and subtract component by component:
       a + b = (1 + 2)i + (2 − 1)j + (−3 + 5)k = 3i + j + 2k
       a − b = (1 − 2)i + (2 + 1)j + (−3 − 5)k = −i + 3j − 8k
       |a + b| = √(9 + 1 + 4) = √14;  |a| = √14, |b| = √30
    TRIANGLE LAW: place b with its tail at the head of a; a + b goes from the
    first tail to the last head (AB + BC = AC). PARALLELOGRAM LAW: with a and b
    from the same point, a + b is the diagonal (and a − b is the other diagonal,
    from the head of b to the head of a). POLYGON LAW: AB + BC + CD + DE = AE,
    and a closed polygon gives 0. The triangle inequality |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|
    says one side of a triangle is at most the sum of the other two; equality
    only when a and b point the same way. Now you try: |a − b| for these
    vectors. (√74)

D4. Show that a = 2i − 3j + k and b = −6i + 9j − 3k are parallel. Find λ so that
    λi + 6j − 4k is parallel to 3i − 9j + 6k. Are 2i + 4j − k and 3i + 6j + 2k
    parallel?
    Answer: b = −3a (parallel, opposite directions). λ = −2. No.
    Teacher explains: Two vectors are parallel when one is a scalar multiple of
    the other, i.e. the ratios of corresponding components are equal:
       −6/2 = 9/(−3) = −3/1 = −3    so b = −3a
    The negative factor means b points the opposite way, and |b| = 3|a|. For λ:
       λ/3 = 6/(−9) = −4/6,  all equal to −2/3,  so λ = −2
    (check the two known ratios agree first: 6/(−9) = −2/3 = −4/6). For the last
    pair: 3/2 = 6/4 = 1.5 but 2/(−1) = −2, so they are NOT parallel. With a zero
    component, compare directly: 2i + 0j is parallel to 5i + 0j but not to
    5i + j. Common mistake: checking only two of the three ratios. Now you try:
    find p and q if 2i + pj + 3k is parallel to 4i − 6j + qk. (p = −3, q = 6)

D5. A is (1, 2, −3) and B is (4, −2, 9). Find AB, the distance AB and the unit
    vector in the direction of AB.
    Answer: AB = 3i − 4j + 12k, |AB| = 13, unit vector
    (3/13)i − (4/13)j + (12/13)k.
    Teacher explains: Let a = i + 2j − 3k and b = 4i − 2j + 9k be the position
    vectors. Going from A to B by way of O: AB = AO + OB = −a + b, so
       AB = b − a = (4 − 1)i + (−2 − 2)j + (9 + 3)k = 3i − 4j + 12k
       |AB| = √(9 + 16 + 144) = √169 = 13
       unit vector = AB/13 = (3/13)i − (4/13)j + (12/13)k
    'End minus start' gives AB; start minus end gives BA = −AB. The length of AB
    is the distance formula of topic 8.26 in vector dress. Common mistake:
    AB = a − b. Now you try: P(2, 0, −1), Q(0, 3, 5): find PQ and |PQ|.
    (−2i + 3j + 6k; 7)

D6. Prove the section formula r = (mb + na)/(m + n). Use it to find the point
    dividing A(1, 2, 3) and B(7, −4, 9) internally in the ratio 1 : 2, and the
    point dividing them externally in the ratio 2 : 1.
    Answer: Internal: 3i + 5k, the point (3, 0, 5). External: 13i − 10j + 15k,
    the point (13, −10, 15).
    Teacher explains: R lies on AB with AR : RB = m : n, so n AR = m RB:
       n(r − a) = m(b − r)   →   nr + mr = mb + na   →   r = (mb + na)/(m + n)
    Internal 1 : 2 (m = 1, n = 2):
       r = (b + 2a)/3 = ((7 + 2)i + (−4 + 4)j + (9 + 6)k)/3 = 3i + 0j + 5k
    External 2 : 1: R is outside, AR : RB = 2 : 1 with R beyond B, and the
    formula becomes r = (mb − na)/(m − n):
       r = (2b − a)/1 = (14 − 1)i + (−8 − 2)j + (18 − 3)k = 13i − 10j + 15k
    Check the external point: B is the midpoint of A and R: ((1 + 13)/2,
    (2 − 10)/2, (3 + 15)/2) = (7, −4, 9). Correct, since AR = 2RB means RB = AB.
    Common mistake: attaching m to a. Now you try: the point dividing a = 2i − j
    and b = 5i + 8j in the ratio 2 : 1 internally. (4i + 5j)

D7. Prove that the medians of a triangle meet at the point with position vector
    g = (a + b + c)/3, and find it for A(1, 2, 3), B(3, −1, 4) and C(−1, 5, 5).
    Answer: g = i + 2j + 4k, the point (1, 2, 4).
    Teacher explains: The midpoint D of BC has position vector d = (b + c)/2.
    The point dividing the median AD in the ratio 2 : 1 is
       (2d + 1a)/3 = (b + c + a)/3
    This expression is SYMMETRIC in a, b, c, so the point dividing BE in the
    ratio 2 : 1 (E the midpoint of CA) and the one dividing CF in 2 : 1 give the
    same vector: all three medians pass through G, with AG : GD = 2 : 1. For the
    triangle:
       g = ((1 + 3 − 1)i + (2 − 1 + 5)j + (3 + 4 + 5)k)/3
         = (3i + 6j + 12k)/3 = i + 2j + 4k
    Check with the median from A: d = (b + c)/2 = i + 2j + 4.5k, and (2d + a)/3
    = ((2 + 1)i + (4 + 2)j + (9 + 3)k)/3 = i + 2j + 4k. The vector proof is
    shorter than any coordinate-geometry proof. Common mistake: dividing by 2
    instead of 3. Now you try: the centroid of A(2, 0, 0), B(0, 3, 0),
    C(0, 0, 6). ((2/3)i + j + 2k)

D8. Show that A(1, −2, −8), B(5, 0, −2) and C(11, 3, 7) are collinear and find
    the ratio in which B divides AC. Find k if P(1, 2, 3), Q(2, k, 5) and
    R(4, 8, 9) are collinear.
    Answer: BC = (3/2)AB, so they are collinear and B divides AC in the ratio
    2 : 3. k = 4.
    Teacher explains: Compute two vectors that share a point:
       AB = 4i + 2j + 6k,   BC = 6i + 3j + 9k = (3/2)(4i + 2j + 6k)
    AB and BC are parallel and share B, so A, B, C lie on one line. Since
    BC = (3/2)AB, AB : BC = 2 : 3 (both in the same direction, so B is between A
    and C). For k: PQ = i + (k − 2)j + 2k and PR = 3i + 6j + 6k. Collinear means
    PR = λPQ: from i and k components λ = 3 and λ = 3, so 6 = 3(k − 2) and
    k = 4. Check: PQ = i + 2j + 2k and PR = 3PQ. Note the clash of letters: k is
    both the unknown and the unit vector, so write the components in brackets
    when in doubt: PQ = (1, k − 2, 2). Common mistake: showing AB ∥ BC is not
    enough for LINES in general; here the shared point B makes it work. Now you
    try: are (0, 1, 2), (1, 3, 5) and (3, 7, 11) collinear? (yes: the second
    difference is twice the first)

D9. Find the direction cosines of a = i − j + √2 k and the angles it makes with
    the axes. Find the vectors of magnitude 2√3 that are equally inclined to the
    three axes.
    Answer: 1/2, −1/2, √2/2; angles 60°, 120°, 45°. ±(2i + 2j + 2k).
    Teacher explains: |a| = √(1 + 1 + 2) = 2, so â = (1/2)i − (1/2)j + (√2/2)k,
    and its components are cos α, cos β, cos γ:
       cos α = 1/2 → α = 60°;  cos β = −1/2 → β = 120°;  cos γ = √2/2 → γ = 45°
    Check: 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/2 = 1. Equally inclined
    means cos α = cos β = cos γ = c, so 3c² = 1, c = ±1/√3. The vector of length
    2√3 is 2√3 × (±1/√3)(i + j + k) = ±(2i + 2j + 2k); check
    |2i + 2j + 2k| = √12 = 2√3. Common mistake: taking direction cosines of a
    vector as its components before dividing by |a|. Now you try: the angles
    that 3i + 4k makes with the axes. (cos α = 3/5, β = 90°, cos γ = 4/5;
    α ≈ 53.1°, γ ≈ 36.9°)

D10. Find the vector of magnitude 9 in the direction of a = 2i − j + 2k, the
     vector of magnitude 5 opposite to 3i + 4k, and the vector of magnitude 14
     along a + b, where b = i + 3j + 4k.
     Answer: 6i − 3j + 6k; −3i − 4k; 6i + 4j + 12k.
     Teacher explains: The recipe is (required length) × (unit vector in the
     required direction):
        |a| = √(4 + 1 + 4) = 3,   â = (2i − j + 2k)/3,   9â = 6i − 3j + 6k
        |3i + 4k| = 5,  opposite unit vector −(3i + 4k)/5,  5 × it = −3i − 4k
        a + b = 3i + 2j + 6k,  |a + b| = √(9 + 4 + 36) = 7
        14 × (3i + 2j + 6k)/7 = 6i + 4j + 12k
     Check the first: |6i − 3j + 6k| = √(36 + 9 + 36) = √81 = 9. 'Opposite to'
     means multiply by −1. Common mistake: multiplying a itself by 9 (giving
     length 27). Now you try: the vector of length 4 in the direction of i − j.
     (2√2 i − 2√2 j)

D11. Use vectors to prove the midpoint theorem: the segment joining the
     midpoints of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half
     as long. Then show that the midpoints of the sides of ANY quadrilateral
     form a parallelogram.
     Answer: If M, N are the midpoints of AB, AC then MN = (1/2)BC. For a
     quadrilateral ABCD with midpoints P, Q, R, S of AB, BC, CD, DA:
     PQ = SR = (1/2)AC.
     Teacher explains: Use position vectors a, b, c. The midpoints are
     m = (a + b)/2 and n = (a + c)/2, so
        MN = n − m = (a + c)/2 − (a + b)/2 = (c − b)/2 = (1/2)BC
     A vector equal to (1/2)BC is parallel to BC and has half its length: that
     is the whole theorem in one line. Quadrilateral (Varignon's theorem):
        PQ = (b + c)/2 − (a + b)/2 = (c − a)/2 = (1/2)AC
        SR = (c + d)/2 − (d + a)/2 = (c − a)/2 = (1/2)AC
     PQ = SR, so one pair of opposite sides of PQRS is equal and parallel, and
     PQRS is a parallelogram, even if ABCD is not convex or not flat! Check with
     numbers: A(0, 0, 0), B(4, 0, 0), C(6, 4, 2), D(0, 2, 4): P(2, 0, 0),
     Q(5, 2, 1), R(3, 3, 3), S(0, 1, 2); PQ = (3, 2, 1) = SR. Now you try: show
     that the diagonals of a parallelogram OACB (OA = a, OB = b) bisect each
     other. (both midpoints are (a + b)/2)

D12. Three ropes pull on a hot-air balloon with forces F₁ = 2i + 3j − k,
     F₂ = −i + 2j + 4k and F₃ = 3i − j + 2k (in kN). Find the resultant force
     and its size. What single extra force would keep the balloon in
     equilibrium?
     Answer: R = 4i + 4j + 5k, |R| = √57 ≈ 7.55 kN; the extra force is
     −4i − 4j − 5k.
     Teacher explains: Forces are vectors, so they add component by component
     (polygon law):
        i:  2 − 1 + 3 = 4
        j:  3 + 2 − 1 = 4
        k: −1 + 4 + 2 = 5          R = 4i + 4j + 5k
        |R| = √(16 + 16 + 25) = √57 ≈ 7.55 kN
     EQUILIBRIUM means the total force is the zero vector, so the extra force
     must be −R = −4i − 4j − 5k, the same size √57 kN in the opposite direction.
     Its direction cosines are −4/√57, −4/√57, −5/√57. Adding magnitudes
     (|F₁| + |F₂| + |F₃| = √14 + √21 + √14 ≈ 12.07) gives a wrong answer unless
     all the forces point the same way. Now you try: forces 3i − j and
     −i + 4j + 2k; the force needed for equilibrium. (−2i − 3j − 2k)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Write AB in the form xi + yj + zk.
    a) A(1, 2, −3), B(4, −2, 9)   b) A(0, 0, 0), B(2, −3, 6)
    c) A(2, 0, −1), B(0, 3, 5)    d) A(1, 1, 1), B(1, 1, 1)
    e) A(3, −1, 2), B(5, 4, −2)   f) A(−2, −4, 1), B(−2, 0, 1)
    g) A(5, 6, 7), B(1, 2, 3)     h) A(0, 3, 0), B(4, 0, 0)
    i) A(1, −2, 4), B(−3, 2, 0)   j) A(1/2, 1, 0), B(3/2, −1, 2)
    k) A(2, 2, 2), B(0, 0, 0)     l) A(−1, 5, −6), B(3, 5, 6)
    m) A(7, −3, 0), B(7, −3, 8)   n) A(4, 1, −1), B(1, 5, 11)
    o) A(0, −2, 5), B(6, 1, 3)    p) A(−3, 3, −3), B(3, −3, 3)
    q) A(10, 0, 0), B(0, 10, 0)   r) A(2, −5, 1), B(8, −3, −2)
    s) A(1, 0, 1), B(0, 1, 0)     t) A(6, 6, −2), B(4, 3, 4)
    Answers: a) 3i − 4j + 12k   b) 2i − 3j + 6k   c) −2i + 3j + 6k   d) 0
             e) 2i + 5j − 4k   f) 4j   g) −4i − 4j − 4k   h) 4i − 3j
             i) −4i + 4j − 4k   j) i − 2j + 2k   k) −2i − 2j − 2k   l) 4i + 12k
             m) 8k   n) −3i + 4j + 12k   o) 6i + 3j − 2k   p) 6i − 6j + 6k
             q) −10i + 10j   r) 6i + 2j − 3k   s) −i + j − k   t) −2i − 3j + 6k

M2. Find the magnitude.

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw arrows for every sum and difference before computing; say
  'end minus start' for AB; line up components in columns (i, j, k) when adding;
  always divide by the MAGNITUDE (not the sum of components) for a unit vector;
  check parallel vectors by writing all three ratios. Harder: prove with vectors
  that the midpoints of the sides of any quadrilateral form a parallelogram
  (Varignon); show that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other;
  prove that if a, b, c are position vectors of A, B, C and αa + βb + γc = 0
  with α + β + γ = 0 (not all zero) then A, B, C are collinear; find the point
  where the line joining a vertex of a tetrahedron to the centroid of the
  opposite face meets the other such lines.


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.29 — DOT PRODUCT AND CROSS PRODUCT; SCALAR TRIPLE PRODUCT
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - DOT (scalar) PRODUCT: a·b = |a||b| cos θ, where θ (0 ≤ θ ≤ π) is the angle
    between a and b. In components a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ — a NUMBER.
    i·i = j·j = k·k = 1 and i·j = j·k = k·i = 0. It is commutative and
    distributive, and a·a = |a|².
  - ANGLE: cos θ = a·b/(|a||b|). a·b > 0: acute; a·b = 0 (a, b ≠ 0):
    PERPENDICULAR; a·b < 0: obtuse. Work done by a force F over a displacement d
    is W = F·d.
  - PROJECTION of a on b: scalar projection a·b/|b| (the signed length of the
    'shadow'); vector projection (a·b/|b|²)b. Identities: |a ± b|² = |a|² ±
    2a·b + |b|² and (a + b)·(a − b) = |a|² − |b|².
  - CROSS (vector) PRODUCT: a × b = |a||b| sin θ n̂, where n̂ is the unit vector
    perpendicular to a and b given by the RIGHT-HAND RULE. In components it is
    the determinant with rows (i, j, k), (a₁, a₂, a₃), (b₁, b₂, b₃): a × b
    = (a₂b₃ − a₃b₂)i − (a₁b₃ − a₃b₁)j + (a₁b₂ − a₂b₁)k.
  - i × j = k, j × k = i, k × i = j (cyclic), and reversing the order changes
    the sign: b × a = −(a × b). a × a = 0; a × b = 0 exactly when a and b are
    parallel (or one is 0). The cross product is distributive but NOT
    commutative and NOT associative.
  - |a × b| = area of the PARALLELOGRAM with sides a, b; the triangle ABC has
    area (1/2)|AB × AC|. Unit vectors perpendicular to both a and b:
    ±(a × b)/|a × b|. Lagrange's identity: |a × b|² + (a·b)² = |a|²|b|². Moment
    (torque) of a force F acting at r about O: τ = r × F.
  - SCALAR TRIPLE PRODUCT [a b c] = a·(b × c) = the 3 × 3 determinant of the
    components of a, b, c (rows in that order). It is unchanged by a CYCLIC
    change, [a b c] = [b c a] = [c a b], and changes sign when two vectors are
    swapped; the dot and cross can be interchanged: a·(b × c) = (a × b)·c.
  - |[a b c]| = VOLUME of the parallelepiped with edges a, b, c; the tetrahedron
    ABCD has volume (1/6)|[AB AC AD]|. a, b, c are COPLANAR exactly when
    [a b c] = 0; four points A, B, C, D are coplanar exactly when
    [AB AC AD] = 0.
  - VECTOR TRIPLE PRODUCT: a × (b × c) = (a·c)b − (a·b)c, which in general
    differs from (a × b) × c = (a·c)b − (b·c)a.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A constant force F = 3i + 4j − 2k newtons pushes a crate from A(1, 1, 0) to
    B(3, 2, 1) (metres). How much work does it do? Explain why i·i = 1 and
    i·j = 0.
    Answer: 8 J.
    Teacher explains: Work = force · displacement. The displacement is
    d = AB = 2i + j + k, so
       W = F·d = 3 × 2 + 4 × 1 + (−2) × 1 = 6 + 4 − 2 = 8 J
    Only the part of the force ALONG the motion does work; a force at right
    angles to the motion does none, and then F·d = 0. From a·b = |a||b| cos θ:
    i·i = 1 × 1 × cos 0 = 1 and i·j = 1 × 1 × cos 90° = 0. Expanding
    (a₁i + a₂j + a₃k)·(b₁i + b₂j + b₃k), the nine products shrink to three,
    because the six mixed ones are 0: a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃. The answer is a
    SCALAR (a number), not a vector. Common mistake: writing F·d = 6i + 4j − 2k.
    Now you try: the work done by F = 2i − j + 3k N over d = 4i + 2j − k m.
    (3 J)

D2. Find the angle between a = i + j and b = j + k, and between a = 2i − j + 2k
    and c = i + 2j − 2k.
    Answer: 60°; arccos(−4/9) ≈ 116.4° (obtuse).
    Teacher explains: cos θ = a·b/(|a||b|):
       a·b = 0 + 1 + 0 = 1,  |a| = |b| = √2,  cos θ = 1/2,  θ = 60°
       a·c = 2 − 2 − 4 = −4,  |a| = |c| = 3,  cos θ = −4/9
       θ = arccos(−4/9) ≈ 116.4°
    A negative dot product always means an obtuse angle. Geometric check of the
    first answer: the points O, P(1, 1, 0) and Q(0, 1, 1) form a triangle with
    OP = OQ = √2 and PQ = √(1 + 0 + 1) = √2, an equilateral triangle, so the
    angle at O is 60°. The angle between two vectors is always between 0 and π
    (0° and 180°). Common mistake: forgetting to divide by BOTH magnitudes. Now
    you try: the angle between i + 2j + 2k and 2i + j − 2k. (arccos(0) = 90°)

D3. Find λ so that 2i + λj + k and i − 2j + 3k are perpendicular. Prove with the
    dot product that the diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular.
    Answer: λ = 5/2.
    Teacher explains: Perpendicular non-zero vectors have dot product 0:
       (2i + λj + k)·(i − 2j + 3k) = 2 − 2λ + 3 = 5 − 2λ = 0,  λ = 5/2
    Check: 2 − 5 + 3 = 0. RHOMBUS: let the sides from one vertex be a and b with
    |a| = |b|. The diagonals are a + b and a − b, and
       (a + b)·(a − b) = a·a − a·b + b·a − b·b = |a|² − |b|² = 0
    because a·b = b·a. So the diagonals are perpendicular (in fact this works
    exactly when |a| = |b|: a parallelogram has perpendicular diagonals only if
    it is a rhombus). Similarly (a + b)·(a + b) = |a|² + 2a·b + |b|² gives the
    cosine rule. Common mistake: setting the CROSS product to zero (that tests
    parallel, not perpendicular). Now you try: λ if λi + 2j − k ⊥ 3i − j + 4k.
    (λ = 2)

D4. Find the scalar and vector projections of a = 2i + 3j + 2k on
    b = i + 2j + k. What does the scalar projection mean geometrically?
    Answer: Scalar projection 10/√6 = 5√6/3 ≈ 4.08; vector projection
    (5/3)(i + 2j + k).
    Teacher explains: The projection is the 'shadow' of a on the line of b when
    light falls perpendicular to b. Its signed length is |a| cos θ = a·b/|b|:
       a·b = 2 + 6 + 2 = 10,   |b| = √6
       scalar projection = 10/√6 = 10√6/6 = 5√6/3
       vector projection = (a·b/|b|²) b = (10/6)(i + 2j + k)
                         = (5/3)i + (10/3)j + (5/3)k
    Check: the remainder a − (5/3)(i + 2j + k) = (1/3)i − (1/3)j + (1/3)k is
    perpendicular to b: 1/3 − 2/3 + 1/3 = 0. So a splits into a part along b and
    a part perpendicular to b, which is how forces are resolved on a slope. A
    negative scalar projection means the shadow points opposite to b. Common
    mistake: dividing by |a| instead of |b|. Now you try: the scalar projection
    of i − j + k on 2i + j + 2k. (1)

D5. |a| = 3, |b| = 4 and the angle between them is 60°. Find a·b, |a + b| and
    |a − b|. Show that if |a + b| = |a − b| then a ⊥ b.
    Answer: a·b = 6, |a + b| = √37 ≈ 6.08, |a − b| = √13 ≈ 3.61.
    Teacher explains: a·b = |a||b| cos θ = 3 × 4 × 1/2 = 6. Magnitudes of sums
    are found by SQUARING (dot a vector with itself):
       |a + b|² = |a|² + 2a·b + |b|² = 9 + 12 + 16 = 37
       |a − b|² = |a|² − 2a·b + |b|² = 9 − 12 + 16 = 13
    (This is the cosine rule in vector form: |a − b| is the third side of the
    triangle with sides 3, 4 and angle 60°.) If |a + b| = |a − b|, subtracting
    the two expansions gives 4a·b = 0, so a·b = 0 and a ⊥ b: a parallelogram
    with equal diagonals is a rectangle. Common mistake: |a + b| = |a| + |b| = 7
    (only true when θ = 0). Now you try: |a| = 2, |b| = 5, a·b = −3; find
    |2a + b|. (√29)

D6. Find a × b for a = 2i + j − k and b = i − j + 2k. Check that it is
    perpendicular to both a and b, and find b × a.
    Answer: a × b = i − 5j − 3k; b × a = −i + 5j + 3k.
    Teacher explains: Write the determinant with i, j, k on top and expand along
    the first row:
               | i   j   k |
       a × b = | 2   1  −1 |
               | 1  −1   2 |
       = (1 × 2 − (−1)(−1))i − (2 × 2 − (−1) × 1)j + (2 × (−1) − 1 × 1)k
       = (2 − 1)i − (4 + 1)j + (−2 − 1)k = i − 5j − 3k
    Watch the MINUS sign on the j term. Checks: a·(a × b) = 2 − 5 + 3 = 0 and
    b·(a × b) = 1 + 5 − 6 = 0, so a × b is perpendicular to both, as it must be.
    Swapping the rows of a determinant changes its sign, so b × a = −(a × b).
    The cyclic table i × j = k, j × k = i, k × i = j (and j × i = −k, etc.)
    gives the same result term by term. Now you try: (i + 2j + 3k) × (i − j).
    (3i + 3j − 3k)

D7. Find the area of the triangle with vertices A(1, 1, 1), B(2, 3, 4) and
    C(4, 3, 2), and the area of the parallelogram with adjacent sides
    a = 3i + j + 4k and b = i − j + k.
    Answer: Triangle: 2√6 ≈ 4.90; parallelogram: √42 ≈ 6.48.
    Teacher explains: |a × b| = |a||b| sin θ = base × height of the
    parallelogram on a and b. The triangle is half of the parallelogram on AB
    and AC:
       AB = i + 2j + 3k,  AC = 3i + 2j + k
       AB × AC = (2 − 6)i − (1 − 9)j + (2 − 6)k = −4i + 8j − 4k
       |AB × AC| = √(16 + 64 + 16) = √96 = 4√6,  area = 2√6
    For the parallelogram:
       a × b = (1 × 1 − 4 × (−1))i − (3 × 1 − 4 × 1)j + (3 × (−1) − 1 × 1)k
             = 5i + j − 4k,   area = √(25 + 1 + 16) = √42
    If the area comes out 0 the points are collinear (or the vectors parallel).
    Common mistake: forgetting the 1/2 for a triangle, or using AB × BC with a
    wrong sign (the magnitude is the same either way). Now you try: the area of
    the triangle with vertices (0, 0, 0), (1, 2, 3), (2, 3, 1). (5√3/2, since
    the cross product is −7i + 5j − k)

D8. Find the unit vectors perpendicular to both a = 3i + 2j + 2k and
    b = i + 2j − 2k. Verify Lagrange's identity |a × b|² + (a·b)² = |a|²|b|² for
    these vectors.
    Answer: ±(1/3)(−2i + 2j + k).
    Teacher explains: a × b is perpendicular to both; divide by its length:
       a × b = (2(−2) − 2 × 2)i − (3(−2) − 2 × 1)j + (3 × 2 − 2 × 1)k
             = −8i + 8j + 4k,   |a × b| = √(64 + 64 + 16) = 12
       unit vectors: ±(−8i + 8j + 4k)/12 = ±(−(2/3)i + (2/3)j + (1/3)k)
    There are TWO answers (up and down). Lagrange: |a|² = 17, |b|² = 9,
    a·b = 3 + 4 − 4 = 3, so |a × b|² + (a·b)² = 144 + 9 = 153 = 17 × 9. This is
    just sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 multiplied by |a|²|b|², and it gives a quick check on
    a cross product. Common mistake: giving only one of the two unit vectors.
    Now you try: a unit vector perpendicular to i + j and j + k.
    (±(1/√3)(i − j + k))

D9. A mechanic pulls on a spanner. The force F = 2i + 3j − k newtons acts at the
    point with position vector r = i − 2j + 3k metres relative to the bolt. Find
    the moment (torque) of F about the bolt and its magnitude.
    Answer: τ = −7i + 7j + 7k N m, |τ| = 7√3 ≈ 12.1 N m.
    Teacher explains: The moment of F about O is τ = r × F (r FIRST):
       τ = ((−2)(−1) − 3 × 3)i − (1 × (−1) − 3 × 2)j + (1 × 3 − (−2) × 2)k
         = (2 − 9)i − (−1 − 6)j + (3 + 4)k = −7i + 7j + 7k
       |τ| = √(49 + 49 + 49) = 7√3 ≈ 12.1 N m
    The direction of τ is the axis about which F tends to turn the spanner
    (right hand rule), and |τ| = |r||F| sin θ = (distance) × (perpendicular part
    of the force): a longer spanner gives more turning effect. Pushing along the
    line of the spanner (F parallel to r) gives τ = 0: no turning at all. Common
    mistake: F × r, which gives −τ. Now you try: τ for F = i + j acting at
    r = 2i. (2k)

D10. Find [a b c] for a = 2i − 3j + 4k, b = i + 2j − k, c = 3i − j + 2k, and the
     volume of the parallelepiped with edges a, b, c. Check that [b c a] gives
     the same number and [b a c] its negative.
     Answer: [a b c] = −7; the volume is 7 cubic units; [b c a] = −7,
     [b a c] = 7.
     Teacher explains: [a b c] = a·(b × c) is the determinant with rows a, b, c:
        | 2  −3   4 |
        | 1   2  −1 |  = 2(4 − 1) + 3(2 + 3) + 4(−1 − 6)
        | 3  −1   2 |  = 6 + 15 − 28 = −7
     b × c is perpendicular to the base parallelogram with area |b × c|, and
     a·(b × c) = (area) × (height along the normal), so |[a b c]| is the volume:
     7. A cyclic shift of the rows (a b c → b c a) is two row swaps, so the
     determinant is unchanged; one swap (b a c) changes the sign. The sign of
     [a b c] tells whether a, b, c form a right-handed (positive) or left-handed
     (negative) set. Common mistake: giving the volume as −7. Now you try:
     [i + j, j + k, k + i]. (2)

D11. Find λ so that 2i − j + k, i + 2j − 3k and 3i + λj + 5k are coplanar. Show
     that A(4, 5, 1), B(0, −1, −1), C(3, 9, 4) and D(−4, 4, 4) are coplanar.
     Answer: λ = −4. [AB AC AD] = 0, so the points are coplanar.
     Teacher explains: Three vectors are coplanar exactly when the
     parallelepiped they make is flat, i.e. [a b c] = 0:
        | 2  −1   1 |
        | 1   2  −3 |  = 2(10 + 3λ) + 1(5 + 9) + 1(λ − 6) = 7λ + 28
        | 3   λ   5 |
     7λ + 28 = 0 gives λ = −4. For four points, use the three edges from A:
        AB = −4i − 6j − 2k,  AC = −i + 4j + 3k,  AD = −8i − j + 3k
        [AB AC AD] = −4(12 + 3) + 6(−3 + 24) − 2(1 + 32)
                   = −60 + 126 − 66 = 0
     so D lies in the plane of A, B, C. Common mistake: using the position
     vectors a, b, c, d directly — [a b c] = 0 says O, A, B, C are coplanar,
     which is a different question. Now you try: are i + j, j + k and i − k
     coplanar? (yes: the determinant is 0, since i − k = (i + j) − (j + k))

D12. Find the volume of the tetrahedron with vertices A(1, 1, 1), B(2, 1, 3),
     C(3, 2, 2) and D(3, 3, 4). Then, with a = i + j, b = j + k, c = k + i,
     check a × (b × c) = (a·c)b − (a·b)c and show that (a × b) × c is different.
     Answer: Volume 5/6. a × (b × c) = −i + j; (a × b) × c = −i + k.
     Teacher explains: A tetrahedron is 1/6 of the parallelepiped on the same
     three edges:
        AB = i + 2k,  AC = 2i + j + k,  AD = 2i + 2j + 3k
        [AB AC AD] = 1(3 − 2) − 0(6 − 2) + 2(4 − 2) = 1 + 4 = 5
        volume = (1/6) × 5 = 5/6
     (1/3 × base × height, where the base triangle is half a parallelogram:
     (1/3)(1/2) = 1/6.) Triple products:
        b × c = (1 − 0)i − (0 − 1)j + (0 − 1)k = i + j − k
        a × (b × c) = (1(−1) − 0 × 1)i − (1(−1) − 0 × 1)j + (1 − 1)k = −i + j
        (a·c)b − (a·b)c = 1(j + k) − 1(k + i) = −i + j        equal
        a × b = i − j + k,   (a × b) × c = (−1 − 0)i − (1 − 1)j + (0 + 1)k
              = −i + k
     So the brackets matter: the cross product is not associative. Memory aid
     for the formula: 'a × (b × c) = b(a·c) − c(a·b)', BAC minus CAB. Now you
     try: the volume of the tetrahedron O(0, 0, 0), (2, 0, 0), (0, 3, 0),
     (0, 0, 4). (4)

M8. Find the unit vectors perpendicular to both vectors.

    b) i + j and j + k
    c) 2i + j − k and i − j + 2k
    d) i + 2j + 3k and i − j

      a) ±(−(2/3)i + (2/3)j + (1/3)k)
      b) ±((√3/3)i − (√3/3)j + (√3/3)k)
      c) ±((√35/35)i − (√35/7)j − (3√35/35)k)
      d) ±((√3/3)i + (√3/3)j − (√3/3)k)
      e) ±(k)
      f) ±((√2/2)j + (√2/2)k)
      g) ±((√2/2)i − (√2/2)k)
      h) ±((3/5)i + (4/5)k)
      i) ±(−(2/3)i + (2/3)j − (1/3)k)
      j) ±((2/3)i − (2/3)j + (1/3)k)
      k) ±((3√13/13)i − (2√13/13)j)
      l) ±(−(√6/6)i − (√6/6)j + (√6/3)k)

M9. Find the scalar triple product [a b c] = a·(b × c).
    a) [2i − 3j + 4k, i + 2j − k, 3i − j + 2k]

M11. Coplanar or not? In the last five parts find the value that makes the
     vectors (or points) coplanar.
     a) 2i − j + k, i + 2j − 3k, 3i − 4j + 5k
     b) i + j, j + k, i − k
     c) i + 2j + 3k, 4i + 5j + 6k, 7i + 8j + 9k
     d) i, j, i + j + k
     e) i − j + 2k, 2i + j + k, 3i + 3k
     f) 2i + 3j + k, i − j + 2k, 4i + j + 5k
     g) points (4, 5, 1), (0, −1, −1), (3, 9, 4), (−4, 4, 4)
     h) points (1, 1, 1), (2, 3, 4), (3, 5, 7), (0, 0, 1)
     i) points (0, 0, 0), (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (1, 1, 1)
     j) points (1, 2, 3), (2, 3, 4), (3, 1, 2), (4, 2, 3)
     k) λ: 2i − j + k, i + 2j − 3k, 3i + λj + 5k
     l) λ: i + j + k, 2i + 3j + λk, i − j + 2k
     m) λ: λi + j, i + λj, i + j + k (two values)
     n) k: points (1, 2, 3), (2, 3, 1), (1, 1, 2), (k, 0, 1)
     o) λ: points (0, 0, 0), (1, 1, 1), (2, 0, λ), (1, 2, 3)
     Answers:
       a) coplanar
       b) coplanar

       d) not coplanar ([a b c] = 1)

       i) not coplanar ([AB AC AD] = 1)
       j) coplanar
       k) λ = −4

       o) λ = −2

M12. a = i + 2j − k, b = 2i + k, c = −i + j + 3k. Compute each expression and
     notice which ones are equal (identity checks).
     a) a × b               b) b × a             c) a·(a × b)
     d) b·(a × b)           e) a × a             f) [a b c]
     g) [b c a]             h) [b a c]           i) (a × b)·c
     j) a × (b × c)         k) (a·c)b − (a·b)c   l) (a × b) × c
     m) |a × b|² + (a·b)²   n) |a|²|b|²          o) (a + b) × (a − b)
     p) −2(a × b)

              g) −17   h) 17   i) −17   j) −3i − j − 5k   k) −3i − j − 5k

              p) −4i + 6j + 8k

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: say 'dot gives a number, cross gives a vector' aloud before each
  question; write vectors in a column layout before multiplying; for cross
  products always write the 3 × 3 determinant and circle the minus sign on j;
  check every cross product by dotting it with both factors (you must get 0);
  use a real box to see why |[a b c]| is a volume. Harder: prove the sine rule
  for a triangle using a × b = b × c = c × a when a + b + c = 0; prove that
  a·(b × c) = 0 when two of the vectors are equal; show that [a × b, b × c,
  c × a] = [a b c]²; find the shortest distance from a point to a line using
  |AP × u|/|u| (used in topic 8.30); prove the cosine rule
  c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C with dot products.


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.30 — LINES AND PLANES IN 3D; ANGLES AND DISTANCES
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - LINE through the point A (position vector a) with direction b: VECTOR form
    r = a + λb (λ any real number). CARTESIAN (symmetric) form through
    (x₁, y₁, z₁) with direction ratios a, b, c:
    (x − x₁)/a = (y − y₁)/b = (z − z₁)/c. Through two points use the direction
    ratios x₂ − x₁, y₂ − y₁, z₂ − z₁. A 0 in a denominator means that coordinate
    is constant along the line.
  - ANGLE between two lines with directions b₁, b₂: cos θ = |b₁·b₂|/(|b₁||b₂|)
    (we take the acute angle). Perpendicular: b₁·b₂ = 0; parallel: b₁ = kb₂.
  - Two lines in space either INTERSECT, are PARALLEL, or are SKEW (neither:
    they do not meet and are not parallel). To decide, solve the equations of
    the general points; to find the intersection, put λ and μ back.
  - SHORTEST DISTANCE between skew lines r = a₁ + λb₁ and r = a₂ + μb₂:
    d = |(a₂ − a₁)·(b₁ × b₂)|/|b₁ × b₂| (d = 0 means they intersect). Between
    PARALLEL lines r = a₁ + λb, r = a₂ + μb: d = |(a₂ − a₁) × b|/|b|. From a
    point P to the line r = a + λb: |(p − a) × b|/|b|.
  - PLANE with normal n through the point a: (r − a)·n = 0; Cartesian
    a(x − x₁) + b(y − y₁) + c(z − z₁) = 0, i.e. ax + by + cz = d, whose normal
    has direction ratios a, b, c. NORMAL FORM r·n̂ = p, or lx + my + nz = p,
    with (l, m, n) the unit normal and p ≥ 0 the distance from O. INTERCEPT form
    x/a + y/b + z/c = 1. Through three points A, B, C: use n = AB × AC.
  - ANGLE between two planes: cos θ = |n₁·n₂|/(|n₁||n₂|); perpendicular planes
    n₁·n₂ = 0; parallel planes have proportional normals. ANGLE between a line
    (direction b) and a plane (normal n): sin φ = |b·n|/(|b||n|); the line is
    parallel to the plane when b·n = 0 and perpendicular to it when b ∥ n.
  - INTERSECTION of a line and a plane: substitute the general point of the line
    into the plane and solve for λ.
  - DISTANCE from (x₁, y₁, z₁) to the plane ax + by + cz + d = 0:
    |ax₁ + by₁ + cz₁ + d|/√(a² + b² + c²). Between PARALLEL planes
    ax + by + cz + d₁ = 0 and ax + by + cz + d₂ = 0 (same a, b, c!):
    |d₁ − d₂|/√(a² + b² + c²). The FOOT of the perpendicular and the IMAGE of a
    point come from the line through the point along n.
  - COPLANAR LINES: r = a₁ + λb₁ and r = a₂ + μb₂ lie in one plane exactly when
    (a₂ − a₁)·(b₁ × b₂) = 0; that plane has normal b₁ × b₂.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A laser beam starts at A(1, 2, 3) and travels in the direction 2i − j + 4k.
    Write the equation of the beam in vector and Cartesian form. Does it hit a
    sensor at (5, 0, 11)? At (3, 1, 6)?
    Answer: r = (i + 2j + 3k) + λ(2i − j + 4k);
    (x − 1)/2 = (y − 2)/(−1) = (z − 3)/4. (5, 0, 11) is on it (λ = 2); (3, 1, 6)
    is not.
    Teacher explains: Every point of the line is 'start + λ × direction':
       r = (i + 2j + 3k) + λ(2i − j + 4k)
       x = 1 + 2λ,  y = 2 − λ,  z = 3 + 4λ
    Making λ the subject of each equation and equating gives the Cartesian form
    (x − 1)/2 = (y − 2)/(−1) = (z − 3)/4. To test a point, find λ from one
    coordinate and check the others: for (5, 0, 11), λ = 2 from x, and then
    y = 2 − 2 = 0 and z = 3 + 8 = 11, all agree: ON the beam (for λ ≥ 0, the ray
    itself). For (3, 1, 6), x gives λ = 1, y gives λ = 1, but z gives λ = 3/4:
    NOT on it. Common mistake: writing (x + 1)/2 for the point (1, 2, 3) (the
    sign in the bracket is the opposite of the coordinate), or putting the
    point's coordinates in the denominators. Now you try: the line through
    (−2, 4, −5) parallel to 3i + 5j + 6k. ((x + 2)/3 = (y − 4)/5 = (z + 5)/6)

D2. Find the Cartesian equation of the line through (−1, 0, 2) and (3, 4, 6),
    and of the line through (3, −2, −5) and (3, −2, 6). Write
    (4 − x)/2 = (y + 1)/3 = z/(−1) in vector form.
    Answer: (x + 1)/1 = y/1 = (z − 2)/1 (i.e. x + 1 = y = z − 2); x = 3, y = −2
    (the line parallel to the z-axis); r = (4i − j) + λ(−2i + 3j − k).
    Teacher explains: Direction ratios from the two points: (3 + 1, 4 − 0,
    6 − 2) = (4, 4, 4), which we may scale to (1, 1, 1). So
    (x + 1)/1 = (y − 0)/1 = (z − 2)/1. For (3, −2, −5) and (3, −2, 6) the
    direction ratios are (0, 0, 11): x and y never change, so the line is x = 3,
    y = −2 (some books write (x − 3)/0 = (y + 2)/0 = (z + 5)/11, meaning the
    numerators are 0). For the last one, first make the coefficient of x equal
    to +1:
       (4 − x)/2 = (x − 4)/(−2)
    so the point is (4, −1, 0) and the direction ratios are (−2, 3, −1):
    r = (4i − j + 0k) + λ(−2i + 3j − k). Common mistake: reading the direction
    as (2, 3, −1) from (4 − x)/2. Now you try: the line through (1, 2, 3) and
    (4, 2, −1). ((x − 1)/3 = (z − 3)/(−4), y = 2)

D3. Find the angle between the lines (x − 2)/2 = (y − 1)/5 = (z + 3)/(−3) and
    (x + 2)/(−1) = (y − 4)/8 = (z − 5)/4. Are the lines
    (x − 5)/7 = (y + 2)/(−5) = z/1 and x/1 = y/2 = z/3 perpendicular?
    Answer: θ = arccos(26/(9√38)) ≈ 62.1°. Yes, they are perpendicular.
    Teacher explains: Only the DIRECTIONS matter (the points do not):
    b₁ = (2, 5, −3), b₂ = (−1, 8, 4).
       b₁·b₂ = −2 + 40 − 12 = 26
       |b₁| = √(4 + 25 + 9) = √38,   |b₂| = √(1 + 64 + 16) = 9
       cos θ = 26/(9√38) ≈ 0.4686,   θ ≈ 62.1°
    We use |b₁·b₂| so that θ is the ACUTE angle between the lines (a line has no
    preferred direction). Second pair: (7, −5, 1)·(1, 2, 3) = 7 − 10 + 3 = 0, so
    they are perpendicular — even though they may not meet (skew lines can be
    perpendicular). Common mistake: using the points instead of the direction
    ratios. Now you try: the angle between x/2 = y/2 = z/1 and
    (x − 5)/4 = (y − 2)/1 = (z − 3)/8. (arccos(2/3) ≈ 48.2°)

D4. Show that the lines (x − 1)/1 = (y − 2)/(−1) = (z − 3)/2 and
    (x − 2)/1 = (y + 2)/2 = (z − 9)/(−2) intersect, and find the point.
    Answer: They meet at (3, 0, 7).
    Teacher explains: Write the general points: (1 + λ, 2 − λ, 3 + 2λ) and
    (2 + μ, −2 + 2μ, 9 − 2μ). They meet when all three coordinates agree:
       x:  1 + λ = 2 + μ         λ − μ = 1
       y:  2 − λ = −2 + 2μ       λ + 2μ = 4
       z:  3 + 2λ = 9 − 2μ       (the check equation)
    From the first two, 3μ = 3, μ = 1, λ = 2. Check z: 3 + 4 = 7 and 9 − 2 = 7,
    equal, so the lines really meet; the point is (1 + 2, 2 − 2,
    3 + 4) = (3, 0, 7). If the third equation had failed, the lines would be
    SKEW (not parallel, since (1, −1, 2) and (1, 2, −2) are not proportional).
    Always use DIFFERENT parameters λ and μ for the two lines. Common mistake:
    using λ for both lines, which only finds points reached at the same
    parameter value. Now you try: do x = y = z and (x − 1)/1 = y/2 = (z + 1)/3
    meet? (yes, at (2, 2, 2))

D5. Find the shortest distance between the skew lines
    r = (i + j) + λ(2i − j + k) and r = (2i + j − k) + μ(3i − 5j + 2k), and
    explain the formula.
    Answer: d = 10/√59 = 10√59/59 ≈ 1.30.
    Teacher explains: The shortest segment between two skew lines is
    perpendicular to BOTH, so it is parallel to b₁ × b₂. Its length is the
    projection of any joining vector a₂ − a₁ on that common normal:
       b₁ × b₂ = (−2 + 5)i − (4 − 3)j + (−10 + 3)k = 3i − j − 7k
       |b₁ × b₂| = √(9 + 1 + 49) = √59
       a₂ − a₁ = (2i + j − k) − (i + j) = i − k
       d = |(i − k)·(3i − j − 7k)|/√59 = |3 + 7|/√59 = 10/√59
    If the numerator (a₂ − a₁)·(b₁ × b₂) is 0, the lines are coplanar and (not
    being parallel) they intersect. If b₁ × b₂ = 0 the lines are parallel and a
    different formula is needed (D6). Common mistake: forgetting the absolute
    value, or dividing by |a₂ − a₁|. Now you try: the shortest distance between
    r = i + λj and r = k + μi. (1)

D6. Find the distance between the parallel lines
    r = (i + 2j − 4k) + λ(2i + 3j + 6k) and
    r = (3i + 3j − 5k) + μ(2i + 3j + 6k). Find also the distance of the point
    P(1, 2, 3) from the line r = λ(i + j + k).
    Answer: √293/7 ≈ 2.45; √2 ≈ 1.41.
    Teacher explains: For parallel lines the joining vector a₂ − a₁ and the
    common direction b make a parallelogram whose height is the distance:
       a₂ − a₁ = 2i + j − k,   b = 2i + 3j + 6k,  |b| = 7
       (a₂ − a₁) × b = (6 + 3)i − (12 + 2)j + (6 − 2)k = 9i − 14j + 4k
       d = √(81 + 196 + 16)/7 = √293/7
    The same idea gives the distance from a point: the line passes through O
    with b = i + j + k, and OP = i + 2j + 3k:
       OP × b = (2 − 3)i − (1 − 3)j + (1 − 2)k = −i + 2j − k
       d = √6/√3 = √2
    Check the second by the foot of the perpendicular: the foot is (2, 2, 2)
    (λ = (1 + 2 + 3)/3 = 2), and P to (2, 2, 2) is √(1 + 0 + 1) = √2. Now you
    try: the distance of (0, 0, 0) from the line r = i + λj. (1)

D7. Reduce 2x − 3y + 6z + 14 = 0 to normal form and find the distance of the
    plane from O and the direction cosines of its normal. Find the plane through
    (1, −1, 2) with normal 2i + 3j − k.
    Answer: −(2/7)x + (3/7)y − (6/7)z = 2: distance 2, direction cosines
    (−2/7, 3/7, −6/7). 2x + 3y − z + 3 = 0.
    Teacher explains: In normal form lx + my + nz = p, (l, m, n) is a UNIT
    normal and p ≥ 0. Here |n| = √(4 + 9 + 36) = 7. Move the constant:
    2x − 3y + 6z = −14. The right side must be positive, so divide by −7:
       −(2/7)x + (3/7)y − (6/7)z = 2
    The distance from O is 2, and the unit normal pointing from O towards the
    plane is (−2/7, 3/7, −6/7). A plane through a point with a given normal:
    every vector in the plane is perpendicular to n, so (r − a)·n = 0:
       2(x − 1) + 3(y + 1) − (z − 2) = 0,   2x + 3y − z + 3 = 0
    Check: 2 − 3 − 2 + 3 = 0. Common mistake: dividing by 7 and keeping −2 on
    the right (p must be non-negative). Now you try: the distance from O to
    x + 2y − 2z = 9. (3)

D8. Find the plane through A(1, 1, 0), B(1, 2, 1) and C(−2, 2, −1), and write it
    in intercept form. Find the plane with intercepts 2, −3 and 4 on the axes.
    Answer: 2x + 3y − 3z = 5, i.e. x/(5/2) + y/(5/3) + z/(−5/3) = 1.
    6x − 4y + 3z = 12.
    Teacher explains: The normal is perpendicular to AB and AC, so take their
    cross product:
       AB = j + k,  AC = −3i + j − k
       n = AB × AC = (−1 − 1)i − (0 + 3)j + (0 + 3)k = −2i − 3j + 3k
       −2(x − 1) − 3(y − 1) + 3(z − 0) = 0,   2x + 3y − 3z = 5
    Check B: 2 + 6 − 3 = 5 and C: −4 + 6 + 3 = 5. For intercept form divide by
    the constant: x/(5/2) + y/(5/3) − z/(5/3) = 1; the plane meets the axes at
    x = 5/2, y = 5/3, z = −5/3. The plane with intercepts 2, −3, 4 is
    x/2 + y/(−3) + z/4 = 1; multiply by 12: 6x − 4y + 3z = 12. If the three
    points are collinear, AB × AC = 0 and there is no unique plane. Now you try:
    the plane through (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (0, 0, 1). (x + y + z = 1)

D9. Find the angle between the planes 2x + y − 2z = 5 and 3x − 6y − 2z = 7. Find
    the plane through (1, 4, −2) parallel to 2x − y + 3z + 7 = 0. Are
    x + 2y − z = 1 and 3x − y + z = 4 perpendicular?
    Answer: arccos(4/21) ≈ 79.0°. 2x − y + 3z + 8 = 0. Yes.
    Teacher explains: The angle between two planes is the angle between their
    normals:
       n₁ = (2, 1, −2), n₂ = (3, −6, −2),  n₁·n₂ = 6 − 6 + 4 = 4
       |n₁| = 3, |n₂| = 7,  cos θ = 4/21,  θ ≈ 79.0°
    A plane parallel to 2x − y + 3z + 7 = 0 has the same normal, so it is
    2x − y + 3z = k; through (1, 4, −2): k = 2 − 4 − 6 = −8, giving
    2x − y + 3z + 8 = 0. Perpendicular planes have perpendicular normals:
    (1, 2, −1)·(3, −1, 1) = 3 − 2 − 1 = 0, yes. Common mistake: using sin
    instead of cos (sin is for a line and a plane, D10). Now you try: the angle
    between x + y = 3 and y + z = 5. (60°)

D10. Find the angle between the line (x − 2)/3 = (y + 1)/4 = (z − 2)/12 and the
     plane x − y + z = 5, and the point where the line meets the plane. How far
     is that point from (−1, −5, −10)?
     Answer: sin φ = 11/(13√3), φ ≈ 29.2°; the point (2, −1, 2); distance 13.
     Teacher explains: The angle φ between a line and a plane is 90° minus the
     angle between the line and the NORMAL, so we use sine:
        b = (3, 4, 12), n = (1, −1, 1),  b·n = 3 − 4 + 12 = 11
        |b| = 13, |n| = √3,  sin φ = 11/(13√3) ≈ 0.489,  φ ≈ 29.2°
     Intersection: the general point (2 + 3λ, −1 + 4λ, 2 + 12λ) is on the plane
     when (2 + 3λ) − (−1 + 4λ) + (2 + 12λ) = 5, i.e. 5 + 11λ = 5, λ = 0: the
     point (2, −1, 2). Distance to (−1, −5, −10): √(3² + 4² + 12²) = √169 = 13.
     If b·n = 0 the line is parallel to the plane (no intersection, or it lies
     in the plane). Common mistake: cos φ = |b·n|/(|b||n|), which gives the
     complement. Now you try: where does x/1 = y/2 = z/3 meet x + y + z = 12?
     ((2, 4, 6))

D11. Find the distance of (2, 5, −3) from 6x − 3y + 2z − 4 = 0, the distance
     between the planes 2x − y + 2z + 3 = 0 and 4x − 2y + 4z + 5 = 0, and the
     foot and image of (1, 3, 4) in the plane 2x − y + z + 3 = 0.
     Answer: 13/7; 1/6; foot (−1, 4, 3), image (−3, 5, 2).
     Teacher explains: Point to plane: substitute the point into the left side
     and divide by |n|:
        |6(2) − 3(5) + 2(−3) − 4|/√(36 + 9 + 4) = |−13|/7 = 13/7
     Parallel planes: first make the coefficients IDENTICAL. The second plane is
     2x − y + 2z + 5/2 = 0, so the distance is
     |3 − 5/2|/√(4 + 1 + 4) = (1/2)/3 = 1/6. Foot and image: the perpendicular
     from P(1, 3, 4) runs along n: (1 + 2t, 3 − t, 4 + t). On the plane:
     2 + 4t − 3 + t + 4 + t + 3 = 0, so 6 + 6t = 0 and t = −1: foot (−1, 4, 3).
     The image is as far beyond the plane: t = −2, giving (−3, 5, 2). Check: the
     midpoint of P and the image is the foot. Common mistake: using |5 − 3|/3
     for the planes without halving the second equation. Now you try: the
     distance from (3, −2, 1) to 2x − y + 2z + 3 = 0. (13/3)

D12. Show that the lines (x + 3)/(−3) = (y − 1)/1 = (z − 5)/5 and
     (x + 1)/(−1) = (y − 2)/2 = (z − 5)/5 are coplanar, and find the plane
     containing them.
     Answer: (a₂ − a₁)·(b₁ × b₂) = 0; the plane is x − 2y + z = 0.
     Teacher explains: a₁ = (−3, 1, 5), b₁ = (−3, 1, 5), a₂ = (−1, 2, 5),
     b₂ = (−1, 2, 5).
        b₁ × b₂ = (5 − 10)i − (−15 + 5)j + (−6 + 1)k = −5i + 10j − 5k
        a₂ − a₁ = 2i + j + 0k
        (a₂ − a₁)·(b₁ × b₂) = −10 + 10 + 0 = 0      coplanar
     The common normal is b₁ × b₂, or (1, −2, 1) after dividing by −5. Through
     (−3, 1, 5): (x + 3) − 2(y − 1) + (z − 5) = 0, so x − 2y + z = 0. Check the
     second line's point (−1, 2, 5): −1 − 4 + 5 = 0. Coplanar lines either meet
     or are parallel; these directions are not parallel, so they meet — in fact
     both pass through the origin: λ = −1 and μ = −1 both give (0, 0, 0). The
     condition is the same as the shortest distance being 0. Now you try: are
     x = y = z and the line through (1, 0, 0) with direction j coplanar? (no:
     i·((i + j + k) × j) = −1 ≠ 0)

     h) z − 2 = 0 and 2z + 6 = 0
     i) foot and image of (1, 3, 4) in 2x − y + z + 3 = 0
     j) foot and image of (0, 0, 0) in x + y + z − 3 = 0
     k) foot and image of (3, −1, 2) in x + 2y − z − 5 = 0
     l) foot and image of (2, 1, 0) in z − 4 = 0
     m) coplanar? (x + 3)/(−3) = (y − 1)/1 = (z − 5)/5 and
        (x + 1)/(−1) = (y − 2)/2 = (z − 5)/5
     n) coplanar? (x − 1)/2 = (y − 2)/3 = (z − 3)/4 and
        (x − 2)/3 = (y − 4)/4 = (z − 5)/5
     o) coplanar? x/1 = y/1 = z/1 and x = 1, z = 0 (parallel to the y-axis)
     p) coplanar? (x − 1)/1 = (z − 1)/(−1), y = 1 and (y − 3)/1 = (z − 1)/2,
        x = 2
     q) coplanar? x = 1, z = 0 (parallel to the y-axis) and y = 0, z = 1
        (parallel to the x-axis)
     r) coplanar? (x − 2)/1 = (y − 1)/1 = z/1 and
        (x − 3)/1 = (y − 2)/(−1) = (z − 1)/2
     Answers:
       a) 1/6
       b) 4
       c) 2
       d) √3
       e) 3
       f) √2
       g) 1
       h) 5
       i) foot (−1, 4, 3), image (−3, 5, 2)
       j) foot (1, 1, 1), image (2, 2, 2)
       k) foot (4, 1, 1), image (5, 3, 0)
       l) foot (2, 1, 4), image (2, 1, 8)
       m) coplanar; plane x − 2y + z = 0
       n) not coplanar ((a₂ − a₁)·(b₁ × b₂) = 1)
       o) not coplanar ((a₂ − a₁)·(b₁ × b₂) = −1)
       p) not coplanar ((a₂ − a₁)·(b₁ × b₂) = −3)
       q) not coplanar ((a₂ − a₁)·(b₁ × b₂) = −1)
       r) coplanar; plane 3x − y − 2z = 5

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: model lines with pencils and planes with books or a sheet of card;
  always write a line as 'point + λ × direction' and read the point and the
  direction off separately; underline the normal (a, b, c) of every plane; for
  any distance question first ask 'point, line or plane?' and choose the formula
  from a table; check intersection points in BOTH equations. Harder: find the
  equation of the plane through the intersection of x + y + z = 6 and
  2x + 3y + 4z + 5 = 0 passing through (1, 1, 1) (20x + 23y + 26z = 69); find
  the image of a line in a plane; find the equations of the common perpendicular
  of two skew lines and its feet; show that the locus of points equidistant from
  two parallel planes is the plane midway between them; find the volume of the
  tetrahedron cut from the first octant by x/a + y/b + z/c = 1 (abc/6).


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.31 — LIMITS: INTUITION, ALGEBRA OF LIMITS, STANDARD LIMITS (sin x / x)
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - MEANING: lim (x → a) f(x) = L means f(x) can be made as close to L as we
    like by taking x close enough to a, but NOT equal to a. The value f(a) (or
    whether it exists) does not matter. Precisely: for every ε > 0 there is
    δ > 0 with |f(x) − L| < ε whenever 0 < |x − a| < δ.
  - ONE-SIDED LIMITS: the left-hand limit (x → a⁻, x < a) and the right-hand
    limit (x → a⁺, x > a). lim (x → a) f(x) exists exactly when both one-sided
    limits exist and are EQUAL.
  - ALGEBRA OF LIMITS: if lim f = L and lim g = M then lim (f ± g) = L ± M, lim
    kf = kL, lim fg = LM, lim f/g = L/M (M ≠ 0), lim fⁿ = Lⁿ, lim ⁿ√f = ⁿ√L
    (L ≥ 0 for even n). So for polynomials, and rational functions with non-zero
    denominator, just SUBSTITUTE x = a.
  - INDETERMINATE FORM 0/0: substitution gives no answer. Remove the common
    factor (x − a) by FACTORISING, by RATIONALISING (multiply by the conjugate
    of the surd expression), or by using a STANDARD LIMIT.
  - STANDARD LIMITS (x in RADIANS): (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) → naⁿ⁻¹ as x → a; sin x/x
    → 1, tan x/x → 1 and (1 − cos x)/x² → 1/2 as x → 0; (eˣ − 1)/x → 1,
    (aˣ − 1)/x → ln a and ln(1 + x)/x → 1 as x → 0; (1 + x)^(1/x) → e as x → 0
    and (1 + 1/x)ˣ → e as x → ∞. More generally sin kx/x → k, (1 + kx)^(1/x) →
    eᵏ.
  - LIMITS AT INFINITY: 1/xⁿ → 0 (n > 0). For a rational function divide top and
    bottom by the highest power of x in the DENOMINATOR: degree of
    numerator < degree of denominator gives 0; equal degrees give the ratio of
    the leading coefficients; a higher numerator degree gives no finite limit
    (±∞). For √(x² + ...) remember √(x²) = |x|, which is −x for x < 0.
  - A LIMIT FAILS TO EXIST when the one-sided limits differ (a jump, as for
    |x|/x at 0), when f grows without bound (1/x² → ∞ is described as 'tends to
    infinity', not a real number limit), or when f oscillates (sin(1/x) at 0).
  - SANDWICH (SQUEEZE) THEOREM: if g(x) ≤ f(x) ≤ h(x) near a and g, h → L, then
    f → L. It proves sin x/x → 1 and x sin(1/x) → 0.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A ball is dropped from a tower; after t seconds it has fallen s = 5t²
    metres. Find its average speed between t = 2 and t = 2 + h, and use a table
    to guess its speed at the instant t = 2. Also guess lim (x → 2)
    (x² − 4)/(x − 2) from a table.
    Answer: Average speed 20 + 5h m/s, which tends to 20 m/s as h → 0; the limit
    is 4.
    Teacher explains: Average speed = distance/time:
       (5(2 + h)² − 5 × 4)/h = (20 + 20h + 5h² − 20)/h = 20 + 5h   (h ≠ 0)
       h         1      0.1     0.01     −0.01    −0.1
       speed     25     20.5    20.05    19.95    19.5
    As h → 0 from either side the average speed approaches 20 m/s: the speed at
    the instant t = 2 is the LIMIT, 20 m/s. At h = 0 the formula is 0/0,
    meaningless, which is why we need limits. Similarly for
    g(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2):
       x       1.9    1.99    1.999    2.001    2.01    2.1
       g(x)    3.9    3.99    3.999    4.001    4.01    4.1
    g(2) is not defined, but g(x) = x + 2 for x ≠ 2, so the graph is the line
    y = x + 2 with a HOLE at (2, 4), and the limit is 4. The limit is about what
    happens NEAR x = 2, not AT x = 2. Now you try: guess lim (x → 1)
    (x² − 1)/(x − 1) from x = 0.9, 0.99, 1.01, 1.1. (1.9, 1.99, 2.01, 2.1: the
    limit is 2)

D2. Find lim (x → 2) (x³ − 2x + 5) and lim (x → 1) (x² + 1)/(x + 3). If lim
    f(x) = 3 and lim g(x) = −2 as x → a, find the limits of 2f − 3g, fg, f/g and
    √(f + 6).
    Answer: 9; 1/2; 12, −6, −3/2, 3.
    Teacher explains: Polynomials: the limit is the value, because limits
    respect sums, products and constant multiples:
       lim (x³ − 2x + 5) = 8 − 4 + 5 = 9
    Quotients: allowed when the denominator's limit is not 0:
       lim (x² + 1)/(x + 3) = (1 + 1)/(1 + 3) = 2/4 = 1/2
    With the given limits, apply the rules one at a time:
       lim (2f − 3g) = 2(3) − 3(−2) = 12
       lim fg = 3 × (−2) = −6,        lim f/g = 3/(−2) = −3/2
       lim √(f + 6) = √(3 + 6) = 3
    The quotient rule FAILS if lim g = 0; then we must simplify first (D3, D4).
    Common mistake: 'substituting' into a 0/0 expression and writing 0/0 = 1 or
    0. Now you try: lim (x → −1) (x² + 3x)/(x − 1). (1)

D3. Find lim (x → 2) (x³ − 8)/(x² − 4) and lim (x → 3) (x² − 5x + 6)/(x² − 9).
    Answer: 3; 1/6.
    Teacher explains: Substitution gives 0/0, so (x − 2) is a factor of BOTH
    numerator and denominator (factor theorem). Factorise and cancel (allowed,
    since x ≠ 2 in a limit):
       (x³ − 8)/(x² − 4) = (x − 2)(x² + 2x + 4)/((x − 2)(x + 2))
                         = (x² + 2x + 4)/(x + 2) → (4 + 4 + 4)/4 = 3
       (x² − 5x + 6)/(x² − 9) = (x − 2)(x − 3)/((x − 3)(x + 3))
                              = (x − 2)/(x + 3) → 1/6
    If after cancelling you still get 0/0, cancel again; if you get
    (non-zero)/0, the limit does not exist (the function blows up). Common
    mistake: cancelling terms instead of factors, e.g. x²/x² in
    (x² − 5x + 6)/(x² − 9). Now you try: lim (x → 1) (x² − 1)/(x² + x − 2).
    (2/3)

D4. Find lim (x → 0) (√(x + 4) − 2)/x and lim (x → 0) (√(1 + x) − √(1 − x))/x.
    Answer: 1/4; 1.
    Teacher explains: With a surd, multiply top and bottom by the CONJUGATE, so
    that (√A − B)(√A + B) = A − B² removes the root:
       (√(x + 4) − 2)/x × (√(x + 4) + 2)/(√(x + 4) + 2)
       = (x + 4 − 4)/(x(√(x + 4) + 2)) = 1/(√(x + 4) + 2) → 1/(2 + 2) = 1/4
       (√(1 + x) − √(1 − x))/x = ((1 + x) − (1 − x))/(x(√(1 + x) + √(1 − x)))
       = 2/(√(1 + x) + √(1 − x)) → 2/2 = 1
    Check the first with a calculator: x = 0.001 gives
    (√4.001 − 2)/0.001 ≈ 0.24998. Do NOT expand the denominator after
    multiplying: the x must stay as a factor so that it cancels. Now you try:
    lim (x → 9) (√x − 3)/(x − 9). (1/6)

D5. Prove that lim (x → 0) sin x/x = 1 (x in radians). What happens if x is in
    degrees?
    Answer: The limit is 1; in degrees sin(x°)/x → π/180 ≈ 0.01745.
    Teacher explains: Draw the unit circle with centre O, A = (1, 0),
    P = (cos x, sin x) with 0 < x < π/2, and let the tangent at A meet OP at T,
    so AT = tan x. Compare three areas:
       triangle OAP   <   sector OAP   <   triangle OAT
       (1/2) sin x    <   (1/2) x      <   (1/2) tan x
    Divide by (1/2) sin x (positive) and take reciprocals:
       1 < x/sin x < 1/cos x,   so   cos x < sin x/x < 1
    As x → 0⁺, cos x → 1, so by the SANDWICH theorem sin x/x → 1;
    since sin(−x)/(−x) = sin x/x, the left-hand limit is the same. Table
    (radians): x = 0.1 gives 0.99833, x = 0.01 gives 0.99998. In degrees,
    x° = πx/180 radians, so sin(x°)/x = (π/180) × sin(πx/180)/(πx/180) → π/180:
    this is why calculus always uses radians. Now you try: lim (x → 0) tan x/x.
    (1, since tan x/x = (sin x/x)(1/cos x))

D6. Find lim (x → 0) sin 5x/(3x), lim (x → 0) tan 2x/sin 3x and
    lim (x → 0) sin(x²)/x.
    Answer: 5/3; 2/3; 0.
    Teacher explains: Make the ANGLE and the DENOMINATOR match, then use sin θ/θ
    → 1 with θ → 0:
       sin 5x/(3x) = (5/3) × sin 5x/(5x) → (5/3) × 1 = 5/3
       tan 2x/sin 3x = (tan 2x/(2x)) × (3x/sin 3x) × (2x/(3x)) → 1 × 1 × 2/3
       sin(x²)/x = (sin(x²)/x²) × x → 1 × 0 = 0
    General results: sin ax/x → a, sin ax/sin bx → a/b, tan ax/tan bx → a/b.
    Common mistake: 'cancelling' the x in sin 5x/(3x) to get sin 5/3 — sin 5x is
    NOT sin × 5x. Another: using sin 5x/(3x) → 5x/(3x) without justifying it
    (the matching step IS the justification). Now you try:
    lim (x → 0) sin 3x/sin 7x. (3/7)

D7. Show that lim (x → 0) (1 − cos x)/x² = 1/2, and find lim (x → 0)
    (1 − cos 4x)/x² and lim (x → 0) (tan x − sin x)/x³.
    Answer: 1/2; 8; 1/2.
    Teacher explains: Use 1 − cos x = 2 sin²(x/2):
       (1 − cos x)/x² = 2 sin²(x/2)/x² = (1/2) × (sin(x/2)/(x/2))² → 1/2
    For 1 − cos 4x = 2 sin² 2x:
       2 sin² 2x/x² = 2 × 4 × (sin 2x/(2x))² → 8
    (or: (1 − cos kx)/x² → k²/2 = 16/2). For the third, factor out tan x:
       tan x − sin x = tan x (1 − cos x)
       (tan x − sin x)/x³ = (tan x/x) × (1 − cos x)/x² → 1 × 1/2 = 1/2
    Check numerically: x = 0.01 gives (1 − cos 0.01)/0.0001 ≈ 0.499996. Common
    mistake: splitting (tan x − sin x)/x³ into tan x/x³ − sin x/x³, which gives
    ∞ − ∞, no information. Now you try: lim (x → 0) (1 − cos 2x)/(x sin x). (2)

D8. A bank pays 100% interest per year, compounded n times a year, on ₹1.
    Tabulate the amount after one year for n = 1, 2, 12, 365 and find the limit.
    Then find lim (x → 0) (1 + 3x)^(1/x), lim (x → 0) (e^(2x) − 1)/x and
    lim (x → 0) (2ˣ − 1)/x.
    Answer: ₹2, ₹2.25, ₹2.6130, ₹2.7146 → e ≈ 2.71828; e³; 2; ln 2 ≈ 0.693.
    Teacher explains: Each period multiplies the money by (1 + 1/n), and there
    are n periods:
       n            1      2       12        365       → ∞
       (1 + 1/n)ⁿ   2      2.25    2.6130    2.7146    → e = 2.71828...
    With x = 1/n this is (1 + x)^(1/x) → e as x → 0. Then
       (1 + 3x)^(1/x) = ((1 + 3x)^(1/(3x)))³ → e³
       (e^(2x) − 1)/x = 2 × (e^(2x) − 1)/(2x) → 2 × 1 = 2
       (2ˣ − 1)/x = (e^(x ln 2) − 1)/(x ln 2) × ln 2 → ln 2
    The last uses 2ˣ = e^(x ln 2) and the standard limit (eᵘ − 1)/u → 1. The
    form 1^∞ is indeterminate: (1 + 3x)^(1/x) is NOT 1 in the limit. Common
    mistake: 'lim (1 + 3x) = 1 and 1 to any power is 1'. Now you try:
    lim (x → 0) ln(1 + 3x)/x. (3)

D9. Prove that lim (x → a) (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = naⁿ⁻¹ for a positive integer n,
    and find lim (x → 2) (x⁵ − 32)/(x − 2) and lim (x → 8)
    (x^(1/3) − 2)/(x − 8). If lim (x → 2) (xⁿ − 2ⁿ)/(x − 2) = 80, find n.
    Answer: 80; 1/12; n = 5.
    Teacher explains: Factorise (check by multiplying out, all middle terms
    cancel):
       xⁿ − aⁿ = (x − a)(xⁿ⁻¹ + xⁿ⁻²a + xⁿ⁻³a² + ... + aⁿ⁻¹)
    Cancel (x − a); the bracket has n terms, each → aⁿ⁻¹ as x → a, so the limit
    is naⁿ⁻¹. (The result also holds for rational n and a > 0.) Now:
       (x⁵ − 32)/(x − 2) = (x⁵ − 2⁵)/(x − 2) → 5 × 2⁴ = 80
       (x^(1/3) − 8^(1/3))/(x − 8) → (1/3) × 8^(−2/3) = (1/3)(1/4) = 1/12
    For n: n × 2ⁿ⁻¹ = 80; try n = 5: 5 × 16 = 80. (n × 2ⁿ⁻¹ increases with n, so
    n = 5 is the only answer.) Common mistake: writing 32 as 2⁴. Now you try:
    lim (x → 1) (x¹⁰ − 1)/(x − 1) and lim (x → 1) (x⁵ − 1)/(x³ − 1). (10; 5/3)

D10. Find the left- and right-hand limits of |x|/x at 0 and of ⌊x⌋ at 2 (⌊x⌋ is
     the greatest integer ≤ x). For which k does lim (x → 1) f(x) exist, where
     f(x) = x² for x < 1 and f(x) = 2x + k for x ≥ 1?
     Answer: |x|/x: −1 and 1, no limit. ⌊x⌋: 1 and 2, no limit. k = −1 (the
     limit is then 1).
     Teacher explains: For x < 0, |x| = −x so |x|/x = −1; for x > 0 it is +1:
        lim (x → 0⁻) |x|/x = −1,     lim (x → 0⁺) |x|/x = 1
     The two sides disagree, so lim (x → 0) |x|/x does NOT exist (the graph
     jumps). Just left of 2, ⌊x⌋ = 1 (e.g. ⌊1.999⌋ = 1); just right, ⌊x⌋ = 2.
     Again no limit, although ⌊x⌋ is defined at 2 (⌊2⌋ = 2). For the piecewise
     function:
        LHL = lim (x → 1⁻) x² = 1,       RHL = lim (x → 1⁺) (2x + k) = 2 + k
     The limit exists exactly when 1 = 2 + k, i.e. k = −1. Common mistake: using
     f(1) as the left-hand limit. Now you try: the one-sided limits of
     |x − 3|/(x − 3) at 3. (−1 and 1)

D11. Find lim (x → ∞) (3x² − 2x + 1)/(5x² + 4), lim (x → ∞) (2x + 1)/(x² + 3),
     lim (x → ∞) (x³ + 1)/(2x² − 1) and lim (x → ∞) (√(x² + x) − x).
     Answer: 3/5; 0; no finite limit (→ ∞); 1/2.
     Teacher explains: Divide top and bottom by the highest power in the
     DENOMINATOR, and use 1/x → 0, 1/x² → 0:
        (3 − 2/x + 1/x²)/(5 + 4/x²) → 3/5
        (2/x + 1/x²)/(1 + 3/x²) → 0/1 = 0
        (x + 1/x²)/(2 − 1/x²) → ∞
     Rule of degrees: lower on top gives 0, equal degrees give the ratio of the
     leading coefficients, higher on top gives ±∞. For √(x² + x) − x (form
     ∞ − ∞), rationalise:
        (x² + x − x²)/(√(x² + x) + x) = x/(√(x² + x) + x)
        = 1/(√(1 + 1/x) + 1) → 1/2
     Numerical check: x = 10⁶ gives 0.4999999. Common mistake:
     √(x² + x) − x ≈ x − x = 0. Now you try: lim (x → ∞) (4x − 7)/(2x + 9). (2)

D12. Explain why lim (x → 0) 1/x, lim (x → 0) 1/x² and lim (x → 0) sin(1/x) do
     not exist, while lim (x → 0) x sin(1/x) = 0. Prove from the ε-δ definition
     that lim (x → 3) (2x + 1) = 7.
     Answer: 1/x: one-sided limits −∞ and +∞; 1/x²: grows without bound (→ ∞);
     sin(1/x): oscillates between −1 and 1; x sin(1/x) → 0 by the sandwich
     theorem. For 2x + 1, δ = ε/2 works.
     Teacher explains: Three ways a limit can fail:
        1/x        x = ±0.001 gives ±1000: the two sides go opposite ways
        1/x²       x = ±0.001 gives 1,000,000: unbounded, 'tends to ∞'
        sin(1/x)   takes every value from −1 to 1 infinitely often near 0
     For sin(1/x): at x = 1/(nπ) it is 0 and at x = 2/((4n + 1)π) it is 1, and
     both kinds of point come arbitrarily close to 0. But
     −|x| ≤ x sin(1/x) ≤ |x| and both bounds → 0, so x sin(1/x) → 0 (sandwich).
     ε-δ: we need |(2x + 1) − 7| < ε, i.e. 2|x − 3| < ε. Choose δ = ε/2: if
     0 < |x − 3| < δ then |(2x + 1) − 7| = 2|x − 3| < 2δ = ε. For example, to be
     within 0.01 of 7 it suffices to be within 0.005 of 3. Now you try: does
     lim (x → 0) x² sin(1/x) exist? (yes, 0, since −x² ≤ x² sin(1/x) ≤ x²)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Find the limit by direct substitution.
    a) x → 2: x³ − 2x + 5                 b) x → −1: 4x² + 3x − 7
    c) x → 3: (x² + 1)/(x + 2)            d) x → 0: (x + 5)/(x − 5)
    e) x → 1/2: 2x³ + 4x                  f) x → 4: √x + x
    g) x → 9: (√x − 1)/(√x + 1)           h) x → π/2: sin x + cos x
    i) x → π/4: tan x                     j) x → π: x cos x
    k) x → 0: eˣ + 1                      l) x → 1: ln x + x²
    m) x → −2: |x − 1|                    n) x → 3: (x² − 9)/(x + 3)
    o) x → 1: (x² + x + 1)/(x² − x + 1)   p) x → 2: ∛(x + 6)
    q) x → 0: (1 + x)¹⁰                   r) x → π/6: 2 sin x − 1
    s) x → e: ln x                        t) x → 5: 7
    Answers: a) 9   b) −6   c) 2   d) −1   e) 9/4   f) 6   g) 1/2   h) 1   i) 1
             j) −π   k) 2   l) 1   m) 3   n) 0   o) 3   p) 2   q) 1   r) 0
             s) 1   t) 7

M2. The limits are of the form 0/0: factorise and cancel.
    a) x → 2: (x² − 4)/(x − 2)
    b) x → 3: (x² − 9)/(x − 3)
    c) x → 2: (x³ − 8)/(x² − 4)
    d) x → 3: (x² − 5x + 6)/(x² − 9)
    e) x → 1: (x² − 1)/(x² + x − 2)
    f) x → −1: (x³ + 1)/(x + 1)
    g) x → 0: (x² + 3x)/x
    h) x → 4: (x² − 16)/(x² − 3x − 4)
    i) x → 1: (x⁴ − 1)/(x − 1)
    j) x → 2: (x² − 3x + 2)/(x² − 4)
    k) x → −3: (x² + x − 6)/(x² + 5x + 6)
    l) x → 1/2: (4x² − 1)/(2x − 1)
    m) x → 0: ((2 + x)² − 4)/x
    n) x → 0: ((x + 1)³ − 1)/x
    o) x → 1: (x³ − 3x + 2)/(x² − 1)
    p) x → 2: (x³ − 2x² − 4x + 8)/(x² − 4x + 4)
    q) x → 0: (1/(x + 1) − 1)/x
    r) x → 3: (1/x − 1/3)/(x − 3)
    s) x → −2: (x³ + 8)/(x⁴ − 16)
    t) x → 5: (x² − 25)/(x − 5)
    Answers: a) 4   b) 6   c) 3   d) 1/6   e) 2/3   f) 3   g) 3   h) 8/5   i) 4
             j) 1/4   k) 5   l) 2   m) 4   n) 3   o) 0   p) 4   q) −1   r) −1/9
             s) −3/8   t) 10

M3. Rationalise (multiply by the conjugate), then find the limit.
    a) x → 0: (√(x + 4) − 2)/x          b) x → 0: (√(1 + x) − √(1 − x))/x
    c) x → 9: (√x − 3)/(x − 9)          d) x → 4: (x − 4)/(√x − 2)
    e) x → 0: x/(√(x + 9) − 3)          f) x → 1: (√(x + 3) − 2)/(x − 1)
    g) x → 0: (√(1 + x²) − 1)/x²        h) x → 2: (√(3x − 2) − 2)/(x − 2)
    i) x → 0: (√(4 + x) − √(4 − x))/x   j) x → 3: (√(x + 1) − 2)/(√(x + 6) − 3)
    k) x → 0: (√(x + 25) − 5)/x         l) x → 16: (√x − 4)/(x − 16)
