TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always try substitution first and write down what you get (a
  number, 0/0, or non-zero/0); make tables of values on a calculator in RADIAN
  mode; draw the graph with an open circle for the hole; keep a card with the
  standard limits and practise 'matching' the angle and the denominator; for
  one-sided limits test x = a − 0.001 and a + 0.001. Harder: prove lim (x → 0)
  (eˣ − 1)/x = 1 from e = lim (1 + 1/n)ⁿ; use the ε-δ definition to prove
  lim (x → 2) x² = 4 (take δ = min(1, ε/5)); find lim (x → 0) (sin x − x)/x³
  (−1/6) by the triple-angle identity; show that lim (n → ∞) (1 + 1/n)ⁿ exists
  by showing the sequence is increasing and bounded by 3; investigate
  lim (x → 0) x⌊1/x⌋ (1).


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.32 — CONTINUITY
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - f is CONTINUOUS at x = a when three things hold: (1) f(a) is defined; (2)
    lim (x → a) f(x) exists (left- and right-hand limits equal); (3) the limit
    equals f(a). In short lim (x → a) f(x) = f(a). f is LEFT-continuous at a if
    lim (x → a⁻) f(x) = f(a), RIGHT-continuous if lim (x → a⁺) f(x) = f(a).
  - f is continuous on an open interval if it is continuous at every point; on
    [a, b] it must also be right-continuous at a and left-continuous at b.
    Informally: the graph can be drawn without lifting the pen. Continuity is
    only asked at points of the DOMAIN.
  - STANDARD CONTINUOUS FUNCTIONS (on their domains): polynomials, rational
    functions (except where the denominator is 0), sin x, cos x, eˣ, aˣ, |x|
    (everywhere), tan x (except x = π/2 + nπ), ln x (x > 0), √x (x ≥ 0,
    right-continuous at 0). Sums, differences, products, quotients
    (denominator ≠ 0) and COMPOSITIONS of continuous functions are continuous.
  - TYPES OF DISCONTINUITY at a: REMOVABLE — the limit exists but is not f(a),
    or f(a) is undefined (redefine f(a) = the limit to repair it); JUMP — both
    one-sided limits are finite but different (jump = RHL − LHL); INFINITE — f →
    ±∞ on at least one side (a vertical asymptote); OSCILLATING — f keeps
    oscillating, as sin(1/x) at 0.
  - SPECIAL FUNCTIONS: ⌊x⌋ (greatest integer ≤ x) is discontinuous (jump 1) at
    every integer and continuous elsewhere; x − ⌊x⌋ likewise; sgn x has a jump
    at 0; |x| is continuous everywhere (it has a corner at 0, which affects
    differentiability, not continuity).
  - FINDING CONSTANTS in a piecewise function: at each joining point, set
    LHL = RHL = f(a) and solve (one equation per join for one unknown, two
    equations when there are two unknowns).
  - INTERMEDIATE VALUE THEOREM (IVT): if f is continuous on [a, b] and k lies
    between f(a) and f(b), then f(c) = k for some c in (a, b). In particular, if
    f(a) and f(b) have OPPOSITE SIGNS, f has a root in (a, b). Halving the
    interval each time (BISECTION) traps the root. The IVT needs continuity on
    the WHOLE closed interval, and it proves existence only (it does not say how
    many roots, or where exactly).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Let f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x − 3) for x ≠ 3. Is f continuous at 3 if (a) f(3) = 6,
    (b) f(3) = 5, (c) f(3) is not defined? Check the three conditions each time.
    Answer: (a) continuous; (b) not continuous (removable discontinuity); (c)
    not continuous at 3 (3 is not in the domain; the discontinuity is
    removable).
    Teacher explains: For x ≠ 3, (x² − 9)/(x − 3) = (x − 3)(x + 3)/(x − 3)
    = x + 3, so lim (x → 3) f(x) = 6 in every case. Now check the three
    conditions:
               f(3) defined?   limit exists?   limit = f(3)?
       (a)     yes (6)         yes (6)         yes          continuous
       (b)     yes (5)         yes (6)         no           not continuous
       (c)     no              yes (6)         —            not continuous
    The graph is the line y = x + 3 with the point at x = 3 either filled in the
    right place (a), lifted to height 5 (b), or missing (c). In (b) and (c) the
    defect is REMOVABLE: define f(3) = 6 and the function becomes continuous.
    Common mistake: stopping after condition (2) — a limit can exist and still
    differ from the value. Now you try: is g(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1) (x ≠ 1),
    g(1) = 2 continuous at 1? (yes: the limit is 2 = g(1))

D2. Where is each function continuous: (a) (x² + 1)/(x² − 5x + 6), (b) tan x,
    (c) √(x − 1) + ln(4 − x), (d) sin(x²) + e^(cos x), (e) |x − 2|?
    Answer: (a) all x except 2 and 3; (b) all x except π/2 + nπ; (c) 1 ≤ x < 4
    (right-continuous at 1); (d) all real x; (e) all real x.
    Teacher explains: Use the building blocks and the rules. (a) A rational
    function is continuous wherever its denominator is not 0:
    x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3), so it fails only at 2 and 3 (not in the
    domain). (b) tan x = sin x/cos x fails where cos x = 0, i.e. x = π/2 + nπ.
    (c) √(x − 1) needs x ≥ 1 and ln(4 − x) needs x < 4; each piece is continuous
    on its domain, so the sum is continuous on [1, 4), right-continuous at the
    end point 1. (d) x² and sin are continuous, so sin(x²) is (composition);
    cos x and eˣ are continuous, so e^(cos x) is; their sum is continuous
    everywhere. (e) x − 2 and |u| are continuous, so |x − 2| is continuous
    everywhere, even at the corner x = 2. Common mistake: calling a function
    'discontinuous at 2' when 2 is not in its domain and then forgetting to say
    so. Now you try: where is 1/(eˣ − 1) continuous? (all x ≠ 0)

D3. An electricity board charges B(u) = 5u rupees for u ≤ 100 units and
    B(u) = 7u + c for u > 100. Find c so that the bill is continuous at
    100 units. Find k so that f(x) = kx + 1 (x ≤ 2), f(x) = 3x − 1 (x > 2) is
    continuous.
    Answer: c = −200; k = 2.
    Teacher explains: At a joining point, the left piece, the right piece and
    the value must agree:
       B(100) = 5 × 100 = 500 = LHL
       RHL = lim (u → 100⁺) (7u + c) = 700 + c
       700 + c = 500   →   c = −200
    With c = −200 there is no sudden jump in the bill when a family uses one
    unit more than 100: a fair tariff. For f: LHL = f(2) = 2k + 1 and
    RHL = 3(2) − 1 = 5, so 2k + 1 = 5 and k = 2. Check: the pieces 2x + 1 and
    3x − 1 both give 5 at x = 2. Common mistake: using the wrong piece for f(2)
    (check where the '=' sign is). Now you try: k if f(x) = x² + k (x < 3),
    f(x) = 4x (x ≥ 3) is continuous. (k = 3)

D4. Find k so that each function is continuous at 0: (a) f(x) = sin 3x/x
    (x ≠ 0), f(0) = k; (b) g(x) = (1 − cos 4x)/x² (x ≠ 0), g(0) = k; (c)
    h(x) = (eˣ − 1)/x (x ≠ 0), h(0) = k.
    Answer: (a) k = 3; (b) k = 8; (c) k = 1.
    Teacher explains: The value must equal the limit, which we find with the
    standard limits of topic 8.31:
       sin 3x/x = 3 × sin 3x/(3x) → 3
       (1 − cos 4x)/x² = 2 sin² 2x/x² = 8 (sin 2x/(2x))² → 8
       (eˣ − 1)/x → 1
    So k = 3, 8 and 1. These are REMOVABLE discontinuities repaired by the right
    choice of value. Check (a) numerically: x = 0.001
    gives sin 0.003/0.001 ≈ 2.9999955. Common mistake: putting x = 0
    into sin 3x/x and deciding k = 0 (0/0 is not 0). Now you try: k if
    f(x) = tan 2x/x (x ≠ 0), f(0) = k is continuous. (k = 2)

D5. Find a and b so that f is continuous at x = 1, where f(x) = ax + 1 for
    x < 1, f(1) = 3 and f(x) = bx² − 1 for x > 1. Then find a and b so that
    g(x) = x² (x ≤ 1), ax + b (1 < x < 3), 2x + 5 (x ≥ 3) is continuous
    everywhere.
    Answer: a = 2, b = 4. For g: a = 5, b = −4.
    Teacher explains: At x = 1 all three must equal 3:
       LHL = a + 1 = 3        →   a = 2
       RHL = b − 1 = 3        →   b = 4
    For g there are TWO joins, giving two equations:
       x = 1:  1² = a + b             a + b = 1
       x = 3:  3a + b = 2(3) + 5      3a + b = 11
    Subtract: 2a = 10, a = 5, b = −4. Check: the middle piece 5x − 4 gives 1 at
    x = 1 and 11 at x = 3, matching both neighbours. Each piece is a polynomial,
    so continuity can fail only at the joins. Now you try: a and b if
    f(x) = x + a (x < 0), f(0) = b, f(x) = x² + 2 (x > 0). (a = 2, b = 2)

D6. Classify the discontinuity: (a) (x² − 1)/(x − 1) at 1, (b) |x|/x at 0, (c)
    1/(x − 2) at 2, (d) sin(1/x) at 0, (e) f(x) = x + 1 (x < 1), f(x) = 5 − x
    (x ≥ 1) at 1.
    Answer: (a) removable; (b) jump; (c) infinite; (d) oscillating; (e) jump of
    2.
    Teacher explains: Find the one-sided limits and compare:
       function            LHL      RHL      type
       (x² − 1)/(x − 1)    2        2        removable (f(1) undefined)
       |x|/x               −1       1        jump (size 2)
       1/(x − 2)           −∞       +∞       infinite (vertical asymptote)
       sin(1/x)            none     none     oscillating
       piecewise (e)       2        4        jump (size 2)
    Only a REMOVABLE discontinuity can be repaired by changing one value. A jump
    cannot: no value at 1 can equal both 2 and 4. Infinite and oscillating
    discontinuities have no finite one-sided limits at all. Note: for (b), 0 is
    not in the domain of |x|/x, but it is still a jump point of the graph. Now
    you try: classify 1/x² at 0 and ⌊x⌋ at 3. (infinite; jump)

D7. A car park charges ₹30 for each hour or part of an hour. Sketch the charge
    C(t) for 0 < t ≤ 4 hours. Where is it discontinuous? Where is f(x) = ⌊x⌋
    continuous? What about x − ⌊x⌋ and ⌊x⌋ + ⌊−x⌋?
    Answer: C jumps by ₹30 at t = 1, 2, 3; ⌊x⌋ is continuous at every
    non-integer and has a jump at every integer; so does x − ⌊x⌋; ⌊x⌋ + ⌊−x⌋ has
    a REMOVABLE discontinuity at each integer.
    Teacher explains: Sketch C(t) = 30 × (number of hours or part hours):
       ₹120                            o--------*
        ₹90                   o--------*
        ₹60          o--------*
        ₹30 o--------*
            0        1        2        3        4   t (hours)
    The charge stays constant, then jumps; the filled dot shows the value at the
    jump and the open dot the missing end (1 hour exactly costs ₹30, just over 1
    hour costs ₹60). ⌊x⌋: near a non-integer it is constant, so continuous; at
    an integer n, LHL = n − 1 and RHL = n = ⌊n⌋: right-continuous, with a jump
    of 1. x − ⌊x⌋ (the fractional part) has LHL 1 and RHL 0 at each integer:
    jump. For ⌊x⌋ + ⌊−x⌋: at a non-integer it equals −1, at an integer it equals
    0; near n both sides give −1 but the value is 0: removable. Now you try: is
    x⌊x⌋ continuous at 0? (yes: both sides → 0 = f(0))

D8. Show that f(x) = √x is continuous on [0, ∞) and that g(x) = √(4 − x²) is
    continuous on [−2, 2]. Is |x| continuous at 0?
    Answer: Yes (right-continuous at 0); yes (one-sided at ±2); yes.
    Teacher explains: On a CLOSED interval we only need one-sided continuity at
    the ends, because the function does not exist beyond them. √x is continuous
    for x > 0, and lim (x → 0⁺) √x = 0 = √0, so it is right-continuous at 0:
    continuous on [0, ∞). g is the upper half of the circle x² + y² = 4: a
    composition of the polynomial 4 − x² ≥ 0 and √, so continuous on [−2, 2],
    with lim (x → 2⁻) g(x) = 0 = g(2) and lim (x → −2⁺) g(x) = 0 = g(−2). For
    |x| at 0: LHL = lim (−x) = 0, RHL = lim x = 0, |0| = 0: continuous. The
    sharp corner at 0 matters for DIFFERENTIABILITY (topic 8.33), not for
    continuity. Now you try: is ln x continuous on (0, ∞)? Can it be continuous
    on [0, ∞)? (yes; no, ln 0 is not defined)

D9. State the Intermediate Value Theorem. Show that x³ − x − 1 = 0 has a root
    between 1 and 2, and use bisection twice to narrow it down.
    Answer: f(1) = −1 < 0 < 5 = f(2), so a root lies in (1, 2); after two
    bisections it lies in (1.25, 1.5), and a third gives (1.25, 1.375). (The
    root is ≈ 1.3247.)
    Teacher explains: IVT: if f is continuous on [a, b] and k is between f(a)
    and f(b), then f(c) = k for at least one c in (a, b). f is a polynomial,
    hence continuous, and it changes sign on [1, 2], so it must cross 0 there.
    BISECTION: test the midpoint and keep the half where the sign changes:
       interval        midpoint m    f(m)                      new interval
       (1, 2)          1.5           3.375 − 1.5 − 1 = 0.875   (1, 1.5)
       (1, 1.5)        1.25          1.953 − 1.25 − 1 = −0.297 (1.25, 1.5)
       (1.25, 1.5)     1.375         2.600 − 1.375 − 1 = 0.225 (1.25, 1.375)
    Each step halves the width (1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, ...), so ten steps give the
    root to within about 0.001. The IVT promises at least one root; here the
    graph rises steadily for x > 1, so there is exactly one. Now you try: show
    that x³ + 2x − 5 = 0 has a root between 1 and 2. (f(1) = −2, f(2) = 7)

D10. Show that cos x = x has a solution between 0 and π/2. A hiker leaves the
     foot of a hill at 6 a.m., reaches the top at 6 p.m., sleeps, and walks down
     the same path next day from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. Show there is a place where
     she was at the same time of day on both days.
     Answer: g(x) = cos x − x has g(0) = 1 > 0 and g(π/2) = −π/2 < 0, so
     g(c) = 0 for some c. For the hiker, apply the IVT to the difference of her
     two heights.
     Teacher explains: Rearrange as g(x) = 0 with g(x) = cos x − x, continuous
     (difference of continuous functions):
        g(0) = cos 0 − 0 = 1 > 0
        g(π/2) = cos(π/2) − π/2 = −π/2 < 0
     So some c in (0, π/2) has cos c = c (c ≈ 0.739). Hiker: let U(t) be her
     height at time t on day 1 and D(t) on day 2; both are continuous. The
     difference h(t) = U(t) − D(t) is (0 − top) < 0 at 6 a.m. and (top − 0) > 0
     at 6 p.m., so h(t) = 0 at some time: same height, same time, hence the same
     place on the path. The IVT gives existence with no formula for the answer.
     Now you try: show that eˣ = 3 − x has a solution in (0, 1).
     (g(x) = eˣ + x − 3: g(0) = −2, g(1) = e − 2 > 0)

D11. Find and classify all the discontinuities of f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x² − 3x + 2),
     and redefine f where possible to remove them.
     Answer: x = 1: removable (limit −2), define f(1) = −2; x = 2: infinite
     (cannot be removed).
     Teacher explains: Factorise: f(x) = (x − 1)(x + 1)/((x − 1)(x − 2)). f is
     continuous except where the denominator is 0, at x = 1 and x = 2.
        at 1: cancel (x − 1): f(x) = (x + 1)/(x − 2) → 2/(−1) = −2
        at 2: (x + 1)/(x − 2) → 3/0: f → −∞ from the left, +∞ from the right
     At x = 1 the limit exists, so defining f(1) = −2 makes f continuous there
     (removable). At x = 2 there is a vertical asymptote: an infinite
     discontinuity, which no value can repair. Rule for rational functions: a
     zero of the denominator that cancels completely with the numerator is a
     hole (removable); one that does not cancel is an asymptote. Now you try:
     find and classify the discontinuities of (x² − 4)/(x² − x − 2). (x = 2
     removable, limit 4/3; x = −1 infinite)

D12. Explain why the IVT fails for f(x) = 1/x on [−1, 1], and why its converse
     is false. Prove that every continuous f: [0, 1] → [0, 1] has a FIXED POINT
     (f(c) = c).
     Answer: 1/x is not continuous on [−1, 1] (undefined at 0), so although
     f(−1) = −1 < 0 < 1 = f(1) there is no root. Converse: x² takes the value 0
     in (−1, 1) without a sign change. Fixed point: apply the IVT to
     g(x) = f(x) − x.
     Teacher explains: The IVT needs continuity on the WHOLE closed interval.
     1/x jumps from −∞ to +∞ across 0 and never takes the value 0: no
     contradiction, because the hypothesis fails. The converse ('if there is a
     root then f changes sign') is false: f(x) = x² has f(−1) = f(1) = 1 > 0 but
     f(0) = 0. FIXED POINT: let g(x) = f(x) − x, continuous on [0, 1]. Since
     0 ≤ f(x) ≤ 1:
        g(0) = f(0) − 0 ≥ 0,      g(1) = f(1) − 1 ≤ 0
     If g(0) = 0 or g(1) = 0 we are done; otherwise g(0) > 0 > g(1) and the IVT
     gives c in (0, 1) with g(c) = 0, i.e. f(c) = c. Example: f(x) = cos x on
     [0, 1] maps into [0, 1] and has the fixed point c ≈ 0.739. The same idea
     proves that every polynomial of ODD degree has a real root (it is negative
     for large negative x and positive for large positive x, or the other way).
     Now you try: show that x⁵ − 3x + 1 = 0 has a root in (0, 1). (f(0) = 1,
     f(1) = −1)

M10. Show that f(x) = 0 has a root in the interval: give f at the end points (f
     is continuous there).
     a) x³ − x − 1 on [1, 2]
     b) x³ + 2x − 5 on [1, 2]

     e) cos x − x on [0, π/2]
     f) eˣ + x − 3 on [0, 1]
     g) x³ − 4x + 1 on [0, 1]
     h) x⁴ − x − 10 on [1, 2]
     i) 2ˣ − 3x on [0, 1]
     j) ln x + x − 2 on [1, 2]
     k) x³ + x² − 1 on [0, 1]
     l) sin x − x/2 on [π/2, π]
     m) x³ − 3x + 1 on [1, 2]
     n) x − e⁻ˣ on [0, 1]
     o) x⁴ − 5x + 2 on [0, 1]
     p) tan x − 1 − x on [1, 3/2]
     Answers:
       a) f(1) = −1, f(2) = 5; sign change, so a root
       b) f(1) = −2, f(2) = 7; sign change, so a root
       c) f(0) = 1, f(1) = −1; sign change, so a root
       d) f(1) = −1, f(2) = 2; sign change, so a root
       e) f(0) = 1, f(π/2) = −π/2; sign change, so a root
       f) f(0) = −2, f(1) = e − 2 ≈ 0.718; sign change, so a root
       g) f(0) = 1, f(1) = −2; sign change, so a root
       h) f(1) = −10, f(2) = 4; sign change, so a root
       i) f(0) = 1, f(1) = −1; sign change, so a root
       j) f(1) = −1, f(2) = ln 2 ≈ 0.693; sign change, so a root
       k) f(0) = −1, f(1) = 1; sign change, so a root
       l) f(π/2) = 1 − π/4 ≈ 0.215, f(π) = −π/2; sign change, so a root
       m) f(1) = −1, f(2) = 3; sign change, so a root
       n) f(0) = −1, f(1) = 1 − 1/e ≈ 0.632; sign change, so a root
       o) f(0) = 2, f(1) = −2; sign change, so a root
       p) f(1) = tan 1 − 2 ≈ −0.443, f(3/2) = tan(3/2) − 5/2 ≈ 11.601; sign
          change, so a root

M11. Find consecutive integers n, n + 1 between which the LARGEST real root
     lies, then do two steps of bisection.
     a) x³ − x − 1 = 0
     b) x³ + 2x − 5 = 0
     c) x³ − 2x − 5 = 0
     d) x³ + x − 1 = 0
     e) x³ − 6x + 2 = 0
     f) x⁴ − 2x − 1 = 0
     g) x³ − 9 = 0
     h) x² − 7 = 0
     i) x³ − 3x² + 1 = 0
     j) x³ + 3x − 6 = 0
     Answers:
       a) (1, 2); (1, 1.5); (1.25, 1.5)
       b) (1, 2); (1, 1.5); (1.25, 1.5)
       c) (2, 3); (2, 2.5); (2, 2.25)
       d) (0, 1); (0.5, 1); (0.5, 0.75)
       e) (2, 3); (2, 2.5); (2.25, 2.5)
       f) (1, 2); (1, 1.5); (1.25, 1.5)
       g) (2, 3); (2, 2.5); (2, 2.25)
       h) (2, 3); (2.5, 3); (2.5, 2.75)
       i) (2, 3); (2.5, 3); (2.75, 3)
       j) (1, 2); (1, 1.5); (1.25, 1.5)

M12. True or false? Give a reason or a counterexample for 'false'.
     a) Every polynomial is continuous at every real number.
     b) If lim (x → a) f(x) exists, then f is continuous at a.
     c) If f is continuous at a, then lim (x → a) f(x) = f(a).
     d) |x| is continuous at 0.
     e) ⌊x⌋ is continuous at x = 2.
     f) tan x is continuous on (−π/2, π/2).
     g) 1/x is continuous on its domain.
     h) If f and g are continuous at a, so is f/g.
     i) If f is continuous and f(1) < 0 < f(2), then f has a root in (1, 2).
     j) If f has a root in (a, b), then f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs.
     k) A jump discontinuity can be removed by redefining f at one point.
     l) The sum of two discontinuous functions is always discontinuous.
     m) sin(1/x), with f(0) = 0, is continuous at 0.
     n) x sin(1/x), with f(0) = 0, is continuous at 0.
     o) Every odd-degree polynomial has at least one real root.
     p) If f is continuous on [0, 1] with values in [0, 1], then f(c) = c for
        some c.
     Answers:
       a) true
       b) false (e.g. f(a) may differ or be undefined)
       c) true
       d) true
       e) false (jump from 1 to 2)
       f) true
       g) true (0 is not in the domain)
       h) false (only if g(a) ≠ 0)
       i) true (IVT)
       j) false (x² on [−1, 1])
       k) false (LHL ≠ RHL, so no value equals both)
       l) false (⌊x⌋ + (−⌊x⌋) = 0)
       m) false (oscillates)
       n) true
       o) true (IVT)
       p) true (fixed point)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw the graph of every piecewise function before deciding; fill
  in a three-column table (f(a), LHL, RHL) for each joining point; say 'no
  lifting of the pen' as the first test; for the IVT always write 'f is
  continuous on [a, b] because ...' before quoting signs. Harder: prove that if
  f is continuous and f(x) = 0 only at x = 1 and x = 3 then f has constant sign
  on (1, 3); show that x = cos x has exactly one solution; prove that a
  continuous function on [0, 2] with f(0) = f(2) takes equal values at two
  points 1 apart (apply the IVT to f(x + 1) − f(x)); study the Dirichlet
  function (1 for rational x, 0 for irrational x), discontinuous everywhere, and
  x times it, continuous only at 0.


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.33 — DERIVATIVE: DEFINITION FROM FIRST PRINCIPLES; GEOMETRIC MEANING
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - AVERAGE RATE OF CHANGE of y = f(x) from x = a to x = a + h is
    (f(a + h) − f(a))/h. On the graph it is the SLOPE OF THE SECANT (chord)
    joining (a, f(a)) and (a + h, f(a + h)).
  - The DERIVATIVE of f at a is f'(a) = lim h→0 (f(a + h) − f(a))/h, when this
    limit exists (as a finite number). Equivalent form: f'(a) = lim x→a
    (f(x) − f(a))/(x − a). Notation: f'(x), dy/dx, y', d/dx (f(x)), Df(x).
    Finding it straight from the limit is called differentiating FROM FIRST
    PRINCIPLES (ab initio).
  - GEOMETRIC MEANING: f'(a) is the slope of the TANGENT to y = f(x) at (a,
    f(a)); the tangent is the limiting position of the secants. Its equation is
    y − f(a) = f'(a)(x − a). PHYSICAL MEANING: the INSTANTANEOUS rate of change
    of y with respect to x (velocity = ds/dt, marginal cost, rate of growth).
  - Standard first-principles results: d/dx (c) = 0; d/dx (xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹ (binomial
    expansion of (x + h)ⁿ); d/dx (ax² + bx + c) = 2ax + b; d/dx (1/x) = −1/x²;
    d/dx (√x) = 1/(2√x) (rationalise the numerator); d/dx (sin x) = cos x and
    d/dx (cos x) = −sin x (x in RADIANS, using lim h→0 sin h/h = 1 and lim h→0
    (1 − cos h)/h = 0); d/dx (eˣ) = eˣ (using lim h→0 (eʰ − 1)/h = 1).
  - LEFT and RIGHT derivatives: Lf'(a) = lim h→0⁻ (f(a + h) − f(a))/h,
    Rf'(a) = lim h→0⁺ (f(a + h) − f(a))/h. f is differentiable at a exactly when
    both exist and are equal.
  - DIFFERENTIABLE ⇒ CONTINUOUS (proof:
    f(a + h) − f(a) = [(f(a + h) − f(a))/h] × h → f'(a) × 0 = 0). The converse
    is FALSE: |x| is continuous at 0 but has a CORNER there (Lf'(0) = −1,
    Rf'(0) = 1); x^(2/3) has a CUSP and ∛x a VERTICAL TANGENT at 0.
  - NUMERICAL DERIVATIVES: the difference quotients for h = 0.1, 0.01, 0.001
    approach f'(a); the central difference (f(a + h) − f(a − h))/(2h) approaches
    much faster.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A stone is dropped from a bridge; after t seconds it has fallen s = 5t²
    metres. Find its average speed from t = 2 to t = 2 + h for h = 1, 0.1, 0.01,
    0.001, and hence its speed at the instant t = 2.
    Answer: Average speed = 20 + 5h m/s: 25, 20.5, 20.05, 20.005. The
    instantaneous speed at t = 2 is 20 m/s.
    Teacher explains: Average speed = distance ÷ time over the small interval:
       (s(2 + h) − s(2))/h = (5(4 + 4h + h²) − 20)/h = (20h + 5h²)/h = 20 + 5h
            h       average speed (m/s)
            1       25
            0.1     20.5
            0.01    20.05
            0.001   20.005
    As h shrinks the averages close in on 20, so the speed AT t = 2 is lim h→0
    (20 + 5h) = 20 m/s. This limit is exactly the derivative ds/dt at t = 2. We
    may cancel h because h ≠ 0 while we compute the quotient; only then do we
    let h → 0. Common mistake: putting h = 0 straight into (s(2 + h) − s(2))/h,
    which gives the meaningless 0/0. Now you try: find the speed at t = 3. (30
    m/s)

D2. Find the derivatives of x² and x³ from first principles. Then prove d/dx
    (xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹ for every positive integer n.
    Answer: d/dx (x²) = 2x, d/dx (x³) = 3x², and in general nxⁿ⁻¹.
    Teacher explains: Always write the definition first, then expand, cancel h,
    take the limit:
       f(x) = x²:  (f(x + h) − f(x))/h = (x² + 2xh + h² − x²)/h = 2x + h → 2x
       f(x) = x³:  ((x + h)³ − x³)/h = (3x²h + 3xh² + h³)/h
                                    = 3x² + 3xh + h² → 3x²
    For xⁿ use the binomial theorem (topic 8.18):
       (x + h)ⁿ = xⁿ + nxⁿ⁻¹h + C(n, 2)xⁿ⁻²h² + ... + hⁿ
       ((x + h)ⁿ − xⁿ)/h = nxⁿ⁻¹ + C(n, 2)xⁿ⁻²h + ... + hⁿ⁻¹ → nxⁿ⁻¹
    Every term after the first still contains h, so it tends to 0. The rule
    "bring the power down, reduce the power by 1" is called the POWER RULE; it
    also holds for negative and fractional powers (see D4, D5 and topic 8.34).
    Common mistake: forgetting the middle terms, as in (x + h)² = x² + h². Now
    you try: find d/dx (x⁴) from first principles. (4x³)

D3. Find from first principles the derivative of f(x) = ax² + bx + c, and use it
    to find the derivative of 3x² − 5x + 2 and its value at x = 1.
    Answer: f'(x) = 2ax + b. For 3x² − 5x + 2 the derivative is 6x − 5, and at
    x = 1 it equals 1.
    Teacher explains: Work out f(x + h) − f(x) first, so the x² and x and c
    parts cancel:
       f(x + h) = a(x + h)² + b(x + h) + c = ax² + 2axh + ah² + bx + bh + c
       f(x + h) − f(x) = 2axh + ah² + bh
       (f(x + h) − f(x))/h = 2ax + ah + b  →  2ax + b   as h → 0
    The constant c disappears: a constant does not change, so its rate of change
    is 0. With a = 3, b = −5, c = 2: f'(x) = 6x − 5 and f'(1) = 1. This also
    shows that differentiation is LINEAR: the derivative of a sum is the sum of
    the derivatives and constants multiply through. Common mistake: writing the
    derivative of −5x as −5x or 5. Now you try: 4x² + 7x − 9. (8x + 7)

D4. Using the definition, show that d/dx (1/x) = −1/x² (x ≠ 0), and find the
    slope of the curve y = 1/x at (2, 1/2).
    Answer: The derivative is −1/x²; the slope at (2, 1/2) is −1/4.
    Teacher explains: Combine the two fractions over a common denominator before
    dividing by h:
       1/(x + h) − 1/x = (x − (x + h))/(x(x + h)) = −h/(x(x + h))
       (1/(x + h) − 1/x)/h = −1/(x(x + h))  →  −1/x²   as h → 0
    This agrees with the power rule for n = −1: d/dx (x⁻¹) = −x⁻². At x = 2 the
    slope is −1/4. The slope is negative everywhere, so y = 1/x is falling on
    each branch. Common mistake: writing 1/(x + h) = 1/x + 1/h (false!). Now you
    try: d/dx (1/x²) from first principles. (−2/x³)

D5. Find d/dx (√x) from first principles (x > 0) and hence the slope of y = √x
    at x = 4.
    Answer: d/dx (√x) = 1/(2√x); at x = 4 the slope is 1/4.
    Teacher explains: A difference of square roots over h gives 0/0; RATIONALISE
    the numerator by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate √(x + h) + √x:
       (√(x + h) − √x)/h × (√(x + h) + √x)/(√(x + h) + √x)
         = ((x + h) − x)/(h(√(x + h) + √x))
         = 1/(√(x + h) + √x)  →  1/(2√x)   as h → 0
    Power-rule check: √x = x^(1/2), so the derivative is
    (1/2)x^(−1/2) = 1/(2√x). At x = 0 the quotient √h/h = 1/√h → ∞, so √x has a
    vertical tangent there and is NOT differentiable at 0. Common mistake:
    "multiplying out" the numerator only and leaving h in the denominator. Now
    you try: find d/dx (√(x + 5)) from first principles. (1/(2√(x + 5)))

D6. Prove that d/dx (sin x) = cos x, x in radians. Why must x be in radians?
    Answer: The difference quotient equals cos(x + h/2) × sin(h/2)/(h/2), which
    tends to cos x × 1 = cos x.
    Teacher explains: Use the formula sin C − sin D = 2 cos((C + D)/2)
    sin((C − D)/2):
       sin(x + h) − sin x = 2 cos(x + h/2) sin(h/2)
       (sin(x + h) − sin x)/h = cos(x + h/2) × sin(h/2)/(h/2)
    As h → 0, cos(x + h/2) → cos x (cosine is continuous) and sin(h/2)/(h/2) → 1
    (standard limit, topic 8.31). So the limit is cos x. The standard limit
    lim θ→0 sin θ/θ = 1 is TRUE ONLY IN RADIANS; in degrees it would be π/180,
    and every trig derivative would carry an extra factor π/180. Check the
    geometry: at x = 0 the slope of y = sin x is cos 0 = 1, so the graph leaves
    the origin along y = x. Common mistake: expanding
    sin(x + h) = sin x + sin h. Now you try: prove d/dx (cos x) = −sin x using
    cos C − cos D = −2 sin((C + D)/2) sin((C − D)/2). (the quotient is
    −sin(x + h/2) × sin(h/2)/(h/2) → −sin x)

D7. Given lim h→0 (eʰ − 1)/h = 1, prove d/dx (eˣ) = eˣ. Check the limit
    numerically for h = 0.1, 0.01, 0.001.
    Answer: (eˣ⁺ʰ − eˣ)/h = eˣ(eʰ − 1)/h → eˣ × 1 = eˣ. The quotients are
    1.051709, 1.005017, 1.000500, approaching 1.
    Teacher explains: Factor out eˣ, which does not depend on h:
       (e^(x + h) − eˣ)/h = eˣ(eʰ − 1)/h  →  eˣ × 1 = eˣ
            h        (eʰ − 1)/h
            0.1      1.051709
            0.01     1.005017
            0.001    1.000500
    So eˣ is its own derivative: at every point the slope of y = eˣ equals its
    height. This is what makes e special; for another base, (aʰ − 1)/h → ln a,
    so d/dx (aˣ) = aˣ ln a (topic 8.35). Common mistake: writing d/dx
    (eˣ) = xeˣ⁻¹ (the power rule is for xⁿ with a FIXED power, not for a
    variable power). Now you try: find d/dx (e³ˣ) from first principles, using
    (e³ʰ − 1)/h = 3(e³ʰ − 1)/(3h) → 3. (3e³ˣ)

D8. Find the slope and the equation of the tangent to y = x² at (3, 9). Show
    that the secant from (3, 9) to (3 + h, (3 + h)²) has slope 6 + h and explain
    how the tangent is the limit of the secants.
    Answer: Slope 6; tangent y = 6x − 9.
    Teacher explains: Secant slope = ((3 + h)² − 9)/h = (6h + h²)/h = 6 + h. For
    h = 1, 0.5, 0.1 the secants have slopes 7, 6.5, 6.1: they swing round and
    settle on the tangent of slope 6.
       y |        /  secant, h = 1 (slope 7)
         |       / .·  tangent (slope 6)
         |      /.·
         |    ·/·        the chord through (3, 9) and (4, 16)
         |  ·  (3, 9)    turns into the tangent as h → 0
         +----------------- x
    Point-slope form: y − 9 = 6(x − 3), so y = 6x − 9. Check: the line meets the
    parabola where x² = 6x − 9, (x − 3)² = 0 — a DOUBLE root, the algebraic sign
    of touching. Common mistake: using the slope formula 2x without putting
    x = 3, and writing "y − 9 = 2x(x − 3)", which is not a line. Now you try:
    the tangent to y = x³ at (1, 1). (slope 3; y = 3x − 2)

D9. The radius of a circular ripple is r cm. (i) Find the rate of change of its
    area A = πr² with respect to r when r = 5. (ii) Show that dA/dr equals the
    circumference. (iii) A cube of side x has volume V = x³; find dV/dx at x = 4
    and interpret it.
    Answer: (i) 10π ≈ 31.42 cm² per cm; (ii) dA/dr = 2πr = circumference; (iii)
    dV/dx = 3x² = 48 cm³ per cm at x = 4.
    Teacher explains: By the power rule dA/dr = π × 2r = 2πr; at r = 5,
    10π ≈ 31.42. Meaning: when r = 5, a small increase δr in the radius
    increases the area by about 10π δr, because the extra area is a thin ring of
    length 2πr and width δr. That is why dA/dr is the circumference. For the
    cube, dV/dx = 3x² = 3 × 16 = 48 at x = 4: the extra volume when the side
    grows by δx is about three square slabs x² δx on three faces. The unit of a
    rate is (unit of y) per (unit of x). Common mistake: giving the area at
    r = 5 (25π) instead of its rate of change. Now you try: V = (4/3)πr³ for a
    sphere: find dV/dr at r = 3. (4πr² = 36π ≈ 113.10 cm³ per cm, the surface
    area)

D10. Show that f(x) = |x| is continuous but not differentiable at x = 0. Then
     prove: if f is differentiable at a, it is continuous at a.
     Answer: Lf'(0) = −1 and Rf'(0) = 1 are different, so f'(0) does not exist,
     while lim x→0 |x| = 0 = f(0). Proof of the theorem below.
     Teacher explains: For |x| at 0 the difference quotient is |h|/h:
        h > 0:  |h|/h = h/h = 1       so  Rf'(0) = 1
        h < 0:  |h|/h = −h/h = −1     so  Lf'(0) = −1
     The graph is a V with a CORNER at the origin: the slope jumps from −1 to 1,
     so there is no single tangent. Yet |x| → 0 = |0| as x → 0, so it is
     continuous. Theorem: if f'(a) exists, then for h ≠ 0
        f(a + h) − f(a) = [(f(a + h) − f(a))/h] × h  →  f'(a) × 0 = 0
     so f(a + h) → f(a): f is continuous at a. The contrapositive is useful: a
     function that is NOT continuous at a (a jump, a hole) cannot be
     differentiable there. The converse fails, as |x| shows. Other failures:
     x^(2/3) has a CUSP at 0 (quotient h^(−1/3) → +∞ on the right and −∞ on the
     left) and ∛x has a VERTICAL TANGENT (quotient h^(−2/3) → +∞). Common
     mistake: thinking "no formula for the whole line" means "not
     differentiable". Now you try: is f(x) = x|x| differentiable at 0? (yes: the
     quotient is h|h|/h = |h| → 0, so f'(0) = 0)

D11. Find a and b so that f(x) = x² for x ≤ 1, f(x) = ax + b for x > 1 is
     differentiable at x = 1. Then decide whether g(x) = x² + 1 for x < 1,
     g(x) = 2x for x ≥ 1 is differentiable at 1.
     Answer: a = 2, b = −1. g is differentiable at 1 with g'(1) = 2.
     Teacher explains: Two conditions: CONTINUITY (the pieces meet) and EQUAL
     one-sided slopes.
        continuity at 1:   1² = a(1) + b          a + b = 1
        left slope:  Lf'(1) = 2x at x = 1 = 2
        right slope: Rf'(1) = a                    a = 2, so b = −1
     So f(x) = 2x − 1 for x > 1: this is exactly the tangent to y = x² at
     (1, 1), which is why the join is smooth. For g: left value 1² + 1 = 2 and
     right value 2(1) = 2, so g is continuous; Lg'(1) = 2(1) = 2 and Rg'(1) = 2,
     equal, so g'(1) = 2. Common mistake: checking only the slopes. If the
     pieces do not meet, the one-sided difference quotient (f(1 + h) − f(1))/h
     blows up and f is not differentiable, whatever the slopes are. Now you try:
     find k so that f(x) = x³ (x < 2), kx − 16 (x ≥ 2) is differentiable at 2,
     and check continuity. (k = 12; 8 = 24 − 16)

D12. For f(x) = x³ at x = 2, compute the forward difference quotients
     (f(2 + h) − f(2))/h and the central differences (f(2 + h) − f(2 − h))/(2h)
     for h = 0.1, 0.01, 0.001. Which approaches f'(2) = 12 faster, and why?
     Answer: Forward: 12.61, 12.0601, 12.006001. Central: 12.01, 12.0001,
     12.000001. The central difference is far more accurate.
     Teacher explains: Algebra explains the table:
        forward: ((2 + h)³ − 8)/h = 12 + 6h + h²      error ≈ 6h
        central: ((2 + h)³ − (2 − h)³)/(2h) = 12 + h²  error = h²
             h        forward       central
             0.1      12.610000     12.010000
             0.01     12.060100     12.000100
             0.001    12.006001     12.000001
     Each time h is divided by 10, the forward error drops about 10 times but
     the central error drops 100 times, because the h terms cancel in the
     symmetric quotient. Calculators and computers use such quotients. Warning:
     for tiny h (say 10⁻¹²) rounding errors in f(2 + h) − f(2) take over, so h
     cannot be made as small as we like on a machine. Common mistake: forgetting
     to divide by 2h in the central difference. Now you try: compute
     sin(0.1)/0.1, the forward quotient of sin x at 0 with h = 0.1. (0.998334,
     close to cos 0 = 1)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Find the average rate of change (the slope of the secant) of f over the
    given interval.
    a) x²; [1, 3]      b) x²; [−2, 0]        c) x³; [0, 2]
    d) x³; [1, 1.1]    e) 3x + 7; [−5, 4]    f) x² − 4x; [0, 4]
    g) 1/x; [1, 4]     h) 1/x; [−2, −1]      i) √x; [4, 9]
    j) √x; [0, 1]      k) 2x² + x; [1, 2]    l) 5 − x²; [−1, 3]
    m) x⁴; [−1, 1]     n) x⁴; [1, 2]         o) sin x; [0, π/2]
    p) cos x; [0, π]   q) eˣ; [0, 1]         r) ln x; [1, e]
    s) 2ˣ; [0, 3]      t) x³ − 3x; [−2, 2]
    Answers: a) 4   b) −2   c) 4   d) 3.31   e) 3   f) 0   g) −1/4   h) −1/2
             i) 1/5   j) 1   k) 7   l) −2   m) 0   n) 15   o) 2/π ≈ 0.6366
             p) −2/π ≈ −0.6366   q) e − 1 ≈ 1.7183   r) 1/(e − 1) ≈ 0.5820
             s) 7/3   t) 1

M2. Write the difference quotient (f(x + h) − f(x))/h in simplified form
    (h ≠ 0). Then let h → 0.

M9. Find the left derivative L and right derivative R at the given point, and
    state whether f is differentiable there.
    a) |x| at 0                          b) |x − 2| at 2

      k) L = −1, R = 1; not differentiable
      l) L = 0, R = 0; differentiable, f'(0) = 0
      m) L = 0, R = 2; not differentiable
      n) L = 0, R = 0; differentiable, f'(0) = 0

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: Start every first-principles question by writing the definition in
  full, then do the algebra in three visible steps: expand or combine, cancel h,
  let h → 0. Use numbers first (x = 3) before letters. Draw a secant and slide
  the second point towards the first; a table of difference quotients (D1, D12)
  makes the limit concrete. For the corner of |x|, draw the V and put a ruler on
  each arm. Harder: Prove d/dx (tan x) = sec²x and d/dx (ln x) = 1/x from first
  principles (use lim (ln(1 + u))/u = 1). Show f(x) = x² sin(1/x), f(0) = 0 is
  differentiable at 0 but f' is not continuous there. If f(x + y) = f(x)f(y) for
  all x, y and f'(0) = 2, f(0) = 1, show f'(x) = 2f(x). Where is
  f(x) = |x² − 4x + 3| not differentiable? (x = 1 and x = 3.)


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.34 — DIFFERENTIATION RULES: PRODUCT, QUOTIENT, CHAIN RULE
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - POWER RULE: d/dx (xⁿ) = nxⁿ⁻¹ for EVERY real n (whole, negative,
    fractional). Rewrite first: 1/x³ = x⁻³, √x = x^(1/2), 1/∛x = x^(−1/3),
    x√x = x^(3/2). d/dx (c) = 0 for a constant c.
  - LINEARITY: (cf)' = cf' and (f ± g)' = f' ± g'. So a polynomial is
    differentiated term by term. Simplify a quotient with a ONE-TERM denominator
    by splitting it before differentiating: (x² + 3x)/x = x + 3.
  - PRODUCT RULE: (uv)' = u'v + uv'. For three factors
    (uvw)' = u'vw + uv'w + uvw'. The derivative of a product is NOT the product
    of the derivatives.
  - QUOTIENT RULE: (u/v)' = (u'v − uv')/v² (v ≠ 0): "low d-high minus high
    d-low, over low squared". The order in the numerator matters. Special case:
    (1/v)' = −v'/v².
  - CHAIN RULE: if y = f(u) and u = g(x), then dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx), i.e.
    (f(g(x)))' = f'(g(x)) × g'(x): differentiate the OUTSIDE function, keep the
    inside unchanged, then multiply by the derivative of the INSIDE. GENERAL
    POWER RULE: d/dx [g(x)]ⁿ = n[g(x)]ⁿ⁻¹ g'(x); e.g. d/dx (3x² + 1)⁵
    = 5(3x² + 1)⁴ × 6x = 30x(3x² + 1)⁴.
  - Useful chain results: d/dx √g = g'/(2√g); d/dx (1/g) = −g'/g²; d/dx
    (ax + b)ⁿ = na(ax + b)ⁿ⁻¹.
  - COMBINING RULES: decide the LAST operation (product, quotient or function of
    a function) and apply that rule first; use the others inside. Take out
    common factors to present answers neatly, e.g. x(x + 1)⁵ gives
    (x + 1)⁴(6x + 1).
  - Rules work with tables of values too: (fg)'(a) = f'(a)g(a) + f(a)g'(a),
    (f∘g)'(a) = f'(g(a)) g'(a).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Differentiate (i) x⁷, (ii) 1/x³, (iii) √x, (iv) 1/∛x, (v) x²√x, (vi)
    6/x^(2/3). Explain why rewriting as a power comes first.
    Answer: (i) 7x⁶; (ii) −3/x⁴; (iii) 1/(2√x); (iv) −1/(3x∛x); (v) (5/2)x√x;
    (vi) −4/x^(5/3).
    Teacher explains: The power rule only works on the form xⁿ, so rewrite every
    root and every reciprocal as a power, differentiate, then tidy up:
       (i)   x⁷            →  7x⁶
       (ii)  1/x³ = x⁻³     →  −3x⁻⁴ = −3/x⁴
       (iii) √x = x^(1/2)   →  (1/2)x^(−1/2) = 1/(2√x)
       (iv)  1/∛x = x^(−1/3) → (−1/3)x^(−4/3) = −1/(3x∛x)
       (v)   x²√x = x^(5/2) → (5/2)x^(3/2) = (5/2)x√x
       (vi)  6x^(−2/3)      →  6 × (−2/3)x^(−5/3) = −4/x^(5/3)
    Subtracting 1 from a negative power makes it MORE negative: −3 − 1 = −4,
    −1/3 − 1 = −4/3. Common mistakes: d/dx (1/x³) = 1/(3x²) (differentiating the
    denominator), and −1/3 − 1 = −2/3. Now you try: x^(−5), ∛(x²), 1/(x√x).
    (−5x⁻⁶; 2/(3∛x); −3/(2x²√x))

D2. A small factory's cost of making x bicycles a day is
    C(x) = 0.01x³ − 0.6x² + 15x + 2,000 rupees. Find the marginal cost C'(x) and
    its value when x = 20 and x = 40. What does it mean?
    Answer: C'(x) = 0.03x² − 1.2x + 15; C'(20) = ₹3 and C'(40) = ₹15 per
    bicycle.
    Teacher explains: Differentiate term by term (sum rule) and keep constants
    as multipliers (constant multiple rule); the fixed cost 2,000 has derivative
    0:
       C'(x) = 0.01 × 3x² − 0.6 × 2x + 15 + 0 = 0.03x² − 1.2x + 15
       C'(20) = 0.03 × 400 − 24 + 15 = 12 − 24 + 15 = 3
       C'(40) = 0.03 × 1,600 − 48 + 15 = 48 − 48 + 15 = 15
    Meaning: at 20 bicycles a day, making one more costs about ₹3 extra; at 40 a
    day, about ₹15 extra (the machines are overloaded). Check with actual costs:
    C(21) − C(20) = 2,143.01 − 2,140 = 3.01 ≈ 3. The fixed cost does not affect
    the marginal cost. Common mistake: forgetting that the derivative of the
    constant 2,000 is 0, not 2,000. Now you try: R(x) = 50x − 0.5x²; find
    R'(30). (R'(x) = 50 − x, R'(30) = 20)

D3. Prove the product rule (uv)' = u'v + uv', and use it to differentiate
    y = (x² + 1)(x³ − 2x). Check by expanding first.
    Answer: y' = 5x⁴ − 3x² − 2.
    Teacher explains: Add and subtract u(x + h)v(x) in the difference quotient:
       u(x + h)v(x + h) − u(x)v(x)
         = u(x + h)[v(x + h) − v(x)] + v(x)[u(x + h) − u(x)]
    Divide by h and let h → 0: u(x + h) → u(x) (differentiable, hence
    continuous), so the limit is uv' + vu'. Now the example, with u = x² + 1 and
    v = x³ − 2x:
       u' = 2x,   v' = 3x² − 2
       y' = 2x(x³ − 2x) + (x² + 1)(3x² − 2)
          = 2x⁴ − 4x² + 3x⁴ + x² − 2 = 5x⁴ − 3x² − 2
    Check: y = x⁵ − x³ − 2x, so y' = 5x⁴ − 3x² − 2. Same. Common mistake:
    (uv)' = u'v', which here gives 2x(3x² − 2) = 6x³ − 4x, wrong. Now you try:
    (2x − 1)(x² + 3) by the product rule. (6x² − 2x + 6)

D4. Differentiate y = (2x + 1)/(x − 3) and y = x²/(x + 1) with the quotient
    rule. Where are these derivatives defined?
    Answer: y' = −7/(x − 3)² (x ≠ 3); y' = (x² + 2x)/(x + 1)² (x ≠ −1).
    Teacher explains: Write u (top), v (bottom), u', v' in a small table first:
       u = 2x + 1   u' = 2      v = x − 3   v' = 1
       y' = (u'v − uv')/v² = (2(x − 3) − (2x + 1)(1))/(x − 3)²
          = (2x − 6 − 2x − 1)/(x − 3)² = −7/(x − 3)²
       u = x²   u' = 2x         v = x + 1   v' = 1
       y' = (2x(x + 1) − x²)/(x + 1)² = (x² + 2x)/(x + 1)² = x(x + 2)/(x + 1)²
    The derivative −7/(x − 3)² is always negative: the graph of the first
    function falls on each side of x = 3. Common mistakes: reversing the
    numerator (uv' − u'v gives the wrong sign), forgetting to square v, and
    dropping brackets so that −(2x + 1) becomes −2x + 1. Now you try:
    (3x − 2)/(x + 4). (14/(x + 4)²)

D5. Differentiate y = (3x² + 1)⁵ using the chain rule. Explain the rule with
    u = 3x² + 1, and explain "rates multiply" with a simple example.
    Answer: dy/dx = 30x(3x² + 1)⁴.
    Teacher explains: Let u = 3x² + 1, so y = u⁵:
       dy/du = 5u⁴,   du/dx = 6x
       dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx) = 5u⁴ × 6x = 30x(3x² + 1)⁴
    In words: bring down the power, keep the bracket as it is, lower the power
    by 1, then MULTIPLY BY THE DERIVATIVE OF THE BRACKET. Why rates multiply: if
    a cyclist's gear makes the wheel turn 3 times per pedal turn (du/dx = 3) and
    each wheel turn moves the bike 2 m (dy/du = 2), the bike moves 6 m per pedal
    turn (dy/dx = 2 × 3). Expanding (3x² + 1)⁵ first would take 6 terms and much
    longer. Common mistake: 5(3x² + 1)⁴ with the factor 6x missing. Now you try:
    (1 − 4x)⁶ and (x² + 5x)³. (−24(1 − 4x)⁵; 3(2x + 5)(x² + 5x)²)

D6. Differentiate y = √(1 + x³) and y = 1/(2x − 5)².
    Answer: y' = 3x²/(2√(1 + x³)); y' = −4/(2x − 5)³.
    Teacher explains: Write as powers, then use the general power rule:
       y = (1 + x³)^(1/2)
       y' = (1/2)(1 + x³)^(−1/2) × 3x² = 3x²/(2√(1 + x³))
       y = (2x − 5)⁻²
       y' = −2(2x − 5)⁻³ × 2 = −4/(2x − 5)³
    Memorise d/dx √g = g'/(2√g): "derivative of the inside over twice the root".
    The first derivative exists for 1 + x³ > 0, i.e. x > −1; the second for
    x ≠ 5/2. Common mistakes: writing 1/(2√(1 + x³)) (no chain factor), and
    treating 1/(2x − 5)² with the quotient rule and losing a sign (possible, but
    the power form is quicker). Now you try: ∛(x² + 7) and 1/√(4 − x).
    (2x/(3∛((x² + 7)²)); 1/(2(4 − x)√(4 − x)))

D7. Differentiate y = x²√(1 − x²) and simplify to a single fraction.
    Answer: y' = (2x − 3x³)/√(1 − x²) = x(2 − 3x²)/√(1 − x²), for −1 < x < 1.
    Teacher explains: The LAST operation is a product, so the product rule comes
    first and the chain rule is used inside it:
       u = x²          u' = 2x
       v = √(1 − x²)   v' = −2x/(2√(1 − x²)) = −x/√(1 − x²)
       y' = 2x√(1 − x²) + x² × (−x/√(1 − x²))
          = (2x(1 − x²) − x³)/√(1 − x²)          (common denominator)
          = (2x − 3x³)/√(1 − x²)
    To combine, multiply the first term top and bottom by √(1 − x²):
    √(1 − x²) × √(1 − x²) = 1 − x². Check at x = 0: y' = 0, and indeed y ≥ 0
    with y(0) = 0, a minimum. Common mistake: forgetting the chain factor −2x.
    Now you try: x(2x + 1)³ and factorise. (y' = (2x + 1)³ + 6x(2x + 1)²
    = (2x + 1)²(8x + 1))

D8. Differentiate y = x/√(x² + 1) and y = (x + 1)²/(x − 1), simplifying fully.
    Answer: y' = 1/(x² + 1)^(3/2); y' = (x + 1)(x − 3)/(x − 1)².
    Teacher explains: Quotient rule outside, chain rule inside:
       u = x, u' = 1;  v = √(x² + 1), v' = x/√(x² + 1)
       y' = (√(x² + 1) − x × x/√(x² + 1))/(x² + 1)
          = ((x² + 1) − x²)/((x² + 1)√(x² + 1)) = 1/(x² + 1)^(3/2)
    For the second: u = (x + 1)², u' = 2(x + 1); v = x − 1, v' = 1:
       y' = (2(x + 1)(x − 1) − (x + 1)²)/(x − 1)²
          = (x + 1)(2x − 2 − x − 1)/(x − 1)² = (x + 1)(x − 3)/(x − 1)²
    Take out the common factor (x + 1) BEFORE expanding: it saves work and shows
    at once that y' = 0 at x = −1 and x = 3. Common mistake: cancelling (x + 1)
    against the denominator (it is not a factor of (x − 1)²). Now you try:
    x/(x² + 4). ((4 − x²)/(x² + 4)²)

D9. The table gives values of f, g and their derivatives.
        x    f(x)   f'(x)   g(x)   g'(x)
        1     3      2       2      −1
        2     5      4       1       3
    Find (fg)'(1), (f/g)'(1), (f∘g)'(1), (f∘g)'(2) and (g∘g)'(1).
    Answer: 1, 7/4, −4, 6, −3.
    Teacher explains: Use the rules with numbers, reading carefully WHERE each
    derivative is evaluated:
       (fg)'(1) = f'(1)g(1) + f(1)g'(1) = 2 × 2 + 3 × (−1) = 1
       (f/g)'(1) = (f'(1)g(1) − f(1)g'(1))/g(1)² = (4 + 3)/4 = 7/4
       (f∘g)'(1) = f'(g(1)) × g'(1) = f'(2) × (−1) = 4 × (−1) = −4
       (f∘g)'(2) = f'(g(2)) × g'(2) = f'(1) × 3 = 2 × 3 = 6
       (g∘g)'(1) = g'(g(1)) × g'(1) = g'(2) × (−1) = −3
    In the chain rule the OUTER derivative is taken at the INNER value g(a), not
    at a. Common mistake: (f∘g)'(1) = f'(1)g'(1) = −2. Now you try: find
    (f²)'(2) and say why (g∘f)'(1) cannot be found from this table.
    ((f²)'(2) = 2f(2)f'(2) = 40; (g∘f)'(1) = g'(f(1))f'(1) = g'(3) × 2 needs
    g'(3), which is not in the table)

D10. Show that (1/v)' = −v'/v², and use it with the product rule to derive the
     quotient rule. Hence prove the power rule for negative integers.
     Answer: (1/v)' = −v'/v² by the chain rule; then
     (u/v)' = (u × v⁻¹)' = (u'v − uv')/v²; and (x⁻ⁿ)' = −nx⁻ⁿ⁻¹.
     Teacher explains: Write 1/v = v⁻¹ and use the chain rule (outer function
     t⁻¹, inner v):
        (v⁻¹)' = −v⁻² × v' = −v'/v²
        (u/v)' = (u × v⁻¹)' = u'v⁻¹ + u(−v'/v²)
               = u'/v − uv'/v² = (u'v − uv')/v²
     For n a positive integer, x⁻ⁿ = 1/xⁿ, so (x⁻ⁿ)' = −nxⁿ⁻¹/x²ⁿ = −nx⁻ⁿ⁻¹,
     which is the power rule with power −n. So one rule covers all integer
     powers. Common mistake: (1/v)' = 1/v' (for v = x² that would give 1/(2x)
     instead of −2/x³). Now you try: use (1/v)' to differentiate 1/(x² + 1).
     (−2x/(x² + 1)²)

D11. A spherical balloon is inflated so that its radius after t seconds is
     r = 2t + 1 cm. Find the rate at which its volume V = (4/3)πr³ is increasing
     when t = 2.
     Answer: dV/dt = 200π ≈ 628.32 cm³/s.
     Teacher explains: V depends on r and r depends on t, so use the chain rule:
        dV/dr = 4πr²,   dr/dt = 2
        dV/dt = (dV/dr)(dr/dt) = 4πr² × 2 = 8πr²
        at t = 2:  r = 5,  dV/dt = 8π × 25 = 200π ≈ 628.32 cm³/s
     Units: (cm³ per cm) × (cm per s) = cm³ per s — the "cm" cancels just like
     du in dy/du × du/dx. The rate is not constant: it grows with r² because a
     bigger balloon has a bigger surface to push out. Common mistake: using
     t = 2 in place of r (dV/dr at r = 2 gives 16π, the wrong quantity). Now you
     try: a circular stain has radius r = 3t cm; find dA/dt at t = 2 for
     A = πr². (dA/dt = 2πr × 3 = 36π ≈ 113.10 cm²/s)

D12. Spot and correct each mistake: (a) d/dx (x² × x³) = 2x × 3x² = 6x³; (b)
     d/dx (2x + 1)⁴ = 4(2x + 1)³; (c) d/dx (5/x²) = 5/(2x); (d)
     d/dx √(x² + 9) = 1/(2√(x² + 9)); (e) d/dx
     (x/(x + 1)) = (x − (x + 1))/(x + 1)².
     Answer: (a) 5x⁴; (b) 8(2x + 1)³; (c) −10/x³; (d) x/√(x² + 9); (e)
     1/(x + 1)².
     Teacher explains: Name the rule each student broke:
        (a) product of derivatives used. x² × x³ = x⁵, so 5x⁴
            (or product rule: 2x × x³ + x² × 3x² = 5x⁴)
        (b) chain factor missing: 4(2x + 1)³ × 2 = 8(2x + 1)³
        (c) differentiated the denominator: 5x⁻² → −10x⁻³ = −10/x³
        (d) chain factor missing: (2x)/(2√(x² + 9)) = x/√(x² + 9)
        (e) numerator reversed: (1 × (x + 1) − x × 1)/(x + 1)² = 1/(x + 1)²
     Build the habit of a quick CHECK: plug in a number and compare with the
     difference quotient on a calculator, or differentiate in two ways (expand
     first, then use the rule). Now you try: find the error in d/dx
     (x/(x + 1)) = ((x + 1) − x)/(x + 1). (the denominator must be squared:
     1/(x + 1)²)

              d) 8x + 2   e) −3/x⁴   f) 1 + 1/√x   g) 2x/(x² + 1)²
              h) −24/(3x − 5)³   i) 4(x + 2)³ − 2(x + 2)   j) x²/∛((x³ + 8)²)
              k) −1/(2x + 7)^(3/2)   l) 2(x³ + x)(3x² + 1)   m) −12(1 − 2x)⁵
              n) −4x/(1 + x²)²

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: Before differentiating, say aloud what the LAST operation is: "a
  product", "a quotient", "a power of a bracket". Write u, u', v, v' in a small
  table every time. For the chain rule, draw a box round the inside:
  differentiate outside with the box untouched, then multiply by the box's
  derivative. Check answers by plugging in x = 1 and comparing with a difference
  quotient on a calculator. Harder: Prove (uvw)' = u'vw + uv'w + uvw' and use it
  on x(x + 1)(x + 2). Find the derivative of |x|³ and of f(f(x)) where
  f(x) = x² + 1. Show that if f is an even function then f' is odd. If
  y = (x + √(x² + 1))ⁿ show that √(x² + 1) y' = ny. Differentiate
  (x² + 1)(x² + 2)...(x² + 10) at x = 0 (answer 0) and at x = 1 (use (uvw...)' /
  (uvw...) = sum of u'/u).


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.35 — DERIVATIVES OF TRIGONOMETRIC, EXPONENTIAL, LOGARITHMIC, INVERSE
             TRIG FUNCTIONS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - Angles are in RADIANS. The six trigonometric derivatives:
    d/dx sin x = cos x; d/dx cos x = −sin x; d/dx tan x = sec²x;
    d/dx cot x = −cosec²x; d/dx sec x = sec x tan x; d/dx cosec x = −cosec x
    cot x. Memory aid: the "co" functions carry a minus sign.
  - Exponential and logarithmic: d/dx eˣ = eˣ; d/dx aˣ = aˣ ln a (a > 0);
    d/dx ln x = 1/x (x > 0); d/dx ln|x| = 1/x (x ≠ 0); d/dx logₐx = 1/(x ln a).
    Use log laws to SIMPLIFY before differentiating: ln(√(1 + x)/(1 − x))
    = (1/2)ln(1 + x) − ln(1 − x).
  - Inverse trigonometric (principal values): d/dx sin⁻¹x = 1/√(1 − x²) and
    d/dx cos⁻¹x = −1/√(1 − x²) (|x| < 1); d/dx tan⁻¹x = 1/(1 + x²);
    d/dx cot⁻¹x = −1/(1 + x²); d/dx sec⁻¹x = 1/(|x|√(x² − 1)) and
    d/dx cosec⁻¹x = −1/(|x|√(x² − 1)) (|x| > 1).
  - With the chain rule (g a function of x): (sin g)' = g' cos g, (eᵍ)' = g'eᵍ,
    (ln g)' = g'/g, (tan⁻¹g)' = g'/(1 + g²), (sin⁻¹g)' = g'/√(1 − g²). Note:
    sin²x = (sin x)², but sin x² = sin(x²) — different functions with different
    derivatives.
  - Proof ideas: tan, cot, sec, cosec by the quotient rule; ln x as the inverse
    of eˣ (x = eʸ gives dx/dy = eʸ = x, so dy/dx = 1/x); the inverse trig
    derivatives from dy/dx = 1/(dx/dy).
  - SIMPLIFY INVERSE-TRIG EXPRESSIONS BY SUBSTITUTION first: with x = tan θ,
    tan⁻¹(2x/(1 − x²)) = 2 tan⁻¹x (|x| < 1), sin⁻¹(2x/(1 + x²)) = 2 tan⁻¹x
    (|x| ≤ 1), cos⁻¹((1 − x²)/(1 + x²)) = 2 tan⁻¹x (x ≥ 0); with x = sin θ,
    sin⁻¹(3x − 4x³) = 3 sin⁻¹x (|x| ≤ 1/2). State the interval: the formula
    changes outside it.
  - If the angle is in DEGREES, sin x° = sin(πx/180) and d/dx sin x° = (π/180)
    cos x°.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Starting from d/dx sin x = cos x and d/dx cos x = −sin x, prove
    d/dx tan x = sec²x and d/dx sec x = sec x tan x.
    Answer: tan x = sin x/cos x gives (cos²x + sin²x)/cos²x = sec²x;
    sec x = 1/cos x gives sin x/cos²x = sec x tan x.
    Teacher explains: Use the quotient rule with u = sin x, v = cos x:
       (tan x)' = (cos x × cos x − sin x × (−sin x))/cos²x
                = (cos²x + sin²x)/cos²x = 1/cos²x = sec²x
    For sec x = (cos x)⁻¹ use the chain rule:
       (sec x)' = −(cos x)⁻² × (−sin x) = sin x/cos²x
                = (1/cos x)(sin x/cos x) = sec x tan x
    Both hold wherever cos x ≠ 0 (x ≠ π/2 + nπ). The slope of y = tan x is
    sec²x ≥ 1, so tan x is increasing on each branch. Common mistake: sign
    errors from (cos x)' — it is −sin x. Now you try: prove
    d/dx cot x = −cosec²x and d/dx cosec x = −cosec x cot x. (quotient rule on
    cos x/sin x: (−sin²x − cos²x)/sin²x = −cosec²x; chain rule on (sin x)⁻¹)

D2. Differentiate y = sin²(3x), y = sin(x²) and y = cos³(2x). Explain the
    difference between sin²x and sin x².
    Answer: 6 sin 3x cos 3x = 3 sin 6x; 2x cos(x²); −6 cos²(2x) sin(2x).
    Teacher explains: Peel the layers from the outside in. For
    sin²(3x) = (sin 3x)² there are THREE layers: square, sine, 3x:
       y = (sin 3x)²
       y' = 2 sin 3x × cos 3x × 3 = 6 sin 3x cos 3x = 3 sin 6x
       y = sin(x²):    y' = cos(x²) × 2x = 2x cos(x²)
       y = (cos 2x)³:  y' = 3cos²(2x) × (−sin 2x) × 2 = −6cos²(2x) sin 2x
    sin²x means (sin x)²: the square is OUTSIDE. sin x² means sin(x²): the
    square is INSIDE. In the last line we used 2 sin A cos A = sin 2A to tidy
    up. Common mistake: d/dx sin²(3x) = 2 sin 3x cos 3x (the factor 3 from the
    innermost layer is lost). Now you try: cos(x³) and tan²x. (−3x² sin(x³); 2
    tan x sec²x)

D3. Show that d/dx aˣ = aˣ ln a. A culture has N = 1,000e^(0.3t) bacteria after
    t hours. Find the growth rate when t = 5.
    Answer: aˣ = e^(x ln a), so (aˣ)' = e^(x ln a) × ln a = aˣ ln a.
    dN/dt = 300e^(0.3t); at t = 5 it is 300e^1.5 ≈ 1,344.5 bacteria per hour.
    Teacher explains: Every positive base can be written as a power of e:
    a = e^(ln a), so aˣ = e^(x ln a). The chain rule with the inside x ln a
    (derivative ln a):
       d/dx aˣ = e^(x ln a) × ln a = aˣ ln a
       d/dx 2ˣ = 2ˣ ln 2,   d/dx 10ˣ = 10ˣ ln 10
       N = 1,000e^(0.3t)  →  dN/dt = 1,000 × 0.3 × e^(0.3t) = 300e^(0.3t)
       t = 5:  300e^1.5 = 300 × 4.48169 ≈ 1,344.5
    Notice dN/dt = 0.3N: the growth rate is proportional to the size, which is
    the hallmark of exponential growth. Common mistakes: d/dx 2ˣ = x2ˣ⁻¹ (power
    rule on a variable power) or = 2ˣ (forgetting ln 2). Now you try: the slope
    of y = 2ˣ at x = 3. (8 ln 2 ≈ 5.545)

D4. Prove d/dx ln x = 1/x using the fact that ln is the inverse of eˣ. Then show
    d/dx ln|x| = 1/x for x ≠ 0 and d/dx logₐx = 1/(x ln a).
    Answer: y = ln x ⇔ x = eʸ; dx/dy = eʸ = x, so dy/dx = 1/x. For x < 0,
    ln|x| = ln(−x) has derivative (−1)/(−x) = 1/x. logₐx = ln x/ln a.
    Teacher explains: If y = ln x, then x = eʸ. Differentiate with respect to x
    (chain rule on the right, since y depends on x):
       1 = eʸ × dy/dx   so   dy/dx = 1/eʸ = 1/x   (x > 0)
    For negative x: ln|x| = ln(−x) and
       d/dx ln(−x) = (1/(−x)) × (−1) = 1/x
    So 1/x is the derivative of ln|x| on BOTH sides of 0 — important later for ∫
    (1/x) dx = ln|x| + C. For other bases change base first: logₐx = ln x/ln a,
    and 1/ln a is just a constant, giving 1/(x ln a). Common mistake:
    d/dx ln 5x = 5/x. In fact ln 5x = ln 5 + ln x, so the derivative is 1/x (or
    by the chain rule 5/(5x) = 1/x). Now you try: d/dx log₁₀x at x = 10. (1/(10
    ln 10) ≈ 0.04343)

D5. Differentiate ln(x² + 1), ln(sin x) and ln(sec x + tan x).
    Answer: 2x/(x² + 1); cot x; sec x.
    Teacher explains: The rule (ln g)' = g'/g: "derivative of the inside over
    the inside".
       (ln(x² + 1))' = 2x/(x² + 1)
       (ln(sin x))' = cos x/sin x = cot x          (sin x > 0)
       (ln(sec x + tan x))' = (sec x tan x + sec²x)/(sec x + tan x)
                            = sec x(tan x + sec x)/(sec x + tan x) = sec x
    The last one is worth remembering: it gives ∫ sec x dx later. Common
    mistake: (ln(x² + 1))' = 1/(x² + 1) (no chain factor). Now you try:
    ln(cos x) and ln(eˣ + 1). (−tan x; eˣ/(eˣ + 1))

D6. Differentiate y = e⁻ˣ sin x, y = x² ln x and y = (ln x)/x. For which x is
    each derivative zero in the last case?
    Answer: e⁻ˣ(cos x − sin x); x(2 ln x + 1); (1 − ln x)/x², zero at x = e.
    Teacher explains: Products and quotients of the new functions follow the
    same rules:
       (e⁻ˣ sin x)' = −e⁻ˣ sin x + e⁻ˣ cos x = e⁻ˣ(cos x − sin x)
       (x² ln x)'  = 2x ln x + x² × (1/x) = x(2 ln x + 1)
       ((ln x)/x)' = ((1/x) × x − ln x × 1)/x² = (1 − ln x)/x²
    (1 − ln x)/x² = 0 when ln x = 1, i.e. x = e: the curve y = (ln x)/x has a
    horizontal tangent (its maximum, 1/e) at x = e. Common mistake: in the first
    one forgetting the chain factor −1 in (e⁻ˣ)' = −e⁻ˣ. Now you try: x ln x − x
    and eˣ(sin x + cos x). (ln x; 2eˣ cos x)

D7. Prove d/dx sin⁻¹x = 1/√(1 − x²) for −1 < x < 1, and
    d/dx tan⁻¹x = 1/(1 + x²).
    Answer: With y = sin⁻¹x, x = sin y and dx/dy = cos y = √(1 − x²) (cos y ≥ 0
    as −π/2 ≤ y ≤ π/2), so dy/dx = 1/√(1 − x²). With y = tan⁻¹x,
    dx/dy = sec²y = 1 + x², so dy/dx = 1/(1 + x²).
    Teacher explains: For an inverse function, dy/dx = 1/(dx/dy):
       y = sin⁻¹x, −π/2 ≤ y ≤ π/2       y = tan⁻¹x, −π/2 < y < π/2
       x = sin y                          x = tan y
       dx/dy = cos y = +√(1 − sin²y)      dx/dy = sec²y = 1 + tan²y
             = √(1 − x²)                        = 1 + x²
       dy/dx = 1/√(1 − x²)                dy/dx = 1/(1 + x²)
    Why the + sign: the principal value y lies in [−π/2, π/2], where cos y ≥ 0.
    At x = ±1 the tangent to y = sin⁻¹x is vertical, so the derivative exists
    only for |x| < 1. Common mistake: confusing sin⁻¹x with 1/sin x = cosec x.
    Now you try: prove d/dx cos⁻¹x = −1/√(1 − x²). (x = cos y, 0 ≤ y ≤ π,
    dx/dy = −sin y = −√(1 − x²))

D8. Differentiate tan⁻¹(√x), sin⁻¹(2x) and tan⁻¹(eˣ).
    Answer: 1/(2√x(1 + x)); 2/√(1 − 4x²); eˣ/(1 + e²ˣ).
    Teacher explains: The chain versions: (tan⁻¹g)' = g'/(1 + g²),
    (sin⁻¹g)' = g'/√(1 − g²):
       (tan⁻¹√x)' = (1/(2√x))/(1 + x) = 1/(2√x(1 + x))           (x > 0)
       (sin⁻¹2x)' = 2/√(1 − (2x)²) = 2/√(1 − 4x²)                (|x| < 1/2)
       (tan⁻¹eˣ)' = eˣ/(1 + (eˣ)²) = eˣ/(1 + e²ˣ)
    Square the WHOLE inside: (2x)² = 4x², not 2x². Common mistake: forgetting g'
    in the numerator. Now you try: sin⁻¹(x/2) and tan⁻¹(x²). (1/√(4 − x²);
    2x/(1 + x⁴))

D9. Find dy/dx for y = tan⁻¹(2x/(1 − x²)), |x| < 1, first by substitution and
    then check by direct differentiation.
    Answer: dy/dx = 2/(1 + x²).
    Teacher explains: Put x = tan θ with −π/4 < θ < π/4 (because |x| < 1):
       2x/(1 − x²) = 2 tan θ/(1 − tan²θ) = tan 2θ
       y = tan⁻¹(tan 2θ) = 2θ          (valid as −π/2 < 2θ < π/2)
       y = 2 tan⁻¹x,   dy/dx = 2/(1 + x²)
    Direct check with g = 2x/(1 − x²):
       g' = (2(1 − x²) + 4x²)/(1 − x²)² = 2(1 + x²)/(1 − x²)²
       1 + g² = ((1 − x²)² + 4x²)/(1 − x²)² = (1 + x²)²/(1 − x²)²
       y' = g'/(1 + g²) = 2(1 + x²)/(1 + x²)² = 2/(1 + x²)
    Same answer, far more algebra. The interval matters: for x > 1,
    tan⁻¹(tan 2θ) = 2θ − π, the constant −π does not change the derivative, but
    the formula y = 2 tan⁻¹x is then wrong. Common mistake: writing y = 2 tan⁻¹x
    for all x. Now you try: sin⁻¹(2x/(1 + x²)), |x| < 1. (x = tan θ gives
    sin 2θ, y = 2 tan⁻¹x, dy/dx = 2/(1 + x²))

D10. Simplify then differentiate: (i) y = cos⁻¹((1 − x²)/(1 + x²)), x > 0; (ii)
     y = tan⁻¹(cos x/(1 + sin x)), −π/2 < x < π/2; (iii) y = sin⁻¹(3x − 4x³),
     |x| < 1/2.
     Answer: (i) 2/(1 + x²); (ii) −1/2; (iii) 3/√(1 − x²).
     Teacher explains: Choose the substitution that turns the inside into a
     known formula:
        (i)   x = tan θ, 0 < θ < π/2:  (1 − tan²θ)/(1 + tan²θ) = cos 2θ
              y = cos⁻¹(cos 2θ) = 2θ = 2 tan⁻¹x   (0 < 2θ < π)
        (ii)  cos x/(1 + sin x) = sin(π/2 − x)/(1 + cos(π/2 − x))
              = tan(π/4 − x/2),  so y = π/4 − x/2
        (iii) x = sin θ, |θ| < π/6:  3 sin θ − 4sin³θ = sin 3θ
              y = 3θ = 3 sin⁻¹x
     For (ii) we used sin A/(1 + cos A) = tan(A/2) with A = π/2 − x. For x < 0
     in (i), 2θ is negative, cos⁻¹(cos 2θ) = −2θ, and the derivative becomes
     −2/(1 + x²): the function has a corner at x = 0. Common mistake: ignoring
     the interval. Now you try: tan⁻¹(√((1 − cos x)/(1 + cos x))), 0 < x < π.
     (the inside is tan(x/2), y = x/2, dy/dx = 1/2)

D11. The height of a seat on a Ferris wheel is h = 20 − 18 cos(πt/15) metres
     after t minutes. How fast is the seat rising at t = 5 and at t = 15? Why
     must calculus use radians? Find d/dx sin x° as well.
     Answer: dh/dt = (6π/5) sin(πt/15): at t = 5, 3√3π/5 ≈ 3.265 m/min; at
     t = 15, 0 (the seat is at the top). d/dx sin x° = (π/180) cos x°.
     Teacher explains: Chain rule with the inside πt/15:
        dh/dt = −18 × (−sin(πt/15)) × π/15 = (6π/5) sin(πt/15)
        t = 5:   (6π/5) sin(π/3) = (6π/5)(√3/2) = 3√3π/5 ≈ 3.265 m/min
        t = 15:  (6π/5) sin π = 0
     At t = 15 the height is 20 + 18 = 38 m, the maximum, where the seat
     momentarily moves horizontally. The formula (sin x)' = cos x was proved
     using sin h/h → 1, true only in radians. In degrees x° = πx/180 radians:
        d/dx sin x° = d/dx sin(πx/180) = (π/180) cos x°
     So all calculus formulas would carry a nuisance factor π/180. Common
     mistake: using a calculator in degree mode for (6π/5) sin(π/3). Now you
     try: find dh/dt at t = 10. ((6π/5) sin(2π/3) = 3√3π/5 ≈ 3.265 m/min)

D12. Use log laws to simplify before differentiating: (i)
     y = ln √((1 + x)/(1 − x)), (ii) y = ln((x² + 1)/(x − 1)³), (iii)
     y = log₂(8x³).
     Answer: (i) 1/(1 − x²); (ii) 2x/(x² + 1) − 3/(x − 1); (iii) 3/(x ln 2).
     Teacher explains: The laws ln(ab) = ln a + ln b, ln(a/b) = ln a − ln b,
     ln aⁿ = n ln a turn one hard derivative into several easy ones:
       (i)   y = (1/2)[ln(1 + x) − ln(1 − x)]
             y' = (1/2)[1/(1 + x) + 1/(1 − x)] = (1/2) × 2/(1 − x²) = 1/(1 − x²)
       (ii)  y = ln(x² + 1) − 3 ln(x − 1)
             y' = 2x/(x² + 1) − 3/(x − 1)
       (iii) y = log₂8 + 3 log₂x = 3 + 3 log₂x,   y' = 3/(x ln 2)
     In (i) watch the sign: d/dx ln(1 − x) = −1/(1 − x), and subtracting it
     gives +1/(1 − x). Laws are valid only where the logs are defined (here
     −1 < x < 1 and x > 1). Common mistake: ln(a + b) = ln a + ln b (false). Now
     you try: ln(x²eˣ) for x > 0. (y = 2 ln x + x, y' = 2/x + 1)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Differentiate (x in radians).
    a) sin 3x            b) cos 5x              c) tan 2x
    d) cot 4x            e) sec 3x              f) cosec 2x
    g) sin(2x + 1)       h) cos(1 − 3x)         i) tan(x/2)

    s) 4 sec(x/2)        t) tan(3 − 2x)

             k) 3 cos x + 4 sin x   l) 5 sec²x + 2 sec x tan x
             m) −cosec²x + cosec x cot x   n) cos(x + π/3)   o) sin(π/4 − x)
             p) −cosec(x/7) cot(x/7)   q) 2 cosec²(2x − 1)
             r) cos x − sin x + sec²x   s) 2 sec(x/2) tan(x/2)
             t) −2 sec²(3 − 2x)

M2. Differentiate (powers and chains of trigonometric functions).
    a) sin²x        b) cos²x          c) sin³x           d) tan²x
    e) sec²x        f) cos⁴(2x)       g) sin²(3x)        h) sin(x²)
    i) cos(√x)      j) tan(x³)        k) √(sin x)        l) 1/cos²x
    m) sin(sin x)   n) cos(1/x)       o) sin²x + cos²x   p) sin⁵x cos x
    q) tan³(x/3)    r) √(1 + tan x)
    Answers: a) sin 2x   b) −sin 2x   c) 3sin²x cos x   d) 2 tan x sec²x
             e) 2sec²x tan x   f) −8cos³(2x) sin 2x   g) 3 sin 6x
             h) 2x cos(x²)   i) −sin(√x)/(2√x)   j) 3x² sec²(x³)
             k) cos x/(2√(sin x))   l) 2 tan x sec²x   m) cos(sin x) cos x
             n) sin(1/x)/x²   o) 0   p) 5sin⁴x cos²x − sin⁶x
             q) tan²(x/3) sec²(x/3)   r) sec²x/(2√(1 + tan x))

M3. Differentiate (products and quotients with trigonometric functions).
    a) x sin x                           b) x² cos x
    c) sin x cos x                       d) sin x/x
    e) x tan x                           f) x/(1 + cos x)
    g) sin x/(1 + cos x)                 h) (1 + sin x)/(1 − sin x)
    i) x sec x                           j) cos x/(1 − sin x)
    k) x² sin 2x                         l) sin 3x cos 2x
    m) (sin x − cos x)/(sin x + cos x)   n) tan x/x
    o) x cot x                           p) sec x + tan x
    q) √x cos x                          r) sin x/(x² + 1)
    Answers:
      a) sin x + x cos x
      b) 2x cos x − x² sin x
      c) cos 2x
      d) (x cos x − sin x)/x²
      e) tan x + x sec²x
      f) (1 + cos x + x sin x)/(1 + cos x)²
      g) 1/(1 + cos x)
      h) 2 cos x/(1 − sin x)²
      i) sec x(1 + x tan x)
      j) 1/(1 − sin x)
      k) 2x sin 2x + 2x² cos 2x
      l) 3 cos 3x cos 2x − 2 sin 3x sin 2x
      m) 2/(1 + sin 2x)
      n) (x sec²x − tan x)/x²
      o) cot x − x cosec²x
      p) sec x(tan x + sec x)
      q) cos x/(2√x) − √x sin x
      r) ((x² + 1) cos x − 2x sin x)/(x² + 1)²

M4. Differentiate (exponential functions).
    a) e³ˣ          b) e⁻ˣ            c) e^(x²)        d) e^(−x²)
    e) e^(5 − 2x)   f) 2ˣ             g) 10ˣ           h) 3^(2x + 1)
    i) e^(sin x)    j) e^(√x)         k) xeˣ           l) x²e⁻ˣ
    m) eˣ/x         n) (eˣ − e⁻ˣ)/2   o) eˣ/(1 + eˣ)   p) e^(x ln 3)
    q) eˣ sin x     r) e²ˣ cos 3x     s) 5ˣ⁺¹          t) e^(tan x)
    Answers: a) 3e³ˣ   b) −e⁻ˣ   c) 2xe^(x²)   d) −2xe^(−x²)   e) −2e^(5 − 2x)
             f) 2ˣ ln 2   g) 10ˣ ln 10   h) 2 ln 3 × 3^(2x + 1)
             i) cos x e^(sin x)   j) e^(√x)/(2√x)   k) (x + 1)eˣ
             l) x(2 − x)e⁻ˣ   m) (x − 1)eˣ/x²   n) (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)/2
             o) eˣ/(1 + eˣ)²   p) 3ˣ ln 3   q) eˣ(sin x + cos x)
             r) e²ˣ(2 cos 3x − 3 sin 3x)   s) 5ˣ⁺¹ ln 5   t) sec²x e^(tan x)

M5. Differentiate (logarithmic functions; assume x lies where each log is
    defined).
    a) ln 5x           b) ln(x² + 1)          c) ln(sin x)
    d) ln(cos x)       e) ln(ln x)            f) log₂x
    g) log₁₀(3x + 1)   h) ln √x               i) (ln x)²
    j) x ln x          k) (ln x)/x            l) ln(sec x + tan x)
    m) ln|2x − 3|      n) ln(x + √(x² + 1))   o) ln(eˣ + 1)
    p) x² ln x         q) ln(tan x)           r) ln(1 + x²)/x
    Answers: a) 1/x   b) 2x/(x² + 1)   c) cot x   d) −tan x   e) 1/(x ln x)

M7. Differentiate (inverse trigonometric functions, principal values; assume x

M8. Differentiate (inverse trigonometric functions combined with other rules).

M9. Simplify by a suitable substitution (x = tan θ, sin θ or cos θ), then
    differentiate on the stated interval.
    a) tan⁻¹(2x/(1 − x²)), |x| < 1

      h) 2/√(1 − x²) (y = 2sin⁻¹x)

M10. Find the value of the derivative at the given point.
     a) y = sin 2x; x = π/6      b) y = cos²x; x = π/4

M12. True or false? If false, give the correct derivative.

     o) d/dx log₃x = 1/(x ln 3)     p) d/dx eˣ⁺² = eˣ⁺²
