TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: Make a three-line checklist for every question — continuous on
  [a, b]? differentiable on (a, b)? f(a) = f(b)? — and tick it before solving.
  Draw the graph and the chord; slide a ruler parallel to the chord until it
  just touches the curve. Always test each c against a < c < b. Harder: Prove
  Cauchy's MVT: (f(b) − f(a))g'(c) = (g(b) − g(a))f'(c), using h(x)
  = (f(b) − f(a))g(x) − (g(b) − g(a))f(x). Show that if f'' > 0 on (a, b) the
  MVT point is unique. Prove eˣ ≥ 1 + x for all x and |tan a − tan b| ≥ |a − b|
  on (−π/2, π/2). If f(0) = 0 and |f'(x)| ≤ |f(x)| on [0, 1], show f = 0 there.


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.41 — APPLICATIONS OF DERIVATIVES: RATE OF CHANGE, TANGENTS AND NORMALS,
             INCREASING AND DECREASING FUNCTIONS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - RATE OF CHANGE: dy/dx is the rate at which y changes per unit change in x;
    its units are (units of y) per (unit of x). dA/dr = 2πr for a circle,
    dV/dr = 4πr² for a sphere. Radians are used throughout.
  - RELATED RATES: when several quantities change with time t, write the
    EQUATION linking them first (Pythagoras, similar triangles, volume formula),
    differentiate BOTH sides with respect to t using the chain rule
    (d/dt(r³) = 3r² dr/dt), and only THEN substitute the values at the instant
    asked. A decreasing quantity has a negative rate.
  - TANGENT at the point (x₁, y₁) with slope m = f′(x₁): y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
    NORMAL (perpendicular to the tangent): slope −1/m, so
    y − y₁ = −(1/m)(x − x₁). If m = 0 the tangent is y = y₁ and the normal is
    x = x₁; if dy/dx is infinite the tangent is vertical, x = x₁.
  - For IMPLICIT curves find dy/dx by implicit differentiation (circle:
    dy/dx = −x/y). For PARAMETRIC curves x = x(t), y = y(t):
    dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), evaluated at the given t. Useful results: the
    tangent to x² + y² = a² at (x₁, y₁) is xx₁ + yy₁ = a², and to
    x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 it is xx₁/a² + yy₁/b² = 1.
  - MONOTONICITY: if f′(x) > 0 on an interval then f is strictly increasing
    there; if f′(x) < 0, strictly decreasing (proof by the Mean Value Theorem:
    f(x₂) − f(x₁) = f′(c)(x₂ − x₁)). A zero of f′ at single points does not
    spoil this (x³ is increasing on ℝ).
  - SIGN CHART: find f′, factorise it, mark the CRITICAL POINTS (f′ = 0 or
    undefined) and points outside the domain on a number line, test the sign of
    f′ in each piece, and read off the intervals. We write open intervals;
    endpoints where f is continuous may also be included.
  - ECONOMICS: marginal cost MC = C′(x) and marginal revenue MR = R′(x)
    approximate the extra cost / revenue of producing one more unit; profit
    P(x) = R(x) − C(x).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Find the rate of change of the area A of a circle with respect to its radius
    r when r = 5 cm, and of the volume V of a sphere with respect to its radius
    when r = 3 cm. Then: for y = 7x − x³, x increases at 4 units per second; how
    fast is the SLOPE of the curve changing when x = 2?
    Answer: dA/dr = 10π ≈ 31.42 cm² per cm; dV/dr = 36π ≈ 113.10 cm³ per cm; the
    slope decreases at 48 units per second (dm/dt = −48).
    Teacher explains: "Rate of change of A with respect to r" means dA/dr: how
    many cm² the area gains per extra cm of radius at that moment.
        A = πr²          dA/dr = 2πr     at r = 5:  2π × 5 = 10π
        V = (4/3)πr³     dV/dr = 4πr²    at r = 3:  4π × 9 = 36π
    Note that dA/dr = 2πr is the circumference: a thin ring of width dr adds
    area ≈ 2πr dr. For the last part the slope is m = dy/dx = 7 − 3x², which
    itself changes with time. By the chain rule
    dm/dt = (dm/dx)(dx/dt) = −6x × 4 = −24x, and at x = 2 this is −48. Common
    mistakes: substituting r = 5 BEFORE differentiating (you get 25π, a
    constant, whose derivative is 0), and forgetting units. Now you try: the
    rate of change of the surface area S = 6a² of a cube with respect to its
    edge a when a = 4 cm. (dS/da = 12a = 48 cm² per cm)

D2. Air is pumped into a spherical balloon at 100 cm³ per second. How fast is
    the radius increasing when the radius is 10 cm? How fast is the surface area
    increasing at that instant?
    Answer: dr/dt = 1/(4π) ≈ 0.0796 cm/s; dS/dt = 20 cm²/s.
    Teacher explains: Step 1: name the variables and write what is given and
    wanted: dV/dt = 100, want dr/dt when r = 10. Step 2: the equation linking V
    and r is V = (4/3)πr³. Step 3: differentiate with respect to t (chain rule):
        dV/dt = 4πr² × dr/dt
          100 = 4π(10)² × dr/dt = 400π × dr/dt
        dr/dt = 100/(400π) = 1/(4π) ≈ 0.0796 cm/s
        S = 4πr²   so   dS/dt = 8πr × dr/dt = 8π × 10 × 1/(4π) = 20
    Notice that dr/dt gets SMALLER as the balloon grows: the same 100 cm³
    spreads over a bigger surface, which is why a balloon seems to inflate
    quickly at first and then slowly. Common mistake: writing dV/dt = 4πr²
    (forgetting the factor dr/dt). Now you try: a spherical soap bubble has
    radius increasing at 0.2 cm/s; find dV/dt when r = 5 cm.
    (dV/dt = 4π × 25 × 0.2 = 20π ≈ 62.83 cm³/s)

D3. A 13 m ladder leans against a vertical wall. Its foot is pulled away from
    the wall along the ground at 0.5 m/s. How fast is the top sliding down the
    wall when the foot is 5 m from the wall? How fast is the angle between the
    ladder and the ground changing then?
    Answer: The top slides down at 5/24 m/s ≈ 0.208 m/s (dy/dt = −5/24); the
    angle decreases at 1/24 rad/s ≈ 0.0417 rad/s.
    Teacher explains: Draw the right triangle: x = distance of the foot from the
    wall, y = height of the top. Pythagoras holds at EVERY instant:
        x² + y² = 169
        2x dx/dt + 2y dy/dt = 0      (differentiate w.r.t. t)
        at x = 5:  y = √(169 − 25) = 12
        5 × 0.5 + 12 × dy/dt = 0
        dy/dt = −2.5/12 = −5/24 m/s
    The minus sign says y is DECREASING. For the angle θ with the ground,
    cos θ = x/13, so −sin θ dθ/dt = (1/13) dx/dt. With sin θ = 12/13: dθ/dt
    = −(0.5/13) ÷ (12/13) = −0.5/12 = −1/24 rad/s. Common mistake: putting x = 5
    into x² + y² = 169 before differentiating, which makes x a constant and
    gives nonsense. Now you try: a 10 m ladder, foot moving away at 1.5 m/s; how
    fast does the top fall when the foot is 6 m from the wall? (y = 8,
    dy/dt = −6 × 1.5/8 = −9/8 = −1.125 m/s)

D4. Water is poured at 8 m³ per minute into a conical tank with its vertex
    pointing down. The tank is 12 m deep and its top has radius 6 m. How fast is
    the water level rising when the water is 4 m deep?
    Answer: dh/dt = 2/π ≈ 0.637 m per minute.
    Teacher explains: The water forms a smaller cone with radius r and depth h.
    By similar triangles r/h = 6/12, so r = h/2. Replace r BEFORE
    differentiating so that only one changing variable is left:
        V = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π(h/2)²h = πh³/12
        dV/dt = (πh²/4) × dh/dt
            8 = (π × 16/4) × dh/dt = 4π × dh/dt
        dh/dt = 8/(4π) = 2/π ≈ 0.637 m/min
    As the water gets deeper the surface is wider, so the level rises more
    slowly. Common mistakes: using the tank's fixed radius 6 as r (r changes
    with h), and differentiating V = (1/3)πr²h treating r as a constant. Now you
    try: same tank, find how fast the water SURFACE radius grows when h = 4 m.
    (r = h/2, dr/dt = (1/2)(2/π) = 1/π ≈ 0.318 m/min)

D5. A man 1.8 m tall walks away from a lamp post 6 m high at 1.4 m/s. How fast
    is his shadow lengthening? How fast is the tip of the shadow moving?
    Answer: The shadow lengthens at 0.6 m/s; the tip moves at 2 m/s.
    Teacher explains: Let x = distance of the man from the post and s = length
    of his shadow. The light ray from the lamp top to the shadow tip makes two
    similar triangles:
           lamp
            |\
          6 |  \
            |    \  man
            |     |\
            |  1.8| \
            +-----+--+
               x    s
        6/(x + s) = 1.8/s  →  6s = 1.8x + 1.8s  →  4.2s = 1.8x
        s = (3/7)x          ds/dt = (3/7) × 1.4 = 0.6 m/s
        tip at x + s:       d(x + s)/dt = 1.4 + 0.6 = 2 m/s
    The answer does not depend on how far away he is: the shadow grows at a
    constant rate. Common mistake: answering 0.6 m/s for the TIP; the tip moves
    with the man AND runs ahead of him. Now you try: a girl 1.5 m tall walks
    away from a 4.5 m lamp at 1.2 m/s. (4.5s = 1.5x + 1.5s, s = x/2: shadow
    grows at 0.6 m/s, tip moves at 1.8 m/s)

D6. Find the equations of the tangent and the normal to y = x³ − 2x + 1 at the
    point where x = 2. Where does the normal meet the x-axis?
    Answer: Tangent y = 10x − 15; normal x + 10y = 52; the normal meets the
    x-axis at (52, 0).
    Teacher explains: Three things are needed: the point, the slope of the
    tangent, and the point-slope formula.
        point:    y(2) = 8 − 4 + 1 = 5, so (2, 5)
        slope:    dy/dx = 3x² − 2, at x = 2: 12 − 2 = 10
        tangent:  y − 5 = 10(x − 2)       →  y = 10x − 15
        normal:   slope −1/10
                  y − 5 = −(1/10)(x − 2)  →  10y − 50 = −x + 2
                                          →  x + 10y = 52
    Check: (2, 5) lies on both lines (10 × 2 − 15 = 5 and 2 + 50 = 52), and the
    slopes multiply to 10 × (−1/10) = −1. Putting y = 0 in the normal gives
    x = 52. Common mistakes: using the slope 10 for the normal too; writing the
    normal slope as +1/10 or −10. Now you try: tangent and normal to
    y = x² − 3x + 2 at x = 3. (point (3, 2), slope 3: tangent y = 3x − 7, normal
    x + 3y = 9)

D7. On the curve y = x³ − 3x² − 9x + 5 find the points where the tangent is (a)
    parallel to the x-axis, (b) parallel to the line y = 15x + 2, (c)
    perpendicular to the line x + 15y = 4.
    Answer: (a) (−1, 10) and (3, −22); (b) (−2, 3) and (4, −15); (c) the same
    two points as (b).
    Teacher explains: Parallel lines have EQUAL slopes; a line parallel to the
    x-axis has slope 0. So set dy/dx equal to the required slope and solve for
    x, then find y from the CURVE (not from the line).
        dy/dx = 3x² − 6x − 9 = 3(x − 3)(x + 1)
        (a) 3(x − 3)(x + 1) = 0    →  x = 3 or −1
            y(3) = 27 − 27 − 27 + 5 = −22,   y(−1) = −1 − 3 + 9 + 5 = 10
        (b) 3x² − 6x − 9 = 15      →  x² − 2x − 8 = 0  →  x = 4 or −2
            y(4) = 64 − 48 − 36 + 5 = −15,   y(−2) = −8 − 12 + 18 + 5 = 3
    (c) The line x + 15y = 4 has slope −1/15; a perpendicular line has slope 15
    (product −1), so this is the same as (b). Common mistake: substituting x
    into dy/dx instead of y to get the y-coordinate. Now you try: the point on
    y = x² − 4x + 1 where the tangent is parallel to y = 2x + 3. (2x − 4 = 2,
    x = 3: the point (3, −2))

D8. Find the tangent and normal to the circle x² + y² = 25 at (3, 4), and the
    tangent to the ellipse x²/16 + y²/9 = 1 at (16/5, 9/5). Show that every
    normal to a circle passes through its centre.
    Answer: Circle: tangent 3x + 4y = 25, normal 4x − 3y = 0 (through O).
    Ellipse: tangent x + y = 5.
    Teacher explains: Differentiate implicitly, remembering that y is a function
    of x, so d/dx(y²) = 2y dy/dx:
        2x + 2y dy/dx = 0   →   dy/dx = −x/y = −3/4 at (3, 4)
        tangent:  y − 4 = −(3/4)(x − 3)  →  4y − 16 = −3x + 9
                                         →  3x + 4y = 25
        normal:   y − 4 = (4/3)(x − 3)   →  4x − 3y = 0
    The normal passes through (0, 0). In general the normal at (x₁, y₁) has
    slope y₁/x₁, so it is y = (y₁/x₁)x, a line through the centre: the radius is
    perpendicular to the tangent (as in topic 7.25). For the ellipse,
    (2x/16) + (2y/9) dy/dx = 0 gives dy/dx = −9x/(16y) = −(9 × 16/5)/(16 × 9/5)
    = −1, so y − 9/5 = −(x − 16/5), x + y = 5. This agrees with the formula
    xx₁/16 + yy₁/9 = 1: x/5 + y/5 = 1. Common mistake: writing d/dx(y²) = 2y.
    Now you try: the tangent to x² + y² = 169 at (5, −12). (5x − 12y = 169)

D9. A curve is given by x = t², y = t³. Find the tangent and the normal at the
    point where t = 2. Where is the tangent horizontal or vertical?
    Answer: At t = 2 the point is (4, 8), dy/dx = 3; tangent y = 3x − 4, normal
    x + 3y = 28. At t = 0, both dx/dt and dy/dt vanish: the curve has a cusp at
    the origin (it touches the x-axis there); it has no other horizontal or
    vertical tangents.
    Teacher explains: For a parametric curve, find dx/dt and dy/dt separately
    and divide:
        dx/dt = 2t,  dy/dt = 3t²,  dy/dx = 3t²/(2t) = 3t/2   (t ≠ 0)
        t = 2:  point (4, 8),  slope 3
        tangent:  y − 8 = 3(x − 4)         →  y = 3x − 4
        normal:   y − 8 = −(1/3)(x − 4)    →  x + 3y = 28
    A horizontal tangent needs dy/dt = 0 with dx/dt ≠ 0; a vertical one needs
    dx/dt = 0 with dy/dt ≠ 0. Here both vanish only at t = 0; the slope 3t/2 → 0
    as t → 0, so the curve (y² = x³, the semicubical parabola) meets the origin
    with a cusp touching the x-axis. Common mistake: computing (dx/dt)/(dy/dt),
    which is dx/dy. Now you try: x = t², y = 2t at t = 2. (point (4, 4),
    dy/dx = 1/t = 1/2: tangent x − 2y + 4 = 0, normal 2x + y = 12)

D10. Find the intervals in which f(x) = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x + 1 is strictly
     increasing and strictly decreasing. Use a sign chart.
     Answer: Increasing on (−∞, 1) and (2, ∞); decreasing on (1, 2).
     Teacher explains: Factorise the derivative completely, then test each piece
     of the number line cut by its zeros:
         f′(x) = 6x² − 18x + 12 = 6(x − 1)(x − 2)
                     x < 1      1 < x < 2      x > 2
         x − 1         −            +            +
         x − 2         −            −            +
         f′(x)         +            −            +
         f           rises        falls        rises
               ------------(1)-----------(2)------------
     A quick test value in each piece also works: f′(0) = 12 > 0,
     f′(1.5) = 6(0.5)(−0.5) < 0, f′(3) = 12 > 0. Values: f(1) = 6, f(2) = 5, so
     the graph rises to 6, falls to 5, then rises for ever. Common mistakes:
     finding the intervals where f(x) > 0 instead of f′(x) > 0; losing the
     factor sign when a factor is (2 − x). Now you try: f(x) = x³ − 12x.
     (f′ = 3(x − 2)(x + 2): increasing on (−∞, −2) and (2, ∞), decreasing on
     (−2, 2))

D11. a) Explain why f(x) = x³ is strictly increasing on ℝ even though f′(0) = 0.
     b) Prove that ln(1 + x) < x for all x > 0. c) Is f(x) = 1/x decreasing on
     its whole domain?
     Answer: a) x₁ < x₂ always gives x₁³ < x₂³; f′ > 0 except at the single
     point 0. b) g(x) = x − ln(1 + x) has g(0) = 0 and g′(x) = x/(1 + x) > 0 for
     x > 0, so g(x) > 0. c) No: it decreases on (−∞, 0) and on (0, ∞)
     separately, but f(−1) = −1 < f(1) = 1.
     Teacher explains: a) "Strictly increasing" means x₁ < x₂ ⇒ f(x₁) < f(x₂).
     f′(x) = 3x² > 0 on (−∞, 0) and on (0, ∞), so f increases strictly on each,
     and f is continuous at 0, so the two pieces join: x₁ < 0 < x₂ gives
     x₁³ < 0 < x₂³. So f′ > 0 is SUFFICIENT but not NECESSARY; an isolated zero
     of f′ is allowed.
     b) To prove an inequality A < B, study the difference:
         g(x) = x − ln(1 + x),    g(0) = 0 − ln 1 = 0
         g′(x) = 1 − 1/(1 + x) = x/(1 + x) > 0   for x > 0
         so g is increasing on [0, ∞) and g(x) > g(0) = 0 for x > 0
     c) f′(x) = −1/x² < 0 wherever f is defined, but the domain has a GAP at 0,
     and the MVT argument only works on an interval. Common mistake: saying
     "f′ < 0 everywhere, so f decreases everywhere". Now you try: prove
     eˣ > 1 + x for x > 0. (h = eˣ − 1 − x, h(0) = 0, h′ = eˣ − 1 > 0 for x > 0)

D12. A factory's total cost of making x toys is
     C(x) = 0.005x³ − 0.02x² + 30x + 5,000 rupees, and its revenue from selling
     x toys is R(x) = 3x² + 36x + 5 rupees. Find the marginal cost when x = 3
     and the marginal revenue when x = 5. What do these numbers mean?
     Answer: MC = C′(3) = ₹30.015 ≈ ₹30.02; MR = R′(5) = ₹66. Making the 4th toy
     costs about ₹30; selling the 6th toy brings about ₹66 more.
     Teacher explains: Marginal means "rate of change with respect to the number
     of units".
         C′(x) = 0.015x² − 0.04x + 30
         C′(3) = 0.015 × 9 − 0.04 × 3 + 30 = 0.135 − 0.12 + 30 = 30.015
         R′(x) = 6x + 36,   R′(5) = 30 + 36 = 66
     The exact extra revenue from the 6th toy is R(6) − R(5) = 329 − 260 = 69,
     close to R′(5) = 66: the derivative is the slope of the tangent, a good
     approximation to the change over one unit. The fixed cost ₹5,000 disappears
     on differentiating: it does not change with x. Common mistake: computing
     C(3) (the total cost) instead of C′(3). Now you try:
     R(x) = 13x² + 26x + 15; find the MR when x = 7. (R′ = 26x + 26 = ₹208)

    n) x = cos³t, y = sin³t; t = π/4
    Answers: a) point (9, 6), dy/dx = 1/3; T: x − 3y = −9; N: 3x + y = 33
             b) point (2, 0), dy/dx = 1; T: x − y = 2; N: x + y = 2
             c) point (1, −1), dy/dx = −3/2; T: 3x + 2y = 1; N: 2x − 3y = 5
             d) point (3, −2), dy/dx = 1; T: x − y = 5; N: x + y = 1
             e) point (3, 6), dy/dx = 1; T: x − y = −3; N: x + y = 9
             f) point (3/2, 5/2), dy/dx = 3/5; T: 3x − 5y = −8; N: 5x + 3y = 15
             g) point (√2/2, √2/2), dy/dx = −1; T: y = −x + √2; N: y = x
             h) point (0, 3), dy/dx = 0; T: y = 3; N: x = 0
             i) point (2, √3), dy/dx = −√3/6; T: x + 2√3 y = 8; N:
                y = 2√3 x − 3√3
             j) point (√2, 1), dy/dx = √2; T: y = √2 x − 1; N: y = −√2/2 x + 2
             k) point (π/2 − 1, 1), dy/dx = 1; T: y = x + 2 − π/2; N:
                y = −x + π/2
             l) point (1, 1), dy/dx = −1; T: x + y = 2; N: x − y = 0
             m) point (1, 2), dy/dx = 1; T: x − y = −1; N: x + y = 3
             n) point (√2/4, √2/4), dy/dx = −1; T: y = −x + √2/2; N: y = x

M8. Find the point(s) on the curve with the stated property.
    a) y = x² − 6x + 5: tangent horizontal
    b) y = x³ − 12x: tangent horizontal

    g) y = x² − 2x + 3: tangent parallel to y = 4x + 1
    h) y = x³: tangent parallel to y = 12x − 5
    i) y = x³ − 3x² + 2: tangent parallel to y = 9x

M9. Find the open intervals in which f is strictly increasing (inc) and strictly
    decreasing (dec).
    a) f(x) = x² − 4x + 3
    b) f(x) = 5 − 6x − x²
    c) f(x) = x³ − 3x
    d) f(x) = x³ − 12x + 5
    e) f(x) = 2x³ − 3x² − 12x + 1
    f) f(x) = −2x³ + 9x² − 12x
    g) f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 4
    h) f(x) = x³ + 3x² + 3x + 2
    i) f(x) = x⁴ − 2x²
    j) f(x) = x⁴ − 4x³
    k) f(x) = 3x⁴ − 4x³ − 12x² + 5
    l) f(x) = x³ − 3x² + 6x
    m) f(x) = (x − 1)²(x + 2)
    n) f(x) = x⁴ − 8x² + 3

             g) inc (−∞, 1) and (3, ∞); dec (1, 3)   h) inc (−∞, ∞); dec nowhere
             i) inc (−1, 0) and (1, ∞); dec (−∞, −1) and (0, 1)

             m) inc (−∞, −1) and (1, ∞); dec (−1, 1)
             n) inc (−2, 0) and (2, ∞); dec (−∞, −2) and (0, 2)
             o) inc (−∞, −3) and (2, ∞); dec (−3, 2)
             p) inc (−∞, −1) and (1, ∞); dec (−1, 1)

M10. Find the intervals of increase (inc) and decrease (dec).
     a) f(x) = x eˣ
     b) f(x) = x e^(−x)
     c) f(x) = x² e^(−x)
     d) f(x) = eˣ − x
     e) f(x) = ln x/x (x > 0)
     f) f(x) = x ln x (x > 0)
     g) f(x) = x − ln x (x > 0)
     h) f(x) = x² − 2 ln x (x > 0)
     i) f(x) = x + 1/x (x ≠ 0)
     j) f(x) = x/(x² + 1)

M11. Find the values of the constant k for which f has the stated property; then
     decide true or false.
     a) f(x) = x³ + kx² + 3x increasing on ℝ
     b) f(x) = x³ − kx increasing on ℝ
     c) f(x) = kx − sin x increasing on ℝ
     d) f(x) = kx + cos x decreasing on ℝ
     e) f(x) = x² − kx + 1 increasing on (1, 2)
     f) f(x) = x² + kx + 1 decreasing on (1, 2)
     g) f(x) = kx³ − 9x² + 9x + 3 increasing on ℝ
     h) f(x) = eˣ + kx increasing on ℝ
     i) f(x) = 2x³ + kx² + 6x increasing on ℝ
     j) f(x) = x + k/x increasing on (1, ∞) (k > 0)
     k) True or false: eˣ ≥ 1 + x for all x
     l) True or false: sin x < x for all x > 0
     m) True or false: ln x ≤ x − 1 for all x > 0
     n) True or false: tan x > x for 0 < x < π/2
     o) True or false: 1/x is decreasing on ℝ without 0
     p) True or false: x³ is strictly increasing on ℝ
     q) True or false: f′(c) = 0 forces f to turn at c
     r) True or false: cos x is decreasing on (0, π)
     Answers: a) −3 ≤ k ≤ 3   b) k ≤ 0   c) k ≥ 1   d) k ≤ −1   e) k ≤ 2
              f) k ≤ −4   g) k ≥ 3   h) k ≥ 0   i) −6 ≤ k ≤ 6   j) 0 < k ≤ 1
              k) true   l) true   m) true   n) true   o) false (f(−1) < f(1))
              p) true   q) false (x³ at 0)   r) true

M12. Economics: find the marginal cost (MC), marginal revenue (MR) or marginal
     profit. Money in rupees.
     a) C(x) = 0.005x³ − 0.02x² + 30x + 5,000: MC at x = 3
     b) C(x) = 2x² + 50x + 1,000: MC at x = 10
     c) C(x) = 0.1x² + 12x + 800: MC at x = 25
     d) C(x) = x³ − 6x² + 15x + 100: MC at x = 4
     e) R(x) = 3x² + 36x + 5: MR at x = 5
     f) R(x) = 13x² + 26x + 15: MR at x = 7
     g) R(x) = 100x − 0.5x²: MR at x = 40
     h) R(x) = x(200 − 2x): MR at x = 30
     i) R(x) = 500x − x²: where is MR = 0?
     j) P(x) = −x² + 60x − 400: marginal profit at x = 20
     k) P(x) = −x² + 60x − 400: where is P increasing?
     l) C(x) = 400 + 5x + x²/100: average cost C/x at x = 200
     Answers: a) ₹30.015   b) ₹90   c) ₹17   d) ₹15   e) ₹66   f) ₹208   g) ₹60
              h) ₹80   i) x = 250   j) ₹20   k) 0 < x < 30   l) ₹9 per unit

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: always draw the diagram for a related-rates problem and label the
  CHANGING lengths with letters, fixed ones with numbers; write "given / wanted"
  before any calculus; differentiate first and substitute last. For tangents,
  write three lines every time: point, slope, equation. For monotonicity,
  factorise f′ fully and build the sign chart row by row. Harder: show that the
  tangent to xy = c² at (ct, c/t) cuts off a triangle of constant area 2c² with
  the axes; find the angle between y = x² and y = √x at (1, 1) (tan θ = 3/4,
  θ ≈ 36.87°); do x² = 4y and 4y + x² = 8 cut orthogonally? (they meet at
  (±2, 1) with slopes 1 and −1: yes); a street light 6 m high, a man 2 m tall
  walking towards it at 1.5 m/s: how fast does the shadow shrink? (0.75 m/s);
  prove that f(x) = x/sin x increases on (0, π/2).


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.42 — MAXIMA AND MINIMA; OPTIMISATION PROBLEMS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - f has a LOCAL MAXIMUM at c if f(c) ≥ f(x) for all x near c, and a LOCAL
    MINIMUM if f(c) ≤ f(x) near c. The ABSOLUTE (global) maximum is the largest
    value on the whole domain or interval.
  - CRITICAL POINTS are the points of the domain where f′(c) = 0 or f′(c) does
    not exist. (Fermat) A local extremum at an interior point where f is
    differentiable must have f′(c) = 0; the converse is false: x³ at 0.
  - FIRST DERIVATIVE TEST: if f′ changes from + to − at c, local max; from − to
    +, local min; no change of sign, neither (a point of inflection with
    horizontal tangent, as for x³).
  - SECOND DERIVATIVE TEST: if f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) < 0, local max; f″(c) > 0,
    local min; f″(c) = 0, the test FAILS (x⁴ has a min, −x⁴ a max, x³ neither):
    go back to the first derivative test.
  - ABSOLUTE EXTREMA on a closed interval [a, b] (they exist when f is
    continuous: Extreme Value Theorem): list f at the critical points inside
    (a, b) and at the ENDPOINTS a and b; the largest is the absolute max, the
    smallest the absolute min.
  - OPTIMISATION: 1) draw and name variables; 2) write the quantity to be
    maximised or minimised; 3) use the constraint to reduce it to ONE variable;
    4) state the domain; 5) differentiate, solve, and JUSTIFY (sign change,
    second derivative, or endpoint comparison); 6) answer the question asked,
    with units.
  - Classic results: fixed perimeter → the square has the largest area; closed
    can of fixed volume with least surface area has h = 2r; box from an a × a
    sheet has largest volume when squares of side a/6 are cut; profit is
    greatest where MR = MC; maximising a distance d is the same as maximising d²
    (easier: no square root).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Find the critical points of f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 1 and use the first
    derivative test to classify them.
    Answer: Local maximum f(1) = 5; local minimum f(3) = 1.
    Teacher explains: Critical points come from f′(x) = 0 (f′ exists everywhere
    here).
        f′(x) = 3x² − 12x + 9 = 3(x − 1)(x − 3) = 0  →  x = 1 or 3
                    x < 1      1 < x < 3      x > 3
        f′(x)         +            −            +
        f           rises   max  falls   min   rises
        f(1) = 1 − 6 + 9 + 1 = 5      f(3) = 27 − 54 + 27 + 1 = 1
    At x = 1 the graph stops rising and starts falling (+ to −): a peak. At
    x = 3 it changes from − to +: a valley. These are LOCAL: f(5) = 21 is bigger
    than the "maximum" 5, and there is no absolute maximum on ℝ because f → ∞.
    Common mistake: giving only the x-values; a maximum or minimum VALUE is
    f(c). Now you try: f(x) = x³ − 3x + 2. (f′ = 3(x − 1)(x + 1): local max
    f(−1) = 4, local min f(1) = 0)

D2. Use the second derivative test to find the local extrema of
    f(x) = x⁴ − 8x² + 3. Then explain what the test says about x⁴, −x⁴ and x³ at
    x = 0.
    Answer: Local maxima: f(0) = 3; local minima: f(−2) = f(2) = −13. At 0 the
    test fails for all three (f″(0) = 0): x⁴ has a minimum, −x⁴ a maximum, x³
    neither.
    Teacher explains: The second derivative measures bending: f″ < 0 means the
    graph bends down like a cap (a peak), f″ > 0 bends up like a cup (a valley).
        f′(x) = 4x³ − 16x = 4x(x − 2)(x + 2) = 0  →  x = −2, 0, 2
        f″(x) = 12x² − 16
        f″(0) = −16 < 0   →  local max,  f(0) = 3
        f″(±2) = 48 − 16 = 32 > 0   →  local min,  f(±2) = 16 − 32 + 3 = −13
    For y = x⁴, y′ = 4x³ and y″ = 12x², so y′(0) = y″(0) = 0 and the test says
    NOTHING. The first derivative test decides: 4x³ goes from − to +, so x⁴ has
    a minimum; for −x⁴, + to −, a maximum; for x³, y′ = 3x² is + on both sides,
    so neither. Common mistake: "f″(c) = 0 means a point of inflection" (false
    for x⁴). Now you try: f(x) = 2x³ − 3x² − 12x + 5. (f′ = 6(x − 2)(x + 1);
    f″(−1) = −18: max f(−1) = 12; f″(2) = 18: min f(2) = −15)

D3. Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of f(x) = 2x³ − 15x² + 36x + 1
    on the interval [1, 5].
    Answer: Absolute maximum 56 at x = 5; absolute minimum 24 at x = 1.
    Teacher explains: On a closed interval the extreme values occur either at a
    critical point inside, or at an ENDPOINT. So make a table of candidates:
        f′(x) = 6x² − 30x + 36 = 6(x − 2)(x − 3)  →  x = 2, 3 (both in [1, 5])
        x        1     2     3     5
        f(x)    24    29    28    56
               min               max
    The local max f(2) = 29 and local min f(3) = 28 are NOT the absolute ones:
    the endpoints win here. Common mistakes: forgetting the endpoints, and
    including critical points that lie OUTSIDE the interval. Now you try:
    f(x) = sin x + cos x on [0, π]. (f′ = cos x − sin x = 0 at π/4; f(0) = 1,
    f(π/4) = √2, f(π) = −1: max √2, min −1)

D4. An open box is made from a square sheet of tin of side 18 cm by cutting
    equal squares from the four corners and folding up the sides. What size of
    square should be cut to make the volume as large as possible? What is that
    volume?
    Answer: Cut squares of side 3 cm; the greatest volume is 432 cm³.
    Teacher explains: Let the cut squares have side x cm. The base is (18 − 2x)
    by (18 − 2x) and the height is x, so V(x) = x(18 − 2x)², with domain
    0 < x < 9.
        V′(x) = (18 − 2x)² + x × 2(18 − 2x)(−2)
              = (18 − 2x)(18 − 2x − 4x) = (18 − 2x)(18 − 6x)
        V′ = 0  →  x = 9 (not allowed) or x = 3
        V″(x) = 24x − 144,  V″(3) = −72 < 0  →  maximum
        V(3) = 3 × 12 × 12 = 432 cm³
    Check the ends: V → 0 as x → 0 or x → 9, so the only critical point in the
    domain must give the maximum. In general for a sheet of side a the best cut
    is a/6. Common mistake: using 18 − x for the base (a square is cut from BOTH
    ends of each side). Now you try: a 24 cm square sheet. (x = 4 cm,
    V = 4 × 16² = 1,024 cm³)

D5. A farmer has 200 m of fencing to enclose a rectangular field along a
    straight river; no fence is needed along the river. Find the dimensions of
    the largest field. Compare with a field fenced on all four sides.
    Answer: 50 m (perpendicular to the river) by 100 m (along it): area
    5,000 m². With four sides fenced, the best is a 50 m square: only 2,500 m².
    Teacher explains: Let x be each side perpendicular to the river; the side
    parallel to the river is 200 − 2x.
        A(x) = x(200 − 2x) = 200x − 2x²,    0 < x < 100
        A′(x) = 200 − 4x = 0  →  x = 50
        A″(x) = −4 < 0  →  maximum
        A(50) = 50 × 100 = 5,000 m²
    Four sides: 2x + 2y = 200 gives A = x(100 − x), maximum at x = 50: a square
    of area 2,500 m². The river saves a whole side, so the area doubles. Common
    mistake: using 2x + 2y = 200 when one side is free. Now you try: 600 m of
    fencing, three sides of a rectangle, the fourth is a wall. (150 m by 300 m,
    area 45,000 m²)

D6. A closed cylindrical can must hold 1,000 cm³ (1 litre). Find the radius and
    height that use the least metal (least total surface area).
    Answer: r = ∛(500/π) ≈ 5.42 cm and h = 2r ≈ 10.84 cm; least
    area ≈ 553.58 cm².
    Teacher explains: The constraint is the volume; the quantity to minimise is
    the area.
        πr²h = 1,000   →   h = 1,000/(πr²)
        S = 2πr² + 2πrh = 2πr² + 2,000/r,     r > 0
        S′(r) = 4πr − 2,000/r² = 0   →   r³ = 500/π
        r = ∛(500/π) ≈ 5.419 cm
        S″(r) = 4π + 4,000/r³ > 0   →   minimum
        h = 1,000/(πr²) = 2 × (500/π)/r² = 2r³/r² = 2r
    So the best can has height equal to its DIAMETER (h = 2r). Area: S
    = 2πr² + 2πr(2r) = 6πr² ≈ 6π × 29.37 ≈ 553.58 cm². Real cans are often
    taller because of other costs (sealing, labels). Common mistake: minimising
    the volume instead of the area, or forgetting the two circular ends. Now you
    try: an OPEN-top cylinder holding 1,000 cm³. (S = πr² + 2,000/r,
    r³ = 1,000/π, r ≈ 6.83 cm, h = r)

D7. Find the points on the parabola y = x² nearest to the point (0, 2), and the
    least distance.
    Answer: (±√6/2, 3/2), that is (±1.22, 1.5); least distance √7/2 ≈ 1.32.
    Teacher explains: A point on the curve is (x, x²). Minimise the SQUARE of
    the distance (same minimum point, no square root):
        D(x) = d² = (x − 0)² + (x² − 2)² = x⁴ − 3x² + 4
        D′(x) = 4x³ − 6x = 2x(2x² − 3) = 0  →  x = 0 or x = ±√(3/2)
        D(0) = 4 (d = 2)     D(±√(3/2)) = 9/4 − 9/2 + 4 = 7/4
        D″(x) = 12x² − 6:  D″(0) = −6 (local max),  D″(±√(3/2)) = 12 (min)
    So the nearest points are (±√(3/2), 3/2) = (±√6/2, 3/2) and the least
    distance is √(7/4) = √7/2. The vertex (0, 0), which many students guess, is
    at distance 2: farther! Check: the normal to the parabola at the nearest
    point passes through (0, 2). Common mistake: differentiating √(...) directly
    and making algebra slips; use d². Now you try: the point on the line
    2x + y = 5 nearest to the origin. (D = x² + (5 − 2x)², x = 2: (2, 1),
    distance √5)

D8. A sweet shop finds that it can sell x boxes of barfi a week when the price
    is p = 120 − 0.5x rupees per box. The weekly cost of making x boxes is
    C(x) = 20x + 1,000 rupees. How many boxes should it make, and at what price,
    for the greatest profit?
    Answer: 100 boxes at ₹70 each; greatest weekly profit ₹4,000.
    Teacher explains: Profit = revenue − cost, and revenue = price × quantity.
        R(x) = x(120 − 0.5x) = 120x − 0.5x²
        P(x) = R(x) − C(x) = 100x − 0.5x² − 1,000
        P′(x) = 100 − x = 0  →  x = 100;   P″(x) = −1 < 0  →  maximum
        price p = 120 − 50 = ₹70;   P(100) = 10,000 − 5,000 − 1,000 = 4,000
    Economists say "produce until marginal revenue equals marginal cost":
    MR = R′(x) = 120 − x and MC = C′(x) = 20 are equal at x = 100. Selling more
    than 100 boxes needs a lower price that loses more than it gains. Common
    mistake: maximising the revenue (x = 120, price ₹60) instead of the profit.
    Now you try: p = 50 − x/10 and C = 10x + 500. (P = 40x − x²/10 − 500,
    x = 200, p = ₹30, profit ₹3,500)

D9. A window is a rectangle topped by a semicircle (a Norman window). Its total
    perimeter (including the curved part) is 10 m. Find the dimensions that let
    in the most light (greatest area).
    Answer: Radius r = 10/(4 + π) ≈ 1.40 m, so the width 2r ≈ 2.80 m; the
    rectangle's height h = r ≈ 1.40 m; greatest area 50/(4 + π) ≈ 7.00 m².
    Teacher explains: Let the semicircle have radius r, so the rectangle is 2r
    wide and h high. The perimeter is two sides, the bottom and the arc:
        2h + 2r + πr = 10   →   h = (10 − 2r − πr)/2
        A = 2rh + (1/2)πr² = r(10 − 2r − πr) + (1/2)πr²
          = 10r − 2r² − (π/2)r²
        A′(r) = 10 − 4r − πr = 0   →   r = 10/(4 + π) ≈ 1.400
        A″(r) = −4 − π < 0   →   maximum
    Then h = (10 − (2 + π)r)/2 = (10 × 2/(4 + π))/2 = 10/(4 + π) = r: the
    rectangle is exactly half as tall as it is wide. Area = 10r − ((4 + π)/2)r²
    = 100/(4 + π) − 50/(4 + π) = 50/(4 + π) ≈ 7.00 m². Common mistakes: counting
    the base of the semicircle in the perimeter (it is inside the window), and
    using πr instead of (1/2)πr² for the semicircle's area. Now you try: a plain
    rectangular window of perimeter 10 m. (a square 2.5 m by 2.5 m, area
    6.25 m², less than the 7.00 m² of the Norman window)

D10. Find the rectangle of largest area that can be inscribed in a circle of
     radius 5 cm. Then find the cylinder of largest volume that fits inside a
     sphere of radius 6 cm.
     Answer: The square of side 5√2 ≈ 7.07 cm, area 50 cm². The cylinder has
     height 4√3 ≈ 6.93 cm, radius 2√6 ≈ 4.90 cm and volume 96π√3 ≈ 522.37 cm³.
     Teacher explains: Rectangle: put the centre at O and a corner at (x, y) on
     the circle, so the rectangle is 2x by 2y with x² + y² = 25.
         A = 4xy = 4x√(25 − x²);  maximise A² = 16x²(25 − x²) = 16(25x² − x⁴)
         d(A²)/dx = 16(50x − 4x³) = 0  →  x² = 25/2,  x = 5/√2 = y
         A = 4 × 25/2 = 50 cm²  (a square of side 2x = 5√2)
     Cylinder of height h in a sphere of radius 6: the radius r satisfies
     r² + (h/2)² = 36 (right triangle from the centre).
     V = πr²h = π(36 − h²/4)h = π(36h − h³/4); V′ = π(36 − 3h²/4) = 0 gives
     h² = 48, h = 4√3, r² = 36 − 12 = 24, V = π × 24 × 4√3 = 96π√3. V″
     = −3πh/2 < 0, a maximum. Common mistake: writing r² + h² = 36 (it is HALF
     the height that reaches the centre). Now you try: the largest rectangle in
     a semicircle of radius 4 (base on the diameter). (2x by y,
     A = 2x√(16 − x²), x = 2√2: 4√2 by 2√2, area 16)

D11. Two positive numbers x and y have sum 15. Find them if x²y³ is as large as
     possible. Also find the number that exceeds its square by the greatest
     amount.
     Answer: x = 6, y = 9 (x²y³ = 26,244). The number is 1/2 (it exceeds its
     square by 1/4).
     Teacher explains: Use the sum to write everything in terms of x:
     y = 15 − x, and f(x) = x²(15 − x)³ with 0 < x < 15.
         f′(x) = 2x(15 − x)³ − 3x²(15 − x)²
               = x(15 − x)²[2(15 − x) − 3x] = x(15 − x)²(30 − 5x)
         f′ = 0 inside (0, 15)  →  x = 6
         sign of f′: + for x < 6, − for 6 < x < 15  →  maximum
         x = 6, y = 9,  x²y³ = 36 × 729 = 26,244
     Notice the pattern: to maximise xᵐyⁿ with x + y fixed, split the sum in the
     ratio m : n (here 2 : 3 of 15). For the second part, g(x) = x − x²,
     g′(x) = 1 − 2x = 0 at x = 1/2, g″ = −2 < 0: maximum g(1/2) = 1/4. Common
     mistake: factorising f′ carelessly; take out the common factor x(15 − x)²
     first. Now you try: two positive numbers with product 64 and least sum. (8
     and 8, sum 16)

D12. A fisherman is in a boat 4 km from the nearest point P of a straight shore.
     His village is 6 km along the shore from P. He rows at 3 km/h and walks at
     5 km/h. Where should he land to reach the village as quickly as possible?
     Answer: Land 3 km from P (3 km short of the village); the least time is
     34/15 h = 2 h 16 min.
     Teacher explains: Let him land x km from P (0 ≤ x ≤ 6). He rows √(16 + x²)
     km and walks 6 − x km. Time = distance ÷ speed:
         T(x) = √(16 + x²)/3 + (6 − x)/5
         T′(x) = x/(3√(16 + x²)) − 1/5 = 0
         5x = 3√(16 + x²)  →  25x² = 9x² + 144  →  x² = 9  →  x = 3
         T(3) = 5/3 + 3/5 = 34/15 h ≈ 2.267 h
         T(0) = 4/3 + 6/5 = 38/15 ≈ 2.533 h,   T(6) = √52/3 ≈ 2.404 h
     This is a CLOSED interval, so compare the critical point with both
     endpoints: x = 3 is the smallest, so it is the absolute minimum. Rowing
     straight to the village (x = 6) or straight to shore (x = 0) are both
     slower. (The same calculation gives Snell's law for light.) Common mistake:
     squaring 5x = 3√(16 + x²) wrongly as 25x² = 9 × 16 + x². Now you try: same,
     but walking at 5 km/h and rowing at 4 km/h. (x/(4√(16 + x²)) = 1/5,
     9x² = 256, x = 16/3 ≈ 5.33 km)

     g) 600 m fence: rectangle split in two by a fence parallel to one side
     h) Boat 4 km offshore, village 6 km along shore; row 3 km/h, walk 5 km/h:
        landing point
     i) Same, but row 4 km/h, walk 5 km/h
     j) Wire 20 cm cut into a square (x cm) and a circle: least total area
     k) Largest rectangle under y = 12 − x² above the x-axis
     l) Isosceles triangle of largest area in a circle of radius 6
     Answers: a) r = h = 10/(π + 4) ≈ 1.40 m; A = 50/(π + 4) ≈ 7.00 m²
              b) r = h = 8/(π + 4) ≈ 1.12 m; A = 32/(π + 4) ≈ 4.48 m²
              c) r = h = 12/(π + 4) ≈ 1.68 m; A = 72/(π + 4) ≈ 10.08 m²
              d) 50 m by 100 m, area 5,000 m²
              e) 150 m by 300 m, area 45,000 m²   f) 30 m by 60 m, area 1,800 m²
              g) x = 100 (3 such sides), other side 150, area 15,000 m²
              h) 3 km from P, time 34/15 h   i) 16/3 km from P, time 9/5 h
              j) x = 80/(π + 4) ≈ 11.20 cm (maximum: all into the circle)
              k) x = 2: 4 by 8, area 32
              l) equilateral, side 6√3, area 27√3 ≈ 46.77

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: insist on a written plan: variables, the formula to optimise, the
  constraint, one-variable function, domain. Draw the figure with the unknown
  marked. Keep a table of "candidates" for closed intervals. For the second
  derivative test, compute f″ symbolically once and substitute each critical
  point. Harder: prove that among all rectangles inscribed in a circle the
  square has the largest area, without calculus (AM-GM, topic 8.61); find the
  shortest ladder that reaches over a 2 m wall to a building 1 m behind it
  ((2^(2/3) + 1)^(3/2) ≈ 4.16 m); show that the semi-vertical angle of the cone
  of greatest volume with given slant height is tan⁻¹√2; a right circular cone
  of greatest volume inscribed in a sphere of radius R has height 4R/3 and
  volume 8/27 of the sphere's; find the point on y² = 4x nearest to (2, 1)
  (d² = (y²/4 − 2)² + (y − 1)² has derivative y³/4 − 2, zero at y = 2: the point
  (1, 2), distance √2).


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.43 — CURVE SKETCHING
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A good sketch shows the SHAPE and the KEY POINTS, not a plotted table. Work
    through the checklist: 1) domain; 2) intercepts (x = 0 and y = 0); 3)
    symmetry (even: f(−x) = f(x), symmetric in the y-axis; odd: f(−x) = −f(x),
    symmetric about the origin; periodic); 4) asymptotes; 5) f′: increasing /
    decreasing, local max / min; 6) f″: concavity and inflection points; 7) a
    table of key points; 8) draw.
  - ASYMPTOTES: VERTICAL x = a where f(x) → ±∞ as x → a (usually a zero of the
    denominator that is not cancelled); HORIZONTAL y = L where f(x) → L as
    x → ±∞; OBLIQUE y = mx + c when f(x) − (mx + c) → 0 (for a rational function
    with degree of top = degree of bottom + 1, divide:
    x²/(x − 1) = x + 1 + 1/(x − 1), asymptote y = x + 1).
  - CONCAVITY: f″ > 0 on an interval: concave UP (holds water, lies above its
    tangents); f″ < 0: concave DOWN. An INFLECTION POINT is a point of the graph
    where the concavity CHANGES. f″(c) = 0 is needed (if f″ exists) but not
    enough: x⁴ has f″(0) = 0 and no inflection.
  - Standard limits used for asymptotes: xⁿe^(−x) → 0 as x → ∞ (the exponential
    wins), ln x/x → 0 as x → ∞, x ln x → 0 as x → 0⁺, and a rational function
    behaves like the ratio of its leading terms for large |x|.
  - Features of cubics: every cubic has exactly one inflection point, and the
    graph is symmetric about it; it has two turning points or none. A repeated
    root (x − a)² means the graph TOUCHES the x-axis at a; a triple root
    (x − a)³ means it crosses with a horizontal tangent.
  - Sketches are also used to COUNT real roots: the number of solutions of
    f(x) = k is the number of times the horizontal line y = k meets the graph of
    f.
  - Notation: x^(2/3) means (∛x)², defined for all real x. In a text sketch, *
    marks the curve, | and - the axes; always label the key points and
    asymptotes in a table beside it.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Sketch y = x³ − 3x² + 4, showing intercepts, turning points and the point of
    inflection.
    Answer: x-intercepts −1 and 2 (touching at 2), y-intercept 4; local max
    (0, 4), local min (2, 0); inflection (1, 2); concave down for x < 1, up for
    x > 1; y → ±∞ as x → ±∞.
    Teacher explains: Follow the checklist. Domain ℝ; no asymptotes (a
    polynomial).
        intercepts: y(0) = 4;  x³ − 3x² + 4 = (x + 1)(x − 2)² = 0
                    → x = −1 (crosses), x = 2 (double root: touches)
        f′(x) = 3x² − 6x = 3x(x − 2):  + for x < 0, − on (0, 2), + for x > 2
                    → max (0, 4), min (2, 0)
        f″(x) = 6x − 6: − for x < 1, + for x > 1 → inflection (1, 2)
        x      −1    0     1     2     3
        y       0    4     2     0     4
             crosses max  infl  min
                        |                              *
                        |                             **
                    **********                        *
                  ***   |    ***                     *
                 **     |      ***                  *
                **      |         ***              *
               **       |           ***          **
              **        |             ****     ***
        ------*---------+----------------******-----------
             *          |
            **          |
            *           |
    The inflection point (1, 2) is exactly halfway between the turning points,
    and the cubic is symmetric about it: this is true for every cubic. Common
    mistake: thinking the graph crosses the axis at x = 2; at a double root it
    only touches. Now you try: sketch y = x³ − 3x. (odd; intercepts 0, ±√3; max
    (−1, 2), min (1, −2); inflection (0, 0))

D2. Sketch y = x⁴ − 4x³. Explain why the origin is a point of inflection with a
    horizontal tangent, and not a turning point.
    Answer: Intercepts (0, 0) and (4, 0); only one turning point: minimum
    (3, −27); inflection points (0, 0) (horizontal tangent) and (2, −16);
    concave up for x < 0 and x > 2, down on (0, 2).
    Teacher explains:
        y = x³(x − 4):  x-intercepts 0 (triple root) and 4
        f′(x) = 4x³ − 12x² = 4x²(x − 3)
                sign: − for x < 0, − on (0, 3), + for x > 3
                → f′(0) = 0 but NO sign change: not an extremum
                → minimum at x = 3: y = 81 − 108 = −27
        f″(x) = 12x² − 24x = 12x(x − 2)
                sign: + for x < 0, − on (0, 2), + for x > 2
                → inflections at x = 0 (y = 0) and x = 2 (y = 16 − 32 = −16)
        x      −1     0     2     3     4
        y       5     0   −16   −27     0
    At x = 0 the graph is falling on both sides (f′ ≤ 0), so it does not turn;
    but it changes from concave up to concave down, and the tangent there is
    horizontal (y = 0). This happens because 0 is a TRIPLE root: near 0,
    y ≈ −4x³, which looks like an upside-down x³. Common mistake: marking every
    stationary point as a max or a min. Now you try: y = 3x⁴ − 4x³. (min
    (1, −1); horizontal inflection (0, 0); inflection (2/3, −16/27))

D3. Test each function for symmetry: f(x) = x⁴ − 2x², g(x) = x³ − 3x,
    h(x) = x³ + x², k(x) = x sin x, m(x) = eˣ. Then use symmetry to sketch
    y = x⁴ − 2x² with half the work.
    Answer: f even, g odd, h neither, k even, m neither. y = x⁴ − 2x²:
    intercepts 0, ±√2; max (0, 0), minima (±1, −1); inflections
    (±1/√3, −5/9) ≈ (±0.58, −0.56); a "W" shape.
    Teacher explains: Replace x by −x and compare:
        f(−x) = x⁴ − 2x² = f(x)             even: mirror in the y-axis
        g(−x) = −x³ + 3x = −g(x)            odd: half-turn about O
        h(−x) = −x³ + x²  (neither ±h(x))   neither
        k(−x) = (−x)sin(−x) = x sin x      even (odd × odd = even)
        m(−x) = e^(−x)                      neither
          *                   |                   *
          *                   |                   *
          *                   |                   *
           *                  |                  *
           **                 |                 **
            *                 |                 *
        -----*-----------***********-----------*-----
              **      ****    |    ****      **
               ********       |       ********
                              |
    For the even function, study x ≥ 0 only and reflect.
    f′(x) = 4x³ − 4x = 4x(x − 1)(x + 1): on x > 0 it falls to a minimum at x = 1
    (f(1) = −1) then rises. f″(x) = 12x² − 4 = 0 at x = 1/√3, where
    y = 1/9 − 2/3 = −5/9. Reflecting gives the W with the second minimum at
    (−1, −1); (0, 0) is a local max. Common mistake: "a function is either even
    or odd"; most are neither (h and m). Now you try: is f(x) = x/(x² + 1) even,
    odd or neither? (odd)

D4. Sketch y = x/(x² + 1): find the asymptote, the extreme values and the three
    points of inflection.
    Answer: Odd function through O; horizontal asymptote y = 0; max (1, 1/2),
    min (−1, −1/2); inflections at x = 0, ±√3, i.e. (0, 0) and
    (±√3, ±√3/4) ≈ (±1.73, ±0.43).
    Teacher explains:
        domain ℝ (x² + 1 ≠ 0), no vertical asymptote; odd
        x → ±∞: y ≈ x/x² = 1/x → 0, so y = 0 is a horizontal asymptote
        f′(x) = ((x² + 1) − 2x²)/(x² + 1)² = (1 − x²)/(x² + 1)²
                + on (−1, 1), − outside → max f(1) = 1/2, min f(−1) = −1/2
        f″(x) = 2x(x² − 3)/(x² + 1)³
                zero at x = 0, ±√3 with sign changes → three inflections
        f(√3) = √3/4 ≈ 0.433
                                 |
                                 | **********
                                 |**        ***********
                                 |*                   *****
        -------------------------*-------------------------
        *****                   *|
            ***********        **|
                      ********** |
                                 |
    The curve starts just below the axis on the far left, falls to −1/2, rises
    through the origin to 1/2 and then sinks back towards the axis from above. A
    horizontal asymptote CAN be crossed (here at O), unlike a vertical one.
    Common mistake: forgetting the quotient rule sign: (v u′ − u v′)/v². Now you
    try: y = 4x/(x² + 4). (max (2, 1), min (−2, −1), asymptote y = 0)

D5. Sketch y = x²/(x − 1). Find its vertical and oblique asymptotes and its
    turning points.
    Answer: Vertical asymptote x = 1; oblique asymptote y = x + 1; local max
    (0, 0), local min (2, 4); concave down for x < 1, up for x > 1; no
    inflection.
    Teacher explains: Divide first: it shows the oblique asymptote at once.
        x²/(x − 1) = x + 1 + 1/(x − 1)     (x² = (x − 1)(x + 1) + 1)
        as x → ±∞, 1/(x − 1) → 0: oblique asymptote y = x + 1
        as x → 1⁺, y → +∞;  as x → 1⁻, y → −∞: vertical asymptote x = 1
        f′(x) = 1 − 1/(x − 1)² = x(x − 2)/(x − 1)²
                → max (0, 0), min (2, 4)
        f″(x) = 2/(x − 1)³:  − for x < 1, + for x > 1
    There is no inflection point: the concavity changes at x = 1, but x = 1 is
    not in the domain. The left branch is an upside-down "U" with top (0, 0);
    the right branch is a "U" with bottom (2, 4), both hugging the two
    asymptotes. Note the local max 0 is LESS than the local min 4: on different
    branches this is allowed. Common mistake: finding a horizontal asymptote
    (there is none, degree 2 over 1). Now you try: y = (x² + 3)/(x − 1).
    (x + 1 + 4/(x − 1): asymptotes x = 1, y = x + 1; max (−1, −2), min (3, 6))

D6. Sketch y = 2x²/(x² − 1). Use symmetry, asymptotes, the first and second
    derivatives.
    Answer: Even; vertical asymptotes x = ±1; horizontal asymptote y = 2; local
    max (0, 0); increasing for x < 0, decreasing for x > 0 (x ≠ ±1); concave up
    for |x| > 1, down for |x| < 1; no inflection. The outer branches lie above
    y = 2.
    Teacher explains:
        even: f(−x) = f(x);  only intercept (0, 0)
        x² − 1 = 0 at x = ±1 → vertical asymptotes; x → ±∞: y → 2
        f′(x) = −4x/(x² − 1)²:  + for x < 0, − for x > 0 → max (0, 0)
        f″(x) = 4(3x² + 1)/(x² − 1)³: sign of (x² − 1)
        near 1:  x → 1⁺ gives y → +∞;  x → 1⁻ gives y → −∞
        x      0     0.5     2     3
        y      0   −2/3    8/3   9/4
    Is y above or below the asymptote y = 2? y − 2 = 2/(x² − 1) > 0 for |x| > 1,
    so the outer branches come down from +∞ and approach 2 from ABOVE. The
    middle branch is a cap between the two vertical asymptotes with top (0, 0).
    Common mistake: joining the branches across x = ±1. Now you try:
    y = 1/(x² − 4). (even, x = ±2, y = 0, max (0, −1/4) on the middle branch)

D7. Sketch y = x eˣ.
    Answer: Domain ℝ; intercept (0, 0); horizontal asymptote y = 0 as x → −∞
    (from below); y → ∞ as x → ∞; minimum (−1, −1/e) ≈ (−1, −0.37); inflection
    (−2, −2/e²) ≈ (−2, −0.27).
    Teacher explains:
        f′(x) = eˣ + x eˣ = (x + 1)eˣ:  − for x < −1, + for x > −1
                → minimum f(−1) = −1/e
        f″(x) = (x + 2)eˣ:  − for x < −2, + for x > −2
                → inflection f(−2) = −2/e²
        as x → −∞: x eˣ = x/e^(−x) → 0 (exponential wins), y < 0
        x     −4      −2      −1      0     1
        y   −0.07   −0.27   −0.37    0    2.72
                                                |      *
                                                |     **
                                                |     *
                                                |    *
                                                |   **
                                                |  **
                                                |***
        **********-----------------------------***--------
                 *******************************|
                                                |
    eˣ > 0 always, so the signs of f′ and f″ are just the signs of (x + 1) and
    (x + 2). The graph creeps along just below the negative x-axis, dips to its
    lowest point at x = −1, then shoots up. Common mistake: saying there is no
    asymptote because "eˣ has none on the right"; look at BOTH ends. Now you
    try: y = x e^(−x). (max (1, 1/e), inflection (2, 2/e²), asymptote y = 0 as
    x → ∞)

D8. Sketch y = ln x/x and deduce which is larger, e^π or π^e.
    Answer: Domain x > 0; x-intercept (1, 0); vertical asymptote x = 0 (y → −∞);
    horizontal asymptote y = 0 as x → ∞; maximum (e, 1/e); inflection (e^(3/2),
    3/(2e^(3/2))) ≈ (4.48, 0.33). Since π > e, ln π/π < 1/e = ln e/e, which
    gives e^π > π^e.
    Teacher explains:
        f′(x) = (1 − ln x)/x²:  + for 0 < x < e, − for x > e
                → maximum f(e) = 1/e ≈ 0.368
        f″(x) = (2 ln x − 3)/x³:  zero at ln x = 3/2, x = e^(3/2)
        x → 0⁺: ln x → −∞ and 1/x → +∞, so y → −∞
        x → ∞:  ln x/x → 0
    Because f is decreasing for x > e and π > e: ln π/π < ln e/e. Multiply by eπ
    (positive): e ln π < π ln e = π, so ln(π^e) < ln(e^π) and π^e < e^π
    (numerically 22.46 < 23.14). Common mistake: forgetting the domain
    restriction x > 0 and drawing a left half. Now you try: which is larger, 3⁴
    or 4³? (4 > 3 > e and f decreases there, so ln 4/4 < ln 3/3,
    3 ln 4 < 4 ln 3: 4³ = 64 < 81 = 3⁴)

D9. Sketch y = x² e^(−x).
    Answer: y ≥ 0; touches the x-axis at the origin (minimum (0, 0)); maximum
    (2, 4/e²) ≈ (2, 0.54); inflections at x = 2 ± √2 ≈ 0.59 and 3.41 (y ≈ 0.19
    and 0.38); asymptote y = 0 as x → ∞; y → ∞ as x → −∞.
    Teacher explains:
        f′(x) = 2x e^(−x) − x² e^(−x) = x(2 − x)e^(−x)
                − for x < 0, + on (0, 2), − for x > 2
                → min f(0) = 0, max f(2) = 4/e²
        f″(x) = (x² − 4x + 2)e^(−x), zero at x = 2 ± √2
        x → ∞: x²/eˣ → 0;   x → −∞: x² e^(−x) → ∞
    Key points table: (0, 0) min; (0.59, 0.19) inflection; (2, 0.54) max;
    (3.41, 0.38) inflection. The graph falls from very high on the left, touches
    O, rises to a hump at x = 2 and then decays towards the axis. Common
    mistake: product rule slips: d/dx(e^(−x)) = −e^(−x). Now you try:
    y = x³e^(−x). (f′ = x²(3 − x)e^(−x): max (3, 27/e³); at 0 no extremum)

D10. Sketch the "bell curve" y = e^(−x²) and explain where it is steepest.
     Answer: Even; always positive; maximum (0, 1); inflections
     (±1/√2, 1/√e) ≈ (±0.71, 0.61); asymptote y = 0 as x → ±∞. It is steepest at
     the inflection points (slope ∓√(2/e) ≈ ∓0.86).
     Teacher explains:
         f′(x) = −2x e^(−x²):  + for x < 0, − for x > 0 → max f(0) = 1
         f″(x) = (4x² − 2)e^(−x²):  zero at x = ±1/√2
         f(±1/√2) = e^(−1/2) = 1/√e ≈ 0.607
         f′(1/√2) = −2(1/√2)e^(−1/2) = −√2/√e = −√(2/e) ≈ −0.858
                                  |
                              *********
                            ***   |   ***
                          **      |      **
                        ***       |       ***
                     ***          |          ***
         ************-------------+-------------************
                                  |
     The slope f′ is largest in size where its own derivative f″ is zero: the
     steepest points of any smooth curve are its inflection points. This curve
     (scaled) is the normal distribution of statistics (topic 8.56). Common
     mistake: writing d/dx(e^(−x²)) = e^(−x²) or −x² e^(−x²−1). Now you try:
     y = 1/(1 + x²). (max (0, 1); inflections (±1/√3, 3/4); asymptote y = 0)

D11. The derivative of a function is f′(x) = (x − 1)²(x + 2). Without finding f,
     describe its graph: where does f increase, where are its extrema and
     inflection points?
     Answer: f decreases on (−∞, −2) and increases on (−2, ∞); local min at
     x = −2; no extremum at x = 1 (horizontal inflection); inflection points at
     x = −1 and x = 1.
     Teacher explains:
         sign of f′: (x − 1)² ≥ 0, so sign = sign of (x + 2)
                 − for x < −2, + for x > −2 (0 at x = 1, no change)
         f″(x) = 2(x − 1)(x + 2) + (x − 1)² = (x − 1)(3x + 3) = 3(x − 1)(x + 1)
                 + for x < −1, − on (−1, 1), + for x > 1
                 → concavity changes at x = −1 and x = 1
     So the graph falls to a minimum at x = −2, rises, bends from concave up to
     concave down at x = −1, flattens to a horizontal tangent at x = 1 (still
     rising) where it bends back to concave up. The rule: a factor of f′ with an
     EVEN power gives no sign change (no extremum); an ODD power gives one.
     Common mistake: listing x = 1 as a max or min. Now you try:
     f′(x) = x³(x − 2)². (min at x = 0; x = 2 is not an extremum)

D12. Sketch y = x^(2/3)(x − 5) (with x^(2/3) = (∛x)²). What happens at the
     origin?
     Answer: Intercepts (0, 0) and (5, 0); a CUSP at the origin, which is a
     local max 0 (f′ is undefined there); local min at x = 2: y = −3∛4 ≈ −4.76;
     inflection (−1, −6); concave down for x < −1, up for x > −1 (x ≠ 0).
     Teacher explains:
         y = x^(5/3) − 5x^(2/3)
         f′(x) = (5/3)x^(2/3) − (10/3)x^(−1/3) = 5(x − 2)/(3∛x)
                 critical points: x = 2 (f′ = 0), x = 0 (f′ undefined)
                 signs: + for x < 0, − on (0, 2), + for x > 2
         f″(x) = 10(x + 1)/(9x^(4/3)):  x^(4/3) > 0, so sign = sign of (x + 1)
         f(2) = 2^(2/3) × (−3) = −3∛4,   f(−1) = 1 × (−6) = −6
     Near 0, f′ → +∞ from the left and −∞ from the right: the two sides of the
     graph meet at a sharp point pointing UP (a cusp) with a vertical tangent.
     The first derivative test still works at points where f′ does not exist.
     Common mistake: thinking x^(2/3) is undefined for x < 0;
     (−1)^(2/3) = (∛(−1))² = 1. Now you try: y = x^(1/3)(x − 4).
     (f′ = 4(x − 1)/(3x^(2/3)): min (1, −3); vertical tangent at 0 but no
     extremum)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Find the domain and the intercepts (x-intercepts where y = 0; y-intercept
    where x = 0).
    a) y = x³ − 4x
    b) y = x³ − 3x² + 4
    c) y = x⁴ − 5x² + 4
    d) y = (x − 1)²(x + 3)
    e) y = (x + 2)/(x − 3)
    f) y = x/(x² − 4)
    g) y = (x² − 1)/(x² + 1)
    h) y = (x² − 9)/(x − 1)
    i) y = √(4 − x²)
    j) y = √(x − 1)
    k) y = ln(x + 2)
    l) y = ln(x² − 1)
    m) y = x ln x
    n) y = eˣ − 2
    o) y = x eˣ
    p) y = e^(1/x)
    q) y = 1/(x² + x − 6)
    r) y = x^(2/3)(x − 5)
    Answers: a) domain ℝ; intercepts x = 0, ±2; y = 0
             b) domain ℝ; intercepts x = −1, 2; y = 4
             c) domain ℝ; intercepts x = ±1, ±2; y = 4
             d) domain ℝ; intercepts x = −3, 1; y = 3
             e) domain x ≠ 3; intercepts x = −2; y = −2/3
             f) domain x ≠ ±2; intercepts x = 0; y = 0
             g) domain ℝ; intercepts x = ±1; y = −1
             h) domain x ≠ 1; intercepts x = ±3; y = 9
             i) domain [−2, 2]; intercepts x = ±2; y = 2
             j) domain x ≥ 1; intercepts x = 1; none on the y-axis
             k) domain x > −2; intercepts x = −1; y = ln 2
             l) domain x < −1 or x > 1; intercepts x = ±√2; none on the y-axis
             m) domain x > 0; intercepts x = 1; none on the y-axis
             n) domain ℝ; intercepts x = ln 2; y = −1
             o) domain ℝ; intercepts x = 0; y = 0
             p) domain x ≠ 0; intercepts none
             q) domain x ≠ −3, 2; intercepts none on the x-axis; y = −1/6
             r) domain ℝ; intercepts x = 0, 5; y = 0

M2. Even, odd or neither? (Even: symmetric in the y-axis; odd: symmetric about
    the origin.)
    a) f(x) = x⁴ − 3x²      b) f(x) = x³ − x        c) f(x) = x³ + 1
    d) f(x) = x⁵ + x³       e) f(x) = x² + x        f) f(x) = 1/x
    g) f(x) = 1/x²          h) f(x) = x/(x² + 1)    i) f(x) = x²/(x² − 4)
    j) f(x) = |x|           k) f(x) = x|x|          l) f(x) = sin x
    m) f(x) = cos x         n) f(x) = x sin x       o) f(x) = x cos x
    p) f(x) = sin²x         q) f(x) = tan x         r) f(x) = eˣ
    s) f(x) = e^(−x²)       t) f(x) = eˣ + e^(−x)   u) f(x) = eˣ − e^(−x)
    v) f(x) = ln|x|         w) f(x) = ln x          x) f(x) = x² + cos x

M9. True or false? Give a reason or counterexample where false.
    a) the graph of an odd function passes through the origin (if f(0) is
       defined)

    c) a cubic always has two turning points

    e) a graph can cross its horizontal asymptote
    f) a graph can cross its vertical asymptote

    h) at a double root the graph touches the x-axis
    i) a local maximum is always greater than a local minimum
    j) eˣ is concave up everywhere
    k) ln x is concave down everywhere on its domain
    l) an even function has f′(0) = 0 if f′(0) exists
    m) the inflection point of a cubic is midway between its turning points
    n) a rational function with degree of top < degree of bottom has y = 0 as an
       asymptote
    o) the number of real roots of f(x) = k equals the number of intersections
       of y = f(x) and y = k

             l) true   m) true   n) true   o) true   p) true
