TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: use the same eight-step checklist every time and fill in a printed
  table: domain / intercepts / symmetry / asymptotes / f′ signs / f″ signs / key
  points / sketch. Check the sketch on Desmos or GeoGebra afterwards and find
  what was missed. Start with cubics, then quartics, then rationals, then eˣ and
  ln x. Harder: sketch y = x^x for x > 0 (min at x = 1/e, y → 1 as x → 0⁺);
  sketch y = (x² − 1)/(x² − 4) and find where it crosses its horizontal
  asymptote (never: y − 1 = 3/(x² − 4) ≠ 0); sketch y = sin x + sin 2x on [0,
  2π]; show that the curve y = (x − 1)/(x² + 1) has three collinear inflection
  points; sketch the curve y² = x²(1 − x) (a loop) using y = ±x√(1 − x).


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.44 — INDEFINITE INTEGRALS; INTEGRATION BY SUBSTITUTION, BY PARTS,
             PARTIAL FRACTIONS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - F is an ANTIDERIVATIVE of f if F′(x) = f(x). All antiderivatives differ by a
    constant, so ∫f(x) dx = F(x) + C. Always write + C, and CHECK every answer
    by differentiating it.
  - STANDARD INTEGRALS: ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) (n ≠ −1); ∫1/x dx = ln|x|;
    ∫eˣ dx = eˣ; ∫aˣ dx = aˣ/ln a; ∫sin x dx = −cos x; ∫cos x dx = sin x;
    ∫sec²x dx = tan x; ∫cosec²x dx = −cot x; ∫sec x tan x dx = sec x;
    ∫cosec x cot x dx = −cosec x; ∫1/(1 + x²) dx = tan⁻¹x;
    ∫1/√(1 − x²) dx = sin⁻¹x (all + C). Linear inside:
    ∫f(ax + b) dx = (1/a)F(ax + b).
  - SUBSTITUTION: if the integrand contains g(x) and (a multiple of) g′(x), put
    u = g(x), du = g′(x) dx, integrate in u, then return to x. Special case:
    ∫f′(x)/f(x) dx = ln|f(x)|, so ∫tan x dx = ln|sec x|, ∫cot x dx = ln|sin x|,
    ∫sec x dx = ln|sec x + tan x|, ∫cosec x dx = ln|cosec x − cot x|.
  - TRIG POWERS: even powers use sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2, cos²x = (1 + cos 2x)/2;
    odd powers keep one factor and use sin²x + cos²x = 1 (∫cos³x dx: put
    u = sin x); products use 2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A − B) etc.;
    tan²x = sec²x − 1.
  - BY PARTS: ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du, from the product rule. Choose u by LIATE
    (Logarithm, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential: the earlier one is
    u). Repeat for x²eˣ; for eˣ sin x the integral comes back: solve for it.
    ∫eˣ(f(x) + f′(x)) dx = eˣf(x).
  - PARTIAL FRACTIONS (proper fractions only; if degree top ≥ degree bottom,
    divide first): distinct linear factors A/(x − a) + B/(x − b); repeated
    (x − a)² gives A/(x − a) + B/(x − a)²; an irreducible quadratic x² + px + q
    gives (Bx + C)/(x² + px + q). Find constants by the cover-up rule or by
    comparing coefficients.
  - SPECIAL FORMS (a > 0): ∫1/(x² + a²) dx = (1/a)tan⁻¹(x/a);
    ∫1/√(a² − x²) dx = sin⁻¹(x/a); ∫1/(x² − a²) dx
    = (1/(2a))ln|(x − a)/(x + a)|; ∫√(a² − x²) dx
    = (x/2)√(a² − x²) + (a²/2)sin⁻¹(x/a). Complete the square first for
    x² + bx + c.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Find ∫(3x² − 4x + 5) dx, ∫(√x + 1/x) dx and ∫(eˣ + sec²x) dx. Why do we add
    a constant C, and how can you check an answer?
    Answer: x³ − 2x² + 5x + C; (2/3)x^(3/2) + ln|x| + C; eˣ + tan x + C. C is
    there because every function F + C has the same derivative; check by
    differentiating.
    Teacher explains: Integration reverses differentiation. For powers: add 1 to
    the power and divide by the new power.
        ∫(3x² − 4x + 5) dx = 3 × x³/3 − 4 × x²/2 + 5x + C
                           = x³ − 2x² + 5x + C
        ∫(x^(1/2) + 1/x) dx = x^(3/2)/(3/2) + ln|x| + C
                           = (2/3)x^(3/2) + ln|x| + C
        check: d/dx[(2/3)x^(3/2)] = (2/3)(3/2)x^(1/2) = √x, correct
    The derivative of any constant is 0, so x³ − 2x² + 5x + 7 and
    x³ − 2x² + 5x − 100 are both answers: + C stands for ALL of them (a family
    of parallel curves). Why ln|x| and not ln x? For x < 0, d/dx
    ln(−x) = (−1)/(−x) = 1/x as well, so ln|x| works on both sides of 0. The
    power rule fails for n = −1 (it would divide by 0): that is the case
    ∫1/x dx. Common mistakes: forgetting + C; writing ∫x² dx = x³ (forgot to
    divide by 3); integrating a product term by term. Now you try:
    ∫(x² − 1)/√x dx. (split: x^(3/2) − x^(−1/2); answer 2x^(5/2)/5 − 2√x + C)

D2. Use the table of standard integrals: find
    ∫(2 sin x − 3 cos x + 4/(1 + x²)) dx and ∫(2ˣ + 5/√(1 − x²)) dx. Then find
    ∫(sin 3x + e^(2x)) dx and ∫(2x + 1)⁴ dx.
    Answer: −2 cos x − 3 sin x + 4 tan⁻¹x + C; 2ˣ/ln 2 + 5 sin⁻¹x + C;
    −(1/3)cos 3x + (1/2)e^(2x) + C; (2x + 1)⁵/10 + C.
    Teacher explains: Read the table backwards from the derivatives you know:
        d/dx(−cos x) = sin x          so ∫sin x dx = −cos x + C
        d/dx(tan⁻¹x) = 1/(1 + x²)     so ∫1/(1 + x²) dx = tan⁻¹x + C
        d/dx(2ˣ) = 2ˣ ln 2             so ∫2ˣ dx = 2ˣ/ln 2 + C
        d/dx(sin⁻¹x) = 1/√(1 − x²)    so ∫1/√(1 − x²) dx = sin⁻¹x + C
    For a LINEAR inside, ax + b, integrate as usual and divide by a (the chain
    rule would multiply by a when differentiating back):
    ∫sin 3x dx = −(cos 3x)/3, ∫e^(2x) dx = e^(2x)/2,
    ∫(2x + 1)⁴ dx = (2x + 1)⁵/(5 × 2). This shortcut is ONLY for linear insides:
    ∫(x² + 1)⁴ dx is NOT (x² + 1)⁵/(10x). Common mistake: the sign of ∫sin x dx
    (it is −cos x). Now you try: ∫(cos 4x − 1/(3x + 2)) dx.
    ((1/4)sin 4x − (1/3)ln|3x + 2| + C)

D3. Integrate by substitution: ∫2x(x² + 1)⁵ dx, ∫x√(x² + 4) dx and
    ∫x e^(−x²) dx.
    Answer: (x² + 1)⁶/6 + C; (1/3)(x² + 4)^(3/2) + C; −(1/2)e^(−x²) + C.
    Teacher explains: Look for a function g(x) whose derivative g′(x) is also
    present (up to a constant factor). Put u = g(x):
        u = x² + 1,  du = 2x dx:   ∫u⁵ du = u⁶/6 = (x² + 1)⁶/6 + C
        u = x² + 4,  du = 2x dx, so x dx = du/2:
             ∫√u (du/2) = (1/2)(2/3)u^(3/2) = (1/3)(x² + 4)^(3/2) + C
        u = −x²,     du = −2x dx, so x dx = −du/2:
             ∫eᵘ(−du/2) = −(1/2)e^(−x²) + C
    Every dx must be replaced: after substituting, NO x may remain. If you are
    left with an x you cannot express in u, the substitution is wrong. Check the
    second answer: d/dx[(1/3)(x² + 4)^(3/2)]
    = (1/3)(3/2)(x² + 4)^(1/2)(2x) = x√(x² + 4), as required. Common mistakes:
    forgetting to change dx; forgetting to substitute back. Now you try:
    ∫sin³x cos x dx. (u = sin x: sin⁴x/4 + C)

D4. Show that ∫f′(x)/f(x) dx = ln|f(x)| + C. Use it to find ∫tan x dx,
    ∫(2x + 3)/(x² + 3x + 5) dx, ∫eˣ/(1 + eˣ) dx and ∫sec x dx.
    Answer: ln|sec x| + C (= −ln|cos x| + C); ln(x² + 3x + 5) + C;
    ln(1 + eˣ) + C; ln|sec x + tan x| + C.
    Teacher explains: Put u = f(x), du = f′(x) dx:
    ∫du/u = ln|u| + C = ln|f(x)| + C. So whenever the TOP is the derivative of
    the BOTTOM, the answer is ln|bottom|.
        tan x = sin x/cos x = −(−sin x)/cos x
        ∫tan x dx = −ln|cos x| + C = ln|sec x| + C
        d/dx(x² + 3x + 5) = 2x + 3:   ln|x² + 3x + 5| + C
        (x² + 3x + 5 > 0 always, so the modulus can be dropped)
        sec x = sec x(sec x + tan x)/(sec x + tan x)
              top = sec²x + sec x tan x = d/dx(sec x + tan x)
        ∫sec x dx = ln|sec x + tan x| + C
    The sec x result is a clever trick (multiply top and bottom by
    sec x + tan x); learn the answer. Common mistake: ∫tan x dx = sec²x (that is
    the DERIVATIVE of tan x). Now you try: ∫1/(x ln x) dx and ∫cot x dx.
    (ln|ln x| + C; ln|sin x| + C)

D5. Find ∫sin²x dx, ∫cos³x dx, ∫tan²x dx and ∫sin 3x cos 2x dx.
    Answer: x/2 − (sin 2x)/4 + C; sin x − (sin³x)/3 + C; tan x − x + C;
    −(cos 5x)/10 − (cos x)/2 + C.
    Teacher explains: There is no rule for ∫sin²x directly: rewrite the
    integrand first.
        sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2:   ∫ = x/2 − (sin 2x)/4 + C
        cos³x = cos²x cos x = (1 − sin²x)cos x;  u = sin x, du = cos x dx
                ∫(1 − u²) du = u − u³/3 = sin x − sin³x/3 + C
        tan²x = sec²x − 1:        ∫ = tan x − x + C
        2 sin 3x cos 2x = sin 5x + sin x
                ∫ = (1/2)(−cos 5x/5 − cos x) = −cos 5x/10 − cos x/2 + C
    Rule of thumb: EVEN powers of sin or cos: double-angle formulas; an ODD
    power: save one factor for du and turn the rest into the other function with
    sin² + cos² = 1; products of different angles: product-to-sum. Common
    mistake: ∫sin²x dx = sin³x/3 (the chain rule would need a cos x). Now you
    try: ∫cos²x dx and ∫sin³x dx. (x/2 + sin 2x/4 + C; −cos x + cos³x/3 + C)

D6. Derive the formula for integration by parts and use it for ∫x eˣ dx and
    ∫x cos x dx. How do you decide which factor is u?
    Answer: ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du. ∫x eˣ dx = x eˣ − eˣ + C = (x − 1)eˣ + C;
    ∫x cos x dx = x sin x + cos x + C.
    Teacher explains: Product rule: d(uv)/dx = u dv/dx + v du/dx. Integrate both
    sides: uv = ∫u dv + ∫v du, so ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du. Choose u so that du is
    SIMPLER, and dv so that you can integrate it.
        ∫x eˣ dx:   u = x,  dv = eˣ dx,  du = dx,  v = eˣ
                  = x eˣ − ∫eˣ dx = x eˣ − eˣ + C
        ∫x cos x dx:  u = x,  dv = cos x dx,  du = dx,  v = sin x
                  = x sin x − ∫sin x dx = x sin x + cos x + C
    LIATE gives the order of preference for u: Logarithms, Inverse trig,
    Algebraic (powers of x), Trig, Exponentials. With u = eˣ and dv = x dx
    instead, you would get (x²/2)eˣ − ∫(x²/2)eˣ dx: worse! Check:
    d/dx[x eˣ − eˣ] = eˣ + x eˣ − eˣ = x eˣ, as required. Now you try:
    ∫x sin x dx. (−x cos x + sin x + C)

D7. Find ∫ln x dx, ∫tan⁻¹x dx and ∫x² eˣ dx.
    Answer: x ln x − x + C; x tan⁻¹x − (1/2)ln(1 + x²) + C; eˣ(x² − 2x + 2) + C.
    Teacher explains: For ∫ln x dx there is only ONE factor: take dv = dx (so
    v = x).
        ∫ln x dx:  u = ln x, dv = dx, du = dx/x, v = x
                 = x ln x − ∫x × (1/x) dx = x ln x − x + C
        ∫tan⁻¹x dx:  u = tan⁻¹x, dv = dx, du = dx/(1 + x²), v = x
                 = x tan⁻¹x − ∫x/(1 + x²) dx = x tan⁻¹x − (1/2)ln(1 + x²) + C
        ∫x² eˣ dx:  u = x², v = eˣ:  = x² eˣ − ∫2x eˣ dx
                 = x² eˣ − 2(x eˣ − eˣ) = eˣ(x² − 2x + 2) + C
    For x² eˣ, parts is used TWICE; each time the power of x drops by 1. A quick
    table method (tabular integration) does the same: derivatives x², 2x, 2, 0
    against integrals eˣ, eˣ, eˣ, with signs +, −, +. Common mistake: losing the
    minus sign in the second round (−2(x eˣ − eˣ) = −2x eˣ + 2eˣ). Now you try:
    ∫x ln x dx. (u = ln x: (x²/2)ln x − x²/4 + C)

D8. Find I = ∫eˣ sin x dx. Then use the result ∫eˣ(f(x) + f′(x)) dx = eˣf(x) + C
    to find ∫eˣ(1/x − 1/x²) dx.
    Answer: I = (eˣ/2)(sin x − cos x) + C; ∫eˣ(1/x − 1/x²) dx = eˣ/x + C.
    Teacher explains: Parts twice brings the ORIGINAL integral back; then solve
    for it like an equation.
        I = ∫eˣ sin x dx:  u = sin x, dv = eˣ dx
          = eˣ sin x − ∫eˣ cos x dx
          = eˣ sin x − [eˣ cos x − ∫eˣ(−sin x) dx]     (u = cos x again)
          = eˣ sin x − eˣ cos x − I
        2I = eˣ(sin x − cos x)   →   I = (eˣ/2)(sin x − cos x) + C
    Keep the SAME type of choice in both rounds (u = trig both times); switching
    to u = eˣ in the second round just undoes the first. For the second part:
    d/dx(eˣf) = eˣf + eˣf′, so when the integrand is eˣ times (a function + its
    derivative) the answer is immediate. Here f = 1/x, f′ = −1/x². Common
    mistake: writing 2I = ... and forgetting to halve. Now you try: ∫eˣ
    cos x dx. ((eˣ/2)(sin x + cos x) + C)

D9. Find ∫(x + 5)/((x − 1)(x + 2)) dx using partial fractions. Then find
    ∫x²/(x² − 1) dx (divide first).
    Answer: 2 ln|x − 1| − ln|x + 2| + C = ln|(x − 1)²/(x + 2)| + C;
    x + (1/2)ln|(x − 1)/(x + 1)| + C.
    Teacher explains: Write the fraction as a sum of simpler fractions, one for
    each linear factor:
        (x + 5)/((x − 1)(x + 2)) = A/(x − 1) + B/(x + 2)
        x + 5 = A(x + 2) + B(x − 1)
        x = 1:   6 = 3A   →  A = 2
        x = −2:  3 = −3B  →  B = −1
        ∫[2/(x − 1) − 1/(x + 2)] dx = 2 ln|x − 1| − ln|x + 2| + C
    Putting x = 1 and x = −2 kills one bracket each time: this is the "cover-up"
    rule (cover the factor x − 1 in the original and put x = 1: 6/3 = 2). For
    x²/(x² − 1) the top has the SAME degree as the bottom, so divide first:
    x²/(x² − 1) = 1 + 1/(x² − 1), and 1/((x − 1)(x + 1))
    = (1/2)/(x − 1) − (1/2)/(x + 1). Common mistake: using partial fractions on
    an improper fraction without dividing. Now you try:
    ∫(3x + 1)/(x² − x − 2) dx. ((3x + 1)/((x − 2)(x + 1))
    = (7/3)/(x − 2) + (2/3)/(x + 1): (7/3)ln|x − 2| + (2/3)ln|x + 1| + C)

D10. Find ∫(3x + 1)/(x − 1)² dx and ∫1/(x(x − 1)²) dx (repeated linear factors).
     Answer: 3 ln|x − 1| − 4/(x − 1) + C; ln|x| − ln|x − 1| − 1/(x − 1) + C.
     Teacher explains: A repeated factor (x − 1)² needs TWO fractions:
     A/(x − 1) + B/(x − 1)².
         (3x + 1)/(x − 1)²: write 3x + 1 = 3(x − 1) + 4
             = 3/(x − 1) + 4/(x − 1)²
             ∫ = 3 ln|x − 1| + 4 × (x − 1)^(−1)/(−1)
               = 3 ln|x − 1| − 4/(x − 1) + C
         1/(x(x − 1)²) = A/x + B/(x − 1) + C₁/(x − 1)²
         1 = A(x − 1)² + Bx(x − 1) + C₁x
         x = 0: A = 1;   x = 1: C₁ = 1;   x² terms: 0 = A + B → B = −1
     So ∫ = ln|x| − ln|x − 1| − 1/(x − 1) + C. The cover-up rule gives A and C₁
     but NOT B: for B compare coefficients (or put another value such as x = 2:
     1 = A + 2B + 2C₁). Note ∫1/(x − 1)² dx = −1/(x − 1): a power, not a
     logarithm. Common mistake: writing only A/x + B/(x − 1)² (missing
     B/(x − 1)). Now you try: ∫(x + 2)/(x + 1)² dx. (1/(x + 1) + 1/(x + 1)²:
     ln|x + 1| − 1/(x + 1) + C)

D11. Find ∫1/((x + 1)(x² + 1)) dx (an irreducible quadratic factor).
     Answer: (1/2)ln|x + 1| − (1/4)ln(x² + 1) + (1/2)tan⁻¹x + C.
     Teacher explains: x² + 1 cannot be factorised over the reals, so its
     fraction has a LINEAR top Bx + C:
         1/((x + 1)(x² + 1)) = A/(x + 1) + (Bx + C)/(x² + 1)
         1 = A(x² + 1) + (Bx + C)(x + 1)
         x = −1:          1 = 2A          →  A = 1/2
         x² terms:        0 = A + B       →  B = −1/2
         constant terms:  1 = A + C       →  C = 1/2
         ∫ = (1/2)ln|x + 1| + ∫(−x/2 + 1/2)/(x² + 1) dx
           = (1/2)ln|x + 1| − (1/4)ln(x² + 1) + (1/2)tan⁻¹x + C
     Split (Bx + C)/(x² + 1) into an f′/f part, which gives a log, and a
     constant over x² + 1, which gives tan⁻¹. Check by differentiating:
     1/(2(x + 1)) − x/(2(x² + 1)) + 1/(2(1 + x²)) combines to
     1/((x + 1)(x² + 1)). Common mistake: using a constant top C/(x² + 1) for a
     quadratic factor. Now you try: ∫2/(x(x² + 1)) dx. (2/x − 2x/(x² + 1):
     2 ln|x| − ln(x² + 1) + C)

D12. Find ∫1/(x² + 9) dx, ∫1/√(4 − x²) dx, ∫√(9 − x²) dx and
     ∫1/(x² + 4x + 13) dx.
     Answer: (1/3)tan⁻¹(x/3) + C; sin⁻¹(x/2) + C;
     (x/2)√(9 − x²) + (9/2)sin⁻¹(x/3) + C; (1/3)tan⁻¹((x + 2)/3) + C.
     Teacher explains: The first two come from the table with x/a in place of x:
         ∫1/(x² + a²) dx = (1/a)tan⁻¹(x/a) + C        (a = 3)
         ∫1/√(a² − x²) dx = sin⁻¹(x/a) + C           (a = 2)
         ∫√(9 − x²) dx:  x = 3 sin θ, dx = 3 cos θ dθ, √(9 − x²) = 3 cos θ
            = ∫9cos²θ dθ = (9/2)(θ + sin θ cos θ)
            = (9/2)sin⁻¹(x/3) + (9/2)(x/3)(√(9 − x²)/3)
            = (x/2)√(9 − x²) + (9/2)sin⁻¹(x/3) + C
         x² + 4x + 13 = (x + 2)² + 9:  (1/3)tan⁻¹((x + 2)/3) + C
     The substitution x = a sin θ turns √(a² − x²) into a cos θ (a TRIGONOMETRIC
     SUBSTITUTION); return to x with sin θ = x/a, cos θ = √(a² − x²)/a. For a
     quadratic with no real roots, complete the square and use the tan⁻¹ form
     with u = x + 2. Common mistake: ∫1/(x² + 9) dx = tan⁻¹(x/3) (the factor 1/3
     is missing). Now you try: ∫1/√(3 + 2x − x²) dx.
     (3 + 2x − x² = 4 − (x − 1)²: sin⁻¹((x − 1)/2) + C)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Integrate (powers and polynomials). Check by differentiating.
    a) ∫x⁵ dx                 b) ∫7 dx
    c) ∫(4x³ − 6x²) dx        d) ∫(3x² + 2x − 1) dx
    e) ∫1/x³ dx               f) ∫√x dx
    g) ∫∛x dx                 h) ∫1/√x dx
    i) ∫x^(2/3) dx            j) ∫(x + 1)² dx
    k) ∫(2x − 3)(x + 1) dx    l) ∫(x² + 1)/x² dx
    m) ∫(x³ − 2x + 5)/x dx    n) ∫x√x dx
    o) ∫(1 + √x)² dx          p) ∫(x − 1)/√x dx
    q) ∫(x⁴ − 1)/(x − 1) dx   r) ∫(3/x + 2x) dx
    s) ∫x^(−5/2) dx           t) ∫(x² − 4)/(x + 2) dx
    Answers: a) x⁶/6 + C   b) 7x + C   c) x⁴ − 2x³ + C   d) x³ + x² − x + C
             e) −1/(2x²) + C   f) (2/3)x^(3/2) + C   g) (3/4)x^(4/3) + C
             h) 2√x + C   i) (3/5)x^(5/3) + C   j) x³/3 + x² + x + C
             k) 2x³/3 − x²/2 − 3x + C   l) x − 1/x + C
             m) x³/3 − 2x + 5 ln|x| + C   n) (2/5)x^(5/2) + C
             o) x + (4/3)x^(3/2) + x²/2 + C   p) (2/3)x^(3/2) − 2√x + C
             q) x⁴/4 + x³/3 + x²/2 + x + C   r) 3 ln|x| + x² + C
             s) −2/(3x^(3/2)) + C   t) x²/2 − 2x + C

M2. Integrate using the standard table.
    a) ∫eˣ dx                           b) ∫3 cos x dx
    c) ∫5 sin x dx                      d) ∫sec²x dx
    e) ∫cosec²x dx                      f) ∫sec x tan x dx
    g) ∫cosec x cot x dx                h) ∫1/(1 + x²) dx
    i) ∫1/√(1 − x²) dx                  j) ∫2^x dx
    k) ∫10^x dx                         l) ∫(2eˣ − 3/x) dx
    m) ∫(4 sin x + 2 cos x) dx          n) ∫sec x(sec x + tan x) dx
    o) ∫(1 + cos²x)/cos²x dx            p) ∫1/(1 + cos 2x) dx
    q) ∫(sin x)/cos²x dx                r) ∫(3/(1 + x²) − 2/√(1 − x²)) dx
    s) ∫(x² + 2)/(x² + 1) dx            t) ∫(eˣ + x^e) dx
    Answers: a) eˣ + C   b) 3 sin x + C   c) −5 cos x + C   d) tan x + C
             e) −cot x + C   f) sec x + C   g) −cosec x + C   h) tan⁻¹x + C
             i) sin⁻¹x + C   j) 2^x/ln 2 + C   k) 10^x/ln 10 + C
             l) 2eˣ − 3 ln|x| + C   m) −4 cos x + 2 sin x + C
             n) tan x + sec x + C   o) tan x + x + C   p) (1/2)tan x + C
             q) sec x + C   r) 3 tan⁻¹x − 2 sin⁻¹x + C   s) x + tan⁻¹x + C
             t) eˣ + x^(e + 1)/(e + 1) + C

M3. Integrate (linear substitution: ∫f(ax + b) dx = (1/a)F(ax + b) + C).
    a) ∫(2x + 1)⁵ dx         b) ∫(3x − 2)⁴ dx
    c) ∫(1 − x)⁷ dx          d) ∫√(4x + 1) dx
    e) ∫1/(2x + 3) dx        f) ∫1/(5 − 2x) dx
    g) ∫1/(3x + 1)² dx       h) ∫1/√(1 − 2x) dx
    i) ∫e^(3x) dx            j) ∫e^(−2x) dx
    k) ∫e^(x/2) dx           l) ∫sin 2x dx
    m) ∫cos 5x dx            n) ∫sin(3x + 1) dx
    o) ∫sec²(4x) dx          p) ∫cos(π − 2x) dx
    q) ∫1/(1 + 4x²) dx       r) ∫1/√(1 − 9x²) dx
    s) ∫3^(2x) dx            t) ∫(4x − 1)^(−3/2) dx
    Answers: a) (2x + 1)⁶/12 + C   b) (3x − 2)⁵/15 + C   c) −(1 − x)⁸/8 + C
             d) (1/6)(4x + 1)^(3/2) + C   e) (1/2)ln|2x + 3| + C
             f) −(1/2)ln|5 − 2x| + C   g) −1/(3(3x + 1)) + C   h) −√(1 − 2x) + C
             i) e^(3x)/3 + C   j) −e^(−2x)/2 + C   k) 2e^(x/2) + C
             l) −(1/2)cos 2x + C   m) (1/5)sin 5x + C   n) −(1/3)cos(3x + 1) + C
             o) (1/4)tan 4x + C   p) −(1/2)sin(π − 2x) + C
             q) (1/2)tan⁻¹(2x) + C   r) (1/3)sin⁻¹(3x) + C
             s) 3^(2x)/(2 ln 3) + C   t) −1/(2√(4x − 1)) + C

M4. Integrate by substitution u = g(x).
    a) ∫2x(x² + 3)⁴ dx
    b) ∫x(x² − 1)⁶ dx
    c) ∫x²(x³ + 2)⁵ dx
    d) ∫x√(x² + 1) dx
    e) ∫x/√(x² + 4) dx
    f) ∫x²/√(x³ + 1) dx
    g) ∫x e^(x²) dx
    h) ∫x² e^(x³) dx
    i) ∫eˣ(1 + eˣ)³ dx
    j) ∫eˣ/(1 + eˣ)² dx
    k) ∫sin x cos x dx
    l) ∫sin⁴x cos x dx
    m) ∫cos³x sin x dx
    n) ∫tan x sec²x dx
    o) ∫(ln x)/x dx
    p) ∫(ln x)³/x dx
    q) ∫e^(√x)/√x dx
    r) ∫sin(√x)/√x dx
    s) ∫cos(ln x)/x dx
    t) ∫(sin⁻¹x)²/√(1 − x²) dx
    u) ∫e^(tan⁻¹x)/(1 + x²) dx
    v) ∫x/(1 + x⁴) dx
    w) ∫x(x + 1)^(1/2) dx
    x) ∫x/(x + 2)² dx
    Answers: a) (x² + 3)⁵/5 + C   b) (x² − 1)⁷/14 + C   c) (x³ + 2)⁶/18 + C
             d) (1/3)(x² + 1)^(3/2) + C   e) √(x² + 4) + C
             f) (2/3)√(x³ + 1) + C   g) (1/2)e^(x²) + C   h) (1/3)e^(x³) + C
             i) (1 + eˣ)⁴/4 + C   j) −1/(1 + eˣ) + C   k) sin²x/2 + C
             l) sin⁵x/5 + C   m) −cos⁴x/4 + C   n) tan²x/2 + C
             o) (ln x)²/2 + C   p) (ln x)⁴/4 + C   q) 2e^(√x) + C
             r) −2 cos(√x) + C   s) sin(ln x) + C   t) (sin⁻¹x)³/3 + C
             u) e^(tan⁻¹x) + C   v) (1/2)tan⁻¹(x²) + C
             w) (2/5)(x + 1)^(5/2) − (2/3)(x + 1)^(3/2) + C
             x) ln|x + 2| + 2/(x + 2) + C

M5. Integrate using ∫f′(x)/f(x) dx = ln|f(x)| + C.
    a) ∫2x/(x² + 5) dx                   b) ∫x/(x² − 4) dx
    c) ∫(3x² + 1)/(x³ + x) dx            d) ∫(2x + 1)/(x² + x + 1) dx
    e) ∫x²/(x³ + 8) dx                   f) ∫eˣ/(eˣ + 3) dx
    g) ∫e^(2x)/(1 + e^(2x)) dx           h) ∫(eˣ − e^(−x))/(eˣ + e^(−x)) dx
    i) ∫tan x dx                         j) ∫cot x dx
    k) ∫tan 3x dx                        l) ∫cos x/(2 + sin x) dx
    m) ∫sin x/(1 − cos x) dx             n) ∫sec²x/tan x dx
    o) ∫1/(x ln x) dx                    p) ∫(1 + ln x)/(x ln x) dx
    q) ∫sec x dx                         r) ∫cosec x dx
    Answers: a) ln(x² + 5) + C   b) (1/2)ln|x² − 4| + C   c) ln|x³ + x| + C
             d) ln(x² + x + 1) + C   e) (1/3)ln|x³ + 8| + C   f) ln(eˣ + 3) + C
             g) (1/2)ln(1 + e^(2x)) + C   h) ln(eˣ + e^(−x)) + C

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep a one-page table of standard integrals and derivatives side
  by side; ALWAYS differentiate the answer to check it. Before integrating,
  classify: standard? linear inside? f′/f? g′(x) present (substitution)? product
  of different types (parts)? rational (partial fractions)? √(a² − x²) (trig
  substitution)? Practise 10 mixed integrals a day, labelled with the method
  first. Harder: find ∫1/(1 + eˣ) dx (x − ln(1 + eˣ) + C); ∫√(tan x) dx via
  u² = tan x (hard, JEE Advanced); ∫dx/(a + b cos x) with t = tan(x/2);
  ∫sec³x dx = (1/2)(sec x tan x + ln|sec x + tan x|) + C by parts; derive a
  reduction formula Iₙ = ∫sinⁿx dx = −sinⁿ⁻¹x cos x/n + ((n − 1)/n)Iₙ₋₂; explain
  why ∫e^(−x²) dx has no elementary antiderivative, yet we can still compute
  areas under it numerically.


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.45 — DEFINITE INTEGRALS AS THE LIMIT OF A SUM; FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM OF
             CALCULUS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - RIEMANN SUMS: split [a, b] into n equal strips of width h = (b − a)/n, with
    points xᵢ = a + ih. The right-endpoint sum is Rₙ = h[f(x₁) + f(x₂) +
    ... + f(xₙ)], the left-endpoint sum Lₙ uses x₀, ..., xₙ₋₁. For a continuous
    f both tend to the same limit, the DEFINITE INTEGRAL: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = lim
    (n → ∞) h Σ f(a + ih).
  - Sums needed: 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n + 1)/2; 1² + 2² +
    ... + n² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6; 1³ + ... + n³ = (n(n + 1)/2)²; a geometric
    sum r + r² + ... + rⁿ = r(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1); and lim (h → 0) (e^h − 1)/h = 1.
  - Reading a limit as an integral: lim (1/n) Σ f(i/n) = ∫₀¹ f(x) dx (i from 1
    to n), because h = 1/n and xᵢ = i/n.
  - MEANING: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx is the SIGNED area between the graph and the x-axis:
    parts below the axis count as negative. ∫ₐᵃ f = 0 and ∫ₐᵇ c dx = c(b − a).
  - FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM, part 1: if f is continuous, F(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt is
    differentiable and F′(x) = f(x). With a variable limit: d/dx ∫ₐ^(g(x))
    f(t) dt = f(g(x)) g′(x), and d/dx ∫_(h(x))^(g(x))
    f(t) dt = f(g(x))g′(x) − f(h(x))h′(x).
  - FUNDAMENTAL THEOREM, part 2: if F′ = f is continuous on [a, b], then ∫ₐᵇ
    f(x) dx = [F(x)]ₐᵇ = F(b) − F(a). No + C is needed (it cancels). The
    integrand must be continuous on [a, b]: ∫₋₁¹ 1/x² dx is NOT −2.
  - SUBSTITUTION in a definite integral: change the limits to the new variable
    (x = a → u = g(a)) and never return to x. By parts: ∫ₐᵇ u dv = [uv]ₐᵇ − ∫ₐᵇ
    v du.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Estimate ∫₀² x² dx using 4 strips, first with right endpoints and then with
    left endpoints. Compare with the exact value 8/3.
    Answer: R₄ = 3.75, L₄ = 1.75; the exact value 8/3 ≈ 2.667 lies between them.
    Teacher explains: Width h = (2 − 0)/4 = 0.5. The strip heights are the
    function values at the chosen endpoints:
        x          0     0.5     1     1.5     2
        x²         0    0.25     1    2.25     4
        R₄ = 0.5 × (0.25 + 1 + 2.25 + 4) = 0.5 × 7.5 = 3.75
        L₄ = 0.5 × (0 + 0.25 + 1 + 2.25) = 0.5 × 3.5 = 1.75
            |               *
            |           +---+
            |          *|   |    right-endpoint rectangles
            |       +---+   |    stick out above the rising
            |     * |   |   |    curve (overestimate)
            |  +--*-+   |   |
            +**+----+---+---+---
            0 0.5   1  1.5  2
    x² is increasing on [0, 2], so right endpoints overestimate and left
    endpoints underestimate. With more strips both approach 8/3: this limit IS
    the definite integral. The average (R₄ + L₄)/2 = 2.75 is the trapezium rule.
    Common mistake: using 5 heights (both ends) in one sum. Now you try: R₄ and
    L₄ for ∫₀⁴ x dx. (h = 1: R₄ = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10, L₄ = 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 6;
    exact 8)

D2. Evaluate ∫₁³ (2x + 1) dx as the limit of a sum, and check with the area of a
    trapezium.
    Answer: 10.
    Teacher explains: Take n strips: h = 2/n and xᵢ = 1 + 2i/n, so
    f(xᵢ) = 2(1 + 2i/n) + 1 = 3 + 4i/n.
        Rₙ = Σ (i = 1 to n) (2/n)(3 + 4i/n)
           = (2/n)[3n + (4/n)(1 + 2 + ... + n)]
           = (2/n)[3n + (4/n) × n(n + 1)/2]
           = (2/n)[3n + 2(n + 1)] = (2/n)(5n + 2) = 10 + 4/n
        as n → ∞:  Rₙ → 10
    Check: the region under y = 2x + 1 from x = 1 to 3 is a trapezium with
    parallel sides f(1) = 3 and f(3) = 7 and width 2: area = (3 + 7)/2 × 2 = 10.
    And by the Fundamental Theorem: [x² + x]₁³ = 12 − 2 = 10. Common mistake:
    writing Σ 3 = 3 instead of 3n (the constant is added n times). Now you try:
    ∫₁³ x dx as a limit. (h = 2/n, Rₙ = (2/n)(n + (2/n)n(n + 1)/2)
    = 4 + 2/n → 4)

D3. Prove from the definition that ∫₀¹ x² dx = 1/3 and hence ∫₀ᵇ x² dx = b³/3.
    Answer: Rₙ = (n + 1)(2n + 1)/(6n²) → 2/6 = 1/3. For [0, b]:
    Rₙ = b³(n + 1)(2n + 1)/(6n²) → b³/3.
    Teacher explains:
        h = 1/n,  xᵢ = i/n,  f(xᵢ) = i²/n²
        Rₙ = Σ (1/n)(i²/n²) = (1/n³)(1² + 2² + ... + n²)
           = (1/n³) × n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6
           = (n + 1)(2n + 1)/(6n²) = (1 + 1/n)(2 + 1/n)/6
        n → ∞:   (1)(2)/6 = 1/3
        on [0, b]:  h = b/n,  Rₙ = (b/n) Σ (bi/n)²
                                  = b³(n + 1)(2n + 1)/(6n²) → b³/3
    Archimedes found this area (the parabolic segment) 2,000 years before
    calculus by a similar limiting argument. Divide top and bottom by n² to see
    the limit clearly. The result matches the antiderivative x³/3, as the
    Fundamental Theorem promises. Common mistake: using the formula for Σ i
    instead of Σ i². Now you try: ∫₀² x³ dx from the definition. (Rₙ
    = (2/n)Σ(2i/n)³ = (16/n⁴)(n(n + 1)/2)² = 4(n + 1)²/n² → 4)

D4. Evaluate ∫₀¹ eˣ dx as the limit of a sum.
    Answer: e − 1 ≈ 1.718.
    Teacher explains: The heights form a GEOMETRIC progression: use its sum
    formula.
        h = 1/n:  Rₙ = h(e^h + e^(2h) + ... + e^(nh))
                  = h × e^h(e^(nh) − 1)/(e^h − 1)
                  = (e − 1) × e^h × h/(e^h − 1)          (nh = 1)
        as n → ∞, h → 0:  e^h → 1 and h/(e^h − 1) → 1
        so Rₙ → e − 1
    The key standard limit is (e^h − 1)/h → 1 as h → 0 (topic 8.31): it is the
    statement that the slope of eˣ at 0 is 1. Check with the antiderivative:
    [eˣ]₀¹ = e − 1. Common mistake: summing a geometric series with the wrong
    number of terms: from e^h to e^(nh) there are n terms. Now you try:
    ∫₀² eˣ dx as a limit. (h = 2/n: (e² − 1) × e^h h/(e^h − 1) → e² − 1 ≈ 6.389)

D5. State the second part of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and use it to
    find ∫₁⁴ (3√x − 1/x²) dx and ∫₀^(π/2) cos x dx. Why is no + C needed?
    Answer: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a) where F′ = f. The integrals are
    53/4 = 13.25 and 1.
    Teacher explains: Find ANY antiderivative, then subtract its values at the
    two limits:
        ∫₁⁴ (3x^(1/2) − x^(−2)) dx = [2x^(3/2) + 1/x]₁⁴
           = (2 × 8 + 1/4) − (2 × 1 + 1) = 16.25 − 3 = 13.25
        ∫₀^(π/2) cos x dx = [sin x]₀^(π/2) = sin(π/2) − sin 0 = 1 − 0 = 1
    If we used F + C instead: (F(b) + C) − (F(a) + C) = F(b) − F(a); the C
    cancels, so we leave it out. Write the square-bracket step: it avoids sign
    errors when subtracting F(a), especially when F(a) is negative. Here
    4^(3/2) = (√4)³ = 8. Common mistakes: computing F(a) − F(b); forgetting to
    evaluate at the lower limit because "it is zero" (only sometimes!). Now you
    try: ∫₁² (x² + 1/x) dx. ([x³/3 + ln x]₁² = 7/3 + ln 2 ≈ 3.026)

D6. Find (a) d/dx ∫₀ˣ √(1 + t³) dt, (b) d/dx ∫₁^(x²) ln t dt, (c) d/dx
    ∫ₓ^(x²) e^(t²) dt, (d) d/dx ∫ₓ³ sin t/t dt.
    Answer: (a) √(1 + x³); (b) 2x ln(x²) = 4x ln x (x > 0); (c)
    2x e^(x⁴) − e^(x²); (d) −sin x/x.
    Teacher explains: FTC part 1: the derivative of an integral with respect to
    its upper limit is the integrand evaluated there. With a function g(x) as
    the limit, multiply by g′(x) (chain rule):
        (a) f(t) = √(1 + t³):             √(1 + x³)
        (b) upper limit x², derivative 2x:   ln(x²) × 2x = 4x ln x
        (c) ∫ₓ^(x²) = ∫₀^(x²) − ∫₀ˣ:        e^(x⁴) × 2x − e^(x²) × 1
        (d) x is the LOWER limit:            −sin x/x
    Why it works: if G is an antiderivative of f, then ∫ₐ^(g(x))
    f(t) dt = G(g(x)) − G(a), whose derivative is G′(g(x))g′(x) = f(g(x))g′(x).
    Note that we never need to find the integral itself; in (a) there is no
    elementary antiderivative at all. Common mistakes: forgetting the factor
    g′(x); forgetting the minus sign for a variable lower limit. Now you try:
    d/dx ∫₀^(sin x) √(1 − t²) dt for 0 < x < π/2. (√(1 − sin²x) × cos x = cos²x)

D7. Explain why the Fundamental Theorem, part 1, is true: if F(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt
    with f continuous, then F′(x) = f(x). Then deduce part 2.
    Answer: F(x + h) − F(x) is the area of a thin strip ≈ f(x) × h, so the
    difference quotient tends to f(x). Part 2 follows because F and any
    antiderivative G differ by a constant.
    Teacher explains:
        F(x + h) − F(x) = ∫ₓ^(x + h) f(t) dt
        if m and M are the least and greatest values of f on [x, x + h]:
            m × h ≤ ∫ₓ^(x + h) f(t) dt ≤ M × h
            m ≤ (F(x + h) − F(x))/h ≤ M
        as h → 0, m and M both → f(x) (f is continuous)
        squeeze: F′(x) = f(x)
    For part 2, let G be ANY antiderivative of f. Then (F − G)′ = f − f = 0, so
    F − G is a constant K (by the Mean Value Theorem, topic 8.40). So ∫ₐᵇ
    f = F(b) = F(b) − F(a) (as F(a) = 0) = (G(b) + K) − (G(a) + K)
    = G(b) − G(a). This theorem joins the two halves of calculus: areas (limits
    of sums) are computed by antiderivatives. Common mistake: thinking FTC needs
    the integrand to be a polynomial; it needs continuity. Now you try: if
    F(x) = ∫₂ˣ (t³ − 1) dt, find F(2) and F′(2). (F(2) = 0, F′(2) = 7)

D8. Evaluate ∫₀² x(x² + 1)³ dx, ∫₀^(π/2) sin³x cos x dx and ∫₁^e (ln x)²/x dx by
    substitution, changing the limits.
    Answer: 78; 1/4; 1/3.
    Teacher explains: When you substitute in a definite integral, convert the
    LIMITS too; then there is no need to go back to x.
        u = x² + 1, du = 2x dx:   x = 0 → u = 1,  x = 2 → u = 5
           ∫₁⁵ u³ (du/2) = (1/2)[u⁴/4]₁⁵ = (625 − 1)/8 = 78
        u = sin x, du = cos x dx:  x = 0 → u = 0,  x = π/2 → u = 1
           ∫₀¹ u³ du = [u⁴/4]₀¹ = 1/4
        u = ln x, du = dx/x:       x = 1 → u = 0,  x = e → u = 1
           ∫₀¹ u² du = [u³/3]₀¹ = 1/3
    Common mistake: changing the variable but keeping the old limits, e.g.
    (1/2)[u⁴/4]₀² = 2 for the first one (wrong). If you prefer, find the
    antiderivative in x first ((x² + 1)⁴/8) and use the ORIGINAL limits:
    (625 − 1)/8 = 78, the same. Now you try: ∫₀¹ x e^(x²) dx. (u = x²:
    (1/2)[eᵘ]₀¹ = (e − 1)/2 ≈ 0.859)

D9. Evaluate ∫₀¹ x eˣ dx, ∫₁^e ln x dx and ∫₀^π x sin x dx by parts.
    Answer: 1; 1; π.
    Teacher explains: Use [uv]ₐᵇ − ∫ₐᵇ v du, evaluating the bracket at once:
        ∫₀¹ x eˣ dx = [x eˣ]₀¹ − ∫₀¹ eˣ dx = e − (e − 1) = 1
        ∫₁^e ln x dx = [x ln x]₁^e − ∫₁^e 1 dx = (e − 0) − (e − 1) = 1
        ∫₀^π x sin x dx = [−x cos x]₀^π + ∫₀^π cos x dx
                        = (−π × (−1) − 0) + [sin x]₀^π = π + 0 = π
    Remember cos π = −1 and ln 1 = 0, ln e = 1. It is often safer to find the
    whole antiderivative first (for x eˣ: (x − 1)eˣ) and then substitute:
    [(x − 1)eˣ]₀¹ = 0 − (−1) = 1. Common mistake: evaluating uv but forgetting
    to put the limits into the second integral. Now you try: ∫₀^(π/2)
    x cos x dx. ([x sin x + cos x]₀^(π/2) = π/2 − 1 ≈ 0.571)

D10. Evaluate ∫₂³ 1/(x² − 1) dx, ∫₀¹ 1/(1 + x²) dx and ∫₀¹ 1/√(4 − x²) dx. Give
     exact values and decimals.
     Answer: (1/2)ln(3/2) ≈ 0.203; π/4 ≈ 0.785; π/6 ≈ 0.524.
     Teacher explains:
         1/(x² − 1) = (1/2)[1/(x − 1) − 1/(x + 1)]
         ∫₂³ = (1/2)[ln|(x − 1)/(x + 1)|]₂³ = (1/2)(ln(2/4) − ln(1/3))
             = (1/2)ln((1/2) × 3) = (1/2)ln(3/2)
         ∫₀¹ 1/(1 + x²) dx = [tan⁻¹x]₀¹ = π/4 − 0 = π/4
         ∫₀¹ 1/√(4 − x²) dx = [sin⁻¹(x/2)]₀¹ = sin⁻¹(1/2) = π/6
     Inverse trig values must be PRINCIPAL values in radians: tan⁻¹1 = π/4, not
     45 and not 5π/4. The second result gives a famous formula: π = 4∫₀¹
     1/(1 + x²) dx, which can be used to compute π numerically. Use the log laws
     to tidy the first: ln a − ln b = ln(a/b). Common mistake:
     ln|(x − 1)/(x + 1)| at x = 2 is ln(1/3), not ln 3. Now you try: ∫₀¹
     1/((x + 1)(x + 2)) dx. ([ln((x + 1)/(x + 2))]₀¹ = ln(2/3) − ln(1/2)
     = ln(4/3) ≈ 0.288)

D11. Explain why ∫₀^(2π) sin x dx = 0, although the region between y = sin x and
     the x-axis has area 4. What goes wrong with "∫₋₁¹ 1/x² dx =
     [−1/x]₋₁¹ = −2"?
     Answer: The integral counts area below the axis as negative: +2 − 2 = 0;
     the total area is 2 + 2 = 4. The second calculation is invalid: 1/x² is not
     continuous (not even defined) at 0; in fact the area is infinite.
     Teacher explains:
         ∫₀^π sin x dx = [−cos x]₀^π = 1 + 1 = 2        (above the axis)
         ∫_π^(2π) sin x dx = [−cos x]_π^(2π) = −1 − 1 = −2   (below)
         signed total:  2 + (−2) = 0;   area:  2 + |−2| = 4
     A definite integral is a SIGNED area. For a geometric area, split the
     interval at the zeros of f and add absolute values (topic 8.47). For the
     second: the FTC needs f continuous on the WHOLE of [a, b]. 1/x² is positive
     everywhere, so its integral can never be negative: the answer −2 is
     obviously wrong. Near 0, ∫_ε¹ 1/x² dx = 1/ε − 1 → ∞. Common mistake:
     applying [F]ₐᵇ blindly across a vertical asymptote. Now you try: ∫₀³
     (x − 1) dx and the area between y = x − 1 and the x-axis on [0, 3]. (3/2;
     area 1/2 + 2 = 5/2)

D12. A particle moves along a line with velocity v(t) = 3t² − 12t + 9 m/s. Find
     its displacement and the total distance travelled from t = 0 to t = 4 s.
     Answer: Displacement 4 m; distance 12 m.
     Teacher explains: Displacement is the integral of velocity; distance is the
     integral of SPEED |v|, so split where v changes sign.
         s(t) = ∫v dt = t³ − 6t² + 9t   (antiderivative)
         displacement = [s]₀⁴ = 64 − 96 + 36 − 0 = 4 m
         v = 3(t − 1)(t − 3): v > 0 on (0, 1), v < 0 on (1, 3), v > 0 on (3, 4)
         s(0) = 0,  s(1) = 4,  s(3) = 0,  s(4) = 4
         distance = |4 − 0| + |0 − 4| + |4 − 0| = 12 m
     The particle goes forward 4 m, comes back 4 m to the start, then goes
     forward 4 m again. The same idea gives total water flow from a rate, total
     cost from marginal cost, and so on: "the integral of a rate of change is
     the total change" (net change theorem). Common mistake: answering 4 m for
     the distance. Now you try: v(t) = t − 2 on [0, 5]. (displacement 5/2 m;
     distance 2 + 9/2 = 13/2 m)

M10. Find the positive constant.
     a) ∫₀ᵏ 2x dx = 9
     b) ∫₀ᵏ x² dx = 9
     c) ∫₁ᵏ 1/x dx = 2
     d) ∫₀ᵏ eˣ dx = 4
     e) ∫₀ᵏ (2x − 1) dx = 6
     f) ∫₁ᵏ (3x² + 2x) dx = 34 (k > 1)
     g) ∫₀ᵏ 1/(1 + x²) dx = π/3
     h) ∫₀ᵏ cos x dx = 1/2 (0 < k < π/2)
     i) ∫₀ᵏ √x dx = 18
     j) ∫₀^a (3x² + 2x + 1) dx = 14 (a > 0)
     k) ∫₀¹ (ax + 1) dx = 3
     l) ∫₀^b x(b − x) dx = 36 (b > 0)
     Answers: a) k = 3   b) k = 3   c) k = e²   d) k = ln 5   e) k = 3
              f) k = 3   g) k = √3   h) k = π/6   i) k = 9   j) a = 2   k) a = 4
              l) b = 6

M11. Limits and functions defined by integrals.
     a) lim (x → 0) (1/x)∫₀ˣ cos(t²) dt
     b) lim (x → 0) (1/x²)∫₀ˣ sin t dt
     c) lim (x → 0) (1/x³)∫₀ˣ sin(t²) dt
     d) lim (x → 0) (1/x)∫₀ˣ e^(t²) dt
     e) lim (x → 0) (∫₀^(x²) cos t dt)/(x sin x)
     f) lim (x → ∞) (1/x)∫₀ˣ 1/(1 + t²) dt
     g) lim (h → 0) (1/h)∫₂^(2 + h) √(t² + 5) dt
     h) f if ∫₀ˣ f(t) dt = x³ + x² for all x
     i) f if ∫₁ˣ f(t) dt = x ln x − x + 1
     j) f(4) if ∫₀^(x²) f(t) dt = x³ for x > 0
     k) a and f if ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt = x² − 9
     l) F′(x) and F″(x) for F(x) = ∫₀ˣ √(1 + t⁴) dt
     Answers: a) 1   b) 1/2   c) 1/3   d) 1   e) 1   f) 0   g) 3
              h) f(x) = 3x² + 2x   i) f(x) = ln x
              j) f(x²) × 2x = 3x², f(4) = 3   k) f(x) = 2x; a = ±3
              l) F′ = √(1 + x⁴), F″ = 2x³/√(1 + x⁴)

M12. Average value (1/(b − a))∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx, displacement / distance, net change.
     a) average of x² on [0, 3]
     b) average of x³ on [0, 2]
     c) average of sin x on [0, π]
     d) average of eˣ on [0, 1]
     e) average of 1/x on [1, e]
     f) average of √x on [0, 4]
     g) average of cos²x on [0, π]
     h) v(t) = t² − 4t + 3 m/s on [0, 3]: displacement, distance
     i) v(t) = 2t − 4 m/s on [0, 5]: displacement, distance
     j) v(t) = cos t m/s on [0, π]: displacement, distance
     k) v(t) = 3t² − 12t + 9 m/s on [0, 4]: displacement, distance
     l) Water flows in at r(t) = 20 + 3t litres/min: litres in the first 10 min
     m) MC = 50 − 0.2x rupees: extra cost of raising output from 0 to 100 units
     Answers: a) 3   b) 2   c) 2/π ≈ 0.637   d) e − 1 ≈ 1.718
              e) 1/(e − 1) ≈ 0.582   f) 4/3   g) 1/2   h) 0 m, 8/3 m
              i) 5 m, 13 m   j) 0 m, 2 m   k) 4 m, 12 m   l) 350 L   m) ₹4,000

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: draw the rectangles for Riemann sums on squared paper before doing
  the algebra; memorise the three power-sum formulas; for the FTC write the
  antiderivative in square brackets, then two substitutions, then subtract. For
  FTC part 1, say aloud: "put the top limit into the integrand, times the
  derivative of the top". Harder: show that lim (n → ∞)
  (1/n)[(n + 1)(n + 2)...(2n)]^(1/n) = 4/e (take logs: ∫₀¹
  ln(1 + x) dx = 2 ln 2 − 1); prove that ∫₀¹ xⁿ dx = 1/(n + 1) from the
  definition using the sum formula for Σ iⁿ for n = 3; evaluate lim Σ (i = 1 to
  n) i/(n² + i²) ((1/2)ln 2); find the local extrema of F(x) = ∫₀ˣ
  (t² − 4t + 3) dt (local max F(1) = 4/3, local min F(3) = 0); if f is
  continuous and ∫₀ˣ f(t) dt = x sin πx, find f(4) (f(x) = sin πx + πx cos πx,
  f(4) = 4π).


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.46 — PROPERTIES OF DEFINITE INTEGRALS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - P0 (dummy variable): ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(t) dt. P1: ∫ᵦᵃ f = −∫ₐᵇ f, and ∫ₐᵃ
    f = 0. P2 (additivity): ∫ₐᵇ f = ∫ₐᶜ f + ∫_cᵇ f for any c; use it to split at
    the corners of |...| and the jumps of ⌊x⌋ and of piecewise functions.
  - P3 ("king's property"): ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(a + b − x) dx; in particular ∫₀ᵃ
    f(x) dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a − x) dx. Proof: put x = a + b − t. Typical use: add the
    integral to its reflected form so that the awkward parts cancel
    (I + I = something easy).
  - P4: ∫₀^(2a) f(x) dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx + ∫₀ᵃ f(2a − x) dx; so it equals 2∫₀ᵃ f
    when f(2a − x) = f(x) and 0 when f(2a − x) = −f(x).
  - P5 (symmetry on [−a, a]): if f is EVEN, ∫₋ₐᵃ f = 2∫₀ᵃ f; if f is ODD, ∫₋ₐᵃ
    f = 0. Split any integrand into its even and odd parts first.
  - P6 (periodic f, period T): ∫ₐ^(a + T) f = ∫₀ᵀ f for every a, and ∫₀^(nT)
    f = n∫₀ᵀ f. Periods: sin x, cos x: 2π; |sin x|, |cos x|, tan x, sin²x: π;
    x − ⌊x⌋ (the fractional part {x}): 1.
  - INEQUALITIES: if f ≤ g on [a, b] then ∫ₐᵇ f ≤ ∫ₐᵇ g; if m ≤ f ≤ M then
    m(b − a) ≤ ∫ₐᵇ f ≤ M(b − a); |∫ₐᵇ f| ≤ ∫ₐᵇ |f|.
  - GREATEST INTEGER ⌊x⌋: constant on each interval [k, k + 1); ⌊x²⌋ jumps at
    x = √1, √2, √3, ... . Always make a table of the pieces.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Given ∫₀² f(x) dx = 5 and ∫₀⁵ f(x) dx = 12, find ∫₂⁵ f(x) dx, ∫₅² f(x) dx
    and ∫₀² (3f(x) − 2) dx. Then evaluate ∫₀³ f(x) dx where f(x) = x² for x ≤ 1
    and f(x) = 3 − x for x > 1.
    Answer: 7; −7; 11; 7/3.
    Teacher explains:
        ∫₀⁵ = ∫₀² + ∫₂⁵   →   12 = 5 + ∫₂⁵   →   ∫₂⁵ f = 7
        ∫₅² f = −∫₂⁵ f = −7                       (reversing the limits)
        ∫₀² (3f − 2) dx = 3 × 5 − 2 × (2 − 0) = 15 − 4 = 11
        piecewise:  ∫₀³ f = ∫₀¹ x² dx + ∫₁³ (3 − x) dx
                  = 1/3 + [3x − x²/2]₁³ = 1/3 + (9/2 − 5/2) = 1/3 + 2 = 7/3
    Additivity works even when c is outside [a, b], and it is how every
    piecewise function is integrated: split exactly where the formula changes.
    Linearity: ∫(3f − 2) = 3∫f − ∫2, and ∫₀² 2 dx = 2 × 2 = 4 (not 2). Common
    mistake: using the wrong formula on one side of the break point. Now you
    try: if ∫₁⁴ g = 6 and ∫₁² g = −1, find ∫₂⁴ g and ∫₄² (g + 1). (7;
    −7 − 2 = −9)

D2. Evaluate ∫₋₁² |x| dx, ∫₀⁴ |x − 1| dx and ∫₋₂² |x² − 1| dx.
    Answer: 5/2; 5; 4.
    Teacher explains: Split the interval where the expression inside the modulus
    changes sign, and drop the modulus with the correct sign on each piece:
        ∫₋₁² |x| dx = ∫₋₁⁰ (−x) dx + ∫₀² x dx = 1/2 + 2 = 5/2
        ∫₀⁴ |x − 1| dx = ∫₀¹ (1 − x) dx + ∫₁⁴ (x − 1) dx = 1/2 + 9/2 = 5
        |x² − 1| is even:  ∫₋₂² = 2∫₀² |x² − 1| dx
           = 2[∫₀¹ (1 − x²) dx + ∫₁² (x² − 1) dx]
           = 2[2/3 + (8/3 − 2 − (1/3 − 1))] = 2[2/3 + 4/3] = 4
    Graphically these are areas of triangles and curved pieces: ∫₋₁² |x| dx is
    two triangles of areas 1/2 and 2. The modulus flips the negative part of the
    graph up above the axis. Common mistake: writing ∫|x − 1| dx = |x − 1|²/2
    over the whole interval without splitting. Now you try: ∫₀³
    |x² − 3x + 2| dx. (split at 1 and 2: 5/6 + 1/6 + 5/6 = 11/6)

D3. Evaluate ∫₀³ ⌊x⌋ dx, ∫₀² ⌊x²⌋ dx and ∫₀² x⌊x⌋ dx, where ⌊x⌋ is the greatest
    integer not exceeding x.
    Answer: 3; 5 − √2 − √3 ≈ 1.854; 3/2.
    Teacher explains: ⌊x⌋ is a step function: constant between consecutive
    integers. Split at every jump:
        ∫₀³ ⌊x⌋ dx = ∫₀¹ 0 + ∫₁² 1 + ∫₂³ 2 = 0 + 1 + 2 = 3
        ⌊x²⌋ jumps when x² = 1, 2, 3, i.e. at x = 1, √2, √3:
        x on        [0, 1)   [1, √2)   [√2, √3)   [√3, 2)
        ⌊x²⌋          0        1          2          3
        ∫₀² ⌊x²⌋ dx = 1(√2 − 1) + 2(√3 − √2) + 3(2 − √3)
                    = 5 − √2 − √3
        ∫₀² x⌊x⌋ dx = ∫₀¹ 0 dx + ∫₁² x dx = 3/2
    The values of ⌊x⌋ at the single jump points do not affect the integral (a
    single point has zero width). The graph of ⌊x⌋ is a staircase, so ∫₀³ ⌊x⌋ dx
    is the total area of the steps. Common mistakes: splitting ⌊x²⌋ at x = 1, 2,
    3 instead of at √1, √2, √3; forgetting that ⌊x⌋ = −1 on [−1, 0). Now you
    try: ∫₋₁¹ ⌊x⌋ dx and ∫₀^(1.5) ⌊x²⌋ dx. (−1 + 0 = −1;
    1 × (√2 − 1) + 2(1.5 − √2) = 2 − √2 ≈ 0.586)

D4. Prove that ∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a − x) dx. Use it to show that
    ∫₀^(π/2) sin x/(sin x + cos x) dx = π/4.
    Answer: Substitute x = a − t. I = π/4.
    Teacher explains:
        put x = a − t, dx = −dt;  x = 0 → t = a,  x = a → t = 0
        ∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx = ∫ₐ⁰ f(a − t)(−dt) = ∫₀ᵃ f(a − t) dt = ∫₀ᵃ f(a − x) dx
        I = ∫₀^(π/2) sin x/(sin x + cos x) dx
        replace x by π/2 − x:  sin → cos, cos → sin
        I = ∫₀^(π/2) cos x/(cos x + sin x) dx
        add:  2I = ∫₀^(π/2) (sin x + cos x)/(sin x + cos x) dx
                 = ∫₀^(π/2) 1 dx = π/2
        I = π/4
    The minus sign from dx = −dt is used to swap the limits back (P1), and the
    last step renames the dummy variable t as x (P0). The strategy "reflect and
    add" works whenever the reflected integrand and the original add up to
    something simple, even though neither can be integrated easily on its own.
    Common mistake: reflecting only part of the integrand; replace EVERY x. Now
    you try: ∫₀^(π/2) sin⁴x/(sin⁴x + cos⁴x) dx. (π/4)

D5. Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) √(sin x)/(√(sin x) + √(cos x)) dx and ∫₂⁵
    √x/(√x + √(7 − x)) dx.
    Answer: π/4; 3/2.
    Teacher explains: For [a, b] use the general form: replace x by a + b − x.
        (1) a + b = π/2: sin ↔ cos, so
            I = ∫₀^(π/2) √(cos x)/(√(cos x) + √(sin x)) dx
            2I = ∫₀^(π/2) 1 dx = π/2   →   I = π/4
        (2) a + b = 7: x → 7 − x
            I = ∫₂⁵ √(7 − x)/(√(7 − x) + √x) dx
            2I = ∫₂⁵ 1 dx = 3   →   I = 3/2
    Recognise the pattern: f(x)/(f(x) + f(a + b − x)) always integrates to half
    the length of the interval, (b − a)/2. Common mistake: using x → 5 − x or
    x → 7 + x; the reflection must swap the two limits. Now you try: ∫₁³
    √(4 − x)/(√x + √(4 − x)) dx. (a + b = 4; answer (3 − 1)/2 = 1)

D6. Use the king's property to find ∫₀^π x sin x dx (without parts) and ∫₀^π
    x sin x/(1 + cos²x) dx.
    Answer: π; π²/4.
    Teacher explains:
        I = ∫₀^π x sin x dx;  x → π − x:  sin(π − x) = sin x
        I = ∫₀^π (π − x) sin x dx = π∫₀^π sin x dx − I
        2I = π × 2   →   I = π
        J = ∫₀^π x sin x/(1 + cos²x) dx;  cos(π − x) = −cos x, cos² unchanged
        2J = π∫₀^π sin x/(1 + cos²x) dx;  u = cos x, du = −sin x dx
           = π∫₋₁¹ du/(1 + u²) = π[tan⁻¹u]₋₁¹ = π(π/4 + π/4) = π²/2
        J = π²/4
    General rule: ∫₀^π x f(sin x) dx = (π/2)∫₀^π f(sin x) dx. The "x" disappears
    because x and π − x average to π/2. J cannot be done by parts easily; the
    property makes it a one-line tan⁻¹. Common mistake: thinking
    cos(π − x) = cos x. Now you try: ∫₀^π x/(1 + sin x) dx. ((π/2)∫₀^π
    dx/(1 + sin x) = (π/2) × 2 = π)

D7. Prove that ∫₋ₐᵃ f(x) dx = 0 for an odd function and 2∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx for an even
    one. Evaluate ∫₋₁¹ (x³ + x cos x + tan⁵x) dx, ∫₋₂² (x² + x³) dx and
    ∫_(−π/2)^(π/2) sin⁷x dx.
    Answer: 0; 16/3; 0.
    Teacher explains:
        ∫₋ₐᵃ f = ∫₋ₐ⁰ f(x) dx + ∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx;  in the first put x = −t:
        ∫₋ₐ⁰ f(x) dx = ∫ₐ⁰ f(−t)(−dt) = ∫₀ᵃ f(−t) dt
        so ∫₋ₐᵃ f = ∫₀ᵃ [f(x) + f(−x)] dx
        odd:  f(−x) = −f(x) → 0;    even:  f(−x) = f(x) → 2∫₀ᵃ f
    x³, x cos x (odd × even) and tan⁵x are all odd, so the first integral is 0
    without any integration. In the second, x³ is odd and x² is even:
    ∫₋₂² = 2∫₀² x² dx = 2 × 8/3 = 16/3. sin⁷x is odd: 0. The interval MUST be
    symmetric, [−a, a]. Picture: an odd function has equal areas above and below
    the axis that cancel. Common mistake: using the odd rule for eˣ, which is
    neither (∫₋₁¹ eˣ dx = e − 1/e). Now you try: ∫₋₁¹ ln((1 − x)/(1 + x)) dx and
    ∫_(−π/2)^(π/2) cos x dx. (0, odd; 2)

D8. Show that I = ∫₀^(π/2) ln(sin x) dx = −(π/2)ln 2.
    Answer: I = −(π/2)ln 2 ≈ −1.089.
    Teacher explains:
        by P3:  I = ∫₀^(π/2) ln(cos x) dx
        2I = ∫₀^(π/2) ln(sin x cos x) dx = ∫₀^(π/2) [ln(sin 2x) − ln 2] dx
           = ∫₀^(π/2) ln(sin 2x) dx − (π/2)ln 2
        put t = 2x:  ∫₀^(π/2) ln(sin 2x) dx = (1/2)∫₀^π ln(sin t) dt
        by P4 (sin(π − t) = sin t):  (1/2) × 2∫₀^(π/2) ln(sin t) dt = I
        2I = I − (π/2)ln 2   →   I = −(π/2)ln 2
    This beautiful result uses P3, a double-angle identity, a substitution and
    P4 together. (Strictly the integral is improper because ln(sin x) → −∞ at 0,
    but it converges.) It is negative, as it must be: sin x ≤ 1 so
    ln(sin x) ≤ 0. Common mistake: ln(sin x cos x) = ln(sin x) × ln(cos x). Now
    you try: ∫₀^(π/2) ln(tan x) dx. (= I − I = 0, or reflect:
    ln(cot x) = −ln(tan x))

D9. Use periodicity to evaluate ∫₀^(100π) |sin x| dx, ∫₀¹⁰ (x − ⌊x⌋) dx and
    ∫₀^(2π) sin²x dx.
    Answer: 200; 5; π.
    Teacher explains:
        |sin x| has period π:   ∫₀^(100π) = 100∫₀^π sin x dx = 100 × 2 = 200
        {x} = x − ⌊x⌋ has period 1 and equals x on [0, 1):
                ∫₀¹⁰ {x} dx = 10∫₀¹ x dx = 10 × 1/2 = 5
        sin²x has period π:     ∫₀^(2π) = 2∫₀^π sin²x dx = 2 × π/2 = π
    For a periodic function, every full period contributes the same amount, and
    the starting point does not matter: ∫ₐ^(a + T) f = ∫₀ᵀ f. So
    ∫_(π/3)^(π/3 + π) |sin x| dx = 2 as well. When the interval is not a whole
    number of periods, split off the full periods first. Common mistake: using
    the period 2π for |sin x| (its period is π). Now you try: ∫₀^(3π/2)
    |cos x| dx. (one full period [0, π] gives 2, plus ∫_π^(3π/2) |cos x| dx = 1:
    total 3)

D10. Use ∫₀^(2a) f(x) dx = ∫₀ᵃ [f(x) + f(2a − x)] dx to evaluate ∫₀^π cos³x dx,
     ∫₀^π sin³x dx and ∫₀^(2π) cos⁵x dx.
     Answer: 0; 4/3; 0.
     Teacher explains:
         ∫₀^π cos³x dx:  2a = π, cos(π − x) = −cos x  →  0
         ∫₀^π sin³x dx:  sin(π − x) = sin x  →  2∫₀^(π/2) sin³x dx
             ∫₀^(π/2) sin³x dx = [−cos x + cos³x/3]₀^(π/2)
                               = 0 − (−1 + 1/3) = 2/3
             so ∫₀^π sin³x dx = 4/3
         ∫₀^(2π) cos⁵x dx:  cos(2π − x) = cos x → 2∫₀^π cos⁵x dx,
             and cos(π − x) = −cos x → ∫₀^π cos⁵x dx = 0
     The graph of cos³x on [0, π] is symmetric about the point (π/2, 0): the
     positive half cancels the negative half. The graph of sin³x is symmetric
     about the line x = π/2: two equal halves. Always test f(2a − x) against
     ±f(x) before integrating. Common mistake: concluding 0 for sin³x on [0, π]
     "because sin³x is odd" (oddness needs a symmetric interval [−a, a]). Now
     you try: ∫₀^π sin⁵x cos x dx. (f(π − x) = −f(x): 0)

D11. Without evaluating, show that 1/2 ≤ ∫₀¹ 1/(1 + x⁴) dx ≤ 1 and that ∫₀¹
     x¹⁰⁰ dx < ∫₀¹ x⁹⁹ dx. Also show 1/e ≤ ∫₀¹ e^(−x²) dx ≤ 1.
     Answer: On [0, 1]: 1/2 ≤ 1/(1 + x⁴) ≤ 1, x¹⁰⁰ ≤ x⁹⁹ and 1/e ≤ e^(−x²) ≤ 1;
     integrate over an interval of length 1. (Actual values: 0.867;
     1/101 < 1/100; 0.747.)
     Teacher explains: Bound the integrand, then use m(b − a) ≤ ∫ₐᵇ
     f ≤ M(b − a):
         0 ≤ x ≤ 1  →  0 ≤ x⁴ ≤ 1  →  1 ≤ 1 + x⁴ ≤ 2  →  1/2 ≤ 1/(1 + x⁴) ≤ 1
         x¹⁰⁰ = x × x⁹⁹ ≤ x⁹⁹ on [0, 1] (not equal on (0, 1))
         0 ≤ x² ≤ 1  →  e^(−1) ≤ e^(−x²) ≤ e⁰ = 1
     These estimates are useful when no antiderivative exists: e^(−x²) has none
     among elementary functions, yet we can trap its integral between 0.368 and
     1 immediately (numerically it is ≈ 0.747). Strict inequality holds when
     f < g on a subinterval of positive length. Common mistake: reversing the
     bounds when taking reciprocals (bigger denominator, smaller fraction). Now
     you try: show 2 ≤ ∫₁³ √(1 + x) dx ≤ 4. (√2 ≤ √(1 + x) ≤ 2 on [1, 3]: bounds
     2√2 ≈ 2.83 and 4, and 2√2 > 2)

D12. Evaluate ∫₀^(π/4) ln(1 + tan x) dx (a well-known JEE problem).
     Answer: (π/8)ln 2 ≈ 0.272.
     Teacher explains:
         x → π/4 − x:  tan(π/4 − x) = (1 − tan x)/(1 + tan x)
         1 + tan(π/4 − x) = (1 + tan x + 1 − tan x)/(1 + tan x) = 2/(1 + tan x)
         I = ∫₀^(π/4) ln(2/(1 + tan x)) dx = ∫₀^(π/4) ln 2 dx − I
         2I = (π/4)ln 2   →   I = (π/8)ln 2
     The key step is the identity 1 + tan(π/4 − x) = 2/(1 + tan x), which turns
     the reflected log into ln 2 minus the original log. The substitution
     x = tan θ shows that ∫₀¹ ln(1 + x)/(1 + x²) dx has the same value,
     (π/8)ln 2. Common mistake: tan(π/4 − x) = 1 − tan x. Now you try: ∫₀¹
     ln(1 + x)/(1 + x²) dx. (put x = tan θ: (π/8)ln 2)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------
M1. Given ∫₀³ f(x) dx = 5, ∫₀⁵ f(x) dx = 8, ∫₀³ g(x) dx = −2 and ∫₀⁵
    g(x) dx = 1, find:
    a) ∫₃⁵ f(x) dx                    b) ∫₅³ f(x) dx
    c) ∫₀³ 2f(x) dx                   d) ∫₀³ (f(x) + g(x)) dx
    e) ∫₀³ (f(x) − 3g(x)) dx          f) ∫₃⁰ g(x) dx
    g) ∫₃⁵ g(x) dx                    h) ∫₀⁵ (2f(x) − g(x)) dx
    i) ∫₀³ (f(x) + 1) dx              j) ∫₀⁵ (4 − f(x)) dx
    k) ∫₃³ f(x) dx                    l) ∫₀³ f(t) dt
    m) ∫₀^(3/2) f(2x) dx (u = 2x)     n) ∫₀³ f(3 − x) dx
    o) ∫₋₃⁰ f(−x) dx                  p) ∫₁² f(x + 1) dx if ∫₂³ f = 4
    Answers: a) 3   b) −3   c) 10   d) 3   e) 11   f) 2   g) 3   h) 15   i) 8
             j) 12   k) 0   l) 5   m) 5/2   n) 5   o) 5   p) 4

M11. True or false? Give a reason or counterexample.
     a) ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = ∫ₐᵇ f(t) dt

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: keep a card with the properties and one example each. Before
  integrating, ask four questions: is the interval symmetric (even / odd)? would
  x → a + b − x simplify it? is it periodic? is there a modulus or floor
  (split)? Sketch the graph for |...| and ⌊...⌋. Harder: show ∫₀^(π/2)
  x/(sin x + cos x) dx = (π/(2√2))ln(√2 + 1); prove ∫₀^π
  x ln(sin x) dx = −(π²/2)ln 2; evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) sin²x/(1 + sin x cos x) dx
  (π/(3√3)); show that ∫₀¹ tan⁻¹(1 − x + x²) dx = ln 2 (hint: tan⁻¹(1 − x + x²)
  = π/2 − tan⁻¹x − tan⁻¹(1 − x)); evaluate ∫₀^(2π) |sin x − cos x| dx (4√2).


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.47 — AREA UNDER AND BETWEEN CURVES
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - AREA UNDER A CURVE: if f(x) ≥ 0 on [a, b], the area between y = f(x), the
    x-axis and the lines x = a, x = b is ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx. If the curve is BELOW the
    axis the integral is negative and the area is |∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx|.
  - A curve that crosses the axis: find the zeros, split the interval there and
    add the absolute values of the pieces. The signed integral (positive parts
    minus negative parts) is NOT the area.
  - AREA BETWEEN TWO CURVES: area = ∫ₐᵇ (upper − lower) dx = ∫ₐᵇ |f − g| dx.
    First find the points of intersection by solving f(x) = g(x); they give the
    limits. If the curves cross inside [a, b], split there.
  - WITH RESPECT TO y: for curves given as x = g(y) (for example y² = 4x,
    x = y²), area = ∫_c^d (right − left) dy. Choose the variable that gives ONE
    integral with no splitting.
  - STANDARD RESULTS (prove them once): circle x² + y² = a²: area πa²; ellipse
    x²/a² + y²/b² = 1: area πab; parabola y² = 4ax cut by its latus rectum
    x = a: 8a²/3; y² = 4ax and x² = 4ay enclose 16a²/3; y = x² and the line
    y = mx + c between the roots α, β: (β − α)³/6. Useful integral:
    ∫√(a² − x²) dx = (x/2)√(a² − x²) + (a²/2)sin⁻¹(x/a) + C.
  - METHOD: (1) sketch the curves and shade the region; (2) find the
    intersections; (3) decide upper / lower (or right / left) on each piece; (4)
    integrate; (5) check that the answer is positive and roughly matches the
    sketch. Areas are in square units.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Find the area of the region between the curve y = x² − 4x and the x-axis.
    Explain why ∫₀⁴ (x² − 4x) dx is negative.
    Answer: ∫₀⁴ (x² − 4x) dx = −32/3, so the area is 32/3 ≈ 10.67 square units.
    Teacher explains:
        zeros: x² − 4x = x(x − 4) = 0  →  x = 0, 4
        test x = 1: y = −3 < 0, so the arch is BELOW the axis on (0, 4)
        ∫₀⁴ (x² − 4x) dx = [x³/3 − 2x²]₀⁴ = 64/3 − 32 = −32/3
        area = |−32/3| = 32/3 square units
           *    |                                    *
            **  |                                  **
             ***|                                ***
        -------**-------------------------------**-------
                ***:::::::::::::::::::::::::::***
                | ***:::::::::::::::::::::::***
                |   ****:::::::::::::::::****
                |      *****:::::::::*****
                |          ***********
                |
    Every strip of the Riemann sum has height f(xᵢ) < 0, so the sum and its
    limit are negative. Area is a positive quantity: take the modulus, or
    integrate (upper − lower) = (0 − (x² − 4x)) = 4x − x². Common mistake:
    giving the area as −32/3. Now you try: the area between y = 3x − x² and the
    x-axis. (zeros 0, 3; area 9/2)

D2. For y = x³ − x on [−1, 2], find the integral ∫₋₁² (x³ − x) dx and the total
    area between the curve and the x-axis. Why are they different?
    Answer: Integral 9/4; area 11/4.
    Teacher explains:
        zeros: x³ − x = x(x − 1)(x + 1) = 0  →  x = −1, 0, 1
        F(x) = x⁴/4 − x²/2:  F(−1) = −1/4, F(0) = 0, F(1) = −1/4, F(2) = 2
        piece      [−1, 0]    [0, 1]     [1, 2]
        integral    +1/4       −1/4       +9/4
        signed integral = 1/4 − 1/4 + 9/4 = 9/4
        area = 1/4 + 1/4 + 9/4 = 11/4
    The integral counts the loop below the axis on (0, 1) as negative, so it
    cancels the loop above the axis on (−1, 0). For AREA, split at every zero
    and add the absolute values. Always sketch or make a sign table before
    integrating. Common mistake: integrating straight from −1 to 2 and calling
    9/4 the area. Now you try: the area between y = sin x and the x-axis for
    0 ≤ x ≤ 2π. (2 + 2 = 4, although ∫₀^(2π) sin x dx = 0)

D3. Find the area enclosed by the parabola y = x² and the line y = x + 2. Draw a
    rough sketch.
    Answer: 9/2 square units; the curves meet at (−1, 1) and (2, 4).
    Teacher explains:
        intersections: x² = x + 2  →  x² − x − 2 = (x − 2)(x + 1) = 0
                       x = −1 (y = 1) and x = 2 (y = 4)
        upper: the line (at x = 0: 2 > 0)
        A = ∫₋₁² (x + 2 − x²) dx = [x²/2 + 2x − x³/3]₋₁²
          = (2 + 4 − 8/3) − (1/2 − 2 + 1/3) = 10/3 + 7/6 = 9/2
                            |                     *    ****
                            |                    *******
        **                  |               ****o**
         **                 |          ******:**
          ***               |     ******::::**
            ***             ******::::::::***
              ***      ******:::::::::::***
                **o****:::::::::::::::***
            ****** ****:::::::::::****
        *****---------*************------------------------
                            |
                            |
    The shaded region is ":"; "o" marks the intersections. Use the vertical
    strip: its height is (upper − lower) = (x + 2) − x², the same formula across
    the whole region, so one integral suffices. A shortcut for a parabola y = x²
    and a chord: area = (β − α)³/6 = 3³/6 = 9/2. Common mistake: subtracting in
    the wrong order and getting −9/2. Now you try: the area enclosed by y = x²
    and y = 2x. (x = 0, 2; ∫₀² (2x − x²) dx = 4/3)

D4. Find the area of the region enclosed by the parabolas y² = 4x and x² = 4y.
    Answer: 16/3 ≈ 5.33 square units.
    Teacher explains:
        intersections: y = x²/4 → (x²/4)² = 4x → x⁴ = 64x
                       x(x³ − 64) = 0 → x = 0, 4: points (0, 0), (4, 4)
        upper: y = 2√x (from y² = 4x, y ≥ 0); lower: y = x²/4
        A = ∫₀⁴ (2√x − x²/4) dx = [(4/3)x^(3/2) − x³/12]₀⁴
          = (4/3)(8) − 64/12 = 32/3 − 16/3 = 16/3
               |                            *
               |                          *******
               |                     ****o***
               |               **********
               |          *****:::::***
               |     *****::::::::***
               |  ****:::::::::***
               |***::::::::*****
               **::::::*****
        *******o********-------------------------
               **
               |*
    Each parabola is the reflection of the other in the line y = x, so the
    region is symmetric about y = x. For y² = 4ax and x² = 4ay the area is
    16a²/3 (here a = 1). Only the upper half y = +2√x of the first parabola
    bounds the region. Common mistake: using y = ±2√x and getting 0. Now you
    try: the area enclosed by y = x² and y = 8 − x². (x = ±2; ∫₋₂²
    (8 − 2x²) dx = 64/3)

D5. Find the area enclosed by the parabola x = y² and the line x − y = 2,
    integrating with respect to y. Then check by integrating with respect to x.
    Answer: 9/2 square units (both ways); intersections (1, −1) and (4, 2).
    Teacher explains:
        as x = g(y):  parabola x = y²,  line x = y + 2
        y² = y + 2  →  (y − 2)(y + 1) = 0  →  y = −1, 2
        right: the line (at y = 0: 2 > 0); left: the parabola
        A = ∫₋₁² (y + 2 − y²) dy = [y²/2 + 2y − y³/3]₋₁² = 9/2
        with respect to x (two pieces, because the lower boundary changes):
          0 ≤ x ≤ 1: between y = −√x and y = √x:  ∫₀¹ 2√x dx = 4/3
          1 ≤ x ≤ 4: between y = x − 2 and y = √x:
              ∫₁⁴ (√x − x + 2) dx = 16/3 − 13/6 = 19/6
          total 4/3 + 19/6 = 27/6 = 9/2
                |                                     ***
                |                                 *****
                |                        *******o********
                |            ************:*****
                |    ********:::::::::*****
                |****:::::::::::::*****
        --------*:::::::::::::*****----------------------
                |****:::::*****
                |    ***o****
                | *****      ************
                ***                      ********
    Use horizontal strips: length (right − left) = (y + 2) − y², the same
    formula from y = −1 to 2. With vertical strips the bottom edge is the
    parabola for x < 1 but the line for x > 1, so two integrals are needed.
    Choose the variable that avoids splitting. Common mistake: using the
    x-limits −1 and 2 in a dx integral. Now you try: the area between x = y² and
    x = 4. (∫₋₂² (4 − y²) dy = 32/3)

D6. Use integration to prove that the area of the circle x² + y² = a² is πa².
    Hence find the area of x² + y² = 16, and the area in the first quadrant
    between the circle x² + y² = 16 and the line x + y = 4.
    Answer: πa²; 16π ≈ 50.27; 4π − 8 ≈ 4.57.
    Teacher explains:
        upper semicircle: y = √(a² − x²); by symmetry A = 4∫₀ᵃ √(a² − x²) dx
        ∫√(a² − x²) dx = (x/2)√(a² − x²) + (a²/2)sin⁻¹(x/a) + C
        ∫₀ᵃ √(a² − x²) dx = (0 + (a²/2)(π/2)) − (0 + 0) = πa²/4
        A = 4 × πa²/4 = πa²;   a = 4:  A = 16π
        segment: quarter circle − triangle = 16π/4 − (1/2)(4)(4) = 4π − 8
          (by integration: ∫₀⁴ [√(16 − x²) − (4 − x)] dx = 4π − 8)
    The substitution x = a sin θ also works: ∫₀^(π/2) a² cos²θ dθ = πa²/4. The
    quarter-circle trick uses the symmetry of the circle in both axes. Common
    mistake: forgetting the factor 4, or writing sin⁻¹(1) = 90 (radians: π/2).
    Now you try: the area inside x² + y² = 9 and above the x-axis.
    (9π/2 ≈ 14.14)

D7. Find the area enclosed by the ellipse x²/9 + y²/4 = 1, and show that the
    ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 has area πab.
    Answer: 6π ≈ 18.85 square units; in general πab.
    Teacher explains:
        upper half: y = (b/a)√(a² − x²);   A = 4∫₀ᵃ (b/a)√(a² − x²) dx
          = 4(b/a) × πa²/4 = πab            (quarter-circle integral)
        here a = 3, b = 2:
        A = 4∫₀³ (2/3)√(9 − x²) dx = (8/3) × 9π/4 = 6π
                            |
                            |
                  *********************
               ****:::::::::::::::::::****
             **:::::::::::::::::::::::::::**
        -----*:::::::::::::::::::::::::::::*-----
             **:::::::::::::::::::::::::::**
               ****:::::::::::::::::::****
                  *********************
                            |
                            |
    An ellipse is a circle stretched by the factor b/a in the y-direction, so
    its area is πa² × (b/a) = πab. When a = b = r this gives πr². Common
    mistake: π(a + b) or πa²b. Now you try: the area inside x²/16 + y²/9 = 1 and
    above the chord x/4 + y/3 = 1. (quarter ellipse − triangle = 3π − 6 ≈ 3.42)

D8. Find the area enclosed between y = sin x and y = cos x from x = π/4 to
    x = 5π/4 (one complete "lens"), and the area between the two curves for
    0 ≤ x ≤ π/2.
    Answer: 2√2 ≈ 2.83; 2√2 − 2 ≈ 0.83.
    Teacher explains:
        sin x = cos x  →  tan x = 1  →  x = π/4, 5π/4 (in [0, 2π))
        on (π/4, 5π/4) sin x is on top (x = π/2: 1 > 0)
        A = ∫_(π/4)^(5π/4) (sin x − cos x) dx = [−cos x − sin x]_(π/4)^(5π/4)
          = (√2/2 + √2/2) − (−√2/2 − √2/2) = 2√2
        on [0, π/2]: cos on top for x < π/4, sin on top for x > π/4
        A = ∫₀^(π/4) (cos x − sin x) dx + ∫_(π/4)^(π/2) (sin x − cos x) dx
          = (√2 − 1) + (√2 − 1) = 2√2 − 2
        |
        ********    ***************
        |      ******:::::::::::::*****
        |    ****  *****::::::::::::::****
        |****          ***::::::::::::::::****
        **----------------***::::::::::::::::***-------------
        |                    ***:::::::::::::::****
        |                      *****:::::::::::::::****  ****
        |                          *****:::::::::::::******
        |                              ***************    ***
        |
    Radians throughout: the x-axis runs from 0 to about 4.3 ≈ 11π/8. When the
    curves cross inside the interval, the upper curve changes, so split there.
    Check: cos(5π/4) = sin(5π/4) = −√2/2. Common mistake: integrating
    (sin x − cos x) from 0 to π/2 and getting 0. Now you try: the area between
    y = sin 2x and y = sin x for 0 ≤ x ≤ π/3. (sin 2x ≥ sin x there:
    [−cos 2x/2 + cos x]₀^(π/3) = 3/4 − 1/2 = 1/4)

D9. Find the area of the smaller region cut off from the circle x² + y² = 4 by
    the line x = 1.
    Answer: 4π/3 − √3 ≈ 2.46 square units.
    Teacher explains:
        the region: 1 ≤ x ≤ 2, between y = −√(4 − x²) and y = √(4 − x²)
        A = 2∫₁² √(4 − x²) dx = 2[(x/2)√(4 − x²) + 2 sin⁻¹(x/2)]₁²
          = 2[(0 + 2 × π/2) − (√3/2 + 2 × π/6)]
          = 2[π − √3/2 − π/3] = 4π/3 − √3
        check with geometry: the chord subtends angle θ = 2π/3 at O,
          segment = (r²/2)(θ − sin θ) = 2(2π/3 − √3/2) = 4π/3 − √3
    At x = 1 the circle has y = ±√3, so the chord runs from (1, −√3) to (1, √3),
    and cos(θ/2) = 1/2 gives θ/2 = π/3. The answer is about 2.46, less than a
    quarter of the circle (π ≈ 3.14): sensible. Common mistake: sin⁻¹(1/2) = 30
    (in radians it is π/6). Now you try: the part of x² + y² = 4 with x ≥ √2.
    (2∫_(√2)^2 √(4 − x²) dx = π − 2 ≈ 1.14)

D10. Find the area between y = eˣ, y = e^(−x) and the line x = 1. Then find the
     area between y = ln x, the x-axis and x = e in two ways.
     Answer: e + 1/e − 2 ≈ 1.09; 1.
     Teacher explains:
         eˣ = e^(−x) → x = 0; for x > 0, eˣ > e^(−x)
         A = ∫₀¹ (eˣ − e^(−x)) dx = [eˣ + e^(−x)]₀¹ = e + 1/e − 2
         ln x = 0 at x = 1:  A = ∫₁ᵉ ln x dx = [x ln x − x]₁ᵉ
                               = (e − e) − (0 − 1) = 1
         with respect to y: x from eʸ (curve) to e (line), 0 ≤ y ≤ 1
           A = ∫₀¹ (e − eʸ) dy = e − (e − 1) = 1
     ∫ln x dx needs integration by parts, but the dy version needs only ∫eʸ dy:
     inverse functions swap the roles of x and y. Check with a picture: the
     region under ln x (area 1) and the region between the y-axis and x = eʸ for
     0 ≤ y ≤ 1 (area e − 1) together fill the rectangle 0 ≤ x ≤ e, 0 ≤ y ≤ 1 of
     area e. Common mistake: writing [eˣ − e^(−x)] (the antiderivative of e^(−x)
     is −e^(−x)). Now you try: the area between y = ln x, the y-axis, y = 0 and
     y = 1. (∫₀¹ eʸ dy = e − 1)

D11. Use integration to find the area of the triangle with vertices A(1, 0),
     B(2, 2) and C(3, 1). Check with the determinant formula.
     Answer: 3/2 square units.
     Teacher explains:
         AB: y = 2x − 2     BC: y = 4 − x     AC: y = (x − 1)/2
         lower side AC throughout; upper side AB for 1 ≤ x ≤ 2, BC for
         2 ≤ x ≤ 3 (the top changes at B, so split at x = 2)
         A₁ = ∫₁² (2x − 2 − (x − 1)/2) dx = ∫₁² (3/2)(x − 1) dx = 3/4
         A₂ = ∫₂³ (4 − x − (x − 1)/2) dx = ∫₂³ (3/2)(3 − x) dx = 3/4
         area = 3/4 + 3/4 = 3/2
         determinant: (1/2)|1(2 − 1) + 2(1 − 0) + 3(0 − 2)| = (1/2)|−3| = 3/2
     Find the three line equations first (two-point form), then decide which
     side is on top over each x-range. The vertex B with the middle x-coordinate
     is where the upper boundary changes. Common mistake: using one integral
     from 1 to 3 with the line AB. Now you try: the area of the triangle bounded
     by y = x + 1, y = 3 − x and the x-axis. (vertices (−1, 0), (3, 0), (1, 2):
     area 4)

D12. The region between y = x² and the line y = 4 is cut into two equal areas by
     the line y = k. Find k.
     Answer: k = 4^(2/3) = 2∛2 ≈ 2.52.
     Teacher explains:
         whole region: ∫₋₂² (4 − x²) dx = 16 − 16/3 = 32/3
         below y = k (horizontal strips): x from −√y to √y
           ∫₀ᵏ 2√y dy = (4/3)k^(3/2)
         set (4/3)k^(3/2) = (1/2)(32/3) = 16/3  →  k^(3/2) = 4
         k = 4^(2/3) = ∛16 = 2∛2 ≈ 2.52
     Horizontal strips make the part below y = k a single simple integral. The
     answer is above 2 (half of 4) because the region is wider at the top: more
     area lies near y = 4. Common mistake: taking k = 2 by "halving the height".
     Now you try: the line x = k halves the area under y = x² from x = 0 to 2.
     Find k. (k³/3 = 4/3: k = ∛4 ≈ 1.59)
