TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: check the four binomial conditions aloud before using the formula;
  write "n = , p = , q = , r = " first; translate "at least / at most / more
  than / fewer than" into ≥, ≤, >, <; for the normal, ALWAYS sketch the bell
  curve and shade the required area; say "z = distance from the mean in SDs";
  use the empirical rule to check that table answers are sensible. Harder: prove
  the mode rule for B(n, p) from the ratio of successive terms; show that the
  normal curve y = e^(−z²/2)/√(2π) has inflection points at z = ±1; evaluate
  Φ(1) − 0.5 from the series of e^(−x²/2) (8.49); compare B(n, p) histograms
  with the normal curve in Desmos or Python for n = 10, 30, 100; learn how the
  Central Limit Theorem (8.57 and Stage 9) explains why the normal curve is
  everywhere.


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.57 — POISSON DISTRIBUTION; SAMPLING DISTRIBUTIONS (INTRODUCTION)
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - The POISSON distribution models the NUMBER OF EVENTS in a fixed interval of
    time, length, area or volume when the events happen singly, at random,
    independently of each other and at a constant average rate. If the mean
    number in the interval is λ, we write X ~ Po(λ) and P(X = r) = e^(−λ) λʳ /
    r!, for r = 0, 1, 2, 3, ... (no upper limit). Give probabilities to 4
    decimal places (4 d.p.).
  - Useful facts: P(X = 0) = e^(−λ); the probabilities add to 1 because Σ λʳ/r!
    = e^λ; the RECURRENCE P(X = r + 1) = P(X = r) × λ/(r + 1) builds a table
    quickly; the MODE is the integer part of λ (if λ is a whole number, both
    λ − 1 and λ are modes). For "at least" use the complement: P(X ≥ 3) = 1 −
    P(X ≤ 2).
  - MEAN = VARIANCE = λ, so SD = √λ. If data have mean ≈ variance, a Poisson
    model is reasonable; variance much bigger or smaller than the mean suggests
    it is not. λ scales with the interval: 3 per hour means λ = 1 for 20 minutes
    and λ = 6 for 2 hours.
  - SUMS: if X ~ Po(λ) and Y ~ Po(μ) are INDEPENDENT, then X + Y ~ Po(λ + μ).
    (X − Y is NOT Poisson, though Var(X − Y) = λ + μ still.)
  - POISSON APPROXIMATION TO THE BINOMIAL: if X ~ B(n, p) with n large and p
    small (rule of thumb n ≥ 50 and p ≤ 0.1, so np ≤ 5 or so), then X is
    approximately Po(np). If p is close to 1, count the failures instead.
  - SAMPLING: a POPULATION has parameters (mean μ, SD σ); a random SAMPLE of
    size n gives statistics such as the sample mean X-bar = (X₁ + ... + Xₙ)/n.
    X-bar varies from sample to sample; its distribution is the SAMPLING
    DISTRIBUTION. E(X-bar) = μ (unbiased), Var(X-bar) = σ²/n, and the STANDARD
    ERROR is SE = σ/√n (4 times the sample size halves the SE).
  - CENTRAL LIMIT THEOREM (CLT): for large n (n ≥ 30 is the usual rule), X-bar
    is approximately N(μ, σ²/n) WHATEVER the shape of the population; if the
    population itself is normal, this is exact for every n. Then z = (X-bar −
    μ)/(σ/√n).
  - CONFIDENCE INTERVALS (idea): an observed sample mean m gives the interval m
    ± z × σ/√n with z = 1.645 (90%), 1.96 (95%), 2.576 (99%). "95% confidence"
    means that 95% of intervals made this way contain the true μ; wider
    interval = more confidence; bigger n = narrower interval.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Calls reach a railway enquiry helpline at random at an average rate of 3 per
    10 minutes. Using a Poisson model, find the probability that in a particular
    10-minute period there are a) no calls b) exactly 2 calls c) at most 2 calls
    d) at least 3 calls.
    Answer: a) 0.0498 b) 0.2240 c) 0.4232 d) 0.5768 (all to 4 d.p.).
    Teacher explains: X = number of calls in 10 minutes, X ~ Po(3). Write the
    formula first, then substitute:
    P(X = r) = e^(−3) × 3ʳ / r!
    P(X = 0) = e^(−3) × 1 / 1       = 0.0498
    P(X = 1) = e^(−3) × 3 / 1       = 0.1494
    P(X = 2) = e^(−3) × 9 / 2       = 0.2240
    P(X ≤ 2) = e^(−3)(1 + 3 + 4.5) = 8.5 e^(−3) = 0.4232
    P(X ≥ 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 2)         = 0.5768
    Keep e^(−3) = 0.049787... unrounded on the calculator and round only the
    final answer. "At least 3" has infinitely many cases (3, 4, 5, ...), so
    ALWAYS use the complement. Common mistakes: forgetting 0! = 1 and the r = 0
    term in P(X ≤ 2); writing P(X ≥ 3) = 1 − P(X ≤ 3). Now you try: P(exactly 4
    calls). (0.1680)

D2. Explain which of these can reasonably be modelled by a Poisson distribution,
    and why. a) The number of misprints on a page of a novel. b) The number of
    heads in 20 tosses of a coin. c) The number of cars passing a toll plaza in
    a minute at 2 a.m. d) The number of customers entering a sweet shop per hour
    over a whole festival day. e) The number of goals scored in a football
    match. f) The number of students absent from a class of 40 during a flu
    outbreak.
    Answer: a) yes b) no, binomial B(20, 0.5) c) yes d) no, the rate is not
    constant e) yes, approximately f) no, absences are not independent (and the
    maximum is 40).
    Teacher explains: Check the four conditions: events occur 1) singly, 2) at
    random, 3) INDEPENDENTLY and 4) at a CONSTANT average rate, with no fixed
    upper limit. a) Misprints are rare, random and independent: Poisson. b)
    There are exactly 20 trials with p = 0.5 and at most 20 heads: this is
    binomial, and p is not small. c) Late-night traffic is light and random at a
    steady rate: Poisson. d) The rate changes during the day (evening rush
    before the festival), so a single λ does not fit; Poisson could work hour by
    hour with different λ. e) Goals are fairly rare and random: a Poisson model
    with λ ≈ 2.5 is often used. f) Flu spreads from child to child, so absences
    are not independent. Common mistake: using Poisson just because something is
    "a count". Now you try: the number of e-mails you receive between 3 a.m. and
    4 a.m. (Poisson: random, independent, steady low rate)

D3. Accidents at a busy junction in Pune occur at random at an average rate of
    0.6 per day. Find the probability of a) no accident on a given day b)
    exactly 3 accidents in a week c) at least one accident in a 2-day period.
    Answer: a) 0.5488 b) 0.1852 c) 0.6988
    Teacher explains: The key step is to SCALE λ to the interval asked about,
    because the mean number is proportional to the length of time:
    1 day:  λ = 0.6         P(X = 0) = e^(−0.6) = 0.5488
    1 week: λ = 7 × 0.6 = 4.2
            P(X = 3) = e^(−4.2) × 4.2³ / 3! = 0.1852
    2 days: λ = 2 × 0.6 = 1.2
            P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − e^(−1.2) = 0.6988
    Common mistake: using λ = 0.6 for the week and multiplying the answer by 7;
    probabilities do not scale, the MEAN does. Now you try: P(no accident in
    5 days). (λ = 3, 0.0498)

D4. a) Prove that if X ~ Po(λ) then E(X) = λ and Var(X) = λ. b) The numbers of
    goals scored by a school team in 100 matches are: 0 goals 30 matches, 1 goal
    36, 2 goals 22, 3 goals 9, 4 goals 3. Find the mean and variance and comment
    on whether a Poisson model fits. Estimate the expected number of matches
    with no goal.
    Answer: a) See the proof. b) mean = 1.19, variance = 1.1139; they are close,
    so Po(1.19) is a reasonable model; expected number with 0 goals = 100
    e^(−1.19) ≈ 30.4 (observed 30).
    Teacher explains: a) The r = 0 term of Σ r P(X = r) is zero, and r/r!
    = 1/(r − 1)!:
    E(X) = Σ r e^(−λ) λʳ/r! = λ e^(−λ) Σ λʳ⁻¹/(r − 1)!
         = λ e^(−λ) × e^λ = λ   (sum from r = 1)
    E(X(X − 1)) = λ² e^(−λ) Σ λʳ⁻²/(r − 2)! = λ²   (sum from r = 2)
    E(X²) = λ² + λ,  Var(X) = E(X²) − (E X)² = λ² + λ − λ² = λ
    b) Σfx = 0 + 36 + 44 + 27 + 12 = 119, Σfx² = 0 + 36 + 88 + 81 + 48 = 253, so
    mean = 119 ÷ 100 = 1.19 and variance = 253 ÷ 100 − 1.19² = 2.53 − 1.4161
    = 1.1139. Mean ≈ variance is the signature of a Poisson distribution.
    Expected frequency of 0 goals = 100 × e^(−1.19) ≈ 30.4. Common mistake:
    dividing Σfx² by 100 and forgetting to subtract the square of the mean. Now
    you try: data with mean 2.0 and variance 5.1: Poisson? (no; the variance is
    far bigger than the mean)

D5. On average 1% of the LED bulbs made by a factory in Noida are defective. A
    box contains 200 bulbs. Find the probability that the box contains at most 2
    defective bulbs a) exactly, using the binomial distribution b) using a
    Poisson approximation. Why does the approximation work?
    Answer: a) 0.6767 b) 0.6767; n is large and p is small, so B(200, 0.01) ≈
    Po(2).
    Teacher explains: X ~ B(200, 0.01). Exactly:
    P(X ≤ 2) = 0.99²⁰⁰ + 200(0.01)(0.99)¹⁹⁹
               + C(200, 2)(0.01)²(0.99)¹⁹⁸
             = 0.1340 + 0.2707 + 0.2720 = 0.6767
    Poisson: λ = np = 200 × 0.01 = 2, so P(X ≤ 2) ≈
    e^(−2)(1 + 2 + 2) = 5e^(−2) = 0.6767. The answers agree to 5 d.p. here
    (0.67668). Reason: as n → ∞ with np = λ fixed, C(n, r)pʳ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ʳ →
    e^(−λ)λʳ/r!, because (1 − λ/n)ⁿ → e^(−λ). Use the rule n ≥ 50, p ≤ 0.1.
    Common mistake: using λ = n or λ = p. Now you try: P(no defective bulb) by
    both methods. (0.1340 and 0.1353)

D6. Two typists prepare a school magazine. Anil makes errors at random at a mean
    rate of 1.5 per page and Bina at 2.5 per page, independently. Each types one
    page. Find the probability that the two pages together contain a) exactly 3
    errors b) at most 1 error. c) What are the mean and variance of the
    DIFFERENCE A − B, and why is A − B not Poisson?
    Answer: a) 0.1954 b) 0.0916 c) mean −1, variance 4; A − B can be negative.
    Teacher explains: Let A ~ Po(1.5), B ~ Po(2.5), independent. Then T = A + B
    ~ Po(1.5 + 2.5) = Po(4).
    P(T = 3) = e^(−4) × 4³ / 3! = 0.1954
    P(T ≤ 1) = e^(−4)(1 + 4) = 5e^(−4) = 0.0916
    Check a) the long way: P(T = 3) = Σ P(A = i)P(B = 3 − i) over i = 0 to 3,
    which gives the same 0.1954. c) E(A − B) = 1.5 − 2.5 = −1 and Var(A − B) =
    Var A + Var B = 4 (variances ADD even for a difference). A Poisson variable
    is never negative and has mean = variance, so A − B is not Poisson. Common
    mistake: using Po(1.5 × 2.5) or forgetting the independence condition. Now
    you try: P(T = 0). (0.0183)

D7. X ~ Po(λ). Find λ if a) P(X = 1) = P(X = 2) b) P(X = 0) = 0.2 c)
    P(X = 3) = 2P(X = 2). In each case find P(X = 0) or P(X = 1) as a check.
    Answer: a) λ = 2 (P(X = 0) = 0.1353) b) λ = ln 5 ≈ 1.6094 (P(X = 1) = 0.2 ln
    5 ≈ 0.3219) c) λ = 6 (P(X = 0) = 0.0025)
    Teacher explains: Write both sides with the formula and cancel e^(−λ):
    a) e^(−λ)λ = e^(−λ)λ²/2  ⇒  λ = λ²/2  ⇒  λ = 2   (λ > 0)
    b) e^(−λ) = 0.2  ⇒  −λ = ln 0.2  ⇒  λ = ln 5
    c) λ³/6 = 2 × λ²/2  ⇒  λ/3 = 2  ⇒  λ = 6
    The recurrence gives c) at once: P(X = 3)/P(X = 2) = λ/3. Reject λ = 0
    because a Poisson mean must be positive. Common mistake: dividing by λ²
    without saying λ ≠ 0, or taking logs of a sum. Now you try: P(X = 2) =
    P(X = 3). (λ = 3)

D8. Show that for X ~ Po(λ), P(X = r + 1) = P(X = r) × λ/(r + 1). Use it to make
    a table for λ = 3.7 and find the most likely value (the mode). What happens
    when λ = 4?
    Answer: mode = 3 for λ = 3.7; for λ = 4, r = 3 and r = 4 are equally likely
    (both 0.1954).
    Teacher explains: Divide consecutive terms: [e^(−λ)λʳ⁺¹/(r + 1)!] ÷
    [e^(−λ)λʳ/r!] = λ/(r + 1). So the probabilities INCREASE while λ/(r + 1) >
    1, i.e. r + 1 < λ, and then decrease. For λ = 3.7 start with P(X = 0) =
    e^(−3.7) and multiply by 3.7/1, 3.7/2, 3.7/3, ...:
    r              0       1       2       3       4       5       6       7
    P(X = r)  0.0247  0.0915  0.1692  0.2087  0.1931  0.1429  0.0881  0.0466
    The ratio 3.7/4 < 1 is the first ratio below 1, so the peak is at r = 3.
    When λ = 4 the ratio at r = 3 is 4/4 = 1, so P(X = 4) = P(X = 3): two modes,
    3 and 4. In general the mode is the integer part of λ. Now you try: the mode
    of Po(0.8). (0)

D9. A bag has four cards marked 2, 4, 6 and 8. Two cards are drawn WITH
    replacement and their mean X-bar is found. a) Find the population mean μ and
    variance σ². b) List the sampling distribution of X-bar. c) Show that
    E(X-bar) = μ and Var(X-bar) = σ²/2.
    Answer: a) μ = 5, σ² = 5 b) see the table c) E(X-bar) = 5,
    Var(X-bar) = 2.5 = 5 ÷ 2.
    Teacher explains: a) μ = (2 + 4 + 6 + 8) ÷ 4 = 5; σ²
    = ((−3)² + (−1)² + 1² + 3²) ÷ 4 = 20 ÷ 4 = 5. b) There are 4 × 4 = 16
    equally likely ordered samples (2, 2), (2, 4), ..., (8, 8). Their means:
    X-bar     2    3     4    5     6    7     8
    count     1    2     3    4     3    2     1
    P      1/16  1/8  3/16  1/4  3/16  1/8  1/16
    c) E(X-bar) = (2 × 1 + 3 × 2 + 4 × 3 + 5 × 4 + 6 × 3 + 7 × 2 + 8 × 1) ÷ 16
    = 80 ÷ 16 = 5 = μ. Var(X-bar) = Σ(x − 5)² P
    = (9 + 8 + 3 + 0 + 3 + 8 + 9) ÷ 16 = 40 ÷ 16 = 2.5 = σ²/2. The sample mean
    is centred on μ but less spread out than a single card. Notice also that the
    distribution of X-bar is symmetric and peaked in the middle even though the
    population is flat: the first sign of the Central Limit Theorem. Now you
    try: the variance of X-bar for samples of 4 cards. (5/4 = 1.25)

D10. Packets of basmati rice are filled by a machine with mean mass 1000 g and
     standard deviation 12 g. A quality inspector weighs a random sample of 36
     packets. a) Find the standard error of the sample mean. b) Find the
     probability that the sample mean is less than 996 g. c) Find
     P(997 < X-bar < 1003). d) Compare with the probability that ONE packet
     weighs less than 996 g.
     Answer: a) SE = 12/√36 = 2 g b) 0.0228 c) 0.8664 d) about 0.37, much
     larger.
     Teacher explains: n = 36 ≥ 30, so by the CLT X-bar ≈ N(1000, 2²) whatever
     the shape of the population.
     a) SE = σ/√n = 12/6 = 2
     b) z = (996 − 1000)/2 = −2,  P(Z < −2) = 0.0228
     c) z = ±1.5,  P(−1.5 < Z < 1.5) = 2Φ(1.5) − 1 = 0.8664
     d) one packet: z = −4/12 ≈ −0.33,  P ≈ 0.3707
     The average of 36 packets is 6 times less spread out than one packet, so a
     mean as low as 996 g is rare (2.3%) and would make the inspector suspect
     the machine. Common mistake: using σ = 12 instead of the SE for a sample
     mean. Now you try: P(X-bar > 1003). (0.0668)

D11. State the Central Limit Theorem. Waiting times for a city bus have a very
     skewed distribution with mean 8 minutes and standard deviation 8 minutes.
     Find the probability that the mean waiting time of 64 randomly chosen
     passengers exceeds 9.5 minutes. Why could we NOT find P(one passenger waits
     more than 9.5 minutes) the same way?
     Answer: P(X-bar > 9.5) = P(Z > 1.5) = 0.0668. For one passenger the
     distribution is skewed, not normal, so the normal table does not apply.
     Teacher explains: CLT: if X₁, ..., Xₙ are independent with mean μ and
     variance σ², then for large n the sample mean X-bar is approximately N(μ,
     σ²/n), even when the X values themselves are not normal. Here μ = 8, σ = 8,
     n = 64:
     SE = 8/√64 = 1
     z = (9.5 − 8)/1 = 1.5
     P(X-bar > 9.5) = 1 − Φ(1.5) = 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668
     The CLT is about AVERAGES of many values; a single waiting time keeps the
     skewed shape of the population. Common mistake: applying the CLT with n = 5
     to a skewed population. Now you try: P(X-bar < 7). (0.1587)

D12. The heights of 100 randomly chosen Class 12 students have mean
     m = 162.4 cm. Assume σ = 8 cm. a) Find a 95% confidence interval for the
     mean height μ of all Class 12 students. b) Explain what "95% confidence"
     means. c) How large a sample would halve the width?
     Answer: a) 162.4 ± 1.96 × 0.8 = (160.832, 163.968) cm b) see below c)
     n = 400.
     Teacher explains: Standard error SE = σ/√n = 8/10 = 0.8. For 95%,
     P(−1.96 < Z < 1.96) = 0.95, so the interval is m ± 1.96 SE:
     margin = 1.96 × 0.8 = 1.568
     interval = 162.4 − 1.568 to 162.4 + 1.568
              = 160.832 to 163.968  (≈ 160.8 to 164.0 cm)
     b) μ is fixed; the INTERVAL is random. If we took many samples of 100 and
     built an interval from each, about 95% of those intervals would contain μ.
     It is wrong to say "μ lies in this interval with probability 0.95". c) The
     width is 2 × 1.96 × σ/√n; halving it needs √n doubled, so
     n = 4 × 100 = 400. Now you try: the 99% interval. (162.4 ±
     2.576 × 0.8 = 160.3392 to 164.4608)

PART B — MATHEMATICAL ONLY
--------------------------

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: write the four Poisson conditions on a card and check them before
  every question; build the probability table with the recurrence × λ/(r + 1);
  always write "X ~ Po(λ)" with λ scaled to the interval; for sampling, list the
  samples of a tiny population (as in D9) before using σ/√n; draw the normal
  curve and shade the region every time. Harder: prove that the sum of
  independent Poissons is Poisson using Σ P(X = i)P(Y = r − i) and the binomial
  theorem; show that P(X = r | X + Y = n) is binomial; simulate 1,000 samples of
  size 30 from a skewed population on a computer and draw the histogram of the
  means; derive the sample-size formula n ≥ (zσ/E)²; compare Po(λ) with N(λ, λ)
  for λ = 20 (continuity correction).


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.58 — LINEAR PROGRAMMING (GRAPHICAL METHOD)
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - A LINEAR PROGRAMMING PROBLEM (LPP) asks for the maximum or minimum of a
    linear OBJECTIVE FUNCTION Z = ax + by subject to linear CONSTRAINTS
    (inequalities such as 3x + 2y ≤ 120) and the NON-NEGATIVITY conditions
    x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. x and y are the DECISION VARIABLES.
  - FORMULATION from words: define x and y with units; turn every resource limit
    into an inequality ("at most" ≤, "at least" ≥, "not more than twice"
    y ≤ 2x); write Z as profit or cost per unit × number of units.
  - The FEASIBLE REGION is the set of points satisfying ALL the constraints:
    draw each boundary line (use its intercepts), test a point such as (0, 0) to
    choose the side, and take the common part. Each point of it is a FEASIBLE
    SOLUTION; the best one is the OPTIMAL solution. If there is no common part
    the problem is INFEASIBLE.
  - CORNER-POINT THEOREM: if the feasible region is bounded, Z has both a
    maximum and a minimum, and each occurs at a CORNER (vertex). Method: find
    every corner by solving the equations of the two lines that meet there,
    CHECK the point satisfies all the other constraints, evaluate Z at every
    corner and compare.
  - UNBOUNDED region: an optimum may not exist. If M is the largest corner
    value, M is the maximum only if the open half-plane ax + by > M has no point
    in common with the region; similarly m (the smallest corner value) is the
    minimum only if ax + by < m has no common point. With positive a and b and a
    region stretching to infinity, the maximum does not exist, but the minimum
    usually does.
  - ISO-PROFIT (iso-cost) LINES ax + by = k are all parallel with slope −a/b;
    slide the line away from the origin to increase k: the last point of the
    region it touches is optimal. If the objective line is PARALLEL to an edge
    at the optimum, both end corners and every point of the edge between them
    are optimal (MULTIPLE OPTIMA).

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. A carpentry workshop in Jaipur makes tables and chairs. A table needs
    3 hours of carpentry and 1 hour of polishing; a chair needs 2 hours of
    carpentry and 2 hours of polishing. Each week at most 120 hours of carpentry
    and 80 hours of polishing are available. The profit is ₹400 per table and
    ₹300 per chair. Formulate an LPP and find how many of each should be made to
    maximise profit.
    Answer: 20 tables and 30 chairs; maximum profit ₹17,000 per week.
    Teacher explains: Let x = tables and y = chairs per week. Maximise
    Z = 400x + 300y subject to
    3x + 2y ≤ 120   (carpentry)
    x + 2y ≤ 80     (polishing)
    x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0
    Intercepts: 3x + 2y = 120 meets the axes at (40, 0) and (0, 60); x + 2y = 80
    at (80, 0) and (0, 40). (0, 0) satisfies both, so shade towards the origin.
    The corners are O(0, 0), A(40, 0), C(0, 40) and B where the lines cross:
    subtract x + 2y = 80 from 3x + 2y = 120 to get 2x = 40, x = 20, y = 30.
    Check B: 60 + 60 = 120 ≤ 120 and 20 + 60 = 80 ≤ 80.
    corner   O(0, 0)   A(40, 0)   B(20, 30)   C(0, 40)
    Z              0     16,000      17,000     12,000
    Maximum ₹17,000 at B. Note (0, 60) is NOT a corner: it breaks the polishing
    limit (0 + 120 > 80). Common mistakes: using every intercept as a corner
    without checking; forgetting x, y ≥ 0. Now you try: if the table profit
    rises to ₹500, what is the best plan? (40 tables, 0 chairs, ₹20,000; B gives
    19,000)

D2. A hostel dietician mixes two foods. Food X contains 2 units of vitamin A and
    1 unit of vitamin B per kg and costs ₹60 per kg; food Y contains 1 unit of A
    and 2 units of B per kg and costs ₹40 per kg. The mixture must contain at
    least 8 units of A and 10 units of B. Find the cheapest mixture. Why does
    the maximum cost not exist?
    Answer: 2 kg of X and 4 kg of Y; minimum cost ₹280. The region is unbounded,
    so the cost can be made as large as we like.
    Teacher explains: x kg of X, y kg of Y. Minimise Z = 60x + 40y subject to
    2x + y ≥ 8 (vitamin A), x + 2y ≥ 10 (vitamin B), x, y ≥ 0. Now (0, 0) does
    NOT satisfy the constraints, so shade AWAY from the origin. The region is
    unbounded (open to the top right). Corners: (0, 8) on the y-axis, (10, 0) on
    the x-axis, and 2x + y = 8, x + 2y = 10 ⇒ (doubling the first) 4x + 2y = 16,
    subtract: 3x = 6, x = 2, y = 4.
    corner   (0, 8)   (2, 4)   (10, 0)
    Z           320      280       600
    Smallest corner value 280. Because the region is unbounded we must check:
    draw 60x + 40y < 280, i.e. 3x + 2y < 14. Every point of the region has
    3x + 2y ≥ 14 (at (2, 4) it equals 14 and the region lies beyond), so there
    is no common point and 280 IS the minimum. Common mistake: claiming a
    maximum of ₹600 at (10, 0); (20, 20) is feasible and costs more. Now you
    try: minimise 50x + 50y on the same region. (300 at (2, 4))

D3. Explain why the maximum of Z = ax + by over a bounded feasible region must
    occur at a corner. Then maximise Z = 3x + 4y subject to x + y ≤ 6,
    x + 3y ≤ 12, 2x + y ≤ 10, x, y ≥ 0, listing and checking every corner.
    Answer: Maximum Z = 21 at (3, 3). Corners: (0, 0), (5, 0), (4, 2), (3, 3),
    (0, 4).
    Teacher explains: Why corners: the points where Z = k form the straight line
    ax + by = k. As k increases the line moves parallel to itself. The region is
    a convex polygon, so the last position where the line still touches it
    passes through a vertex (or along a whole edge, which contains two
    vertices). A point in the middle of the region cannot be best: we can always
    move a little further in the direction that increases Z.
    Corners: on the axes (0, 0), (5, 0) (from 2x + y = 10; check 5 ≤ 6 and
    5 ≤ 12) and (0, 4) (from x + 3y = 12). Then pairs of lines:
    x + y = 6,   x + 3y = 12:  2y = 6, y = 3, x = 3     → (3, 3)
    x + y = 6,   2x + y = 10:  x = 4, y = 2             → (4, 2)
    x + 3y = 12, 2x + y = 10:  x = 18/5, y = 14/5
        check x + y = 32/5 > 6                        → reject
    corner   (0, 0)   (5, 0)   (4, 2)   (3, 3)   (0, 4)
    Z             0       15       20       21       16
    So Z(max) = 21 at (3, 3). The rejected intersection shows why every corner
    must be checked against ALL the constraints. Now you try: maximise Z = 4x +
    y. (Z = 20 at (5, 0))

D4. Use iso-profit lines to maximise Z = 3x + 4y subject to x + 2y ≤ 10, 3x +
    y ≤ 15, x, y ≥ 0. Explain, using slopes, why the optimum is at the
    intersection of the two lines.
    Answer: Z(max) = 24 at (4, 3).
    Teacher explains: Draw the lines 3x + 4y = 12 and 3x + 4y = 24; they are
    parallel with slope −3/4. Slide the line away from O: it leaves the region
    last at the corner (4, 3) (solve x + 2y = 10 and 3x + y = 15: from the first
    x = 10 − 2y, so 30 − 6y + y = 15, y = 3, x = 4). Slopes: the edge
    x + 2y = 10 has slope −1/2 and the edge 3x + y = 15 has slope −3. The
    objective slope −3/4 lies BETWEEN −3 and −1/2, so the iso-profit line is
    steeper than one edge and flatter than the other and touches only the corner
    between them. Corner check: O 0, (5, 0) 15, (4, 3) 24, (0, 5) 20. Common
    mistake: drawing the iso-profit line with slope −4/3 (the slope of ax + by =
    k is −a/b). Now you try: maximise Z = x + 3y on the same region. (slope −1/3
    is flatter than −1/2: Z = 15 at (0, 5))

D5. Find the minimum and the maximum (if they exist) of Z = 3x + 5y subject to
    x + 3y ≥ 3, x + y ≥ 2, x, y ≥ 0.
    Answer: Minimum Z = 7 at (3/2, 1/2); no maximum.
    Teacher explains: Both constraints are "≥", so the region lies away from the
    origin and is unbounded. Corners: (3, 0) (x + 3y = 3 on the x-axis; check
    3 ≥ 2), (0, 2) (x + y = 2 on the y-axis; check 6 ≥ 3), and x + 3y = 3, x +
    y = 2 ⇒ 2y = 1, y = 1/2, x = 3/2.
    corner   (3, 0)   (3/2, 1/2)   (0, 2)
    Z             9            7       10
    Test the smallest value: the half-plane 3x + 5y < 7 has no point in common
    with the region, so 7 is the minimum. For the maximum, the largest corner
    value is 10, but 3x + 5y > 10 does meet the region (for example (10, 10)); Z
    grows without limit, so NO maximum exists. Common mistake: announcing
    "max = 10" from the table without drawing the region. Now you try: minimise
    Z = x + y on the same region. (2, at every point of the segment from (3/2,
    1/2) to (0, 2))

D6. On the region x + 2y ≤ 10, 3x + y ≤ 15, x, y ≥ 0 maximise a) Z = 2x + 4y b)
    Z = 6x + 2y. What is special about these answers?
    Answer: a) Z(max) = 20 at (0, 5) and (4, 3), and at every point of the
    segment joining them b) Z(max) = 30 at (5, 0) and (4, 3) and every point
    between. Multiple optimal solutions.
    Teacher explains: Corner table: a) O 0, (5, 0) 10, (4, 3) 20, (0, 5) 20 b) O
    0, (5, 0) 30, (4, 3) 30, (0, 5) 10. A tie at two ADJACENT corners means the
    iso-profit line is parallel to the edge between them: 2x + 4y = 2(x + 2y),
    so Z = 2 × 10 = 20 all along x + 2y = 10; and 6x + 2y = 2(3x + y) = 30 all
    along 3x + y = 15. E.g. (2, 4) gives 2 × 2 + 4 × 4 = 20. Every point (x,
    y) = (4t, 5 − 2t), 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, is optimal in a). In business terms the
    manager may choose any of these plans. Common mistake: reporting only one
    corner. Now you try: show that (4.5, 1.5) is also optimal in b). (it lies on
    3x + y = 15, and 6 × 4.5 + 2 × 1.5 = 27 + 3 = 30)

D7. Two ration godowns A and B hold 100 and 50 quintals of wheat. Three shops D,
    E, F need 60, 50 and 40 quintals. Transport costs in ₹ per quintal are: A→D
    6, A→E 3, A→F 2.50, B→D 4, B→E 2, B→F 3. How should the wheat be sent to
    minimise the transport cost?
    Answer: A sends 10 to D, 50 to E, 40 to F; B sends 50 to D, 0 to E, 0 to F.
    Minimum cost ₹510.
    Teacher explains: Use only TWO variables: let A send x to D and y to E.
    Everything else follows from the totals (supply 150 = demand 150):
    A→F = 100 − x − y      B→D = 60 − x
    B→E = 50 − y           B→F = 40 − (100 − x − y) = x + y − 60
    All six amounts ≥ 0 give the constraints x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, x + y ≤ 100, x ≤ 60,
    y ≤ 50, x + y ≥ 60. Cost Z = 6x + 3y + 2.5(100 − x − y) + 4(60 − x) + 2(50 −
    y) + 3(x + y − 60) = 2.5x + 1.5y + 410.
    corner   (60, 0)   (60, 40)   (50, 50)   (10, 50)
    Z            560        620        610        510
    Minimum ₹510 at (10, 50). Check the amounts: A→F = 40, B→D = 50, B→E = 0,
    B→F = 0, all non-negative and the totals match. Common mistake: using six
    variables and getting lost; or forgetting the hidden constraint x + y ≥ 60
    that comes from B→F ≥ 0. Now you try: the maximum possible cost. (₹620 at
    (60, 40))

D8. Write each condition as a linear inequality in x and y (x = kg of cashew
    mix, y = kg of almond mix packed per day). a) At most 60 kg can be packed in
    total. b) At least 10 kg of almond mix must be packed. c) The cashew mix
    must be not more than twice the almond mix. d) Cashew mix needs 2 hours per
    10 kg and almond mix 3 hours per 10 kg, with 15 hours available. e) The
    ratio of cashew to almond must be at least 1 : 3. Then write the objective
    if the profit is ₹80 per kg of cashew mix and ₹60 per kg of almond mix.
    Answer: a) x + y ≤ 60 b) y ≥ 10 c) x ≤ 2y d) 0.2x + 0.3y ≤ 15, i.e.
    2x + 3y ≤ 150 e) 3x ≥ y. Maximise Z = 80x + 60y, with x, y ≥ 0.
    Teacher explains: Translate word by word: "at most" ↔ ≤, "at least" ↔ ≥,
    "not more than twice y" ↔ x ≤ 2y. d) Time per kg: 2/10 = 0.2 h and
    3/10 = 0.3 h, so 0.2x + 0.3y ≤ 15; multiply by 10 to clear decimals. e) x :
    y ≥ 1 : 3 means x/y ≥ 1/3, and since y > 0, 3x ≥ y. Always state the units
    of x and y and add x, y ≥ 0. Common mistakes: writing "twice" the wrong way
    round (2x ≤ y), and cross-multiplying an inequality by a quantity that could
    be negative. Now you try: "the almond mix cannot exceed the cashew mix by
    more than 20 kg". (y − x ≤ 20)

D9. a) Show that the LPP maximise Z = x + y subject to x + y ≤ 2, x + y ≥ 5, x,
    y ≥ 0 has no solution. b) In the LPP maximise Z = 2x + y subject to x +
    y ≤ 8, x ≤ 3, 2x + y ≤ 20, x, y ≥ 0, one constraint is REDUNDANT. Which, and
    what is the optimum?
    Answer: a) The feasible region is empty (infeasible). b) 2x + y ≤ 20 is
    redundant; Z(max) = 11 at (3, 5).
    Teacher explains: a) The two constraints ask for x + y to be at most 2 and
    at least 5 at the same time: the half-planes are on opposite sides of
    parallel lines and do not overlap. No feasible point, so no optimum; this
    usually means the problem was set up wrongly. b) On the region x + y ≤ 8,
    x ≤ 3 we have 2x + y = x + (x + y) ≤ 3 + 8 = 11 < 20, so 2x + y ≤ 20 is
    always satisfied and removing it changes nothing. Corners (0, 0), (3, 0),
    (3, 5), (0, 8) give Z = 0, 6, 11, 8: maximum 11 at (3, 5). Now you try: is
    x ≤ 10 redundant in x + y ≤ 8, x, y ≥ 0? (yes, x ≤ 8 already)

D10. Meera has at most ₹1,00,000 (one lakh, 100,000 in international commas) to
     invest in a fixed deposit paying 8% a year and a bond fund paying 10% a
     year. She wants at least ₹20,000 in the fixed deposit, at most ₹60,000 in
     the bond fund, and the fixed deposit must be at least half of the bond
     amount. How should she invest to maximise her annual return?
     Answer: ₹40,000 in the fixed deposit and ₹60,000 in bonds; return ₹9,200 a
     year.
     Teacher explains: x = ₹ in the deposit, y = ₹ in bonds. Maximise
     Z = 0.08x + 0.10y subject to x + y ≤ 100,000, x ≥ 20,000, y ≤ 60,000, x ≥
     y/2 (i.e. 2x − y ≥ 0), y ≥ 0. Corners:
     corner (₹)   (20,000, 0)   (100,000, 0)
     Z (₹)              1,600          8,000
     corner (₹)   (40,000, 60,000)   (30,000, 60,000)   (20,000, 40,000)
     Z (₹)                   9,200              8,400              5,600
     For example (30,000, 60,000) comes from 2x − y = 0 and y = 60,000, and
     (40,000, 60,000) from y = 60,000 and x + y = 100,000. Best: ₹9,200 at
     (40,000, 60,000). The answer makes sense: bonds pay more, so put the
     maximum allowed in bonds and the rest in the deposit. Now you try: the best
     plan if the bond limit is removed. (x = 100,000/3 ≈ ₹33,333,
     y = 200,000/3 ≈ ₹66,667, return ≈ ₹9,333)

D11. Spot the mistakes. To maximise Z = 5x + 4y subject to 2x + y ≤ 12, x +
     y ≤ 8, x + 3y ≤ 18, x, y ≥ 0, Ravi lists the corners (0, 0), (6, 0), (0,
     8), (4, 4), (3, 5) and says "Z(max) = 5 × 0 + 4 × 8 = 32 at (0, 8)". Find
     the correct maximum.
     Answer: Z(max) = 36 at (4, 4). (0, 8) is not feasible; the missing corner
     is (0, 6).
     Teacher explains: Check every listed point against ALL constraints: (0, 8)
     gives x + 3y = 24 > 18, so it is outside the region (it is only the
     intercept of x + y = 8). The true corner on the y-axis comes from
     x + 3y = 18: (0, 6). Also check (3, 5): 2(3) + 5 = 11 ≤ 12, 3 + 5 = 8 ≤ 8,
     3 + 15 = 18 ≤ 18: feasible (three lines pass through it). Correct table:
     corner   (0, 0)   (6, 0)   (4, 4)   (3, 5)   (0, 6)
     Z             0       30       36       35       24
     So Z(max) = 36 at (4, 4). Lesson: an intersection of two boundary lines is
     a corner only if it satisfies every other inequality. Now you try: the
     maximum of Z = x + 2y on this region. (13 at (3, 5))

D12. On the region x + 2y ≤ 10, 3x + y ≤ 15, x, y ≥ 0, the profit is Z = cx + 4y
     (c > 0). For which values of c is (4, 3) an optimal corner? What happens
     outside this range?
     Answer: 2 ≤ c ≤ 12. For c < 2 the optimum moves to (0, 5); for c > 12 it
     moves to (5, 0); at c = 2 or c = 12 there are multiple optima.
     Teacher explains: (4, 3) stays optimal while the slope of the objective
     line, −c/4, lies between the slopes of the two edges meeting there, −3
     (3x + y = 15) and −1/2 (x + 2y = 10):
     −3 ≤ −c/4 ≤ −1/2   ⇔   1/2 ≤ c/4 ≤ 3   ⇔   2 ≤ c ≤ 12
     Check with corners: Z(4, 3) = 4c + 12, Z(0, 5) = 20, Z(5, 0) = 5c.
     4c + 12 ≥ 20 ⇔ c ≥ 2, and 4c + 12 ≥ 5c ⇔ c ≤ 12. This is SENSITIVITY
     ANALYSIS: how much a price may change before the best plan changes. Now you
     try: for Z = 3x + ky (k > 0), when is (4, 3) optimal? (1 ≤ k ≤ 6)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: use squared paper and draw each line from its two intercepts;
  shade the UNWANTED side so the feasible region stays clear; label every corner
  with the two lines that make it; keep a three-column table (corner, check, Z)
  and never skip the check column; for word problems make a table of resources
  before writing inequalities. Harder: prove that a linear function on a segment
  takes its extreme values at the end points, and deduce the corner-point
  theorem; do sensitivity analysis (ranges of profit coefficients); try an LPP
  in three variables and see why the graphical method fails (the simplex method
  is Stage 9); solve integer-programming questions where the LP optimum is
  fractional; use GeoGebra or Desmos sliders to move iso-profit lines.


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.59 — OLYMPIAD NUMBER THEORY: MODULAR ARITHMETIC, FERMAT'S LITTLE
             THEOREM, DIOPHANTINE EQUATIONS
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - CONGRUENCE: a ≡ b (mod n) means n divides a − b, i.e. a and b leave the same
    remainder on division by n. Congruences can be added, subtracted, multiplied
    and raised to powers: if a ≡ b and c ≡ d (mod n) then a + c ≡ b + d, ac ≡ bd
    and aᵏ ≡ bᵏ. You may DIVIDE both sides by k only when gcd(k, n) = 1. Use
    negative residues to save work: 99 ≡ −1 (mod 100).
  - MODULAR INVERSE: a has an inverse mod n (a number a′ with aa′ ≡ 1) exactly
    when gcd(a, n) = 1; find it with the extended Euclidean algorithm (write 1 =
    ax + ny). Then ax ≡ b (mod n) has the unique solution x ≡ a′b. In general ax
    ≡ b (mod n) has d = gcd(a, n) solutions mod n if d | b, and none otherwise.
  - FERMAT'S LITTLE THEOREM: if p is prime and p does not divide a, then aᵖ⁻¹ ≡
    1 (mod p); for every a, aᵖ ≡ a (mod p). EULER: if gcd(a, n) = 1 then a^φ(n)
    ≡ 1 (mod n), where φ(n) counts 1 ≤ k ≤ n coprime to n; φ(n) =
    n(1 − 1/p₁)(1 − 1/p₂)... over the distinct primes dividing n. To reduce aᴺ,
    reduce the exponent N modulo p − 1 (or φ(n), or the length of the cycle of
    powers).
  - LAST DIGITS: the last digit is the remainder mod 10, the last two digits mod
    100. Powers of any number repeat in a cycle (2, 4, 8, 6 for powers of 2 mod
    10).
  - CHINESE REMAINDER THEOREM (CRT): if m₁, m₂, ..., mₖ are pairwise coprime,
    the system x ≡ rᵢ (mod mᵢ) has exactly one solution modulo m₁m₂...mₖ. Solve
    by substitution: x = r₁ + m₁t, then fit the next congruence.
  - LINEAR DIOPHANTINE EQUATION ax + by = c (integers): solvable iff d = gcd(a,
    b) divides c. If (x₀, y₀) is one solution, ALL solutions are x =
    x₀ + (b/d)t, y = y₀ − (a/d)t, t an integer. For non-negative solutions find
    the range of t.
  - PYTHAGOREAN TRIPLES: every primitive solution of a² + b² = c² (b even) is
    a = m² − n², b = 2mn, c = m² + n² with m > n > 0, gcd(m, n) = 1 and m, n of
    opposite parity; all triples are multiples k(a, b, c). PELL equation
    x² − 2y² = 1: from (3, 2) all solutions come from xₖ + yₖ√2 = (3 + 2√2)ᵏ.
  - Proof tools: look at an equation modulo a small number (squares are 0, 1 mod
    3 and mod 4, and 0, 1, 4 mod 8; cubes are 0, ±1 mod 9) to show it has no
    solutions; factorise (n⁵ − n = n(n − 1)(n + 1)(n² + 1)); use "d | a and d |
    b ⇒ d | ax + by".

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Find the remainder when 2¹⁰⁰ is divided by 7, and when 17 × 23 + 45 × 99 is
    divided by 5, without a calculator. Explain which rules of congruences you
    used.
    Answer: 2¹⁰⁰ ≡ 2 (mod 7); 17 × 23 + 45 × 99 ≡ 1 (mod 5).
    Teacher explains: Look for a small power that is ≡ 1: 2³ = 8 ≡ 1 (mod 7).
    Divide the exponent by 3: 100 = 3 × 33 + 1, so
    2¹⁰⁰ = (2³)³³ × 2 ≡ 1³³ × 2 = 2  (mod 7)
    For the second: 17 ≡ 2, 23 ≡ 3, 45 ≡ 0, 99 ≡ 4 (mod 5), so the expression ≡
    2 × 3 + 0 × 4 = 6 ≡ 1 (mod 5). Check:
    17 × 23 + 45 × 99 = 391 + 4,455 = 4,846, which ends in 6, remainder 1 on
    division by 5. We used: congruences can be multiplied, added and raised to
    powers. Common mistake: reducing the EXPONENT mod 7 (writing 2¹⁰⁰ ≡ 2²
    because 100 ≡ 2 mod 7); exponents are reduced mod the CYCLE LENGTH (here 3).
    Now you try: 3⁵⁰ mod 8. (3² = 9 ≡ 1, so 3⁵⁰ ≡ 1)

D2. State Fermat's little theorem and outline a proof. Use it to find 3¹⁰⁰ mod
    13 and 10¹⁰⁰ mod 17.
    Answer: 3¹⁰⁰ ≡ 3 (mod 13); 10¹⁰⁰ ≡ 4 (mod 17).
    Teacher explains: Theorem: p prime, p ∤ a ⇒ aᵖ⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod p). Proof idea:
    the numbers a, 2a, 3a, ..., (p − 1)a are all different mod p (if ia ≡ ja
    then p | (i − j)a, so p | i − j, so i = j) and none is ≡ 0. So they are 1,
    2, ..., p − 1 in some order. Multiply them all: aᵖ⁻¹ (p − 1)! ≡ (p − 1)!
    (mod p), and (p − 1)! is coprime to p, so we may cancel it: aᵖ⁻¹ ≡ 1.
    3¹² ≡ 1 (mod 13);  100 = 12 × 8 + 4
    3¹⁰⁰ ≡ 3⁴ = 81 = 6 × 13 + 3,  so 3¹⁰⁰ ≡ 3 (mod 13)
    10¹⁶ ≡ 1 (mod 17); 100 = 16 × 6 + 4
    10⁴ = 10,000 = 588 × 17 + 4,  so 10¹⁰⁰ ≡ 4 (mod 17)
    Common mistakes: using p instead of p − 1 as the exponent; applying the
    theorem when p divides a (e.g. 13¹⁰⁰ ≡ 0 mod 13) or when the modulus is not
    prime (use Euler instead). Now you try: 2²⁰²⁶ mod 11. (2¹⁰ ≡ 1,
    2,026 = 202 × 10 + 6, 2⁶ = 64 ≡ 9)

D3. Find a) the last digit of 2²⁰²⁶ b) the last two digits of 7²⁰²⁶ c) the last
    two digits of 3²⁰²⁶.
    Answer: a) 4 b) 49 c) 29
    Teacher explains: a) Powers of 2 end in 2, 4, 8, 6, 2, 4, ... (cycle of
    length 4). 2,026 = 4 × 506 + 2, so 2²⁰²⁶ ends like 2², in 4. b) 7² = 49,
    7⁴ = 2,401 ≡ 1 (mod 100). 2,026 = 4 × 506 + 2, so 7²⁰²⁶ ≡ 7² = 49 (mod 100).
    c) Euler: φ(100) = 100 × (1/2) × (4/5) = 40 and gcd(3, 100) = 1, so 3⁴⁰ ≡ 1
    (mod 100). 2,026 = 40 × 50 + 26, so we need 3²⁶ mod 100:
    3⁵ = 243 ≡ 43,  3¹⁰ ≡ 43² = 1,849 ≡ 49,  3²⁰ ≡ 49² = 2,401 ≡ 1
    (so the cycle is really 20)  3²⁶ = 3²⁰ × 3⁵ × 3 ≡ 1 × 43 × 3 = 129 ≡ 29
    So 3²⁰²⁶ ends in 29. Repeated squaring keeps every number small. Common
    mistake: working mod 10 when two digits are asked for. Now you try: the last
    two digits of 9¹⁰⁰⁰. (01)

D4. Compute φ(36), φ(100) and φ(97). Use Euler's theorem to find the remainder
    when 11¹⁰⁰ is divided by 36. Why can we NOT use it for 10¹⁰⁰ mod 36?
    Answer: φ(36) = 12, φ(100) = 40, φ(97) = 96; 11¹⁰⁰ ≡ 25 (mod 36). gcd(10,
    36) = 2 ≠ 1.
    Teacher explains: φ(n) = n × Π(1 − 1/p): 36 = 2² × 3²,
    φ = 36 × 1/2 × 2/3 = 12 (the numbers 1, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, 25, 29,
    31, 35). 100 = 2² × 5², φ = 100 × 1/2 × 4/5 = 40. 97 is prime, so φ = 96.
    Now gcd(11, 36) = 1, so 11¹² ≡ 1 (mod 36); 100 = 12 × 8 + 4:
    11² = 121 = 3 × 36 + 13 ≡ 13
    11⁴ ≡ 13² = 169 = 4 × 36 + 25 ≡ 25
    11¹⁰⁰ ≡ 11⁴ ≡ 25  (mod 36)
    For 10¹⁰⁰: 10 and 36 share the factor 2, so no power of 10 is ≡ 1 mod 36.
    Split instead: mod 4, 10¹⁰⁰ ≡ 0; mod 9, 10 ≡ 1 so 10¹⁰⁰ ≡ 1; the number ≡ 0
    (mod 4) and ≡ 1 (mod 9) is 28. Now you try: φ(60). (16)

D5. Solve 17x ≡ 5 (mod 43) using the extended Euclidean algorithm. Check your
    answer.
    Answer: x ≡ 18 (mod 43).
    Teacher explains: Run Euclid on 43 and 17, then work backwards to write 1 as
    a combination:
    43 = 2 × 17 + 9        1 = 9 − 8
    17 = 1 × 9 + 8           = 9 − (17 − 9) = 2 × 9 − 17
     9 = 1 × 8 + 1           = 2(43 − 2 × 17) − 17
                             = 2 × 43 − 5 × 17
    So −5 × 17 ≡ 1 (mod 43): the inverse of 17 is −5 ≡ 38. Multiply both sides
    of 17x ≡ 5 by 38: x ≡ 38 × 5 = 190 = 4 × 43 + 18 ≡ 18. Check:
    17 × 18 = 306 = 7 × 43 + 5. ✓ Common mistake: "dividing" 5 by 17 as a
    fraction; in modular arithmetic division means multiplying by the inverse.
    Now you try: solve 7x ≡ 3 (mod 26). (7⁻¹ ≡ 15, x ≡ 19)

D6. A vendor at the Pushkar fair has a basket of eggs. When she counts them in
    2s, 3s, 4s, 5s or 6s there is always 1 egg left over, but in 7s there is
    none left. What is the smallest possible number of eggs, and what are the
    other possibilities?
    Answer: 301 eggs; in general 301 + 420k (k = 0, 1, 2, ...).
    Teacher explains: "1 left over when counted in 2, 3, 4, 5, 6" means x − 1 is
    divisible by lcm(2, 3, 4, 5, 6) = 60, so x ≡ 1 (mod 60). Also x ≡ 0 (mod 7).
    60 and 7 are coprime, so by the CRT there is exactly one solution mod 420.
    Substitute x = 1 + 60t:
    1 + 60t ≡ 0 (mod 7)
    1 + 4t ≡ 0          (60 = 8 × 7 + 4)
    4t ≡ −1 ≡ 6,  t ≡ 6 × 4⁻¹ ≡ 6 × 2 = 12 ≡ 5   (4 × 2 = 8 ≡ 1)
    x = 1 + 60 × 5 = 301
    Check: 301 = 43 × 7 and 300 is divisible by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. ✓ Next solutions
    721, 1,141, ... (add lcm(60, 7) = 420). Common mistake: solving each
    congruence separately and multiplying the answers. Now you try (Sunzi, 3rd
    century): x ≡ 2 (mod 3), x ≡ 3 (mod 5), x ≡ 2 (mod 7). (23)

D7. Pens cost ₹12 and notebooks ₹30. Priya spends exactly ₹246. Find all the
    possible numbers of pens and notebooks. Also show that she cannot spend
    exactly ₹250.
    Answer: (pens, notebooks) = (18, 1), (13, 3), (8, 5), (3, 7). 250 is not a
    multiple of gcd(12, 30) = 6.
    Teacher explains: 12x + 30y = 246. gcd(12, 30) = 6 and 6 | 246, so divide:
    2x + 5y = 41. A particular solution by inspection: y = 1 gives 2x = 36,
    x = 18. Since 2 and 5 are coprime, the general solution is
    x = 18 − 5t,  y = 1 + 2t   (t an integer)
    x ≥ 0 ⇒ t ≤ 3.6;  y ≥ 0 ⇒ t ≥ −0.5;  so t = 0, 1, 2, 3
    giving (18, 1), (13, 3), (8, 5), (3, 7). Check one:
    12 × 8 + 30 × 5 = 96 + 150 = 246. ✓ For ₹250: the left side is always a
    multiple of 6 and 250 is not, so there is no solution at all. Common
    mistakes: writing x = 18 + 5t, y = 1 + 2t (the signs must be opposite so
    that the changes cancel) and forgetting to divide by the gcd first (steps of
    30 and 12 miss solutions). Now you try: all non-negative solutions of
    3x + 7y = 40. ((11, 1), (4, 4))

D8. Prove that a) 4,003 is not a sum of two squares b) x² − 3y² = 2 has no
    integer solutions c) no number of the form 8k + 7 is a sum of three squares.
    Answer: Squares are 0 or 1 mod 4 (a), 0 or 1 mod 3 (b), 0, 1 or 4 mod 8 (c).
    Teacher explains: Work modulo a small number and list ALL cases:
    x mod 4:  0  1  2  3        x mod 8:  0  1  2  3  4  5  6  7
    x² mod 4: 0  1  0  1        x² mod 8: 0  1  4  1  0  1  4  1
    a) x² + y² mod 4 can only be 0 + 0, 0 + 1 or 1 + 1, i.e. 0, 1 or 2. But
    4,003 = 4 × 1,000 + 3 ≡ 3 (mod 4). Impossible. b) Mod 3 the equation says x²
    ≡ 2; but x² mod 3 is 0 (x ≡ 0) or 1 (x ≡ ±1). Impossible. c) Sums of three
    numbers chosen from 0, 1, 4, taken mod 8, give 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 (e.g.
    4 + 1 + 1 = 6) but never 7. Common mistake: checking a few values of x and
    y; the proof must cover every residue class. Now you try: show x² +
    y² = 1,999 has no solutions. (1,999 ≡ 3 mod 4)

D9. a) Show that a = m² − n², b = 2mn, c = m² + n² always gives a² + b² = c². b)
    List all PRIMITIVE Pythagorean triples with hypotenuse less than 50. c) Find
    every right triangle with integer sides that has a leg of length 12.
    Answer: b) (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (7, 24, 25), (8, 15, 17), (9, 40, 41),
    (12, 35, 37), (20, 21, 29) c) (5, 12, 13), (9, 12, 15), (12, 16, 20), (12,
    35, 37).
    Teacher explains: a) (m² − n²)² + (2mn)² = m⁴ − 2m²n² + n⁴ + 4m²n² =
    m⁴ + 2m²n² + n⁴ = (m² + n²)². b) Take m > n, coprime, one odd and one even,
    with m² + n² < 50: (m, n) = (2, 1) 3-4-5, (3, 2) 5-12-13, (4, 1) 15-8-17,
    (4, 3) 7-24-25, (5, 2) 21-20-29, (5, 4) 9-40-41, (6, 1) 35-12-37, (6, 5)
    11-60-61 is too big, (7, 2) 45-28-53 too big. c) Put the leg 12 = a: 144 =
    c² − b² = (c − b)(c + b). The two factors have the same parity (their sum 2c
    is even) and product 144, so both are even: 2 × 72 → c = 37, b = 35; 4 × 36
    → c = 20, b = 16; 6 × 24 → c = 15, b = 9; 8 × 18 → c = 13, b = 5. (12 × 12
    gives b = 0.) A computer search confirms exactly these four. Now you try:
    triangles with a leg 15. ((8, 15, 17), (15, 20, 25), (15, 36, 39), (15, 112,
    113))

D10. Prove that for every integer n: a) 6 | n³ − n b) 30 | n⁵ − n c) 7 | 2³ⁿ − 1
     (n ≥ 0). d) Decide whether 3 | 4ⁿ + 5 for every n ≥ 0.
     Answer: a), b), c) are true for all n. d) is also TRUE: 4ⁿ + 5 ≡ 1 + 2 = 3
     ≡ 0 (mod 3).
     Teacher explains: a) n³ − n = (n − 1)n(n + 1), three consecutive integers:
     one is even and one is a multiple of 3, so 6 divides the product. b) By
     Fermat, n⁵ ≡ n (mod 5); also n⁵ − n = n(n⁴ − 1) = (n³ − n)(n² + 1),
     divisible by 6 from a). 2, 3, 5 are coprime, so 30 | n⁵ − n. c) 2³ⁿ = 8ⁿ
     and 8 ≡ 1 (mod 7), so 8ⁿ − 1 ≡ 1 − 1 = 0. d) 4 ≡ 1 (mod 3), so 4ⁿ + 5 ≡
     1 + 5 = 6 ≡ 0. Check n = 2: 16 + 5 = 21 = 3 × 7. ✓ Congruences turn "for
     every n" into a finite calculation. Common mistake: proving only for n = 1,
     2, 3; a few examples are not a proof. Now you try: prove 7 | 3²ⁿ⁺¹ + 2ⁿ⁺²
     for n ≥ 0. (3 × 9ⁿ + 4 × 2ⁿ ≡ 3 × 2ⁿ + 4 × 2ⁿ = 7 × 2ⁿ ≡ 0 mod 7, since 9 ≡
     2)

D11. Find the three smallest solutions in positive integers of the Pell equation
     x² − 2y² = 1, and a rule that produces all of them. What do they tell us
     about √2?
     Answer: (3, 2), (17, 12), (99, 70); (x, y) → (3x + 4y, 2x + 3y); x/y is a
     very good approximation to √2.
     Teacher explains: Try y = 1, 2, 3, ...: 2y² + 1 = 3, 9 ✓ (x = 3), 19, 33,
     ... So the smallest is (3, 2). Key identity: (x² − 2y²)(3² − 2 × 2²)
     = (3x + 4y)² − 2(2x + 3y)², which comes from multiplying (x +
     y√2)(3 + 2√2) = (3x + 4y) + (2x + 3y)√2. So from (3, 2) we get (17, 12),
     then (99, 70), then (577, 408); it can be shown that these are ALL the
     solutions. Since x² = 2y² + 1, x/y is slightly more than √2:
     17/12 = 1.41666..., 99/70 = 1.414285..., 577/408 = 1.4142156...
     (√2 = 1.4142135...). A computer search up to y = 500 finds only 2, 12, 70,
     408. Now you try: the smallest solution of x² − 3y² = 1. ((2, 1); next (7,
     4))

D12. Find all integers n for which n + 1 divides n² + 1.
     Answer: n = −3, −2, 0, 1.
     Teacher explains: Divide: n² + 1 = (n + 1)(n − 1) + 2. Since n + 1 divides
     (n + 1)(n − 1), it divides n² + 1 exactly when it divides 2. So n + 1 ∈
     {−2, −1, 1, 2}, giving n = −3, −2, 0, 1. Check: n = −3: 10 ÷ (−2) = −5 ✓;
     n = −2: 5 ÷ (−1) ✓; n = 0: 1 ÷ 1 ✓; n = 1: 2 ÷ 2 ✓. In congruence language:
     n ≡ −1 (mod n + 1), so n² + 1 ≡ 1 + 1 = 2. This "replace n by −1" trick is
     the standard olympiad move. Common mistakes: forgetting the negative
     divisors, and dividing by n + 1 when n = −1. A brute-force search over
     −1,000 ≤ n ≤ 1,000 finds only these four. Now you try: n − 2 divides
     n³ − 1. (n³ − 1 ≡ 7, so n − 2 ∈ {±1, ±7}: n = −5, 1, 3, 9)

TEACHING TIPS
  Struggling: build residue tables (x, x², x³ mod n) by hand before using them;
  always write the cycle of powers and underline the "1"; use the extended
  Euclid table with columns for the quotient and the coefficients; check every
  congruence answer by direct multiplication; use a spreadsheet or Python pow(a,
  e, n) to test claims before proving them. Harder: prove Wilson's theorem
  ((p − 1)! ≡ −1 mod p) by pairing each residue with its inverse; show that the
  order of a mod p divides p − 1; prove there are infinitely many primes ≡ 3
  (mod 4); solve x² − y² = 2,026 (no solutions: x² − y² is never ≡ 2 mod 4);
  find all solutions of 2ˣ + 1 = y² (x = 3, y = 3); read about quadratic
  reciprocity and the RSA cipher, which uses Euler's theorem.


================================================================================
TOPIC 8.60 — OLYMPIAD COMBINATORICS: PIGEONHOLE PRINCIPLE, INVARIANTS, EXTREMAL
             PRINCIPLE, DOUBLE COUNTING, GRAPH-THEORY PUZZLES
================================================================================
WHAT THE CHILD MUST LEARN
  - PIGEONHOLE PRINCIPLE: if more than n objects go into n boxes, some box gets
    at least 2. GENERAL form: N objects in k boxes ⇒ some box has at least ⌈N/k⌉
    objects (⌈ ⌉ = round up). The art is choosing the BOXES (remainders, pairs
    {1, 2}, {3, 4}, ..., odd parts, small squares). To GUARANTEE m in one of k
    boxes you need k(m − 1) + 1 objects.
  - INVARIANTS: a quantity that NO allowed move changes (parity of a sum, a sum
    mod n, the number of black squares covered). If the start and the target
    have different values, the target is unreachable. COLOURING a board is an
    invariant in disguise. A MONOVARIANT always goes up (or down), so a process
    on finitely many states must stop.
  - EXTREMAL PRINCIPLE: look at the largest, smallest, longest or closest object
    (a longest path, the smallest counterexample). Its extremality usually
    forces the structure you need.
  - DOUBLE COUNTING: count one set in two ways and equate. HANDSHAKE LEMMA: in
    any graph the sum of the degrees is 2E (each edge has two ends), so the
    number of odd-degree vertices is even. Committee arguments prove identities
    such as Σ k C(n, k) = n × 2ⁿ⁻¹.
  - GRAPHS: vertices joined by edges; degree = number of edges at a vertex. Kₙ
    has n(n − 1)/2 edges; K(m, n) (complete bipartite) has mn. A TREE is a
    connected graph with no cycle: V − E = 1, and every tree with at least 2
    vertices has at least 2 leaves. A graph is BIPARTITE (2-colourable) iff it
    has no odd cycle.
  - EULER: a connected graph has a closed trail using every edge exactly once
    (Euler circuit) iff every degree is even, and an open one (Euler path) iff
    exactly two degrees are odd; the path must start and end at the odd
    vertices.
  - RAMSEY: R(3, 3) = 6. Among any 6 people there are 3 mutual friends or 3
    mutual strangers; 5 people are not enough (colour the sides of a pentagon
    red and its diagonals blue). Other known values: R(3, 4) = 9, R(3, 5) = 14,
    R(4, 4) = 18.

PART A — DESCRIPTIVE
--------------------
D1. Explain, using the pigeonhole principle: a) in any group of 13 students two
    were born in the same month b) in any group of 367 people two share a
    birthday c) a drawer has 10 black and 10 white socks; in the dark, how many
    must you take to be SURE of a matching pair, and how many to be sure of a
    BLACK pair?
    Answer: a), b) boxes = months (12) and days (366) c) 3 socks for a pair; 12
    for a black pair.
    Teacher explains: Pigeonhole: more objects than boxes forces a box with two
    objects. a) 13 students, 12 months. b) 367 people, at most 366 possible
    birthdays (with 29 February). c) The boxes are the 2 colours: 3 socks in 2
    colour-boxes must include two of one colour. Two socks are not enough (one
    black, one white). For a black pair think of the WORST case: you could pick
    all 10 white socks first, then need 2 black: 10 + 2 = 12. The general
    method: imagine an opponent making your draws as unlucky as possible, then
    add one. Common mistake: answering 2 for a pair, or 11 for a black pair. Now
    you try: socks in 5 colours (plenty of each); how many for a sure pair? (6)

D2. Eleven numbers are chosen from 1, 2, ..., 20. Prove that a) two of them are
    consecutive (so two are coprime) b) one of them divides another. Show that
    10 numbers are not enough for either statement.
    Answer: Boxes {1, 2}, {3, 4}, ..., {19, 20} for a); boxes by odd part for
    b). 10 numbers: 1, 3, 5, ..., 19 has no consecutive pair; 11, 12, ..., 20
    has no divisor pair.
    Teacher explains: a) Make 10 boxes {1, 2}, {3, 4}, ..., {19, 20}. Eleven
    numbers in 10 boxes: one box holds two numbers, and they are consecutive.
    Consecutive numbers are coprime (a common divisor divides their difference
    1). b) Write every number as 2ᵏ × m with m odd: 12 = 2² × 3, 20 = 2² × 5,
    7 = 2⁰ × 7. The odd part m is one of 1, 3, 5, ..., 19: 10 boxes. Two chosen
    numbers have the same odd part, 2ᵃm and 2ᵇm with a < b, and then the smaller
    divides the larger. For 10 numbers: the odd numbers 1, 3, ..., 19 contain no
    two consecutive numbers, and in 11, 12, ..., 20 any multiple of a number is
    at least 22. A computer check confirms both examples. Common mistake:
    choosing boxes that are not disjoint or do not cover every number. Now you
    try: from 1 to 2n choose n + 1 numbers; show two add up to 2n + 1. (boxes
    {1, 2n}, {2, 2n − 1}, ...)

D3. Use the general pigeonhole principle. a) Among any 37 integers, at least how
    many leave the same remainder when divided by 6? b) Five points are placed
    inside a square of side 2 cm. Prove that two of them are at most √2 cm
    apart. c) In a school of 1,000 students, at least how many share a birthday
    (not a leap year)?
    Answer: a) 7 b) see below c) 3.
    Teacher explains: General form: N objects in k boxes ⇒ some box has at least
    ⌈N/k⌉. Reason: if every box had at most ⌈N/k⌉ − 1 < N/k objects, the total
    would be less than N. a) 6 remainder-boxes: ⌈37/6⌉ = ⌈6.17⌉ = 7. b) Cut the
    square into four 1 cm × 1 cm squares. Five points, four small squares: two
    points lie in the same small square, and the farthest two points of a unit
    square are opposite corners, distance √(1² + 1²) = √2. c) ⌈1,000/365⌉ =
    ⌈2.74⌉ = 3. Common mistake: using ⌊N/k⌋ (round down) or N/k + 1. Now you
    try: 50 pigeons in 7 holes: some hole has at least? (⌈50/7⌉ = 8)

D4. Prove that from ANY n integers a₁, a₂, ..., aₙ one can choose a block of
    consecutive ones aᵢ + ... + aⱼ whose sum is divisible by n. Find such a
    block for 8, 3, 11, 6, 14.
    Answer: 3 + 11 + 6 = 20, divisible by 5.
    Teacher explains: Look at the n PREFIX SUMS S₁ = a₁, S₂ = a₁ + a₂, ..., Sₙ.
    If one of them is ≡ 0 (mod n) we are done. Otherwise their remainders lie in
    1, 2, ..., n − 1: n numbers in n − 1 boxes, so two are equal, Sᵢ ≡ Sⱼ with
    i < j. Then Sⱼ − Sᵢ = aᵢ₊₁ + ... + aⱼ ≡ 0 (mod n). For the example (n = 5):
    k         1   2   3   4   5
    Sₖ        8  11  22  28  42
    Sₖ mod 5  3   1   2   3   2
    S₁ ≡ S₄ ≡ 3, so a₂ + a₃ + a₄ = 3 + 11 + 6 = 20 = 28 − 8, divisible by 5. (S₃
    ≡ S₅ also gives 6 + 14 = 20.) This is pigeonhole with boxes = remainders.
    Now you try: find a block for 1, 4, 2, 2 (n = 4). (4 or 2 + 2; prefix sums
    1, 5, 7, 9 have remainders 1, 1, 3, 1)

D5. Two opposite corner squares are removed from an 8 × 8 chessboard. Can the
    remaining 62 squares be covered by 31 dominoes (each covering two adjacent
    squares)? What if two squares of DIFFERENT colours are removed?
    Answer: No: 32 squares of one colour and 30 of the other remain, but each
    domino covers one black and one white. With two different colours removed, a
    tiling always exists (Gomory).
    Teacher explains: Colour the board as usual. Opposite corners have the SAME
    colour (say both white: (1, 1) and (8, 8), and 1 + 1 and 8 + 8 are both
    even). After removing them: 32 black, 30 white. A domino always covers one
    black and one white square, so 31 dominoes cover 31 of each: impossible. The
    invariant is "black covered − white covered = 0". Counting squares alone (62
    is even) is not enough to decide. If one black and one white square are
    removed, a clever snake-shaped tour of the board shows a tiling always
    exists. Common mistake: trying many tilings by hand and concluding "I could
    not find one"; that is not a proof. Now you try: can a 5 × 5 board with the
    centre removed be tiled? (colour count 12 and 12: the colour test allows it;
    yes, it can: tile the ring around the centre)

D6. The numbers 1, 2, 3, ..., 10 are written on a board. A move: erase two
    numbers a and b and write |a − b|. After 9 moves one number is left. Can it
    be 0? What about 1, 2, ..., 12?
    Answer: No, for 1 to 10 the last number is odd. For 1 to 12 it is even.
    Teacher explains: Find an INVARIANT: the PARITY of the sum of all numbers on
    the board. |a − b| has the same parity as a + b (they differ by 2 × min(a,
    b)), so replacing a and b by |a − b| changes the sum by an even number. At
    the start the sum is 1 + 2 + ... + 10 = 55, odd; so the sum is always odd,
    and the final single number is odd, never 0. For 1 to 12 the sum is 78,
    even, so the last number is even. (A computer search over all move orders
    for 1 to 6, sum 21, finds only odd final values.) Common mistake: trying a
    few move orders and concluding it is impossible; the invariant gives a
    proof. Now you try: with a + b instead of |a − b|, what is the last number
    for 1 to 10? (always 55)

D7. Prove, using the extremal principle, that if every vertex of a finite graph
    has degree at least 2, then the graph contains a cycle. Extend the idea: if
    every degree is at least d, there is a cycle of length at least d + 1.
    Answer: Take a LONGEST path; its end vertex has all its neighbours on the
    path, which closes a cycle.
    Teacher explains: Let P = v₁v₂...vₖ be a path with as many vertices as
    possible (it exists because the graph is finite). The end vertex v₁ has
    degree at least 2, so it has a neighbour w other than v₂. If w were not on
    P, then wv₁v₂...vₖ would be a longer path: contradiction. So w = vᵢ for some
    i ≥ 3, and v₁v₂...vᵢv₁ is a cycle. For degree ≥ d: ALL neighbours of v₁ lie
    on P (same argument); there are at least d of them, so the farthest one is
    vᵢ with i ≥ d + 1, and the cycle v₁...vᵢv₁ has at least d + 1 vertices. The
    extremal choice (longest path) did all the work. Common mistake: "start
    anywhere and keep walking" without saying why the walk must return; the
    longest path makes it precise. Now you try: show that a tree (no cycles)
    with at least 2 vertices has a vertex of degree 1. (the ends of a longest
    path are leaves)

D8. a) At a party of 9 people, can everyone shake hands with exactly 3 others?
    b) Prove that in any group, the number of people who have shaken an ODD
    number of hands is even. c) A graph has 12 edges and every vertex has degree
    3. How many vertices does it have?
    Answer: a) No b) handshake lemma c) 8.
    Teacher explains: Count the pairs (person, handshake that person is in) in
    two ways. Adding the degrees counts every handshake twice (once for each
    person), so Σ deg = 2E, always EVEN. a) 9 × 3 = 27 would have to equal 2E:
    27 is odd, impossible. b) Σ deg is even; the even degrees add to an even
    number, so the odd degrees also add to an even number, which needs an even
    count of odd terms. c) 3V = 2 × 12 = 24, V = 8 (the cube is an example).
    Common mistake: dividing by 2 the wrong way, e.g. E = Σ deg. Now you try: 7
    people each shake hands with exactly 5 others? (7 × 5 = 35 is odd:
    impossible)

D9. Prove by double counting that Σ k C(n, k) = n × 2ⁿ⁻¹ (sum from k = 0 to n),
    and check it for n = 5. Then prove Σ C(n, k)² = C(2n, n).
    Answer: Both sides count committees with a chairperson. For n = 5:
    0 + 5 + 20 + 30 + 20 + 5 = 80 = 5 × 16.
    Teacher explains: From a class of n students, count the ways to pick a
    committee (any size) AND a chairperson from it. Way 1: first choose the size
    k and the committee, C(n, k) ways, then the chair, k ways: total Σ k C(n,
    k). Way 2: first choose the chair, n ways, then decide for each of the other
    n − 1 students whether to join: 2ⁿ⁻¹ ways. Total n × 2ⁿ⁻¹. Same set, so the
    answers are equal. For n = 5: 1 × 5 + 2 × 10 + 3 × 10 + 4 × 5 + 5 × 1 = 80
    = 5 × 2⁴. Second identity: choose n people from n boys and n girls: C(2n,
    n). Or choose k boys and n − k girls: C(n, k) C(n, n − k) = C(n, k)², summed
    over k. Check n = 6: 1 + 36 + 225 + 400 + 225 + 36 + 1 = 924 = C(12, 6). Now
    you try: prove Σ C(n, k) = 2ⁿ by counting subsets. (each element in or out)

D10. a) Königsberg had 4 land areas joined by 7 bridges: area A had 5 bridges,
     B, C and D had 3 each. Explain why no walk crosses every bridge exactly
     once. b) A "house" is drawn as a square with both diagonals and a
     triangular roof on top. Can it be drawn without lifting the pen or
     retracing a line? Where must you start?
     Answer: a) Four odd vertices, so no Euler path. b) Yes; exactly two
     vertices (the bottom corners) have odd degree 3: start at one of them and
     end at the other.
     Teacher explains: Model: land areas = vertices, bridges = edges. Each time
     a walk passes THROUGH a vertex it uses 2 edges (in and out), so every
     vertex except the start and the end has even degree. Hence an Euler path
     needs 0 or 2 odd vertices (Euler 1736); Königsberg has 4. b) Label the
     square bottom-left 1, bottom-right 2, top-right 3, top-left 4 and the roof
     apex 5. Degrees: 1 and 2 have 3 (two sides and a diagonal), 3 and 4 have 4
     (two sides, a diagonal and a roof edge), 5 has 2. Exactly two odd vertices,
     so start at 1 and finish at 2, e.g. 1-2-3-4-1-3-5-4-2. A computer search
     over all trails confirms: path yes, closed circuit no. Common mistake:
     starting at the roof apex. Now you try: can K₅ (5 points, all 10 segments)
     be drawn in one closed stroke? (yes, all degrees are 4)

D11. a) Prove that every tree with V vertices has E = V − 1 edges. b) 32 teams
     play a knockout cricket tournament (the loser of each match is out, no
     draws). How many matches are played? c) Which of these graphs are
     bipartite: a 6-cycle, a 7-cycle, a tree, the cube?
     Answer: a) induction on V b) 31 c) the 6-cycle, every tree and the cube are
     bipartite; the 7-cycle is not.
     Teacher explains: a) A tree with V ≥ 2 has a leaf (an end of a longest
     path). Remove the leaf and its edge: still a tree, with one fewer vertex
     and one fewer edge. Repeat until one vertex and 0 edges remain: V − E = 1
     at the end, and it never changed. b) Double counting: every match
     eliminates exactly one team, and 31 teams must be eliminated to leave a
     champion: 31 matches (no need to draw the bracket). The bracket is a tree!
     c) Try to 2-colour: an even cycle alternates colours; an odd cycle forces
     two neighbours with the same colour. A tree has no cycles at all. The cube:
     colour a vertex (x, y, z) by the parity of x + y + z. Common mistake:
     thinking "bipartite" means "has two parts that are not joined". Now you
     try: a knockout with 20 teams (some get byes). (19 matches)

D12. Prove that among any 6 people there are 3 who all know each other or 3 who
     are all strangers to each other. Show that this can fail for 5 people.
     Answer: R(3, 3) = 6. For 5 people: a pentagon of "knows" edges and a
     pentagram of "strangers" edges has no one-colour triangle.
     Teacher explains: Draw 6 points; colour a segment red if the two people
     know each other, blue if not. Pick one person P. P has 5 segments, 2
     colours: by pigeonhole at least ⌈5/2⌉ = 3 have the same colour, say red to
     A, B, C. If any of AB, BC, CA is red, it makes a red triangle with P. If
     none is red, ABC is a blue triangle. Either way we win. For 5 people:
     colour the 5 sides of a regular pentagon red and the 5 diagonals blue. The
     red graph is a 5-cycle and the blue graph is also a 5-cycle (the
     pentagram), and a 5-cycle has no triangle. A computer check of all 2¹⁰
     colourings of K₅ finds colourings with 0 one-colour triangles, while every
     one of the 2¹⁵ colourings of K₆ has at least 2. Now you try: show that 6 is
     exactly the number of vertices where the result starts to hold: why does
     the proof fail for 5? (P then has only 4 segments, and ⌈4/2⌉ = 2 is not
     enough)
